articles.title: Capitalizing on Controversy: Humor, Scandal Entrepreneurship, and the Rise of the Far Right
articles.authors: Dick Zijp; giselinde kuipers
articles.abstract: Right-wing public figures, from comedians to politicians, increasingly use humor strategically to provoke scandal. While scandals are typically understood to damage the reputations of norm transgressors, the rise of successful right-wing scandal makers challenges this assumption. In this article, we introduce the concept of ‘scandal entrepreneur’ to theorize the rise of celebrity figures who deliberately create or amplify scandals for personal or political gain. Integrating insights from political scandal research, sociological work on cultural and moral entrepreneurship, and critical humor studies, we develop an innovative approach to scandal that combines dramaturgical and conjunctural analysis. Drawing on a quantitative mapping of Dutch humor scandals between 1990 and 2024 and an in-depth qualitative analysis of two cases, we trace both the steep rise in humor scandals in the early twenty-first century and the increasing professionalization of scandal entrepreneurship, which has turned scandal-making into a profitable business model. Based on our analysis of the Nekschot cartoon scandal (2008) and the VI-Akwasi scandal (2020), we demonstrate that, within the current cultural conjuncture, right-wing actors are best positioned to capitalize on scandals and successfully dramatize social and cultural divides through humor. Our approach offers valuable analytical tools for humor and scandal scholarship and the field of right-wing studies, providing a critical lens through which to examine wider cultural changes.

articles.title: The Influence of Greek, Egyptian, and Hindu Mythology on Human Behaviour and Morality
articles.authors: Sahana Anand Sabharwal; Gokul Prabhu; Ananta Ganjoo
articles.abstract:
Mythology has been used by human cultures throughout history to make sense of death, give
death moral meaning, and deal with the unknown. People’s stories of death and the afterlife
influence individual conduct, systems of ethics, and collective norms across civilisations, not
merely mirror cultural beliefs. This review discusses how three of the world’s most influential
ancient mythologies, Greek, Egyptian, and Hindu, present death and the afterlife and how these
presentations continue to inform human psychology and moral conduct. This paper uses a
comparative theoretical analysis of primary mythological narratives and their associated
religious structures to explore the ways in which beliefs about the afterlife influence death
anxiety, life satisfaction, and moral decision-making. It draws upon the figures, rituals, and
cosmological frameworks embedded within each custom, including the tripartite judgment of
the Greek underworld and the Erinyes, the weighing of the heart against the feather of Ma’at,
and the karmic cycle of samsāra and the pursuit of moksha in Hinduism, to understand how
different spiritual systems produce distinct moral obligations. Together, these traditions reveal
that while religious belief is not the only source of morality, mythological narratives are among
the most enduring and broad structures that individuals and societies use to make sense of life,
death, and the choices in between. Therefore, this paper explores the profound and multifaceted
impact of these ancient mythologies on the ethical frameworks and behavioural norms within
and across societies, examining how foundational narratives shape moral reasoning and
societal structures.

articles.title: AI Parasocial Relationships and The Potential Role of Miswanting in Loneliness and Emotional Distress: A Theoretical Review
articles.authors: Ashly Mathew
articles.abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence has led to the development of more advanced AI systems that can create human like conversation. This increases the usage of AI chatbots into sources of social interaction, emotional support, and companionship. Recent researches have examined their potential benefits and risk but less attention has been given to the individuals expectations regarding the emotional benefits of artificial intelligence. The present theoretical review proposes miswanting as a central theme for understanding the discrepancy between anticipated and actual emotional fulfilment in human- AI relationship. Drawing upon the theories of miswanting, parasocial relationship, self-determination and loneliness theories this review highlights the conceptual framework linking pre-existing loneliness and unmet emotional needs to AI companion use, emotional attachment, expectations of fulfilment, and subsequent psychological outcomes. The framework proposes that individuals may initially experience AI companionship as emotionally comforting and socially supportive and develops expectations that such interaction can satisfy long term emotional and relatedness needs. When experienced outcomes don’t match with these expectations, an expectation- reality discrepancy occurs which may eventually lead to persistent loneliness, emotional. Importantly, the framework does not assume that AI companionship is inherently harmful; rather, it highlights the potential importance of miswanting theory to the emerging context of AI companionship. This review offers a novel conceptual perspective and generates testable propositions for future empirical research.

articles.title: What research culture is for: a six-dimensional framework co-created to cultivate researcher wellbeing
articles.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Karel Svadlenka; Yukiko Watanabe; Sano Satoshi; Ayako Y. Murayama; Akane Tezuka; Ataru Igarashi; Norihiro Sadato; Kazuhiro Hayashi
articles.abstract: Research culture, the soil in which scientific inquiry grows, shapes the quality and sustainability of research, yet remains invisible to science, technology and innovation indicators. Three converging crises signal deteriorating conditions for research: the reproducibility crisis, the productivity paradox, and a global crisis of researcher wellbeing. Reform initiatives have transformed how outputs are assessed, but no validated, internationally comparable framework captures the cultural conditions of research practice. This article reports a six-dimensional research culture framework. The framework was co-created through structured stakeholder dialogue on a principle of equal voice: a workshop of researchers, administrators, funders and policymakers, then an open symposium of approximately 300 participants. It was iteratively refined through domestic and international expert consultation, with a transparent audit trail of what entered at each stage and why. Subjective experience sits at the core, surrounded by social, epistemic, methodological, temporal and evaluative dimensions. Each is operationalised as three items on a common 0–10 scale, in Japanese and English within an instrument pairing internationally standardised wellbeing measures with the Interdependent Happiness Scale, and visualised as a radar chart for team-level dialogue, not institutional ranking. A crosswalk locates the contribution: reform effort concentrates on the evaluative dimension, while the instruments that do measure address only two of the six, the social and the evaluative, treating the other four as symptoms or facets of other constructs, if at all. A nationwide survey planned for fiscal year 2026 provides the first psychometric test, under a design fixed in advance: the six-dimension structure will be compared with rivals in a held-out half of the sample. Grounded in human flourishing theory and aligned with ISO 25554:2024, the framework treats research culture not as a variable to be audited but as a capability to be cultivated.

articles.title: How has the disciplinary composition and preregistration practice of psychology evolved on the OSF (2020–2025)? A meta-science analysis of the diffusion of preregistration.
articles.authors: Albie Duffy
articles.abstract: Preregistration has become one of psychology's most prominent methodological reforms, but its uptake has been characterised at field level, leaving open where within psychology the practice has spread and whether the registrations themselves have changed. This study analysed 47,524 psychology preregistrations carrying a subdiscipline label on the Open Science Framework, created between 2020 and 2025 and retrieved via the public OSF API. Cochran-Armitage trend tests examined change in each subdiscipline's share of the labelled corpus, and a nested regression examined a six-item, text-derived indicator of methodological thoroughness net of document length, registration template, and year. The labelled corpus grew 2.37-fold. All eight subdisciplines predicted a priori to rise showed significant positive trends after false discovery rate correction, and no other subdiscipline did; Clinical Psychology expanded from 9.7% to 18.5% of the labelled field. Social and Cognitive Psychology declined in share while continuing to grow in absolute number. Subdiscipline was associated with registration template (bias-corrected V = .125) and explained incremental variance in the thoroughness indicator after adjustment (ΔR² = .014), with all six rising subdisciplines that survived pooling scoring below the Social Psychology reference. Once disciplinary composition was held constant, no independent temporal trend in thoroughness remained. The composition of psychological preregistration therefore changed substantially across six years while the textual detail of individual registrations did not, indicating that the diffusion of a practice and the development of its content are separable dimensions.

articles.title: Estimation and inference for step-function selection models in meta-analysis with dependent effects
articles.authors: James E Pustejovsky; Martyna Citkowicz; Megha Joshi
articles.abstract: Meta-analyses in social science fields face multiple methodological challenges arising from how primary research studies are designed and reported. One challenge is that many primary studies report multiple relevant effect size estimates, leading to a data structure with dependent observations. Another is selective reporting bias, which arises when the availability of study findings is influenced by the statistical significance of results. Although many selective reporting diagnostics and bias-correction methods have been proposed, few are suitable for meta-analyses involving dependent effect sizes. Among available methods, step-function selection models are conceptually appealing and have shown promise in previous simulations, but tend to understate uncertainty in parameter estimates if dependent effects are ignored. We study methods for estimating step-function models from data involving dependent effect sizes, focusing specifically on estimating parameters of the marginal distribution of effect sizes and accounting for dependence using cluster-robust variance estimation or bootstrap resampling. We describe two estimation strategies, demonstrate them by re-analyzing data from a previous synthesis on ego depletion effects, and evaluate their performance through an extensive simulation study under both univariate and multivariate selection processes. Simulation findings indicate that selection models provide low-bias estimates of average effect size and clustered bootstrap confidence intervals provide acceptable coverage levels for meta-analyses with at least 30 studies. Although unadjusted estimates are more efficient when selective reporting is absent or minimal, the proposed methods provide a robust and useful approach for evaluating the potential biases arising when selective reporting is present in meta-analyses with dependent effects.

articles.title: Shared Identity and Felt Understanding in the Context of Sexual Minority Stress:  Who Gets Me, and Why?
articles.authors: Emma Laurel McGorray; Khava Gillespie; Elsie Newburg; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract: Although sexual minority stress often predicts lower well-being, LGBQ+ people may be protected against these effects if they receive support that helps them feel understood. What processes are linked to greater felt understanding? Across four studies, we tested the hypothesis that LGBQ+ people feel more understood by LGBQ+ (vs. heterosexual) support providers and tested two possible explanations for this relationship: (1) LGBQ+ support providers offer higher-quality support (the support quality explanation) and (2) people’s beliefs about shared identity are linked to how they evaluate support (the interpretive filter explanation). Using varied methodologies—participants reflecting on their close relationships and evaluating both genuine and experimentally manipulated support messages—we found limited evidence for the former explanation but more robust evidence for the latter. These findings underscore the power of sharing an identity with a support provider when experiencing minority stress, while also suggesting that mere beliefs about shared identity may be a major source of that power.

articles.title: The cogmod R Package: Easy-to-Use Bayesian Cognitive Models for Reaction Times, Choices and Subjective Ratings, with Applications to Computational Neuropsychology
articles.authors: Dominique Makowski
articles.abstract: Cognitive tasks produce structured distributions of reaction times, choices, and subjective ratings, yet these data are often reduced to condition means before analysis. This can obscure differences in variability, distributional shape, and the latent processes that generate behaviour. We introduce `cogmod`, an R package that brings Bayesian cognitive models into the regression workflow used by psychologists. `cogmod` implements descriptive response distributions, evidence accumulation models, and models for bounded ratings as brms custom families, allowing model parameters to be predicted by covariates and random effects using familiar formula syntax. Fitted models remain standard brmsfit objects and therefore support established tools for priors, diagnostics, posterior predictive checks, model comparison, and post-processing. Across worked examples, we show that this framework enables direct comparison of competing decision models, quantifies the reliability of model parameters as individual-level measures, and reveals clinically relevant differences that are invisible in conventional mean-based analyses. By placing models spanning the descriptive-to-generative continuum within a common Bayesian regression framework, `cogmod` lowers the practical barrier to richer analyses of cognitive data and makes the choice of model an empirical question rather than a software constraint. `cogmod` is openly available at .

articles.title: A ‘Basin of Attraction’ Theory of Speech Initiation and Stuttering
articles.authors: Frank H H Guenther; Soo-Eun Chang; Jonathan Cannon
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Purpose. Recent work in motor neuroscience suggests that well-learned actions are implemented as stable, stereotyped trajectories in neural state space. The purpose of this article is to propose a theory of stuttering that formalizes this idea for speech production and identifies a specific neural impairment underlying speech dysfluency.
Method. We advance a conceptual and computational framework in which the motor program for a familiar word corresponds to a stable neural trajectory with an associated basin of attraction. We integrate findings from primate motor control, human speech neuroscience, and basal ganglia physiology to specify the role of cortico–basal ganglia–thalamo–cortical (BGTC) circuits in initiating these trajectories.
Results. We propose that fluent speech depends on the ability of the BGTC circuit to initialize the distributed speech motor network within the basin of attraction of the upcoming word’s motor program. Stuttering arises when this initialization process is unreliable or poorly coordinated, preventing the motor program from being executed until the neural state is corrected or the effective basin of attraction is broadened through compensatory mechanisms.
Conclusions. This basin-of-attraction framework provides a unifying account of diverse behavioral and neural findings in stuttering, aligns stuttering theory with contemporary dynamical systems approaches to motor control, and generates testable predictions for future neurophysiological and neuroimaging studies.

articles.title: Measurement Invariance and Sociodemographic Differences at the Lowest Level of the Psychopathology Hierarchy: An Analysis of the German HiTOP-SR
articles.authors: Benno T. T. Trummer; Leon Patrick Wendt; Ulrich Schroeders; Johannes Zimmermann
articles.abstract: Comparisons of mental health problems between sociodemographic groups are interpretable only if measures function equivalently across groups, yet measurement invariance has rarely been tested at the lowest level of the psychopathology hierarchy. Using the validation sample of the German Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology Self-Report (HiTOP-SR; N = 1,049 general-population adults), we tested measurement invariance across sex, age, and socioeconomic status (SES) for all 87 facets in ordinal multigroup confirmatory factor analyses and, where scalar invariance held, estimated standardized latent mean differences. Of the 261 cases (87 facets × 3 grouping variables), 74.3% reached scalar invariance, 14.6% showed non-invariance (usually small to medium in magnitude) and 11.1% were not estimable owing to low base rates. On invariant facets, women scored higher on internalizing and lower on externalizing facets, symptom levels declined with age, and higher SES was associated with lower symptom levels, with facet-level heterogeneity revealing where these differences were most pronounced. The results identify which facets permit meaningful sociodemographic comparisons and inform future revisions of the instrument.

articles.title: Editorial Perspective: Connecting Transdiagnostic Mechanisms Targeted in Cognitive Behavioral Therapies with Empirically-Based Symptom Dimensions
articles.authors: Kasey Stanton; Jack D Burke; Helena Towne; Isabella Whitesides
articles.abstract: Various avenues of transdiagnostic research hold promise for improving diagnosis and treatment but remain fragmented in some ways. We provide recommendations for integrating dimensional assessment guided by the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) framework into clinical practice by more effectively connecting the HiTOP with social-cognitive vulnerability (SCV) mechanisms targeted in cognitive behavioral and third-wave therapies. Specifically, we present concrete ideas for (a) comprehensively understanding HiTOP symptom dimension-SCV associations, (b) integrating measure development efforts spanning the HiTOP and SCV literatures, and (c) sharpening terminology for improving construct description and clinical communication. We draw on studies from the 2026 Special Issue of JCPP Advances on Transdiagnostic Approaches to Child and Adolescent Mental Health (e.g., Carrington et al., 2026; Lloyd et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026) that provide helpful examples illustrating these points, and we use these study examples to demonstrate how HiTOP-based assessment connects with personalized treatment planning.

articles.title: Conventional psychometric practices preordain support for unidimensionality of diagnostic criteria sets: DSM-5 substance use disorder as a case example
articles.authors: Joseph F. Sexton; Abbe Knutsson; Ashley L. Watts
articles.abstract: Psychometric methods are inseparable from contemporary psychiatric classification efforts but were not developed with psychopathology in mind. Here, we consider how conventional psychometric approaches are ill-equipped to characterize the structure of mental disorders and lead researchers to adopt unidimensional conceptualizations of them. Using the DSM-5 substance use disorder criteria set as a case example, we examine the validity of a unidimensional factor model in a large epidemiologic sample (n = 104,944) across 11 classes of psychoactive drugs. Traditional fit indices, factor loadings, and eigenvalues appeared to justify a unidimensional model, but evidence for unidimensionality faltered when using updated model fit indices, model-based fit benchmarks, and manipulating the extent of skew by restricting analyses to symptomatic individuals. Exploratory factor analyses further underscored evidence of multidimensionality in substance use disorder. We situate our findings in the historic literature that documents the hazards of underfactored models and offer suggestions for future classification efforts.

articles.title: Loneliness and Resting Parasympathetic Activity Interact to Influence Approach Motivations
articles.authors: Anita Restrepo; Mary Mousa; Alexander C. Henoch; Emily M. Silver; Gregory Norman; Kelly E. Faig; Karen E Smith
articles.abstract: Loneliness, or perceived social isolation, increases motivation to approach and reaffiliate while simultaneously enhancing sensitivity to potential threats, allowing individuals to avoid further social threats. Some individuals successfully leverage these competing motivations to reduce feelings of loneliness. However, others further withdraw, perpetuating a harmful cycle of loneliness. What drives this variability in responses to loneliness is still not well understood. Prior research found that resting parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) activity, linked to increased regulatory capacity and more flexible adaptation, moderates responses to loneliness. Individuals with higher resting PNS activity and higher levels of loneliness demonstrate enhanced approach of both positive and negative information. Here, we aimed to replicate and expand on this research, examining whether this effect is more pronounced for social information. 107 participants (ages 18 to 56 years) completed an approach-avoidance task in which they made decisions about whether to approach or avoid positive and negative social or non-social images. For individuals with higher resting PNS activity, loneliness was associated with reduced approach of negative information, but no differences in approach of positive information. These effects were comparable for social and non-social stimuli. Our findings suggest lonely individuals with higher resting PNS activity may be better able to flexibly leverage shifts in approach and avoidance motivations in a context-dependent manner, contributing to the field’s understanding of how loneliness shapes motivated behaviors as a function of environmental context, particularly the social nature of incoming valenced information.

articles.title: Neural Representations of Personally Familiar and Experimentally Familiar Faces Across Adulthood
articles.authors: Stefani Morgan; Emma Tripp; Sophie D. Allen; Chris B. Martin
articles.abstract: Face recognition is thought to reflect complementary functions of two brain networks. A core system is thought to support perceptual processing of faces, whereas an extended system represents affective and biographical knowledge that supports familiarity-based discrimination. However, the representational format of face-evoked responses within structures comprising each system is not well understood. Here, we applied RSA to fMRI data to characterize the representational structure of personally familiar, experimentally familiar, and novel faces in younger and older adults. This approach revealed that perirhinal cortex (PRC), a node in the extended face processing system, represented personally familiar and experimentally familiar faces in distinct patterns of activity in young adults; personally familiar faces were repelled from one another, whereas experimentally familiar faces were drawn near one another. Corresponding results from PRC in older adults demonstrated that the representational distinctiveness of experimentally familiar faces, but not personally familiar faces, was preserved across the lifespan. In contrast to young adults, a representationally distinct code for personally familiar faces was revealed only in the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) of older adults, which is a key node in the core face processing system. Comparing across regions of interest also revealed that pSTS was representationally distinct from both the extended system and other structures comprising the core system. Lastly, we found that activity patterns in the fusiform face area and occipital face area of young adults predicted response times on a behavioral oddball task in which personally familiar and novel faces were pitted against one another.

articles.title: Double-check listening effort in adults with cochlear implants, and precise effort timing by listeners with typical hearing
articles.authors: Matthew Winn; Lexi Olson; Abbey L. Thomas; Miski Mohamed; Katherine Teece
articles.abstract:
Objectives
Effortful listening can be a persistent source of strain for people who have hearing loss. Previous experiments have mainly described effort as varying from less to more, overlooking how listening goals might call for more effort at specific moments and less effort at other moments. This study tested listeners’ ability to aim listening effort at specific times containing key speech information, and to reduce effort when it is less needed. 
Design
Adults with typical hearing (TH) or with cochlear implants (CIs) completed a speech perception task where sentences were presented twice in immediate succession. If the sentence were initially presented clearly and in full, its repetition contained no new information. Alternatively, the initial presentation could contain a word masked by noise, demanding the listener seek out that specific word when the sentence was repeated with that word restored. Listening effort was assessed using concurrent measures of pupil dilation, microsaccade rate, and blinks. Each was analyzed using generalized additive mixed-effects modeling to determine when effort increased and decreased. 
Results
Adults with TH devoted less effort to speech repeated with no new information, showing less pupil dilation, less microsaccade inhibition, and less blink inhibition, compared to their responses to the first presentation of the sentence. They also showed stronger responses timed precisely to the moment of a restored key word when it became available in the repetition. However, listeners with CIs showed notable deviation from these patterns, including increased rather than a decreased pupil dilation when listening to a repetition of a sentence already heard fully intact. Additionally, their pupil dilations, microsaccades, and blinks were less precisely timed to key words previously missed.
Conclusions
Listeners with typical hearing can aim their effort at precise moments where information is needed, and reduce effort when listening is not necessary. Listeners with cochlear implants spread their effort across a wider range of time, and exert extra effort of “double-checking” their perceptions. The temporal control of effort is discussed as a dimension of listening that could underlie reports of fatigue and listening strain among people who use cochlear implants.

articles.title: Music as mindfulness: Focused listening reduces negative mind-wandering and strengthens attention networks
articles.authors: Carl-Richard Villanger Løberg; Stefan Koelsch
articles.abstract: Negative mind-wandering, a core component of rumination, is a transdiagnostic risk factor for psychiatric conditions. Here we tested a new focused music-listening method in which music served as the object of a mindfulness-like attentional practice, with sensorimotor synchronization used to stabilize attention. Healthy adults with elevated propensity for rumination (N = 77; Music n = 22, active control n = 30, passive controls n = 25) were randomized to a four-week intervention. Participants in the Music group assembled playlists of personally meaningful, positively valenced songs and practiced focused listening combined with simple sensorimotor synchronization, such as tapping or paced breathing. The active control group used a Cognitive Behavioral Therapy-informed micro-learning app, while passive controls completed experience sampling only. Daily smartphone-based experience sampling revealed reductions over time in negative mind-wandering in both active intervention groups, whereas passive controls showed no comparable change. Weekly questionnaire measures showed similar but weaker effects. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (n = 39 with complete sessions) demonstrated a pre- to post-intervention increase in task-evoked activity of the Extrinsic Mode Network in the Music group only, suggesting training-related enhancement of externally oriented attention systems. These findings identify focused music listening as a scalable form of music-based mindfulness, link its behavioral benefits to large-scale attention-network activity, and highlight its translational potential for mental health interventions and everyday well-being.

articles.title: TripTally: An Open-Access Calculator of Labor Costs Across Psychedelic Therapy Delivery Models
articles.authors: Amanda Downey; Ellen Bradley; Daniel Dickison; Joshua Woolley
articles.abstract: Psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy is generating substantial clinical interest, yet despite growing economic scrutiny, a practical question has received surprisingly little attention: how do specific delivery decisions drive cost? Labor costs—typically the dominant cost component of psychedelic therapy delivery—depend on a tangle of interacting design choices: the number, length, and staffing of treatment sessions (including provider qualifications, group versus individual format, and medical backup requirements), and local hourly wage rates. Together, these factors can produce order-of-magnitude differences in per-patient cost that resist easy estimation and are rarely modeled explicitly, making rational planning difficult. As psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy moves from clinical trials and state-licensed programs toward anticipated Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval, each stage bringing distinct staffing, regulatory, and reimbursement conditions, the need for flexible cost modeling is clear. To make these trade-offs visible and tractable, we developed TripTally (https://danieldickison.github.io/pat-calculator/), an open-access web calculator that, unlike existing economic analyses of fixed scenarios, allows any researcher, clinician, or policymaker to estimate labor costs using staffing configurations and wage rates specific to their own context.

articles.title: That’s Just Like Your Opinion, Man: Effort Legibility in The Big Lebowski
articles.authors: Emily Zohar; Michael Inzlicht
articles.abstract: The cult classic The Big Lebowski helped normalize a slacker lifestyle, inviting viewers to “take it easy”. Here, we use the film to examine a puzzle in the psychology of effort: why observers so often get it wrong. The contrast between Jeffrey “The Dude” Lebowski and Mr. Lebowski reveals a gap between actual and perceived effort. The Dude appears lazy–unemployed, broke, dishevelled, and often smoking a joint–yet repeatedly exerts effort toward intrinsically valued goals, including replacing his “valued rug”. Mr. Lebowski, by contrast, is celebrated as an “Achiever” and insists that he's a very busy man, despite frequently delegating his efforts to others. This misalignment matters because effort is largely private. Observers infer it from visible cues such as strain, struggle, and reward, but these cues can mislead. We argue that people are praised and punished based on effort legibility–how effortful they appear–rather than how much effort they exert. The film reveals what observers routinely miss: the Achiever may be coasting while the slacker is working, and whether we notice depends on which cues we’re seeing. Or, as the Dude puts it, “Yeah, well, that’s just, like, your opinion, man”.

articles.title: An agent’s partial knowledge of a hidden array impacts infants’ representations of object quantity
articles.authors: Melissa M. Kibbe; Jessica Beal Applin
articles.abstract: Infants can represent the quantity of a set of hidden objects, but if the number of objects hidden in a location exceeds three, infants experience “catastrophic forgetting”, failing to represent even a subset of the objects. Infants’ representations of an object also are impacted by other agents’ visual access to an object; infants represent what an agent observed about an object instead of what they themselves observed. Here, we asked whether an agent’s partial visual access to a set of objects would impact infants’ representations of the set’s quantity, and if so, whether this impact would apply when infants’ own representational limits are exceeded. Ten-14-month-olds (n=85) completed an ordinal choice task in which they watched an experimenter distribute different quantities of crackers across two containers, and were allowed to crawl to one of the containers to obtain its contents. We manipulated whether the quantities hidden were within or outside of infants’ capacity limits (1 vs. 2 or 1 vs. 4) and whether a second experimenter, who infants saw had also observed the crackers being distributed, had partial knowledge of the arrays (observing 1 vs. 1 or 1 vs. 2, respectively) or no knowledge. Infants’ container choices suggested that they used the observing agent’s perspective to represent quantity whenever she had partial knowledge of the arrays. Our results suggest that an agent’s quantity representations may mandatorily supplant infants’ own, and this may allow infants to represent a subset of objects in situations in which they would normally experience catastrophic representational failure.

articles.title: Debunking decreases mistaken causal inferences: A direct replication of Irving et al. (2022)
articles.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Keyi Zhang; James Edward Bartlett
articles.abstract: We conducted a direct replication of Irving et al. (2022) examining whether a debunking statement reduces mistaken causal inferences from correlational evidence. We randomly allocated participants to read a news article containing either a correction statement (n = 65) or a no-correction control (n = 64). Participants in the correction group made fewer causal inferences (delta = 0.65, 95% HDI [0.30, 1.00]) and more correlational inferences (delta = 0.72, 95% HDI [0.36, 1.07]) compared to the no correction group. In exploratory analyses, we also supported the robustness of their findings to alternative modelling choices. Our findings represent a successful direct replication of Irving et al.

articles.title: Relationship between purely verbal and numerical–verbal long-term memory in the standard conjoint recognition model
articles.authors: Michał Obidziński; Nina Bażela; Kinga Szafron; Mateusz Hohol
articles.abstract: Research on verbatim and gist long-term memory (LTM) within Fuzzy-Trace Theory (FTT) has largely employed verbal and pictorial materials, with limited attention to numbers. This study compares LTM for sentences without numerical content (purely verbal memory) and sentences containing Arabic digits (numerical–verbal memory) and examines the applicability of the standard Conjoint Recognition (CR) paradigm to numerical–verbal material. Participants completed six counterbalanced CR blocks: three assessing purely verbal memory and three assessing numerical–verbal memory. Results showed a strong correlation between performance across material types, with no significant difference in overall accuracy. However, significant differences emerged in underlying memory processes measured by multinomial processing tree modeling: familiarity parameters were higher for numerical–verbal memory, whereas identity and bias parameters were higher for purely verbal memory. These findings suggest that although LTM for purely verbal and numerical–verbal materials is closely related, it differs in underlying processes.

articles.title: Thought Probe Response Options, but not Probe Frequency,  Affect Thought Report Validity in a Cued Recall Episodic Memory Task
articles.authors: Samuel W. Cox; Michael J. Kane; Christopher N. Wahlheim
articles.abstract: The ability to maintain focus on task-relevant information is often measured using thought probes requiring participants to report their momentary attentional states. Research using this approach demonstrates substantial heterogeneity in thought probe features, raising concerns about measurement validity. In episodic memory tasks, such variation may systematically affect the precision of estimating attention–memory relationships. Two between-subjects experiments examined effects of varying thought probe response options and frequency on thought reports, subsequent recall, and their association. Participants completed paired-associate, cued recall tasks including thought probes during study. In Experiment 1, 128 participants received probes with either two response options (on-task vs. off-task) or three (on-task vs. task-related vs. off-task). Including a task-related option reduced on-task more than off-task reports between groups. Recall was more accurate for items presented during on- than off-task states, especially when the task-related option was included. In Experiment 2, 128 participants received two or four probes during study, always with three response options. Thought report rates and memory accuracy did not differ significantly between probe frequencies. These findings suggest that, within cued recall paradigms, attention–memory associations are generally robust to thought probe variation, but three-option probes that isolate task-related thoughts may characterize attentional states more precisely.

articles.title: Reimagining Empirical Aesthetics Through Cross-Cultural Perspectives
articles.authors: Kohinoor Monish Darda; Dyutiman Mukhopadhyay; Nandini Chatterjee Singh
articles.abstract: Cross-cultural empirical aesthetics examines how aesthetic experience converges and varies across cultural contexts. In this short review, we synthesize recent work on visual art, music, and dance, with emphasis on the audience perspective within the psychology of art: how viewers, listeners, and observers perceive, feel, evaluate, and make meaning from artworks and performances. Evidence suggests that some perceptual and affective cues, such as harmony, contour, tempo, loudness, rhythm, and synchrony, can support partially shared responses, while aesthetic judgments are shaped by enculturation, expertise, familiarity, identity, context, and culturally patterned attention. These findings suggest that aesthetic experience arises from dynamic interactions between universal perceptual mechanisms and culture-specific interpretive frameworks. Using rasa theory from Indian aesthetics as a test case, we argue that cross-cultural empirical aesthetics should embrace a pluralistic, culturally grounded approach that employs theoretical constructs that best capture aesthetic experience within diverse artistic traditions.

articles.title: Attentional network processing in children and adults shows comparable behavioural effects but distinct ERP and time–frequency activity
articles.authors: Praghajieeth Raajhen Santhana Gopalan; Otto Loberg; Jarmo Hamalainen; Paavo H. T. Leppänen
articles.abstract: Visual attention comprises alerting, orienting, and executive-control networks. Although these networks are behaviourally evident in childhood, age differences in the neural processes supporting them remain unclear. Typically developing 12–13-year-old children (n = 77) and 19–33-year-old adults (n = 21) performed the Attention Network Test while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Behavioural performance was assessed using reaction time and accuracy. Neural processing was examined using event-related potentials (N1 and P3 amplitudes and latencies) and induced time–frequency analyses of theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), and beta (13–25 Hz) band activity. Significant alerting, orienting, and executive-control effects were observed in reaction time, with children responding more slowly overall than adults. Children showed longer N1 latencies than adults during the orienting comparison, indicating slower early target-related processing. Alerting cues increased target-related N1 amplitudes similarly in both groups. Children, but not adults, showed larger P3 amplitudes during incongruent than congruent trials, suggesting greater conflict-related neural processing during executive control in late childhood. Time–frequency analyses showed that alerting modulated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity similarly in both groups. Orienting-related theta activity differed between age groups, with children showing higher theta power for spatial- than centre-cue trials, whereas adults showed lower theta power for spatial- than centre-cue trials. Alpha-band activity also differed between orienting conditions similarly in both groups. These findings indicate that children and adults can show comparable behavioural attentional network effects despite differences in neural processing. The results further suggest that electrophysiological measures of attentional processing continue to mature beyond late childhood.

articles.title: Mental Health, Functional Impairment, and Self-Efficacy in Teachers: The Role of Stress-Management Strategies
articles.authors: Raquel Messi Falcoski; Fernando Eduardo Padovan-Neto
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Teachers frequently experience psychological symptoms that may impair occupational functioning. This study examined the associations between sociodemographic, professional, and psychological factors and mental health, functional impairment, and self-efficacy, with a focus on stress-management strategies within a social cognitive framework.
Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted using snowball sampling with 536 teachers and 307 adults from the general population. Participants completed validated measures of anxiety (GAD-7), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), perceived stress (PSS-10), functional impairment (WHODAS 2.0), and teacher self-efficacy (TSES-SF). Additional data included sociodemographic and professional characteristics, mental health diagnosis, treatment status, and engagement in stress-management strategies. Group differences were analyzed using chi-square and t-tests, while Spearman correlations and multiple linear regressions were used to identify predictors.
Results: Teachers reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, depressive symptoms, perceived stress, and functional impairment compared to the general population. Within the teacher sample, older age and engagement in stress-management strategies were consistently associated with lower psychological distress. Functional impairment and perceived stress negatively predicted self-efficacy.
Conclusion: These findings highlight the importance of behavioral strategies and contextual factors in supporting teachers’ mental health and professional functioning. Interventions targeting stress management may help reduce functional impairment and promote self-efficacy in educational settings.

articles.title: Validation Study of the Swedish Child Post-Traumatic Cognitions Inventory in Maltreated Children
articles.authors: Ole Hultmann; James Stålsjö; Valgeir Thorvaldsson; Anke de Haan
articles.abstract:
Background: 
Dysfunctional post-traumatic cognitions (PTCs) play a central role in the development and maintenance of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The Child Post-Traumatic Cognitions Inventory (CPTCI) is a self-report questionnaire assessing dysfunctional PTCs in minors, available in a 25-item original version (CPTCI-25) and a 10-item short form (CPTCI-10). 

Objective: 
This study evaluated the psychometric properties of the Swedish CPTCI (CPTCI-Swe) in its original and short form.  

Method: 
The sample consisted of 77 patients (9-17 years) at a Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) clinic, all with histories of exposure to intimate partner violence and/or child abuse. Data was collected prior to treatment. 

Results: 
Confirmatory factor analyses supported the two-factor structure - permanent and disturbing change (CPTCI-PC) and fragile person in a scary world (CPTCI-SW) - for both versions. Internal consistency was good across the four subscales, although lower for the CPTCI-10 Scary World subscale. The observed associations between dysfunctional PTCs and psychopathology were not as consistent as in previous studies, but we nevertheless consider convergent validity for both the CPTCI-25 and CPTCI-10 established. Neither the CPTCI-25 nor the CPTCI-10 predicted PTSD diagnosis. However, both subscales of the CPTCI-25 emerged as significant predictors of continuous clinician-assessed posttraumatic stress symptoms. 

Conclusions: 
Overall, the CPTCI-Swe is a reliable and valid instrument for assessing dysfunctional PTCs in maltreated children. Depending on time-constraints or when the CPTCI is used repeatedly for monitoring purposes, the CPTCI-10 might be a good alternative to the CPTCI-25. More validation studies on the CPTCI-10 across trauma types are needed to fully understand its clinical utility

articles.title: Trends in well-being of liberal women
articles.authors: Paul H. P. Hanel
articles.abstract: Conservative influencers, politicians, and writers have repeatedly claimed that feminism has made liberal women unhappier. Using an 11-wave repeated cross-sectional design spanning from 2002 to 2023 across 15 European countries (N = 279,530), we found no support for this claim. Well-being did not decline for liberal women aged 14-17, 18-29, and 30-44, nor did it for liberal men, or for moderate or conservative women and men. In fact, the well-being of liberal women aged 45 years or older rose over the study period, as did the well-being of conservatives and moderates, for women and men. These findings remain robust across different operationalisations of well-being, political orientation, and age grouping. Cross-sectionally, well-being declined with age, even as the older groups' well-being rose over the study period. Further, conservatives reported higher well-being consistently across age, gender, and survey rounds. Together, our findings contradict a central claim of prominent conservative writers and politicians.

articles.title: The risk-stigma paradox: How risk-focused HIV prevention produces and distorts vulnerability
articles.authors: Sarah E. Stutterheim
articles.abstract: We currently have a diverse toolbox of HIV prevention modalities that can be leveraged to reduce new HIV infections. Unfortunately, a focus on changing risk perceptions in HIV prevention persist despite limited evidence. In this viewpoint, I describe how an individual-level focus on risk perception fuels stigma while stigma obscures risk perception. I argue that efforts to bolster HIV prevention should focus first and foremost on ascertaining the various determinants of uptake for the various prevention modalities available, and acknowledge that people’s preferences for prevention strategies are neither universal nor static. We should therefore engage in ongoing monitoring of the many sociocognitive and structural determinants of the different prevention modalities over time, and make our sexual health services free from stigma, judgment, and risk eligibility criteria.

articles.title: Image Database for Everyday Affective Spaces (IDEAS): an open-access database of high-quality and standardized affective images of indoor environments
articles.authors: Fatih Deniz; Yvonne A. W. de Kort; Linghan Zhang; Kynthia Chamilothori
articles.abstract: We spend about 90% of our time in indoor environments. These environments strongly influence our health, behavior, and psychological well-being, yet we know surprisingly little about how indoor characteristics shape our affective and approach-avoidance responses. This gap exists partly because previous studies relied on small, self-curated image sets created based on differing criteria, limiting generalizability and reproducibility. To address this, we introduce the Image Database for Everyday Affective Spaces (IDEAS), an open-access dataset of 1,800 high-quality, real-world photographs from the six most frequented indoor environments: offices, living rooms, dining rooms, kitchens, bedrooms, and restaurants. These images were rated by 900 participants on valence, tense arousal, energetic arousal, and approach-avoidance in two online studies. We examined the relationship between valence, tense arousal, and energetic arousal in our dataset using seven theoretical models. Our analyses revealed a strong negative correlation between valence and tense arousal ratings of indoor scenes, whereas valence and energetic arousal, as well as energetic arousal and tense arousal, were largely independent, providing support for the three-dimensional core affect model. Demographic variables had minimal influence on affective ratings, while participants showed high inter-rater reliability. IDEAS offers a valuable resource for advancing environmental preference and broader environmental psychology research, enabling more nuanced investigation of how specific indoor environments and their characteristics shape emotional experience. Beyond normative affective scores, the dataset includes a comprehensive set of low-, mid-, and high-level visual features, individual ratings, demographic data, and copyright information. The IDEAS dataset is available on the OSF (https://osf.io/g9ze5) and GitHub (https://github.com/FatihcDeniz/Image-Database-for-Everyday-Affective-Spaces).

articles.title: Effects of Triangular Human-Machine Interface Icons on Takeover Performance from L3 automation: Behavioural, Ocular, and Psychophysiological Insights
articles.authors: Courtney Michael Goodridge; Gaëtan Merlhiot; Natasha Merat
articles.abstract: Augmented Reality (AR) can create interactive Human-Machine Interfaces (HMIs) that adapt to the road environments and/or attract driver attention to important information. Higher levels of automation may take humans out-of-the-loop, hence effective HMIs are paramount for facilitating fast and safe takeovers. This driving simulator study investigated whether low-level visual features of AR-HMI icons impacted the orientation of driver attention and consequential takeover performance. Drivers (N = 14) in a within-participants experimental design used an SAE Level 3 automated driving system, either with or without a mentally loading non-driving related task (NDRT), before being presented with a takeover request (TOR) to merge into ongoing traffic whilst travelling on a 2-lane motorway. TORs were either urgent (time to collision [TTC] = 7 s) or planned (TTC = 30 s) and consisted of an auditory tone paired with a circular icon, a triangular icon, or no icon. Eye movements, electrodermal activity, and vehicle dynamics were recorded to investigate driver takeover performance. Results indicated that triangular AR-HMI icons were associated with an earlier physiological arousal response, faster takeover times, and increased minimum TTCs for urgent TORs. Conversely, no evidence was found for beneficial takeover performance for the planned TORs. These results indicate that HMI icon shape may facilitate faster and safer takeovers during critical events. We discuss how angular shapes are linked to improved takeover behaviours and why the benefits may only be present if drivers have optimal mental workload.

articles.title: Tailoring relative phase estimation methods to movement shape. A practical approach to estimate the Arnold tongue with testing codes on human data and simulation of discrete and continuous signals.
articles.authors: Martin Le Guennec; julien lagarde
articles.abstract: The relative phase ϕis a key variable in the study of coordination dynamics across many disciplines. Several estimation methods exist and are used interchangeably in the study of sensorimotor synchronization, despite the limitations of certain methods when analyzing inharmonic (aka discrete) movements. In this study, we document differences in estimates of key variables used to describe coordination dynamics, the mean ϕand its standard deviation, calculated using a pointwise method and using the Hilbert transform with signal centering or with a correction of the non-linearity. We applied these methods to experimental data from a tapping task with an incremental increase in metronome frequency. The increase in frequency allowed us to observe differences between methods in inharmonic movements at low synchronization frequencies and in near-sinusoidal movements at higher frequencies. To complement this analysis, we conducted stochastic numerical simulations of non-linear oscillators and with ghost attractors to mimic signals from discrete movements. We compared the mean and SD ϕestimates to a gold standard based on the Arnold tongues framework. Our experimental and simulation results show that the mean and SD ϕestimates obtained from the Hilbert transform are biased for inharmonic signals, we recommend using the pointwise method in this context. With near-sinusoidal signals, both methods provide equivalent results. We propose a practical approach to estimate the quality of synchronization, sharing free testing codes, human data and simulation of discrete or continuous movements.

articles.title: The Sound of Meaning: Prosody Distinguishes Affirmation from Negation in Early Speech Input
articles.authors: Sakine Cabuk-Balli; Volker Dellwo; Aylin C. Küntay; Paul Widmer; Sabine Stoll
articles.abstract: A central feature of human language acquisition is the ability to extract meaning from the linguistic input children encounter. Prosody, a fundamental component of spoken communication, conveys broad communicative intent, but it remains unclear whether it also provides reliable cues to support the learning of more fine-grained semantic distinctions. This study investigates whether prosody can in principle serve as a meaningful signal for distinguishing negative from affirmative declarative utterances in the speech that surrounds children. By analyzing child-directed and child-surrounding speech, we assess whether the prosodic patterns available in learner's input are sufficiently systematic to support the acquisition of these semantic contrasts. We tested (i) whether machines and humans can differentiate between affirmative and negative utterances, and (ii) whether humans are able to categorize specific negative functions (prohibition, rejection, non-existence, and inability) based on their acoustic features. Our dataset comprises affirmative and negative declarative utterances drawn from longitudinal child language acquisition corpora in five typologically diverse languages: Chintang, English, Indonesian, Kurdish, and Turkish.  First, using Support Vector Machines, we evaluate the extent to which prosodic cues (pitch and duration) contribute to the classification of affirmative and negative utterances. The results reveal high accuracy in distinguishing between affirmative and negative utterances across all five languages.  Second, in two behavioral experiments with 300 native and non-speakers of three languages (English, Kurdish, and Turkish), we examined whether there is a difference between the two speaker groups in classifying utterances based on intonational contours. Experiment 1 revealed that native speakers successfully distinguished affirmative from negative utterances based on pitch and amplitude, an ability not shared by non-speakers. Experiment 2 demonstrated that prohibition is identified with the greatest accuracy by both speaker groups. The characteristic elevated pitch of prohibitive utterances appears to function as a universal prosodic marker that facilitates their recognition irrespective of linguistic background. We conclude that prosodic cues in child-surrounding speech form a dynamic and functionally rich acoustic framework that serves as universal signals. These cues facilitate children’s ability to discern meaning and to identify essential negative functions, thereby supporting foundational processes in early semantic interpretation.

articles.title: Strategy Use Determines the Changing-State Effect: Evidence from a Strategy Instruction Manipulation
articles.authors: Philipp Radloff; Judith Schweppe
articles.abstract: The changing-state effect (CSE), the finding that changing-state sound disrupts working memory more than steady-state sound, is a robust empirical phenomenon of auditory distraction. Attentional capture accounts and interference-by-process accounts make opposing predictions under which condition the effect occurs. Only interference-by-process accounts predict that the CSE depends on order processing in the focal task. Previous demonstrations of a CSE in non-order-based tasks have been interpreted as evidence for attentional capture, but quasi-experimental evidence indicates that participants’ use of order-based strategies in the non-order-based missing scan task may have caused the CSE (Hughes & Marsh, 2020). However, this finding was not replicated in a subsequent study (Radloff & Schweppe, 2026). Therefore, we manipulated strategy use experimentally in a missing scan task under steady-state and changing-state sound by instructing participants to apply rehearsal (order-based) or a checklist strategy (non-order-based). The findings are consistent with interference-by-process accounts with a significant interaction between sound and instructed strategy such that a significant CSE was observed only in the rehearsal group. Moreover, Bayesian effect size estimation indicated strong evidence for a null effect in the checklist condition.

articles.title: Momentary Associations of Autonomic Nervous System Activity Measured via Heart Rate Variability with Affective and Arousal States
articles.authors: Justin Hachenberger; Anna Exner; Denny Kerkhoff; Sebastian Ludyga; Axel Mayer; Christian Rominger; Andreas R. Schwerdtfeger; Angelina Sutin; Claudia Voelcker-Rehage; Sakari Lemola
articles.abstract: Affective and biophysiological states are inherently linked, which is partly due to the activity of the autonomic nervous system. Heart rate variability is a commonly used indicator of autonomic nervous system activity. The present study examines the associations between heartrate variability indicators with perceived arousal and affective states using two 14-day experience sampling studies combined with ambulatory assessment of physical activity and heart rate variability. A total of 197 individuals (72.1% female) aged 18 to 29 years provided 11,269 measurements with complete surveys and corresponding valid accelerometry and electrocardiography data. In particular, we investigated heart rate and the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) as indicators for cardiac activity. We found a positive within-person association between heart rate with positive affect and perceived energetic arousal, while the association was negative for RMSSD. The opposite pattern was found for negative affect. No associations of heart rate or RMSSD with perceived tense arousal or generally on the between-person level were found. Mediation analyses revealed that the associations between heart rate variability and affect were partly mediated by perceived energetic arousal. The results of this study suggest that intraindividual fluctuations in heart rate variability indicators are associated with fluctuations in energetic arousal and affect. This study suggests a primarily state-dependent nature of the relationship between the autonomic nervous system activity and affect and highlights perceived energetic arousal as a potential mediator between them.

articles.title: The impact of problematic social media use on loneliness, procrastination and self-esteem: a cross-sectional study in Greece
articles.authors: Zoe Katsiroumpa; Polyxeni Mangoulia; Evmorfia Koukia; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE To explore the impact of problematic social media use on loneliness, procrastination and self-esteem. Additionally, we examined sex and generation differences. METHOD We carried out a cross-sectional study involving a convenience sample of 1033 individuals, all of whom had at least one social media account. To assess problematic social media use, we employed the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Additionally, we evaluated loneliness, procrastination, and self-esteem using the UCLA 3-Item Loneliness Scale, the Irrational Procrastination Scale, and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, respectively. To control for confounding variables such as sex, age, educational level, socioeconomic status, daily social media usage, and the number of social media accounts, we conducted multivariable linear regression analysis. RESULTS Our findings revealed a positive association between problematic social media use and both loneliness and procrastination, while a negative association was observed with self-esteem. Stratification analysis indicated a stronger link between problematic social media use and procrastination among females and Generation Z. Furthermore, the association between problematic social media use and loneliness was more pronounced in Generation X and Millennials, while the association with self-esteem was stronger in Generation Z. CONCLUSIONS Our findings support the association between problematic social media use and issues such as loneliness, procrastination, and self-esteem, with notable differences based on sex and generation. As social media usage continues to rise, healthcare professionals should remain vigilant in identifying high-risk groups susceptible to problems stemming from problematic social media use

articles.title: Revisiting Singularity and Compassion Fade: Replication and extensions of Experiments 1a and 3 in Västfjäll et al. (2014)
articles.authors: Lewend Mayiwar; Shubin Yu; Yooeun Jeong; Richard Rekdal; Tuan Viet; Ihor Rudko; Matilda Dorotic; Gilad Feldman
articles.abstract: Västfjäll et al. (2014) found support for “compassion fade”, that affective reactions and charitable donations decrease as the number of victims increases. In a pre-registered experiment with a U.S. sample recruited through CloudResearch Connect (N = 1207), we conducted a replication and extension of Studies 1a and 3 from Västfjäll et al. (2014). In the replication of Study 1a, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims (one vs. two children) on hypothetical donation amount, positive- or negative affect, perceived impact of donations (all |d|s ≤ 0.16) or for any mediation effects. In the replication of Study 3, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims or relatedness on donation amount, perceived need, positive affect, or negative affect of donations (all ηp2 ≤ 0.012). Bayesian analyses indicated moderate to strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for most effects, and equivalence testing indicated that seven of eight effects were smaller than our conservative smallest effect size of interest. Overall, our findings fail to replicate the original compassion fade effects and suggest limitations on their generalizability across various dependent measures and contexts. Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A2TGB

articles.title: Autistic Burnout Severity Items – French Translation (ABSI-Fr)
articles.authors: Capucine Rebours; Patrick Raynal; Jeanne Kruck
articles.abstract: Autistic burnout is increasingly recognized in the literature as a state of profound physical and mental exhaustion, distinct from occupational burnout and depression, experienced by autistic adults. The Autistic Burnout Severity Items (ABSI), developed by Arnold et al. (2023), is among the few tools designed to capture the severity and multidimensional nature of this experience. Here we present the ABSI-Fr, a French-language translation and cultural adaptation of the ABSI. The translation followed a structured process: an initial French translation was produced and reviewed by an independent translator, then examined for clarity and acceptability by two successive panels of autistic adults (n = 12 and n = 8), whose feedback informed revisions to wording and phrasing. The finalized version was back-translated into English and compared to the original by an independent translator to verify conceptual equivalence. The ABSI-Fr comprises 26 items distributed across six dimensions (emotional and somatic distress, social withdrawal and communication, cognitive dysfunction and slowing, general exhaustion, autistic self-awareness and self-regulation, and memory disruption), plus three additional items assessing meltdown-related behaviours, reported separately and excluded from the total score. Items are rated on a 7-point Likert scale, with a "not applicable" option for items that do not apply to the respondent's situation. This preprint provides the instrument, administration instructions, and scoring guidelines to make the ABSI-Fr available to French-speaking researchers and clinicians. A separate psychometric validation study, examining the factor structure, reliability, and validity of the ABSI-Fr, is currently underway and will be reported elsewhere.

articles.title: Selective attenuation of neural responses to own infant's face in early motherhood: A longitudinal MEG study
articles.authors: Elisa Vuoriainen; Piia Astikainen; Xueqiao Li; Qianru Xu; Santeri Yrttiaho; Mikko J. Peltola
articles.abstract: The transition to parenthood is associated with heightened neural responsiveness to infant cues, particularly to one’s own infant. Yet it remains unclear how this sensitivity changes with caregiving experience. Magnetoencephalography was recorded from 16 first time mothers viewing images of their own infant, an unfamiliar infant, and an unfamiliar adult at two timepoints spanning infancy and early toddlerhood. We examined early orbitofrontal activity (~140 ms), structural face encoding (M170, ~170 ms), and later motivated attention indexed by the late positive potential (LPP, ~300–600 ms). Source-level brain data were analyzed with a depth-weighted minimum-norm estimate. Results showed that early LPP responses in the fusiform cortex and late LPP responses in fusiform and occipital regions were larger for own infant faces at the first session but decreased to the level of other faces by the second session. In contrast, early orbitofrontal activity and M170 responses were not modulated by face type or session, and M170 responses showed high temporal stability. These findings indicate that neural activity associated with motivated attention to one’s own infant attenuates across early motherhood, whereas early responses reflecting perceptual and affective processes remain stable. The findings provide longitudinal evidence for changes in maternal neural reactivity to one’s own infant.

articles.title: The significance of SIGs: Reflections from the first five years of the EHPS Habit Special Interest Group
articles.authors: Benjamin Gardner; Robert Edgren; Daniel John Phipps; Eike Kofi Buabang; Eleonoora Hintsa Figueiredo; Barbara Mullan; Phillippa Lally
articles.abstract: Since 2011, the EHPS has supported several Special Interest Groups (SIGs). SIGs are networks designed to connect EHPS members who have shared interests, facilitate knowledge exchange, and establish collaborations outside of the annual conference. Fifteen years on, seven SIGs exist within the Society, supporting networks of members including those with interests in methodological approaches, social justice and representation, theory and application. In this paper, we draw on our experiences of five years of running the EHPS ‘Habit’ SIG to illustrate some of the benefits that SIGs confer on their members, and the broader health psychology community. We provide examples of how the Habit SIG has allowed its members to steer the course of habit research in health psychology, created a forum for generating and debating new ideas, and strengthened collaborations and community while also supporting career development among early career researchers. We present the Habit SIG as a blueprint for how specialisms within the EHPS can flourish through the establishment and maintenance of SIGs.

articles.title: Symptom Recognition, Help-seeking behaviour, and Joint Decision-making among Parents of Children with Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder
articles.authors: Quirina Engels; Lilian Lechner; Yil Severijns
articles.abstract:
Objective: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) is a relatively new diagnosis for the eating disorder in which children avoid food due to lack of interest, sensory characteristics, or fear of aversive consequences of food. Early recognition and treatment of ARFID is crucial, as delays in diagnosis can lead to serious medical consequences and increased psychosocial burden for both the child and the parents. In the Netherlands a qualitative study was conducted with the research question "Which factors influence parental help-seeking behaviour when suspecting ARFID in their child, and what differences exist between fathers and mothers?".
Methods: Ten semi-structured interviews were conducted with parents of children with ARFID (aged 4-12 years). Nine parental couples and one single parent (N=19) were interviewed. The data were analysed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA).
Results: Parents recognized various symptoms of ARFID in their child, with growth problems and selective eating behaviour being most common. Parents help-seeking behaviour was stimulated by urgent medical consequences and concerns about psychosocial limitations in their child. However, it was hindered by a lack of reference framework with a first child and a wait-and-see attitude of healthcare providers, who viewed the eating problems as a neophobic phase. Differences that emerged between parents were that mothers more often took the initiative to seek help and experienced more guilt about eating behaviour, while fathers more often applied coercion during mealtimes.
Conclusion: The diagnostic trajectory of ARFID was stressful for parents, experiencing frustration, powerlessness, guilt, and lack of support from both healthcare providers and their environment. Recommended is peer support, training of healthcare providers in recognition of ARFID, and a family-centred approach with attention to emotional support.

articles.title: The Perceived Impact of Confidence on Therapeutic Process and Effectiveness: An International Qualitative Exploration with Schema Therapists
articles.authors: Liam Spicer; Andy Allen; Robert Brockman; Clare Wilson; Joanne Brooker
articles.abstract:
Therapist confidence is increasingly recognised as an important variable that influences the
therapeutic alliance, technique delivery, and client outcomes. Within schema therapy, confidence
may be shaped by the therapists’ own early maladaptive schemas and mode activation, yet little
empirical work has explored how schema therapists understand this relationship. This qualitative
study examined schema therapists’ perceptions of the factors that influence their confidence,
how confidence shapes their therapeutic work, and how confidence develops over time. Twenty-
two schema therapists, either accredited with or in the process of accreditation with the
International Society of Schema Therapy, completed an anonymous online qualitative survey.
Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes and 10 subthemes were
generated. The first theme, lack of confidence and perceived impacts, described the influence of
personal schemas including defectiveness, failure, and self-sacrifice on therapists’ confidence,
emotional attunement, and engagement with schema therapy techniques. The second theme,
changes in confidence, outlined how self-awareness, personal therapy, supervision, accreditation,
and client outcomes contributed to the development of confidence across the professional
lifespan. The third theme, perceived benefits of confidence on client work, highlighted how
confidence supported emotional attunement, flexibility in the use of therapeutic techniques, and
creativity in session. Overall, the findings show that confidence is a dynamic and relational
process that interacts with therapists’ own schemas and professional experiences. Supporting
therapist confidence through schema focused supervision, personal schema work, experiential
learning, and training may enhance attunement and the effective delivery of schema therapy.
Implications for supervision, training, and future research are discussed.

articles.title: Tales of the unexpected: psychedelic trial design solutions
articles.authors: Robin Carhart-Harris; Will Alexander Lucas; Lorenzo Pasquini; Alexa Molinaro; Hannes Kettner; Patrick A. McConnell; Jennifer Mitchell
articles.abstract: This article spotlights problematic assumptions and practices in clinical psychedelic research that together hamper the field’s ability to demonstrate causal identification, contributing to confusion and misunderstanding: (1) the main problematic assumption is that pretreatment expectancy causes therapeutic response; while expectancy predicts response to most treatments, it is becoming increasingly clear that the same is not true for psychedelic therapy—and we offer a plausible hypothesis for why; (2) the main problematic practice is the double-blind procedure, which is ecologically invalid, ethically questionable, and fails to achieve its purpose (causal identification) due to functional unblinding; we propose alternative trial designs that can circumvent the need for participant blinding while improving our ability to draw strong inferences regarding the causal action of psychedelic therapy.

articles.title: Scaling Fidelity Across States: The Effects of Fidelity of Delivering of the Pathways-to- Success Identity-based Motivation Program on Student Trajectories
articles.authors: Daphna Oyserman; Alysia Burbidge; Yahan Huang; Nicholas Sorensen
articles.abstract: Students commonly wish for futures requiring educational credentials but (mis)interpret their metacognitive difficulty when thinking about or working on school tasks and goals as implying that these futures are not for them, undermining their goal striving and outcomes. Prior research documents that teachers can train other teachers to deliver Pathways-to-Success–a supporting identity-based motivational program–and that students who receive it with fidelity have more positive academic trajectories. This paper addresses the concern that promising program results often fail to replicate across contexts and at scale by examining the effects of the fidelity with which Pathways-to-Success is delivered on student trajectories across context and at scale. In six cohorts in two federally funded cluster-randomized trials, we assess the total effects of fidelity on student trajectories, controlling for their baseline scores on outcomes of interest and whether their school was randomly assigned to treatment or delayed treatment. We nest students (N=4892) in the classrooms in which they received Pathways-to-Success (n=200). Our structural equation models reveal that students who receive Pathways-to-Success with higher fidelity have better trajectories–they attain higher GPA and standardized math proficiency scores, are at lower risk of course failure, miss a smaller proportion of instructional days, and score higher in social-emotional competency. Regarding depression, almost half of students in our sample are at risk of depression (>CES-D cutoff score); fidelity directionally but not significantly reduces symptom frequency. Receiving Pathways-to-Success with fidelity provides a scalable, context-stable path to support students’ identity-based motivation and bolster their academic and well-being trajectories.

articles.title: Investigating the role of coping strategies, personality traits and mindfulness with self-care in leukemia patients
articles.authors: Fatemeh Khajeh Hasani Rabari; Fatemeh Rezaei; Fatemeh Mirzai; Fatemeh Sedighi
articles.abstract:
Objective: Leukemia is one of the most common cancers, and several factors play a role in aggravating the disease process. The purpose of this study was to investigate the relationship between coping strategies, personality traits, and mindfulness with self-care in leukemia patients.
Materials and Methods: The research design was descriptive-correlation. The statistical population of the research included patients with leukemia in Shariati and Sina hospitals in Tehran in the second half of 2023. 250 people were selected by the convenience sampling method. The data were collected using the Coping with Stressful Situation Questionnaire (CISS), the Neo Five-Factor Personality Characteristics Questionnaire, the Freiburg Mindfulness Questionnaire Short Form (FMI-SF), and the Self-Efficacy Self-Care Questionnaire (SUPPH) and analyzed with a step-by-step regression test with SPSS software.
Findings: The results showed that the relationship between self-care and problem-oriented, emotion-oriented and avoidance strategies and the characteristics of extroversion, openness to experience, adaptability, conscientiousness and mindfulness has a significant positive relationship and a significant negative relationship with neuroticism. Also, the results showed that mindfulness, problem-oriented strategy, neuroticism, openness to experience and conscientiousness predict a total of 58% of the variance of self-care in patients with leukemia.
Conclusion: Considering the effect of problem-oriented strategy, neuroticism, openness to experience and conscientiousness in self-care, it is suggested to organize courses to improve self-care in order to improve psychological health and increase self-care in patients with leukemia.

articles.title: Does Looking Like Meat Help? Visual Similarity and Consumer Evaluations of Plant-Based Steaks
articles.authors: Bojana Većkalov; Femke van Horen
articles.abstract: Plant-based meat alternatives (PBMAs) are often developed to be as similar to animal meat as possible, yet the extent to which such similarity benefits consumer preference remains unclear. Across two online studies (total N = 809), we examined how visual similarity to meat, as a central cue guiding consumers’ decision making at point-of-purchase, shapes evaluations of plant-based steaks using a comparative judgment paradigm. In both studies, plant-based steaks that were perceived as more similar to meat steaks were generally liked more. However, this relationship was not uniform across consumers. Vegans and vegetarians, as well as frequent PBMA consumers preferred lower levels of visual similarity, with evidence for diminishing returns at very high levels of similarity. Omnivores preferred visual similarity to be as high possible, whereas flexitarians fell in between. In sum, our findings suggest that visual similarity is generally beneficial, but the strength and shape of this relationship shifts depending on consumer segment and characteristics. These findings have implications for sustainable product design and marketing.

articles.title: Musica ex Machina: Towards AI-Supported Research into Mechanisms of Music-Based Therapies and Interventions
