articles.authors: Daniela Ruiz; Alejandra Perez; King-Chi Yau; Mok Che Ling Michelle; Vincent Zhong; Martina de Witte; Mario Valderrama; Mark Ettenberger; Artur Jaschke
articles.abstract:
Background: The expanding literature on music-based therapies and interventions makes it increasingly difficult for clinicians and researchers to identify relevant evidence on treatment mechanisms, moderators, mediators, and outcomes. 

Objective: This study explored whether artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP) methods could support the organisation and retrieval of information from this literature.
Methods: An automated PubMed search using the terms “music therapy”, “music intervention”, and “sound therapy” retrieved 4,396 articles. Four approaches were evaluated: (i) expert-defined terminology, (ii) KeyBERT-based keyword extraction with k-means clustering, (iii) Word2Vec-based abstract representations with k-means clustering, and (iv) a BERT-based question-answering (QA) system for retrieving specific answers and source passages.

Results: The expert-defined approach identified a limited set of frequently occurring terms, whereas KeyBERT generated a broader vocabulary and 10 clusters of related abstracts. Word2Vec produced 50 clusters, but the mean silhouette coefficient was 0.20, indicating weak cluster separation. The QA system retrieved potentially relevant passages from source articles. However, its answers and scores changed when the amount of input text or wording of the query was modified.

Conclusions: AI-supported clustering and QA methods may help clinicians and researchers navigate the growing literature on music-based therapies and interventions. However, these findings are preliminary. Further work should focus on improving domain-specific model performance and representativeness. Such systems should support literature retrieval and professional judgment rather than replace clinical expertise.

articles.title: Mental Health Profiles in Aging: A Dual-Factor Approach Using Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
articles.authors: Arielle Bonneville-Roussy; Sophie Rochette Bragg; Alexanne Landry; Laurence Perrier; Olivier Vivier; Isabelle Rouleau; Sébastien Grenier
articles.abstract:
Objectives. 
Mental health (MH) is increasingly conceptualized, according to the dual-factor model (DFM), as the coexistence of well-being and ill-being rather than simply the absence of illness. However, this model has seldom been applied to aging populations. This study aims to move beyond deficit-based models of aging by examining the DFM in older adulthood using indicators of well-being and ill-being. In addition, we examined the profiles’ invariance across age cohorts, their sociodemographic correlates, and validated them against clinical diagnoses of mental illnesses.
Methods. 
We used a sample of 44,528 participants aged 46 to 92 years from the baseline (Time 0) and first follow-up (Time 1) waves of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. Validated measures of well-being (life satisfaction and social support) and ill-being (depression and loneliness) served as the MH variables at T1. We conducted Latent Profile Analysis and assessed measurement invariance to identify distinct MH profiles and their stability across age cohorts. We then used multinomial logistic regression to examine sociodemographic correlates (T0) of the profiles and their relationships with clinical diagnoses of MH disorders.
Results. 
Five distinct, age-invariant profiles emerged, each characterized by different levels of well-being and ill-being. The most adaptive profiles accounted for over 80% of the sample across age groups. Among the clinical diagnoses, mood disorder showed the largest effect across profiles.
Discussion.
The results are consistent with Keyes' (2002) conceptualization of the DFM. Our findings underscore the importance of focusing on MH and highlight the protective role of well-being in the aging population.

articles.title: How the Paradoxical Timetable Cure (PTC) Fosters Post-Traumatic Growth and Self-Compassion Among Long-Term Grief Sufferers Following COVID-19 Bereavement
articles.authors: Mehrdad Etemadi; Mohammad Nabiei; Yoones Rajaei; Mohamad Reza Naeiji; Mahdieh Rahmanian; Erfan Abdollahi Chirani; Amirmahdi Amraei; Fatemeh Mirzai
articles.abstract:
Objective: The present study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of the Paradoxical Timetable Cure (PTC) on post-traumatic growth and self-compassion among long-term grief sufferers following COVID-19 bereavement.

Methods and Materials:  Employing a pre-test, post-test design with a control group, this study included a two-month follow-up period. Thirty individuals in Kermanshah, identified in 2023 as suffering from prolonged grief disorder (PGD) as per the Prolonged Grief Disorder Scale (PGD-13-R; Prigerson et al., 2021), were purposively selected based on specific criteria. Subsequently, they were randomly assigned into two equal groups: an experimental group receiving PTC and a control group with no intervention. Data were collected using the Post-Traumatic Growth Questionnaire (PTGQ; Tedeschi & Calhoun, 1996) and the Self-Compassion Scale (SCS; Neff et al., 2003). Statistical analysis was performed using univariate and multivariate analyses, along with repeated measures ANCOVA, in SPSS version 25.

Findings: The analysis revealed that the PTC significantly improved post-traumatic growth (P < 0.001, F = 7.40) and self-compassion (P < 0.001, F = 4.75) among participants coping with long-term grief following COVID-19 bereavement.

Conclusion: The study's findings indicate that PTC is effective in fostering post-traumatic growth and self-compassion among long-term grief sufferers after COVID-19 bereavement. The efficacy of PTC in enhancing these constructs suggests its value as a therapeutic approach for individuals experiencing prolonged grief due to the pandemic.

articles.title: Screening for paternal perinatal affective symptoms: Psychometric properties of the Perinatal Assessment of Paternal Affectivity (PAPA 2.0) in the Polish context
articles.authors: Grażyna Kmita; Diana Puzio; Eliza Kiepura-Nawrocka; Alicja Niedźwiecka; Karolina Waśkiewicz; Justyna Hermaniuk; Franco Baldoni; Francesca Agostini; Michele Giannotti
articles.abstract: Paternal perinatal mental health has been gaining considerable attention in contemporary scientific literature. Correlational and longitudinal associations have been established between paternal depressive and anxiety symptoms,  maternal mental health and child development. Yet, we still lack assessment instruments tailored to fathers’ specific affective symptom profile that could prompt early detection and intervention. The present study examined the psychometric properties of the Polish adaptation of the Perinatal Assessment of Paternal Affectivity questionnaire (PAPA version 2.0), which represents a further development of PAPA tool published in 2022. The prenatal assessment included 213 fathers in the third trimester of their partners’ pregnancy, while 72 fathers participated in the postnatal phase. Reliability, concurrent validity, factorial structure and associations between prenatal and postnatal scores were evaluated. PAPA 2.0  demonstrated high internal consistency before and after childbirth. Its total scores showed moderate-to-high positive correlations with depressive symptoms, perceived stress, global psychological distress and postnatal EPDS scores, indicating satisfactory concurrent validity. Exploratory factor analysis suggested a two-factor structure with one item - describing risky behaviors - showing poor item discrimination, which may point to the need for this item’s reformulation in future studies. Prenatal and postnatal PAPA scores were significantly associated, suggesting relative stability of paternal affective symptoms across the perinatal period. The study is limited by its convenience sample, high educational and urban bias as well as pandemic-related substantial postnatal attrition. Despite these limitations, the findings support PAPA 2.0 as a promising screening tool for identifying paternal perinatal affective symptoms in Polish fathers.

articles.title: Reframing Self-Perception: Efficacy of Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP) on Self-Disgust, Physical Appearance Perfectionism, and Self-Esteem in Girls with Anorexia Nervosa
articles.authors: Fatemeh Mirzai; Niloofar Nikbakht; Zahra Norouziani; Erfan Abdollahi Chirani; Farshid Fathy Karkaragh; Pardis Mazroei
articles.abstract:
Background: Anorexia nervosa (AN) presents unique psychological challenges, including deep-seated feelings of self-disgust, rigid physical appearance perfectionism, and diminished self-esteem. The aim of this study was to investigate the effectiveness of intensive short-term dynamic psychotherapy (ISTDP) on self-disgust, physical appearance perfectionism, and self-esteem in girls with AN.

Methods: This semi-experimental study used a pre-test, post-test, and follow-up design with a control group. The statistical population of the research included all girls with AN in Tehran, Iran, who had been referred to counselling centers and nutritionists in 2023. Forty of them aged 14 to 19 were selected using the convenience sampling method. Initially, 20 participants were selected for each group, but 3 participants from the control group were excluded due to absence of more than three sessions. The experimental group received 15 sessions of ISTDP, while the control group received no intervention. Data were collected through the use of the Overton et al. Self-Disgust Scale (SDS), Yang and Stoeber Physical Appearance Perfectionism Scale (PAPS), and Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES). Data were analyzed using univariate, multivariate, and repeated measures of covariance in SPSS software.

Results: ISTDP effectively reduced self-disgust (P = 0.001, F = 0.151) and physical appearance perfectionism (P = 0.001, F = 8.830), and enhanced self-esteem (P = 0.001, F = 52.388) in girls with AN.

Conclusion: ISTDP was able to reduce self-disgust and physical appearance perfectionism and increase self-esteem, and this change continued in the follow-up.

articles.title: Online Discourse is Falsely Polarized by Self-Selection
articles.authors: Will Schulz; Claire Elizabeth Robertson; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Ashwini Ashokkumar; Lisa Oswald; JungHwan Yang; Simon Munzert; Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Andrew Markus Guess
articles.abstract: We present comprehensive evidence quantifying the magnitude and scope of false polarization (i.e. the impression that opinions on political issues are more polarized than they actually are) on social media, driven by users' selective posting behavior. Using more than a decade of social media behavior connected to individual ideological attitudes in 1.7 million posts, a series of controlled experiments, and a large global survey covering 40 countries (total N = 49,222), we find that (1) strong ideologues post their opinions significantly more often than moderate individuals, and (2) extreme attitudes are posted more often than moderate attitudes. This general pattern replicates robustly across 40 countries, spanning diverse political cultures. Indeed, across studies we find extreme opinions are overrepresented on social media by at least 6% and up to 22% compared to their true prevalence in our samples. Furthermore, the opinions that users post are more hostile and toxic than the beliefs they keep to themselves.  These results were not explained by political interest or consistent left-right differences, suggesting that political extremity has an independent effect on social media behavior. Thus, most of the observed polarization of online discourse in recent years may be attributable to the systematic over-representation of pre-existing extreme political views, rather than the causal effects of platforms.

articles.title: There is No Good Reason to Not Follow-Up on an Intervention
articles.authors: John Protzko
articles.abstract: While experimental interventions are popular in the psychological sciences, we are not taking full advantage of them. In this paper, we show between 1/3 to ½ of interventions that could plausibly create long-term change in people simply conduct no follow-up after the intervention ended. The results attained p < .05, were written up, but no investigation of long-term effects were conducted. We highlight how long-term follow-up provides deeply valuable information not only about the intervention but about the underlying theory, regardless of the permanence of the intervention effects. We highlight how fadeout or persistence can inform feedback loops or the power of contextual effects. We provide information on how to practically conduct long-term follow-up after an intervention, and highlight unique problems to the intervention with long-term follow-up. Overall, we argue there is no good reason for not following-up on an intervention.

articles.title: BLM-Hum1800: A Human-Validated Benchmark for Linguistic Competence in English and French
articles.authors: Marion Bouffier; Giuseppe Samo; Chunyang Jiang; Vivi Nastase; Paola Merlo; Valentina Borghesani
articles.abstract:
Evaluating the fine-grained linguistic competence of Large Language Models (LLMs) requires diagnostic
benchmarks anchored by controlled syntactic paradigms and human behavioral baselines. Here, we
present a bilingual dataset comprising 1,800 human-validated linguistic problem instances across English
and French. Based on the Blackbird Language Matrices (BLM) framework, the dataset targets three core
grammatical phenomena (i.e., Subject-Verb Agreement, Change-of-State and Object Drop verb
alternations) across three levels of lexical variability (Types I, II, and III). In BLM-Hum1800, we provide
item-level behavioral data from 1,349 human participants, capturing selection accuracy, reaction times,
and click counts, alongside baseline evaluations from two modern LLMs tested across two distinct
reasoning configurations. BLM-Hum1800 serves as a standardized resource for evaluating syntactic rule
extraction and pattern generalization in artificial intelligence models, as well as for comparative
psycholinguistic and cognitive modeling in humans. All problem instances, raw and aggregated behavioral
data, anonymized participant demographics, and evaluation scripts are publicly available in an
open-access repository.

articles.title: Common and distinct effects of age and depression on cognitive effort-based decision-making
articles.authors: Mengzhe Wei; Jennifer Lee Crawford; Joset A. Etzel; Tammy English; Renee J Thompson; Todd Samuel Braver
articles.abstract: Cognitive control is central to decision-making and goal-directed behavior, but the mental effort it requires is often perceived as costly, especially in the context of aging. Although age-related differences in cognitive effort discounting have primarily been studied in healthy adults, major depressive disorder (MDD), which is associated with altered reward valuation, may modify these patterns. In this preregistered study, we examined whether age was differentially associated with cognitive effort discounting in adults with and without MDD (N=134, ages 35-74). We first estimated subjective value (SV), indexing cognitive effort costs, then assessed choices between options that varied in SV. Replicating prior work, SV declined as cognitive load increased, suggesting less willingness to engage in more effortful tasks. Age-related differences in this discounting pattern were only evident among individuals with MDD but not among healthy controls. Specifically, among individuals with MDD, older age was associated with lower SV at low loads, but a shallower decline in SV as difficulty increased. Across diagnostic groups, the positive association between task accuracy and SV weakened with older age. Finally, the relative SV of the more cognitively demanding task (compared to the less demanding task) predicted the willingness to engage with it. This association was also weakened with age across diagnostic groups, suggesting that as individuals get older, their decisions may be less guided by the SV difference between high- and low-effort options. Together, these findings showcase the combined and distinct effects of aging and MDD in altering the mechanisms of cognitive effort evaluation and decision-making.

articles.title: Framing Effects in Choices With Somewhat Risky Options
articles.authors: Prachiti Garge; Michael L DeKay
articles.abstract: When a certain option and a risky option are both described as potential gains, people typically choose the certain option; when the same two options are described as potential losses, people typically choose the risky option. This famous preference pattern is the risky-choice framing effect. Despite the seeming rarity of sure things and all-or-none risks in real life, surprisingly little research on this effect has involved options with intermediate levels of risk. In this research, we identified four types of “somewhat risky” options, combined them with each other and with certain and all-or-none options to create 15 risk comparisons in both gains and losses in each of four domains (cancer, drought, investment, and wildfire), and conducted two preregistered experiments in which we varied risk comparisons between or within participants in both student and online samples (N = 2,586 after exclusions). We found significant framing effects in almost all risk comparisons, greatly expanding the range of decisions in which framing is relevant. In addition, we assessed how well 12 versions of risky-choice theories accounted for participants’ choices. Across experiments and samples, versions of prospect theory (PT) and transfer-of-attention-exchange theory (TAX) generally outperformed versions of fuzzy-trace theory (FTT), the priority heuristic, and other accounts. PT’s and TAX’s performance was largely due to the S-shaped value function rather than the theories’ other mechanisms (e.g., PT’s loss aversion, TAX’s weight transfer). FTT’s performance was harmed by its failure to predict framing effects in choices between certain options and somewhat risky options without zero outcomes.

articles.title: Feasibility and clinical outcomes of a virtual psychotherapy platform for moderate to severe depression and anxiety: a pilot randomized controlled trial
articles.authors: Mindy Hong; David Yadush; Siddharth Suri; Madelyn Frumkin; Russell DuBois
articles.abstract: Mental health disorders are a leading contributor to global disability and are associated with reduced quality of life, increased morbidity and increased healthcare utilization. In recent years, technology-enabled virtual therapy platforms, which integrate multiple synchronous and asynchronous care components, have emerged as scalable approaches for expanding access to therapeutic support. However, randomized evidence supporting efficacy is limited. A pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted to examine feasibility, engagement and clinical outcomes of a virtual therapy platform (BetterHelp) versus a waitlist control group on adults with moderate-to-severe anxiety or depression. 86 participants (51.2% female, 72.1% White) were randomized to receive 12 weeks of virtual therapy or waitlist control. Patient-reported anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9), stress (PSS-10), sleep quality (JSS-4) and workplace productivity (WPAI-GH) outcomes were collected at baseline, 4 weeks and 12 weeks. Adjusted linear mixed effects models were conducted to evaluate the change in clinical outcomes over time. Engagement was measured through the number of individual and support group therapy sessions completed, number of worksheets completed, and number of messages exchanged with a therapist. At 12 weeks, 76.5% and 64.7% of the intervention group achieved MCID in anxiety and depression, respectively, compared to 48.5% and 43.8% of the control group. Among participants randomized to the virtual therapy group who engaged in individual or support group therapy (21/44, 47.7%), participants completed 3.4 therapy sessions, 2.4 worksheets, sent 41.7 messages to their therapists, and reported an Net Promoter Score (NPS) of 8.7. Virtual therapy participants had significantly lower GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores compared to the control group at both 4 (GAD-7: AMD: -1.9 [-3.7, -0.2], p = 0.03, g = -0.46; PHQ-9: AMD: -2.0 [-4.0,-0.01], p = 0.049, g = -0.43) and 12 weeks (GAD-7: AMD: -3.0 [-4.7, -1.3], p < 0.001, g = -0.72; PHQ-9: AMD: -2.4 [-4.3, -0.4], p = 0.02, g = -0.51). No significant differences in stress, sleep quality and workplace productivity outcomes were observed between groups. Although this pilot study lacks statistical power to draw definitive conclusions about treatment efficacy, findings suggest a multimodal approach combining therapist support across both synchronous and asynchronous modalities may help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression among adults with higher clinical severity.

articles.title: The Impact of Culture on the Processing of Spatial Frequencies during Recognition of Homogeneous Objects
articles.authors: Alex Cousineau; Francis Gingras; Émilie Désaulniers; Daniel Fiset; Caroline Blais
articles.abstract: Psychological research often relies on Western participant samples, neglecting global diversity and overlooking cultural influences on visual perception. Studies show that cultural upbringing affects how people process visual stimuli, with East Asians displaying broader attentional patterns and different eye movements compared to Westerners, leading to variations in spatial frequency (SF) processing during face recognition. This study examined whether these cultural differences in SF processing extend beyond faces to Greebles. Participants (50 East Asians and 83 Westerners) took part in an online study that used a data-driven SF sampling method to measure their SF tunings to Greebles. Results showed that East Asians relied more on lower SF, ranging from 2 to 4 cycles per object, than Westerners. These findings suggest that cultural differences in SF processing are not restricted to faces but may extend to other visually homogeneous object categories that share face-like structural properties.

articles.title: Transnational Activism and Civic Engagement among Burmese American Refugee Youth
articles.authors: Xiang Zhou; Phoebe Tu-Phi Pham; Mengxi Zhang; Jenni Thang
articles.abstract: Research on refugee youth has predominantly centered on challenges and deficits, often overlooking their resilience, contributions, and the positive roles they play in their new communities, including activism and civic engagement (ACE). This study addresses that gap by focusing on Burmese refugee youth, one of the largest resettled groups in the U.S. in recent history. Specifically, we examined four types of activities—protesting, donating, distributing information, and signing petitions—across three domains: ethnic/local (Burmese American causes), transnational (Myanmar causes), and general (other causes). The sample comprised 99 Burmese American adolescents from refugee backgrounds. Over half engaged in at least one ACE activity in the last six months. Transnational engagement was most common, followed by ethnic and general ACE. An explorative person-centered analysis revealed three profiles: moderately engaged (60%), transnationally engaged (11%), and highly engaged (20.7%). Results were discussed in the context of the global refugee crisis and the 2021 February 1 Myanmar coup d'état. These findings have important implications to expand the current conceptual model of activism and civic engagement among refugee and migrant youth.

articles.title: Beyond Seeing and Knowing: The Development of an Intuitive Theory of Attention
articles.authors: Rui Zhang; Marlene Berke; Julian Jara-Ettinger
articles.abstract:
Where someone looks, and for how long, is a remarkably rich signal about their mind. It reveals
what they find interesting, what they like, and what is new to them. These inferences are
possible because as adults, we understand that people don’t just encode whatever is visible to
them. This is instead modulated by what they choose to attend to, and for how long. Across
four experiments (N = 220), we asked whether children understand these nuances. We found
that unlike adults, children showed only partial expectations about what draws attention,
expecting longer looking for larger sets by age six, but not for more complex or more varied
objects (Exp. 1). However, children as young as five understood that an agent who looked
longer formed a more accurate representation of what they saw (Exp. 2), and that they are more
likely to look longer at things they find desirable (Exp. 3). Finally, six-year-olds, but not five-
year-olds, inferred that agents who already know about a toy are less likely to look for an
extended duration (Exp. 4). Together, these results suggest that an intuitive theory of attention
is partly in place by age five and continues to develop past age six.

articles.title: Statistical Assessment of a Synastry Algorithm for Personal Relationships and High-Performance Dyads: A Blind Replication Study
articles.authors: Phillip Thompson
articles.abstract: Carl Jung and many others have attempted to validate astrology with the scientific method. This research used an algorithm based on the ancient process of synastry to examine the combined birth charts for pairs of people and to calculate a number that measures astrological compatibility, the Starscore. The average Starscore for participant-blind Prolific and CloudResearch survey respondents who provided the birthdate and location for themselves and their closest relationship was statistically higher than the average for one million random Starscores with small effect sizes. In addition, the Starscore for champion pairs in artistic swimming, figure skating, doubles tennis and for winners and runners-up of The Amazing Race were significantly different from the random group. False discovery rate and family-wise error rate analyses supported the statistical significance of the close relationship surveys. While not proof of causation, these correlations support Jung’s theory that the positions of the planets in our solar system could be related to the development of human life, and they support Jung’s belief that studying astrology may contribute to our understanding of human behavior. If independent researchers replicate these findings, the resulting evidence could provide a stronger empirical basis for evaluating astrology’s potential relevance to psychology.

articles.title: A Bayesian Model of Sequential Collaboration: Understanding Dependent Numerical Judgments Through Expertise and Social Influence
articles.authors: Maren Mayer
articles.abstract: The wisdom-of-crowds phenomenon demonstrates that aggregating judgments across multiple individuals can produce remarkably accurate estimates. However, research has shown that dependent judgments in sequential collaboration, where contributors revise or maintain previous judgments, can equal or outperform traditional aggregation methods based on independent judgments. Recently, a computational model of sequential collaboration has been proposed, but its assumptions and predictions could only be tested qualitatively. To address this limitation, a Bayesian model of sequential collaboration was developed that relies on the same cognitive processes and allows model parameters to be estimated directly from observed judgments and decisions. Simulation studies demonstrated accurate parameter recovery across a wide range of sample sizes and item sets. Applying the model to four empirical datasets showed that estimated parameters aligned with empirical findings for sequential collaboration. Model comparisons further revealed that accounting for response biases substantially improved model fit in homogeneous estimation tasks, whereas other model variations received no support. These findings extend the theoretical framework of sequential collaboration by enabling quantitative testing of cognitive mechanisms underlying dependent judgments. More broadly, the model integrates ideas from wisdom-of-crowds research, cultural consensus theory, anchoring, and group decision making, providing a foundation for future research on collective judgment and social influence.

articles.title: Tailoring relative phase estimation methods to movement shape. A practical approach to estimate the Arnold tongue with testing codes on human data and simulation of discrete and continuous signals.
articles.authors: Martin Le Guennec; julien lagarde
articles.abstract: The relative phase ϕis a key variable in the study of coordination dynamics across many disciplines. Several estimation methods exist and are used interchangeably in the study of sensorimotor synchronization, despite the limitations of certain methods when analyzing inharmonic (aka discrete) movements. In this study, we document differences in estimates of key variables used to describe coordination dynamics, the mean ϕand its standard deviation, calculated using a pointwise method and using the Hilbert transform with signal centering or with a correction of the non-linearity. We applied these methods to experimental data from a tapping task with an incremental increase in metronome frequency. The increase in frequency allowed us to observe differences between methods in inharmonic movements at low synchronization frequencies and in near-sinusoidal movements at higher frequencies. To complement this analysis, we conducted stochastic numerical simulations of non-linear oscillators and with ghost attractors to mimic signals from discrete movements. We compared the mean and SD ϕestimates to a gold standard based on the Arnold tongues framework. Our experimental and simulation results show that the mean and SD ϕestimates obtained from the Hilbert transform are biased for inharmonic signals, we recommend using the pointwise method in this context. With near-sinusoidal signals, both methods provide equivalent results. We propose a practical approach to estimate the quality of synchronization, sharing free testing codes, human data and simulation of discrete or continuous movements.

articles.title: Generative AI Use in Entrepreneurship: An Integrative Review and an Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
articles.authors: Jackson G. Lu; Gerui Gloria Zhao; Anna Zheng
articles.abstract: Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to understand how GenAI can both empower and entrap entrepreneurs, highlighting GenAI’s role as a double-edged sword at each stage of the entrepreneurial process. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality but introduce hallucinations and training data biases; boost entrepreneurial self-efficacy but heighten entrepreneurial overconfidence; increase functional breadth but decrease relational embeddedness; and boost productivity but fuel “workslop” and erode critical thinking, learning, and memory. Moreover, we identify core features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. We also explore boundary conditions (e.g., entrepreneurs’ metacognition, domain expertise, and entrepreneurial experience) that shape the magnitude of these effects. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework offer practical implications for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically throughout the entrepreneurial process while managing its risks.

articles.title: Effects of diagnostic labelling on self-reported depression symptoms: A randomized controlled experimental study
articles.authors: Michael P. Hengartner; Lorenz A. Juen
articles.abstract:
Background: Psychiatric diagnostic labels alter how people interpret common emotional distress, but it is unclear if psychiatric labelling increases reporting of depression symptoms. 
Methods: University students (n=260) recruited during the stressful exams period completed the PHQ-8, a popular depression rating scale, and were then randomized 1:1 to labelling intervention (automated feedback indicating increased depression scores plus definition of depression) or control group (no feedback; only definition of mental wellbeing). Both groups then completed the PHQ-8 a second time and convenience subsample (n=131) also a third time 24 hours later, in addition to a brief measure of individual depression concepts assessing whether people differentiate between depression episodes and acute stress reactions (stringent concept) or not (expanded concept). 
Results: PHQ-8 baseline scores indicated at least mild depression in three-fourths and moderate-to-severe depression in one-third of the sample. Depression labelling, relative to control condition, caused reductions in PHQ-8 scores. Independent of the labelling intervention, expanded depression concepts were associated with more stable PHQ-8 scores and stringent depression concepts with marked reductions.
Conclusion: Contrary to our hypothesis, imposing a depression label on people experiencing acute stress did not increase depression scores. Instead, we found that labelling was associated with reductions in depression scores, as were stringent depression concepts. This suggests that people with initially inflated depression scores who perceive depression as conceptually different to acute stress reactions tend to adjust their scores on a depression rating scale. Further research into the expansiveness of depression concepts and the reporting of symptoms is required to verify this interpretation.

articles.title: Measurement Reliability, Construct Validity, and Transparent Reporting in Original and Replication Psychological Research
articles.authors: Cas Goos; Marjan Bakker; Jelte M. Wicherts; Michele B. Nuijten
articles.abstract: While published (replication) studies using measures to assess psychological phenomena need to transparently report information on measurement procedures, validity, and reliability to allow verification and use in future (replication) research, earlier results highlighted common poor reporting of psychological measurement. Here, we investigated the measurement reporting in a sample of 77 measures within 56 Many Labs replications and related original articles (Ebersole et al., 2016, 2020; Klein et al., 2014, 2018) and found that the information relevant for reusing measures was reported in full in around half the replication measures, and only 5.2% in the original studies. We also observed that only around a third of multiple-item measures in original studies and 11.4% in replications reported reliability coefficients, with comparable proportions for reporting any convergent, discrimant, predictive, or factorial validity evidence. We performed checks of the reliability and unidimensionality of multiple-item measures using the openly available Many Labs item response data. We observed that the reliability and unidimensionality of the measures was rarely stable across labs. These results corroborate existing findings that measurement reporting in published research lacks transparency, and that poor measurement reporting often obscure insufficient reliability and validity. We offer suggestions on how to improve measurement reporting practices and increase the use of validated measures.

articles.title: Biopsychosocial Moderators of Links between Maternal Depressive and Anxiety Symptoms during Pregnancy and Child Socioemotional Outcomes: A Multi-Cohort Study
articles.authors: Annaleena Holopainen; Jana Runze; Luisa Bergunde; Jasminka Štefulj; Gabija Jarašiūnaite-Fedosejeva; Alexia Karain; Jonathan Handelzalts; Danny Horesh; Bea Van den Bergh; Mary Carmen Hernández Martínez
articles.abstract:
Background
Prenatal exposure to maternal depressive and anxiety symptoms may have lasting effects, such as increased internalizing and externalizing behavior during childhood. However, not all children are equally affected. The Multidimensional Conceptualization of Prenatal Influences on Psychological and Health Outcomes Across the Lifespan Framework highlights biopsychosocial factors that may moderate this association and require further investigation. 

Methods
This study combined data from four European cohorts (N = 7,597) to examine biopsychosocial factors – child sex, mode of birth, subjective birth experience, child temperament, social support, and parity – as potential moderators of the associations between maternal prepartum depressive or anxiety symptoms and child internalizing or externalizing behavior at 3-5 years of age. 

Results
Higher prepartum depressive symptoms were associated with higher child internalizing and externalizing behavior, while higher trait and state anxiety symptoms were associated with higher externalizing behavior only. Associations between state anxiety symptoms and both internalizing and externalizing behavior were stronger for first-born children, while findings regarding the moderating role of mode of birth were inconsistent. Child sex, subjective birth experience, child temperament, and social support were not significant moderators.

Conclusions
Prepartum depression and anxiety presage emotional and behavioral difficulties perceived in the child, in particular externalizing problems. Mode of birth and birth order emerged as moderators of these associations. Yet, as most candidate moderators were not empirically supported, they may operate through pathways other than modifying susceptibility to prenatal maternal distress.

articles.title: Future Anxiety Affects Youth’s Democratic Support and Engagement
articles.authors: Olaf Borghi; Katharina Lawall; Kaat Smets; Manos Tsakiris
articles.abstract: Many of today’s young people are anxious about the future. Yet the consequences of their anxiety on democratic support and engagement remain underexplored. In this preregistered survey experiment we tested the causal effects of future anxiety on youth’s democratic attitudes. We exposed young people (N = 1,895; ages 16–26) to social media posts about the cost of living which were manipulated to induce future anxiety, reduce it through hope, or serve as a control. Increasing their future anxiety (vs. hope) resulted in a small but precisely estimated decrease in democratic support (−2.5 percentage points; 95% CI [−4.3, −0.8]), but without any effects on a behavioural candidate-choice task or on self-reported willingness to participate in politics. Conversely, hope (vs. control and anxiety) increased young people’s likelihood to seek information on how to get democratically involved (+6.9 percentage points; 95% CI [1.7, 12.0]). These findings provide experimental evidence that future-oriented feelings shape youth’s democratic support amidst multiple crises.

articles.title: Low-Level Visual and Auditory Features Predict Preferences of Commercials
articles.authors: Valentina Parada; Inbal Gur Arie; Levy Dino
articles.abstract: Video content has become a dominant form of digital marketing, increasing the need to understand which features make videos more appealing and effective. Prior studies showed that low-level visual features in static images affect saliency and consumer preferences, while low-level auditory features influence preferences for music clips. However, it remains unclear how these features and their interaction shape preferences for dynamic stimuli such as video commercials. In this study, 165 participants watched 100 video commercials and rated how much they liked each commercial and their willingness to pay (WTP) for the advertised product. We extracted low-level visual and auditory features from the commercials (e.g., colorfulness, scene frequency, loudness, zero-crossing rate) and used them as inputs to linear and non-linear prediction models. Both visual and auditory low-level features significantly predicted liking and WTP, with the combined model performing best. Importantly, these low-level features also predicted the aggregate engagement metrics at the population level as measured on YouTube, demonstrating the generalizability of our findings and their external validity. These findings show that low-level sensory information influences consumer preferences and ad effectiveness and demonstrate how computational tools can be used to evaluate video effectiveness.

articles.title: Revisiting Singularity and Compassion Fade: Replication and extensions of Experiments 1a and 3 in Västfjäll et al. (2014)
articles.authors: Lewend Mayiwar; Shubin Yu; Yooeun Jeong; Richard Rekdal; Tuan Viet; Ihor Rudko; Matilda Dorotic; Gilad Feldman
articles.abstract: Västfjäll et al. (2014) found support for “compassion fade”, that affective reactions and charitable donations decrease as the number of victims increases. In a pre-registered experiment with a U.S. sample recruited through CloudResearch Connect (N = 1207), we conducted a replication and extension of Studies 1a and 3 from Västfjäll et al. (2014). In the replication of Study 1a, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims (one vs. two children) on hypothetical donation amount, positive- or negative affect, perceived impact of donations (all |d|s ≤ 0.16) or for any mediation effects. In the replication of Study 3, we found no support for the impact of the number of victims or relatedness on donation amount, perceived need, positive affect, or negative affect of donations (all ηp2 ≤ 0.012). Bayesian analyses indicated moderate to strong evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for most effects, and equivalence testing indicated that seven of eight effects were smaller than our conservative smallest effect size of interest. Overall, our findings fail to replicate the original compassion fade effects and suggest limitations on their generalizability across various dependent measures and contexts. Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A2TGB

articles.title: Lexical and affective organizers of (novel) meaning
articles.authors: Celia Martínez Tomás; Fritz Guenther; Daniele Gatti; José Antonio Hinojosa
articles.abstract: Novel (or pseudo-) words lack stored lexical representations and thus are (often) assumed to be semantically empty. Although, challenging this idea, recent studies showed that novel words can evoke semantic and affective responses, these findings do not directly reveal the semantic content that speakers attribute to these unfamiliar forms. We tested this by asking participants to generate open-ended definitions for real and novel valenced words. Definitions were represented via sentence embeddings and examined through consensus, representational similarity and content decoding analyses. Definitions independently generated for the same pseudoword were more semantically similar than definitions generated for different pseudowords, demonstrating cross-speaker convergence in attributed meaning. Participants who produced better-fitting definitions for real words also tended to do so for pseudowords, indicating cross-domain individual differences in semantic-definition behavior. Valence was recoverable from definition embeddings for both real words and pseudowords, and it consistently organized the semantic geometry of pseudoword definitions across four different embedding models. Together, these findings show that unfamiliar word forms constrain the meanings generated by different speakers in systematic and (partly) shared ways, drawing on semantic and affective knowledge also involved in familiar-word processing. Theoretically, this work has implications for theories of language learning by demonstrating that novel meaning acquisition is a structured process driven by general semantic competence, rather than arbitrary association. It also challenges embodied views of language by showing that abstract emotional knowledge (rather than transient affective states) serves as a primary organizing geometry for processing unfamiliar linguistic stimuli.

articles.title: Vibe shift or partisanship: Unequal changes between and within American political groups’ perception of misinformation and its solutions after the 2024 US Election
articles.authors: Tobia Spampatti; Laura K. Globig; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract: Citizens across the globe are torn between addressing misinformation versus guaranteeing individual freedom of expression. Democratic elections provide a chance for not only selecting among competing policies, but also for shifting societal norms about societal issues. The 2024 US Presidential election was heralded as a “vibe shift” with public support swinging away from content moderation and towards freedom of speech. However, the shift in societal norms may have been illusory and Americans may have remained highly polarized along partisan lines. In this preregistered study with data collected before and after the 2024 Presidential Elections (N = 1,377 representative US sample), we tested how electoral results, interpreted according to partisan identity, changed attitudes towards misinformation and censorship, perceived prevalence of misinformation, and support for approaches to curtail misinformation (i.e., digital content moderation) over protecting freedom of expression. Post-election, Americans worried more about misinformation, misinformation spreaders, and censorship. Supporting a partisanship hypothesis, Americans identifying as Democrats worried more about misinformation and spreaders of misinformation than Republicans post-election. Exploratory analyses suggest that, post-election, Democrats supported content moderation strategies even more after the election of Donald Trump while lean Republicans became more likely to choose to protect free speech, whereas strong Republicans were relatively more likely to prefer preventing misinformation from spreading. These results suggest that people’s perception of misinformation and censorship changed after the election, and these perceptions were determined by partisanship rather than reflecting a broader societal shift in social norms.

articles.title: When Democracy Is Worth the Effort: Seeing the Other Side as Willing Strengthens Pro-Democratic Motivation
articles.authors: Olaf Borghi; Manos Tsakiris; Mariana Von Mohr
articles.abstract: Democracy takes effort, and these efforts do not always benefit one’s own political side. Across two preregistered studies (total N = 916), we used computational modeling of effortful behavior to measure US partisans’ motivation to strengthen democratic engagement in rural (traditionally Republican-leaning), urban (traditionally Democratic-leaning), or all US areas. Study 1 showed that participants were generally willing to make pro-democratic efforts, but less so when efforts benefited out-group areas, particularly among more affectively polarized participants. We hypothesized that this asymmetry is sustained by misperceptions about out-partisans’ willingness to engage in cross-partisan pro-democratic efforts. Study 2 showed that most participants (87%) underestimated out-party effort willingness. Importantly, correcting this misperception increased motivation to support out-group areas without significantly reducing in-group motivation. These findings suggest that cross-partisan pro-democratic motivation is common but partly obscured by misperceptions about out-partisans’ willingness, and that making this willingness visible might help sustain the collective effort democracy depends on.

articles.title: Virtual Empathy Scale (VES): Development and Psychometric Validation Among Indian Young Adults
articles.authors: Aishu S Gowda; Akash Nethravathi Raju; Dhiksha J
articles.abstract:
This research was targeted at constructing and testing the virtual empathy scale (VES) that is intended to assess the empathy that is realized in the online communication between young college-going adults. It is based on multidimensional empathy models and is composed of three: empathic expression, cognitive empathy, and affective empathy. There was a generation of a pool of 49 items, and it underwent the face and content validity examination by experts reducing the pool to 41 items. Then we performed EFA on a sample of 421 college going students. This gave a 32-item scale, and good factor loading. We subsequently applied CFA to another sample of 331 students, and this supported the three-factor model, with reasonable fit statistics (CFI= .90, TLI=.899, RMSEA=.061). To conduct the reliability analysis, it was demonstrated that the results had high internal consistency (α > 0.87, ω > 0.87) in all three factors. The scale demonstrated convergent validity as demonstrated in high factor loading and composite reliability, however, the average variance extracted was a little below the optimal thresholds. And lastly, discriminant validity with some factor correlation approaching upper limits was determined with the use of HTMT. This scale has demonstrated high psychometric characteristics and is a potentially useful instrument to measure empathy in digital communication and can be used in a variety of psychological studies, online learning, and digital wellbeing intervention.
Keywords: virtual empathy, digital communication, psychometric validation, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, young adults.

articles.title: Interpreting FMS and SSQ Cybersickness Ratings via User Tolerance in Virtual Reality
articles.authors: Jonathan Kelly; Michael Dorneich; Stephen Gilbert
articles.abstract: Cybersickness remains a persistent challenge limiting the usability of virtual reality (VR), yet commonly used subjective measures such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) and the Fast Motion Sickness (FMS) scale are often difficult to interpret in terms of user outcomes. In particular, there is limited guidance on how specific values on these scales relate to user tolerance or the likelihood that users will discontinue a VR experience due to discomfort. This work addresses this gap by calibrating cybersickness severity interpretations against early termination of a VR experience. In Study 1 (N = 183), participants played an immersive VR game for up to 20 minutes and were free to terminate the experience at any time. Using a Behavioral Risk Banding (BRB) framework, logistic regression linked a modified 0-10 version of the FMS (FMS-10) and post-exposure SSQ scores to dropout probability, yielding behaviorally grounded risk severity bands (mild, moderate, severe, extreme). Survival analyses then showed how these bands mapped onto tolerance over time, revealing a transitional region marked by heightened individual variability. Study 2 (N = 304) evaluated the robustness of these categories across variation in VR content and mitigation context by applying the Study 1 thresholds without re-estimation. Although absolute dropout risk varied, the ordering and behavioral meaning of severity categories were preserved. Together, these results provide a practical, behaviorally grounded framework for interpreting cybersickness ratings in terms of user tolerance and usability across VR contexts.

articles.title: The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts
articles.authors: Milena Philomena Maria Musial; Sam Hall-McMaster; Kanji Shimomura; Ayaka Kato; Erik Lukas Bode; Clarissa Grundmann; Claudia Ebrahimi; Kenji Morita; Samuel J. Gershman; Tanja Endrass
articles.abstract: The successor representation (SR) is a learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (n=260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (n=260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant, particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy and instead more on model-free control in alcohol-related contexts. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.

articles.title: Language preference of adults with lived experience of ADHD: a cross-country study
articles.authors: Joske Rijmen; Oana Denisa Mateut; Erica Fongaro; Madeleine Groom; Diane Purper-Ouakil; Jan R. Wiersema; Blandine French
articles.abstract:
Terminology used to describe neurodevelopmental conditions is increasingly contested, reflecting tensions between medical and neurodiversity-informed frameworks. While a growing body of research has examined terminology preferences within autism, comparable empirical work focusing specifically on Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) remains notably limited. We examined ADHD-related language preferences among adults with lived experience across three languages and four countries. 
An online cross-sectional survey was completed by 2,340 adults with lived experience of ADHD: 359 English-speaking (United Kingdom), 1,749 French-speaking (France), and 232 Dutch-speaking (Belgium and the Netherlands). Linear mixed-effects models were used to test the effects of term, spoken language, and their interaction, with participant as a random intercept. 
Preferences varied by spoken language. English- and Dutch-speaking participants favoured neurodiversity-aligned terms (e.g., “neurodivergent person”, “brain difference”, “traits”), whereas French-speaking participants more strongly endorsed medicalised descriptors (e.g., “person with ADHD”, “disorder”, “symptoms”). However, explicitly deficit-oriented terms (e.g., “abnormal”, “deficits”) were broadly opposed across spoken languages. 
There is no cross-language consensus on ADHD terminology and even within one language preferences vary substantially. These findings caution against the use of universal, prescriptive guidance and underscore the need for culturally and linguistically sensitive language in research, clinical, and policy contexts.

articles.title: How does familiarity impact the computational processes that support face recognition?
articles.authors: Fournier Raphaël; Paul Downing; Richard Ramsey
articles.abstract: Recognising a familiar face is a fundamental social cognitive ability, yet the computational mechanisms that underlie this capacity remain poorly understood. Prior research has established that familiarity affects face recognition performance, but has relied primarily on manifest measures — accuracy and response time — that cannot distinguish between qualitatively different sources of performance change. Here, we used evidence accumulation modelling across a series of experiments to ask not merely whether familiarity affects face recognition, but how — specifically, which latent computational processes are modulated. Experiments 1 and 2 examined visual familiarity (briefly learned faces versus novel faces) and Experiments 3, 4 and 5 examined person knowledge (famous versus novel faces). Fitting linear ballistic accumulator models to recognition data revealed a consistent computational signature across experiments: novel faces produced substantially higher drift rates than familiar faces, accompanied by a smaller but reliable increase in response caution. The dominance of the drift rate effect localises familiarity’s primary influence to the quality of evidence accumulation — how cleanly the perceptual system extracts decision-relevant information — rather than to response bias. We interpret thes findings as reflecting a novelty pop-out effect combined with unstable memory traces for familiar faces. These findings demonstrate that computational modelling reveals dissociable mechanisms underlying face recognition that are invisible to manifest measures alone, and provide a foundation for understanding how familiarity shapes the decision processes that support social perception.

articles.title: Working with Lived-Experience Advisory Groups to Advance Equity in Health Psychology Research in the Netherlands and Flanders
articles.authors: Nadine van der Waal; Maité Van Alboom; Maya Braun; Klaske Tiemstra; Thomas Gültzow; Meeke Hoedjes; Gera Nagelhout; maya schroevers; Laurens van Gestel; Dimitri Van Ryckeghem
articles.abstract:
Persistent health disparities, rooted in unequal distributions of power, resources and opportunities, emphasize the urgent need for more inclusive research practices in health psychology. This paper presents citizen advisory groups, composed of individuals with lived experience of health inequities, as a feasible approach to foster such practices. Citizen advisory groups provide researchers with insight into the lived experience of these individuals, facilitating research that is aligned with their context and needs. Compared to full-scale participatory research, these groups require relatively modest resources while still enabling meaningful community engagement.
In the Netherlands and Flanders, citizen advisory groups have gained traction in recent years. Drawing on experiences from existing groups, literature, and researchers’ input from conference roundtables, this paper aims to disseminate experiences with, and lessons learned from working with advisory groups. Thereby, this paper contributes to researchers’ knowledge about the use and implementation of advisory groups. This helps to support researchers in assessing whether a citizen advisory group is suitable for their work, aiming to lower the barriers to start one. 
This paper covers how citizen advisory groups may overcome researchers’ barriers to inclusive research, the value of advisory groups across different phases of the research process, and how to overcome challenges in the implementation and sustainability of citizen advisory groups. Ultimately, the paper presents citizen advisory groups as a concrete step towards more inclusive research practices in health psychology.

articles.title: Neuroplasticity in Adolescents: The role of sleep, resilience and continuous connectivity.
articles.authors: Maanya Sharma; Ananta Ganjoo; Gaurangi Khetwal
articles.abstract: Neuroplasticity refers to the brain’s inherent capacity to reorganise its structure and function in response to experience, learning, and stress across the lifespan. Psychological resilience, in turn, reflects an individual’s ability to adapt, cope, and maintain functional stability in the face of adversity. Research increasingly suggests that these processes are not independent; rather, they are deeply interwoven and sensitive to disruptions in basic biological systems such as sleep. This paper therefore explores the relationship among sleep deprivation, neuroplasticity, psychological resilience, and cognitive decision-making during adolescence. It examines how the highly susceptible and adaptable adolescent brain responds to environmental influences, particularly sleep patterns and continuous digital connectivity. The paper explores the biological mechanisms underlying neuroplasticity and how these processes support learning, emotional regulation, and adaptive functioning. It also considers how sleep contributes to synaptic reorganisation, memory consolidation, and overall brain efficiency during a critical development period. Furthermore, researchers examine how modern lifestyle factors, including increased screen exposure, may interact with sleep and neural development. The research integrates psychological and neurobiological perspectives to provide an understanding of adolescent brain function. Ultimately, it aims to highlight the importance of sleep and balanced environmental engagement in supporting healthy cognitive and developmental outcomes.

articles.title: FEEDBACK Faces: An Image Data Base With Communicative Facial Expressions of Appreciation and Criticism
articles.authors: Ronja Ochs; Elisabeth Prestele; Christine Altstötter-Gleich; Ulrike Basten
articles.abstract: Facial expressions of appreciation and criticism play an important role for positive and negative reinforcement in social communication. Existing databases of face stimuli for experimental research, however, mainly cover basic emotions and lack specific expressions of positive and negative reinforcement. The aim of the current study was to develop an image database of communicative facial expressions of appreciation and criticism (FEEDBACK Faces) that can be used for experimental research on social reinforcement. In a first step, to generate new photo stimuli, we took pictures of appreciative, critical, and neutral facial expressions from 30 models using three different instruction techniques (imagination of predefined scenarios, recall of personal experiences, and imitation of prototypical expressions). In a second step, we conducted a validation study in which 33 participants rated the extent to which they recognized appreciation vs. criticism in the photographed expressions. Based on the ratings, we selected two separate sets of stimuli for the final database: (A) The set FEEDBACK-AC contains unambiguous expressions with correct identification rates of 88.21% for appreciation, 97.30% for criticism, and 92.76% for neutral expressions (54 images of 18 models, 9 female, 9 male). (B) The set FEEDBACK-AC-Ambiguous contains particularly ambiguous expressions that allow for interpretation as either appreciation or criticism and are intended for research on interpretation biases (16 images of 16 models, 8 female, 8 male). The stimuli can be used for a wide range of applications in behavior research and are freely available for scientific purposes (find link to database website in project repository https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20284150).

articles.title: Growing up in an Age of Economic Inequality: A Social-Cognitive Developmental Framework
articles.authors: Eddie Brummelman; Katherine McAuliffe; Jamie Amemiya
articles.abstract: Economic inequality has reached extreme levels worldwide, and children will bear its burden. How do children perceive and explain economic inequality? And how do these perceptions and explanations, in turn, shape their development? We address these questions by proposing an integrative social-cognitive developmental framework. According to the framework, when children enter a new context, they consider a series of questions: (1) Is there inequality? (2) What causes inequality? (3) What does inequality say about me? (4) What does inequality say about us? (5) And do I address inequality? We suggest that children’s perceptions and explanations of economic inequality—above and beyond exposure to the inequality in itself—have profound consequences for mental health, social relationships, motivation, and egalitarianism (e.g., whether children rectify or perpetuate inequality). Children’s perceptions and explanations, then, might serve as levers for intervention to help children navigate the current age of inequality.

articles.title: When the self makes things look clearer: Self-association biases perceptual evaluation rather than sensory processing
articles.authors: Xueyan Jiang; Ruizhe Zhang; Zhiqiang Luo; Hu Chuan-Peng; Chuyao Yan
articles.abstract: Self-associated information receives privileged access during perceptual processing, but does this priority alter perception itself or how perceptual evidence is interpreted and evaluated? Across seven experiments (N = 302), we tested this question using perceived stimulus clarity as a direct measure of subjective visual experience while systematically manipulating physical stimulus clarity. Using reconstruction and two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) tasks, we first found that self-associated stimuli were consistently perceived as clearer than other-associated stimuli across different levels of physical clarity. However, this subjective clarity advantage reflected a shift in clarity criterion, as self-associated stimuli were more likely to be judged as clear despite showing no improvement in the ability to discriminate physical clarity differences. Beyond clarity judgments, we further examined subjective confidence and found that self-association increased confidence when sensory evidence was ambiguous. However, when perceptual performance was assessed using an objective visual feature, orientation, no self-associated advantage was observed in orientation estimation or discrimination. Finally, hierarchical Bayesian observer modeling provided evidence that the self-associated bias arose from later decision processes rather than changes in sensory evidence. Together, these findings demonstrate that self-association does not enhance sensory representations but instead modulates the evaluation of perceptual evidence, biasing subjective judgments such that self-associated stimuli appear clearer without greater perceptual sensitivity.

articles.title: A cross-linguistic, multi-construct survey for assessing children's beliefs about learning experiences and environments
articles.authors: Lijin Zhang; Amy Lightbody; Robert Zane Sparks; Mika Braginsky; Nichola Jenkins; Daniel Ansari; Maria Camila Perfetti; Julián P. Mariño; Luise Hornoff; Manuel Bohn
articles.abstract: Children's beliefs about their learning experiences and environments play a central role in shaping academic engagement, motivation, and developmental trajectories. Constructs such as academic perception, belonging, and growth mindset are widely studied in developmental and educational research, yet most measures have been developed and validated within limited cultural and linguistic contexts. This raises concerns about whether these instruments capture the same constructs across diverse settings. The present study introduces a cross-linguistic, multi-construct survey for children aged 5-12 years across multiple international sites. The instrument is designed to assess learning-related attitudes across five key constructs: academic perception, belonging, growth mindset, peer relationships, and teacher-student relationships. Using data from three sites in Canada, Colombia, and Germany, we evaluated the reliability and validity of these survey tools. The scales demonstrated good reliability, structural validity, and discriminant validity. The measurement structure was largely invariant across sites, with only a small number of parameters showing noninvariance that did not substantially affect factor score estimation. We further examined relationships among constructs and how these associations vary with age. These findings support the use of the survey instrument to capture developmental and contextual variation in children's attitudes toward learning.

articles.title: Bounded rationality and human development
articles.authors: Samuel David Jones
articles.abstract: Although multi-scale, multi-directional feedback between genes, brain, cognition, and behaviour is the cornerstone of well-evidenced interactionist models of human development (e.g., Gottlieb, 2007), contemporary theories of neurodevelopmental variation and disorder characteristically describe only unidirectional cascades across this hierarchy. To complement this view, I present a new theory of the cognitive and behavioural origins of individual differences in human development. This account is grounded in the ideas of restricted search and satisficing that are central to the bounded rationality paradigm (Simon, 1955, 1956, 1990), and which set this account apart from claims that agents optimise utility functions or maximise their learning. I outline a simple model of adaptive restricted search and satisficing that incorporates reciprocal influences on development and learning, and integrate a broad contemporary empirical literature in support of this model. This work motivates the novel position that adaptive restricted search and satisficing not only amplify neurodevelopmental differences beyond their primary neurogenetic origins (explaining developmental multifinality) but also provide a route by which disparate primary causal processes are anchored to common phenotypes (explaining developmental equifinality). While the primary focus of this paper is on early developmental variation and conditions of clinical significance, I argue that bounded rationality offers a general paradigm through which to understand the emergence of individual differences across the lifespan, from delay, to psychopathology, to expertise. The recommendation of this report is that cognitive and behavioural feedback – specifically bounded rational choice – should be embedded more widely into causal process models of the origins of individual differences in human development.

articles.title: “Suicide is cringe!”: Content analysis of 46,071 mental health videos from adolescents’ TikTok feeds
articles.authors: Rebecca Godard; Amber van der Wal; Ine Beyens
articles.abstract: This manuscript presents a content analysis of 46,071 mental health videos viewed by adolescents over a span of five years. The most frequently-discussed topics included mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g., autism, ADHD, depression), mental health symptoms and experiences (e.g., anxiety and depressive symptoms, trauma), positive aspects of mental health (e.g., recovery, coping, healing), and mentla health treatment (e.g., therapy, inpatient treatment, medication). Videos were primarily personal stories and often contained humorous elements and supportive messages. Yet areas of concern, such as videos that encourage harmful behaviour (e.g., suicide, self-harm, disordered eating) and false of misleading claims of expertise from video creators, also emerged.  Findings highlight the need for a nuanced approach to studying mental health content and its impacts on adolescents, with the aim of empowering youth to harness the potential benefits of this content while minimizing its potential harms.

articles.title: The Deservingness Mismatch and Political Discontent
articles.authors: Troels Siegumfeldt Bøggild; Michael Bang Petersen
articles.abstract: Political discontent is high across many Western democracies, with ramifications for regime stability and social cohesion. We argue that discontent—proxied by political distrust, dissatisfaction with democracy, populism, powerlessness, and low efficacy— reflects a deservingness mismatch: the gap between which groups citizens believe should receive help and their perceptions of who actually does. Using observational and experimental survey data from the United States and Denmark (total N = 4,892), we present three findings. First, citizens experience substantial mismatches, and these predict all five indicators of discontent. Second, citizens prefer that most groups receive more help, implying that correcting the mismatch would require expanding help across many groups simultaneously—a politically and fiscally daunting task. Third, the mismatch operates over and above political ideology and personal group identification, suggesting the existence of a broadly shared moral disenfranchisement with contemporary society. We reconceptualize political discontent as a wicked problem rooted in deep-seated psychological intuitions with strong inertia due to practical and political barriers in aligning politics with citizens’ moral expectations.

articles.title: Reconciling principles of cortical organisation: A historical review of areas and gradients
articles.authors: Casey Paquola; Simon Eickhoff; Matthias Kirschner; Jonathan Smallwood; Boris C. Bernhardt
articles.abstract: A debate is raging in human neuroscience over the foundational principles of cortical organisation, chiefly whether the cortex is best characterised by discrete areas or continuous gradients. Though fuelled by recent insights from in vivo neuroimaging, the debate is in fact centuries old. Classic works in neuroanatomy and neurophysiology hold insights that can still shape our theories today. Tracing the origins of these schools of thought also sheds light on where prevailing models simplify cortical organisation for purposes of utility. In this scoping historical review, traversing across methods as varied as vivisection, skull morphology, neuropathological lesions, histology and modern neuroimaging, we trace a persistent tension between modular and integrative accounts of cortical organisation. Yet several principles consistently emerge, even among competing schools, (i) hard boundaries are the exception rather than the rule, (ii) parcellations and gradients can be thought of as complementary descriptions operating at different spatial scales, and (iii) a more realistic cortical map would be multi-dimensional. We close by reflecting on how a multi-scale, multi-dimensional conceptualisation of the cortex offers a flexible framework for investigating how dynamic cortical function maps onto relatively stable cortical structure.

articles.title: Impaired functional double dissociation in motor-to-sensory transformation mediates aberrant predictive coding in auditory verbal hallucinations
articles.authors: Fuyin YANG; Chen Zhang; Chunbo Li; Xing Tian
articles.abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations (AVHs), the experience of hearing voices in the absence of corresponding external stimuli, are widely attributed to failures of self-monitoring. However, theoretical models and empirical investigations have primarily localized the underlying dysfunction to abnormalities within auditory cortices. Recent studies have revealed that the motor system exerts predictive regulation over auditory processing, suggesting that AVHs are not merely an abnormal auditory processing but also involve distinct, functionally dissociable impairments in motor-to-sensory transformation. How these impairments dynamically manifest in motor-to-sensory neural circuits remains unclear. This review synthesizes recent findings on the functional interactions between motor and sensory systems and proposes a hierarchical neurobiological framework for predictive coding in AVHs across two dimensions: temporal precision and spatial circuit architecture. In the temporal dimension, mismatches between motor-based predictions and sensory feedback disrupt the precision of predictive coding and Bayesian inference, giving rise to three forms of predictive dysfunction: excessively weak predictive signals, excessively strong predictive signals, and impaired predictive updating. In the spatial dimension, we characterize the spatiotemporal disintegration of the frontal-temporal-thalamic circuit underlying AVHs, focusing on both circuit-level disruption and hierarchical computational misalignment between predictive and perceptual signals. By explicitly linking the temporal precision of predictive coding to the spatial architecture of sensorimotor circuits, this study provides a unified mechanistic framework that bridges cognitive, computational, neurobiological, and clinical perspectives on AVHs.

articles.title: Perspective Taking Shapes Creative Performance in Human–AI Collaboration
articles.authors: Man Zhang; Yang Peng; Yajie Wang; Huiqing Hu; Shi Chen; Qingbai Zhao
articles.abstract: This study compared human–human and human–AI collaboration in creative performance and perspective-taking behavior and further examined whether the relationship between perspective-taking and creative performance differed between the two forms of collaboration. According to the actor–partner interdependence model, an individual’s creative performance is influenced not only by their own perspective-taking behavior (actor effect) but also by their partner’s perspective-taking behavior (partner effect). The results showed that: (1) In both the Alternative Uses Task (AUT) and Product Improvement Task (PIT), human–AI collaboration produced significantly higher mean idea novelty and more frequent perspective-taking behavior than human–human collaboration. (2) The effects of perspective-taking on creative performance differed between the two forms of collaboration. In human–human collaboration, both actor and partner effects of perspective-taking significantly and positively predicted idea fluency in both tasks; in the PIT, partner perspective-taking also significantly and positively predicted idea flexibility. In human–AI collaboration, in the AUT, AI’s immediate perspective-taking significantly and positively predicted both its own and its human partner’s idea fluency, whereas humans’ immediate perspective-taking significantly and negatively predicted both their own and AI’s idea flexibility. In the PIT, humans’ delayed perspective-taking significantly and positively predicted both their own and their AI partner’s idea fluency and flexibility, whereas AI’s delayed perspective-taking significantly and negatively predicted both its own and its human partner’s idea novelty. These findings indicate that perspective-taking operates differently in human–AI collaboration than in human–human collaboration and that its effects vary by collaborator role for specific tasks and creativity indicators, providing new evidence for understanding the mechanisms of creative interaction in human–AI collaboration.

articles.title: Articulation Through Iteration: The Career Readiness Pathway as a Boundary-Crossing Framework for Student Development and Stakeholder Alignment
articles.authors: Caleb Braxton Bragg
articles.abstract: The Career Readiness Pathway (CR Path; Bragg & Conway, 2026) presents career readiness as achieved through four iterative components: career-specific knowledge, skills, and abilities (CS-KSAs); core competencies; experiential learning opportunities (ELOs); and career mentorship. The framework emerged from a gap in the career readiness, higher education, and workforce development literatures: no existing framework connected students, faculty, employers, and administrators within a shared logic for understanding what college produces and why it matters. This paper extends the original framework in three ways. First, I present iteration, not sequence, as the mechanism through which career readiness develops.
