The original paper acknowledged that the path was not strictly sequential; this paper makes a stronger claim: iteration is the framework's developmental engine, a distinction whose consequences only became visible through operationalization. Second, I identify the articulation problem, the systematic inability of students in non-professional fields to name what they have learned in language that travels beyond the classroom, and describe the tools built to address it. Third, I follow the iterative logic to its conclusion: some CS-KSAs constitutively require multiple disciplinary perspectives to reach proficiency and cannot complete their development within any single department. For those skills, the CR Path does not break—it extends, pointing toward the pedagogical architecture such skills demand: the Translational Literacy Framework (Bragg, 2026b). Throughout, I argue that the CR Path functions not merely as a pedagogical recommendation but as a coordination framework, a shared language linking what students do in college to everyone who needs to understand it.

articles.title: Learning to Speak Up: Oral Comprehensive Examinations and the Preparation of Health Students at a Hispanic-Serving Institution
articles.authors: Amanda Almond
articles.abstract: At Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), equitable education requires more than access to knowledge; it requires practice articulating that knowledge in contexts shaped by power and hierarchy. This article presents an equity-oriented assessment model, scaffolded oral comprehensive examinations, in an undergraduate health psychology course at an urban HSI in which health service degree programs account for nearly one in five degrees offered. It argues that oral examinations cultivate professional competency by requiring students to explain structural inequity, translate complex health concepts in real time, and engage figures of authority. The article describes the exam design, the learning shifts observed across two administrations, and the implications, limitations, and future directions for HSI health educators.

articles.title: Turning to AI Chatbots to Cope with Loneliness and Social Isolation: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Online Perceptions and Experiences
articles.authors: Ahmed Al-Asmar; Edy Henich; Vincent Paquin
articles.abstract: Loneliness is a public health concern, and people increasingly turn to AI chatbots for social and emotional needs. Empirical research on whether AI chatbots alleviate loneliness remains mixed and is constrained by a lack of naturalistic data that may not capture highly isolated individuals. This study characterized public perceptions and experiences of AI chatbot use in the context of loneliness and social isolation, drawing on naturalistic discussions from Reddit. We retrieved 930 posts and 1,095 comments from AI- and loneliness-focused subreddits. A pipeline combining LLM-assisted screening, sentiment analysis, and perspective classification with CAST topic modelling identified 79 topics organized into five themes: loneliness as a driver, bonding with an AI companion, instrumental and bounded use, dependency, and macro-level debate over the practice. Human raters verified the LLM-assisted outputs, yielding strong agreement. Chatbot use was more often positioned as a reflection of loneliness than its cause. Users held a dual stance, calling the companion “code” while continuing to relate to it as meaningful, engaging with it on terms distinct from human connection. Users credited constant availability, non-judgmental responsiveness, and memory with providing comfort, and blamed the same features for diminishing returns and dependent use. Stigma relocated disclosure into identity-affirming communities for some users while deterring it for others, deepening isolation and discouraging help-seeking. These findings position social chatbot use as a marker of unmet relational need, and carry implications for clinical practice, companion technology design, and retention-focused regulation.

articles.title: Development of noisy-channel parsing: Age-related changes in children’s prior expectations
articles.authors: Yi Ting Huang; Kuan-Jung Huang; Mackensie Blair; Chloe Wright; Sam Van Horne; Giovanna Morini; Amanda Van Horne
articles.abstract: Compared to adults, school-aged children parse sentences more slowly, incorporate discourse and world knowledge less readily, and often misinterpret infrequent and garden-path structures. While prior research focuses on isolating the cause of developmental differences, there remains a fundamental need to characterize how children’s parsing strategies interact with context properties. Adopting an eye-tracking paradigm, the current study investigates the extent to which typically developing 4- to 9-year-olds rely on prior expectations when interpreting sentence meanings in contexts that induces substantial uncertainty about who did what to whom. Across transitive and relative clause structures, children revealed distinct performance in off-line vs. on-line comprehension. While action accuracy improved with age for all sentence types, analysis of correct fixations after disambiguation revealed greater age-related changes for canonical (actives, subject RCs) compared to non-canonical structures (passives, object RCs). Age effects on comprehension of canonical structures persisted even when off-line construction-specific accuracy was accounted for. Our findings are consistent with the development of noisy-channel parsing, whereby children solve uncertainty about signal properties across development through enhanced reliance on prior expectations, which are structured according to frequent representations that generate cross-situational variability over the entirety of their language.

articles.title: The SPOT Grid: Naturalistic Images with Predefined Settings, Patterns, Objects, and Textures
articles.authors: Zall Hirschstein; Mariam Aly; Christopher Baldassano
articles.abstract:
In the natural world, higher-level visual features (e.g., scenes and objects) systematically covary
with specific lower-level constituent features (e.g., textures and patterns). This natural covariation
makes it diﬃcult to isolate aspects of behavior or brain activity that are specific to a single level of
the feature hierarchy. For example, a particular neural or behavioral response may reflect
recognition of a “jungle” scene, or it may reflect sensitivity to the lower-level features — leaf
textures, dense vertical lines, etc.
— that constitute jungle scenes. To address this challenge, we
developed a novel approach for partially decoupling higher- and lower-level features in
naturalistic images. We employed a Stable Diﬀusion image generation framework to create a
naturalistic image set in which setting–object pairings and texture–pattern pairings are factorially
combined, enabling systematic manipulation of higher-level and lower-level image content. To
validate our approach, we used state-of-the-art image processing models to confirm that
higher-level features are represented similarly regardless of their lower-level constituent features
and, conversely, that lower-level features are represented similarly regardless of the higher-level
objects/settings they constitute. We then confirmed that human participants can readily and
rapidly categorize these features in our generated images. We present the image generation
framework and introduce the SPOT (Settings, Patterns, Objects, Textures) Grid, a publicly
available stimulus set accompanied by image-specific metrics (upon request:
forms.gle/X2HpzRYUGigFS1S27). This resource provides new opportunities for investigating
hierarchical visual representations, feature binding, and abstraction across perception, behavior,
and the brain.

articles.title: Changing Contributions of Emotion and Reward Information to Learning Through Adolescence
articles.authors: Camille Phaneuf-Hadd; Elizabeth A. Phelps; Leah Somerville
articles.abstract: From childhood to adulthood, individuals’ learning and decision-making may be differentially impacted by two salient value signals for adolescents: emotions and rewards. This study superimposed these information sources to assess their independent and joint influences on learning and choice processes. Participants ages 8-22 years completed a reinforcement learning task, in which monetary rewards conveyed information integral to making reward-maximizing choices, while emotional expressions conveyed information incidental to this goal. In some conditions, emotion and reward invoked congruent approach-avoid tendencies; following either information source promoted making reward-maximizing (“correct”) choices. In other conditions, emotion and reward invoked incongruent approach-avoid tendencies; following the emotion cue impeded reward capture. Participants completed several measures indexing the persistence of emotion and reward information on choice and evaluations of these signals. Statistical and computational models revealed that emotion-reward incongruence hindered early learning through an incidental emotion bias on value estimates. The emotion bias decayed as reward learning progressed in adolescents and adults but endured in children. Moreover, reward-based choice increased with age across the additional measures. Although participants of all ages were initially affected by incidental emotion cues, adults’ shift toward prioritizing integral reward outcomes indicates that goal-relevant information comes to dominate choice with age.

articles.title: Cross-Linguistic Consistency and Validation of the Mental Health Quotient (MHQ) Across 21 Languages in the Global Mind Project
articles.authors: Jennifer Newson; Oleksii Sukhoi; Tara Thiagarajan
articles.abstract: The Mental Health Quotient (MHQ), the core instrument of the Global Mind Project (GMP), has previously been validated in English across measures of internal consistency, test–retest reliability, and criterion validity against clinical and functional outcomes. As the MHQ is now administered in 23 languages, corresponding validation of its translated versions has not previously been reported. Here we assess two properties of the MHQ across 21 languages with more than 10,000 responses each (and, for five additional lower-volume languages, more than 1,000 responses) collected in the GMP in 2025: (1) convergent and discriminant validity, evaluated as the correlation between conceptually similar and dissimilar item pairs, and (2) sampling stability, evaluated as the coefficient of variation (CV%) of the aggregate MHQ score across repeated random samples of varying size. Similar item pairs showed consistently high absolute correlation across languages (mean r ≈ 0.6), while dissimilar item pairs showed consistently low correlation (mean r ≈ 0.08–0.13), with narrow variation across languages and across country groups sharing the same language. The sampling-stability CV% was likewise low and consistent across languages, averaging 2.8% at n = 1,000 and rising to 6.6% at n = 200, with the least consistent language (Tamil) still showing acceptable stability. These results extend the MHQ's validation beyond English, supporting both the fidelity of its translations and the stability of the GMP's online data acquisition methodology across linguistic and cultural contexts.

articles.title: Beyond Trait Prediction:  What Personality Computing Can Contribute to Personality Psychology
articles.authors: Eric Grunenberg; Ramona Schoedel; Jana Berkessel; Gabriela S. Blum; Kristin Jankowsky; Niclas Kuper; Le Vy Phan; Cornelia Sindermann; Larissa Sust
articles.abstract: Personality computing refers to the integration of machine learning methods with digital data to address personality-relevant research questions. To date, the approach has often been narrowly equated with the prediction of personality traits, leaving much of its potential untapped. This article broadens that view and outlines what personality computing can contribute to personality psychology beyond trait prediction. We discuss four domains in which the approach speaks to questions currently shaping the field: (1) informing personality theories, (2) sharpening the focus on within-person processes and the individual, (3) grounding research in observable behavior, and (4) developing tailored personality interventions. We then situate this within the wider interdisciplinary landscape, where computer science and computational social science have developed the approach along partly different lines, and where personality psychology has a distinct contribution to make. Realizing this potential will require large and intensive longitudinal datasets, methodological expertise within the field, shared standards for how such work is conducted and reported and sustained attention to the ethical questions raised by personality-relevant digital data. Personality computing is neither a panacea nor a replacement for established approaches, but a complementary set of tools that can extend the methodological repertoire of personality research.

articles.title: Embodied Models of Health: A Theoretical Framework of Mind-Body Unity
articles.authors: Peter J Aungle; Pierre-Marie Matta; Daniel L. Chen; Ellen Langer
articles.abstract: In this article, we review the literature on placebo effects and its overlap with the literature on health mindsets. We propose an Embodied Models of Health theoretical framework to account for the array of mind-body effects discussed in our literature review. While beliefs and expectations are widely acknowledged as fundamental drivers of placebo effects – physiological improvements that result exclusively and directly from psychological processes – the role of attention is often neglected in theoretical accounts of the placebo phenomenon and remains poorly understood. We argue that placebo effects and health mindsets are a product of continuous interaction between attention, beliefs, and expectations. We end by discussing novel predictions generated by the Embodied Models of Health framework and highlight opportunities to leverage the role of attention in mind-body dynamics to improve health and wellbeing.

articles.title: Policy, Ethics, and Youth Digital Rights
articles.authors: Kelila Kahane; Chaden Noureddine; John Torous
articles.abstract:
The youth mental health crisis is well established, and social media has emerged as
a putative contributor. In the last three years, legislators, courts, schools, communities, and
industry itself have pursued a range of strategies to change how adolescents engage with social
media. Some government approaches focus on banning social media based on age, with
Australia's national ban taking effect in December 2025, and France and the UK to follow in
2027. Some US states have suggested changes to the ways adolescents are shown content on
social media, and others have suggested warning labels akin to cigarette packs, which as of this
writing have not been shown to users. At the same time, there has been some push for industry to
self-regulate and schools and families have introduced their own standards, with at least 39 states
as of this writing banning phones in schools to some degree. In sum, the landscape is fragmented
and changing quickly, but understanding its core features is essential for anyone working with
and advising children and families. In this chapter, we will map the evolving layers of regulation.
We will then examine the legal, practical, and rights-based challenges that complicate policy.
Lastly, we will close with the clinician's role in this shifting space and four priorities for future
youth social media policy.

This is a preprint of a chapter to be published in Teens, Screens, and Social Connection: An Evidence-Based Guide to Key Problems and Solutions, 2nd edition (Springer).

articles.title: Modeling Environmental Behavior: Lessons from Social Computational Neuroscience
articles.authors: Veronika Wendler; Anne Saulin; Tony Craig; Caroline Moraes; Yansong Li; Chunliang Feng; Lei Zhang
articles.abstract: Addressing climate change requires a better understanding of environmental behavior. Yet environmental-behavior research has largely focused on single observed outcomes, with limited use of computational models to identify the processes through which these behaviors emerge. Many environmental decisions are also socially interdependent, meaning individuals often must weigh personal costs against benefits for others, future generations, and collective outcomes. Social computational neuroscience provides formal models for examining precisely such value-based and social decisions, making it a useful foundation for environmental research. However, environmental decisions also have distinctive features, as their consequences are often delayed, uncertain, and difficult to observe directly. We therefore propose that repeated, computationally structured tasks can complement conventional environmental experimental designs by estimating latent decision processes rather than only measuring behavioral outcomes. We introduce computational frameworks from social computational neuroscience, focusing on subjective-value, reinforcement-learning, drift-diffusion, and agent-based models, and discuss how to adapt them to study environmental behavior. We illustrate this approach with an eco-product choice task integrating product design, learning from feedback, visual attention, and choice. Overall, we propose social computational neuroscience as a framework for linking individual decision mechanisms to socially situated and collective environmental behavior, contributing to the emerging field of environmental social neuroscience.

articles.title: Upstream of Ideology: Measuring the Values That Generate Political Positions
articles.authors: Jason W. Payne; Aisha Mir; Nathan Oesch; David Samson
articles.abstract: Existing political psychology instruments tend to measure political orientation by aggregating known political positions. As such, the resulting instruments are contaminated with the very political content they are meant to predict. Alternatively, underlying value commitments could be used but historically these have been measured only piecemeal and without a framework specifying how values produce position-taking. Sowell (2007) proposes such a framework. Sowell makes claims about human nature, knowledge, and social processes from which political orientations may be derived. The present instrument seeks to operationalize these commitments at the value level. In a large adult sample (N = 1,532), confirmatory and exploratory analyses converged on five value dimensions. Correlations with Right-Wing Authoritarianism, Social Dominance Orientation, and Conway's Left-Wing Authoritarianism showed only partial overlap. An instrument that measures values independently of positions permits questions that current tools cannot ask: whether values predict voting and other downstream behaviour more strongly under effortful reasoning, and whether ideological change is value change or merely repackaging of the same commitments.

articles.title: The Tug of War between Taxonomic and Thematic Relations in Young Toddlers
articles.authors: Kim Plunkett; Irina Lepadatu; Janette Chow; Armando Quetzalcóatl Angulo-Chavira
articles.abstract:
Adult semantic memory contains distinct taxonomic and thematic memory systems.
Whether these systems are anatomically separate or should best be characterized as
functionally separable is unclear. We review evidence for the emergence of these
memory systems during infancy and toddlerhood and describe an experiment that
pits taxonomically and thematically related objects against each other in a visual
world task. The results of the experiment indicate that toddlers (and adults) prefer to
fixate both types of foils, as compared to unrelated foils, though thematic foils tend
to attract more fixations during the later stages of an experimental trial. The latency
of initial fixations towards these semantic foils do not differ. Similar results were
obtained for adults using the same set of stimuli, though their interest in the taxo-
nomic foil evaporated halfway through a trial. These results show that toddlers are
not only sensitive to the taxonomic and thematic relations between named objects but
that the processing of these relations are different. One possibility is that taxonomic
relations are processed in a fast and automatic fashion whereas thematic relations are
also processed under more strategic both during the early stages of lexico-semantic
development and in adulthood. We also discuss the possibility that maintenance of
interest in taxonomic foils throughout a trial might reflect a development of feature
specificity in toddlers.

articles.title: Inconclusive evidence for prospective links between self-efficacy and depression during adolescence: reanalysis and commentary on Nguyen et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Drawing on statistically significant cross-lagged parameters, Nguyen et al. argued that self-efficacy and depressive symptoms exert reciprocal longitudinal influences during adolescence. However, cross-lagged estimates in observational data may reflect statistical artifacts rather than genuine influencing processes. To evaluate the robustness of these conclusions, we applied multiple analytic approaches to data simulated to reproduce the correlations and sample characteristics reported by Nguyen et al. Across models, estimated effects varied markedly in both magnitude and direction, yielding evidence for both decreasing and increasing associations between the constructs. Meta-analytic synthesis of these alternative estimates produced effects that were not significantly different from zero. These findings suggest that the conclusions drawn by Nguyen et al. may be premature and that the reported cross-lagged associations could reflect statistical artifacts. Consistent with multiverse principles, we recommend evaluating prospective associations across several plausible models and basing substantive conclusions on the overall pattern of findings.

articles.title: No convincing evidence for prospective effects between perceived social support, school adaptation, and depression: A reanalysis and comment on Meng et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using cross-lagged panel analyses, Meng et al. concluded that perceived social support, school adaptation, and depression exert reciprocal longitudinal influences among Chinese vocational students. However, cross-lagged coefficients may reflect statistical artifacts rather than true prospective effects. To evaluate this possibility, we analyzed simulated data constructed to reproduce the sample characteristics and correlation structure reported by Meng et al. Alternative analytic approaches yielded markedly different conclusions, including positive, negative, and near-zero prospective effects among the study variables. When these estimates were synthesized meta-analytically, the resulting overall effects were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that the reported longitudinal influences may not provide reliable evidence of prospective relationships. Consistent with multiverse principles, we recommend evaluating hypotheses across multiple plausible models and basing conclusions on the combined evidence rather than on a single analytic specification.

articles.title: Authoritarianism in Action
articles.authors: Ana P. Gantman; Jordan Wylie; Wil Cunningham; Nicolette Dakin; Connie Pui Yee Chiu; Brendan Michael Fee
articles.abstract: In this paper, we take a behavioral approach to the psychological study of authoritarianism. We specify authoritarian behavior as the products of interactions between people and official systems of power, which forward the personal and political interests of some over others, at the expense of the rule of law. In doing so, we focus on hybrid authoritarianism, or the leveraging of legitimate systems of adjudication for quashing pluralism and consolidating power.  We seek to explain current and historical authoritarian tactics—punishing dissidents, persecuting minorities, and codifying ingroup norms into law–as satisfying immediate motives like retribution or obedience, and made more or less likely by existing predispositions (e.g., for conformity) and particular environments (e.g., anomie). Our view highlights the unique affordances for social control that official systems of power make available, and in doing so, we also identify new tactics that meet our criteria of authoritarian behavior (e.g., selective rule enforcement, inequitable administrative burden). In sum, we provide a framework for understanding authoritarianism from a behavioral perspective, provide a bridge between individual ideology and current and historical authoritarian tactics, and highlight novel avenues for the psychological study of both authoritarianism and punishment more broadly.

articles.title: Organizational Narcissism as an Adaptive Strategy in Contemporary Academia
articles.authors: Elisabeth Julie Vargo
articles.abstract: Universities around the world are undergoing a marketisation process in order to respond to consumer-oriented demands. Despite priority shifts, universities have remained traditionally hierarchical and elitist. Moreover, a new and growing generation of academic researchers has found it increasingly difficult to integrate in academia. Systems and patterns of behaviour breeding cultural narcissism, intended as a value and cultural system characterised by an investment in false self-projections backed by Machiavellian attainment, exist and appear to thrive in academic institutions. This organizational adaptation for survival is now embedded in higher education and interlinked with mobbing, workplace bullying and academic misconduct. The problematics we are witnessing today in many academic settings (high rates of mental health issues, widespread cases research misconduct scandals and loss of credibility of academic research) are a by-product of an organizational narcissistic culture. Amidst economic shifts, it might seem reasonable to adopt measures aimed at increasing assets, invest in highly entrepreneurial academics who attract financial resources to universities and use any means to salvage the reputations of educational institutions. Yet these strategies might be promoting and perpetuating value systems that are undermining academic integrity, and therefore contributing to the scientific credibility crisis and failure of these institutions.

articles.title: Misidentification Delusion Contents and Aberrant Prediction Errors in the General Population
articles.authors: Martin Meyer; Deanna Greco; Constance Lubinski; Philip R. Corlett
articles.abstract: Misidentification delusions – e.g., "My partner is an impostor” – occur most strikingly in rare neuropsychological cases, which are relatively immune to empirical study. Theorizing from these cases augurs commitments to a modular mental ontology. But what if misidentification beliefs were common? This would open the field to empirical study as never before. Moreover, if these beliefs could pre-date the index brain damage (albeit in attenuated form), it would challenge explanatory accounts which posit modular mechanisms for aberrant belief formation. We find that misidentification belief contents are prevalent in the general population; about a quarter of our online sample endorsed at least one (111 of 395 were endorsers). Furthermore, endorsing misidentification predicted relatively weaker Kamin blocking – an index of aberrant prediction error processing. Intriguingly, domain-general computational motifs related to particular phenomenological contents. Overall, these results invite an experimental exploration of misidentification delusions and further development of explanatory theories, beyond the status quo.

articles.title: A pilot study assessing the clinical significance of neurorehabilitation: A retrospective study using FIM+FAM, NPDS, and RCS-E.
articles.authors: Bipana Thapa; Adenekan Oyefeso
articles.abstract: This pilot study assessed the impact of neurorehabilitation by analysing changes in patient outcomes from admission to discharge using three key measures: the Functional Independence Measure, the Functional Assessment Measure (FIMFAM), the Northwick Park Dependency Scale (NPDS), and the Rehabilitation Complexity Scale-Extended (RCS-E). A retrospective analysis was conducted on the records of 31 patients admitted to a neurorehabilitation centre between April 2021 and March 2023. Paired t-tests were performed to assess statistically significant changes in these outcome measures, and the Reliable Change Index (RCI) was calculated to determine the clinical significance of observed changes. Significant improvements were found across all the measures. The FIM+FAM scores indicated enhanced motor and cognitive function (p<.0001), with the average score increasing by 28.19. NPDS scores reflected reduced care needs (avg. scores reduced by 8.42, p<.0001), similar to the reduced average scores (2.45) from the RCS-E (p<.0001), signifying decreased rehabilitation needs. The results exceeded RCI thresholds across measures, indicating clinically meaningful improvement; future work will include MDC thresholds for service-level benchmarking.

articles.title: Neural Representations of Personally Familiar and Experimentally Familiar Faces Across Adulthood
articles.authors: Stefani Morgan; Emma Tripp; Sophie D. Allen; Chris B. Martin
articles.abstract: Face recognition is thought to reflect complementary functions of two brain networks. A core system is thought to support perceptual processing of faces, whereas an extended system represents affective and biographical knowledge that supports familiarity-based discrimination. However, the representational format of face-evoked responses within structures comprising each system is not well understood. Here, we applied RSA to fMRI data to characterize the representational structure of personally familiar, experimentally familiar, and novel faces in younger and older adults. This approach revealed that perirhinal cortex (PRC), a node in the extended face processing system, represented personally familiar and experimentally familiar faces in distinct patterns of activity in young adults; personally familiar faces were repelled from one another, whereas experimentally familiar faces were drawn near one another. Corresponding results from PRC in older adults demonstrated that the representational distinctiveness of experimentally familiar faces, but not personally familiar faces, was preserved across the lifespan. In contrast to young adults, a representationally distinct code for personally familiar faces was revealed only in the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) of older adults, which is a key node in the core face processing system. Comparing across regions of interest also revealed that pSTS was representationally distinct from both the extended system and other structures comprising the core system. Lastly, we found that activity patterns in the fusiform face area and occipital face area of young adults predicted response times on a behavioral oddball task in which personally familiar and novel faces were pitted against one another.

articles.title: School Distress and Attendance Difficulties for Neurodivergent Pupils: A Complex Interplay of Drivers, Feelings, and (A Lack of) Support
articles.authors: Chloe Fielding; Deborah M Riby; Sinead Mullally; Rachel Jewers; Mary Hanley
articles.abstract: School distress is a key driver of increasing attendance difficulties among neurodivergent children and young people (CYP) in the UK. Despite this, public and policy discourse often frames attendance difficulties as CYP ‘won’t’ rather than ‘can’t’ attend school, prioritising attendance over wellbeing. Research centring the lived experiences of neurodivergent CYP is needed to understand key contributors to attendance difficulties, their emotional experiences, and ways to improve support. 139 CYP and their parents/carers completed online questionnaires, including standardised measures of anxiety and sensory differences. CYP rated statements about school life and answered qualitative questions about school challenges, feelings about attendance difficulties, support, and suggested changes. Qualitative and quantitative findings identified anxiety and sensory experiences as key drivers of attendance difficulties. CYP described complex, mixed emotions about attendance, often feeling relieved yet simultaneously worried when absent from school. Although around 30% reported feeling supported by a trusted adult, many felt they received no helpful support. Participants highlighted the need for more inclusive sensory environments and greater staff understanding and support. School distress and attendance difficulties are complex and multifaceted. Effective interventions and policies must prioritise CYP’s wellbeing in parallel with attendance, rather than focusing solely on numerical attendance targets.

articles.title: Explaining Emotion Co-Occurrence: Comparison of Parsimonious, Formal Theories Using Multimodal, Within-Person Data
articles.authors: Sebastian Kueppers; Janis Zickfeld; Shukoofeh Ghadertootoonchi; Jens Lange
articles.abstract: Emotion theories should explain when and how emotions co-occur. Investigating emotion co-occurrence, Lange and Zickfeld (2023) found support for the network theory of emotions. This theory suggests that emotions co-occur because the networks of interacting components that represent emotions partly overlap. However, Lange and Zickfeld’s evidence is limited to self-reports and between-person analyses. We substantially extended their work by applying between- and within-person network analytic tools to self-report, physiological (i.e., heart rate, respiration rate, skin conductance, goosebumps), and facial expression data of awe and fear. We compared five parsimonious, formalized theories of emotion co-occurrence derived from distinct emotion, network, and dimensional approaches to emotions. Consistent with Lange and Zickfeld’s (2023) findings, between-person analyses showed that the network theory best explains the co-occurrence of awe and fear. In contrast, the within-person analyses did not allow definitive conclusions regarding the competing theories. We discuss the utility of theory formalization, and highlight the need for the collection of within-person, multimodal emotion data for advancing research on emotion co-occurrence.

articles.title: Beyond the Normative Trajectory: Understanding Individual Differences in Adolescent Reward- Related Motivation and Risk for Psychopathology
articles.authors: Ashley C Parr; Valerie J. Sydnor; Beatriz Luna
articles.abstract: Adolescence is characterized by pronounced changes in incentive motivation that support exploration, learning, and the transition to independence in adulthood. Population-average developmental models have been instrumental in defining these normative changes and have shaped contemporary theories of adolescent neurodevelopment. However, growing evidence indicates that individuals differ substantially in how reward-related motivational systems mature. Despite this, the developmental sources and long-term consequences of this variability remain poorly understood. In this Review, we suggest that individual differences in developmental trajectories – including their timing, tempo, duration, and overall shape – represent an important framework for understanding vulnerability and resilience across psychopathology. We propose that reward-related motivational trajectories emerge through continual interactions between neuroplasticity and environmental experience. Early life experiences scaffold the developmental conditions from which incentive motivational systems mature, whereas ongoing experiences during adolescence calibrate these trajectories through experience-dependent plasticity. Using dopamine (DA)-sensitive mesocorticolimbic circuitry as the primary developmental system supporting reward and incentive motivation, we review evidence from longitudinal neuroimaging, animal models, and behavioral studies demonstrating how neurobiological maturation and environmental experience interact to shape developmental trajectories. We highlight growing evidence that person-centered developmental trajectories better characterize heterogeneity in substance use and other neuropsychiatric outcomes in comparison to population-average developmental trends. Finally, we discuss emerging methodological approaches – including dense longitudinal designs, flexible nonlinear modeling, normative developmental modeling, and person-centered trajectory analyses – that provide new opportunities to identify when developmental trajectories diverge, which biological and environmental mechanisms drive these individual differences, and how they relate to long-term outcomes. By shifting the focus from describing normative developmental change to understanding why individuals diverge from expected developmental trajectories, this framework provides a foundation for identifying mechanistically informed developmental phenotypes, individualized windows of vulnerability and resilience, and developmentally timed prevention and intervention strategies.

articles.title: (Dis)Embodied Joint Agency in Human-Virtual Agents Interactions
articles.authors: Altea Vanni; Jan Pohl; Shihan Liu; Jiaqi Yin; Sylvia Xueni Pan; Antonia Hamilton; Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Anna Ciaunica
articles.abstract: The sense of agency is a fundamental feature of the human mind and deeply connected with its embodied roots. Recent advances in artificial agents such as robots and Virtual Reality (VR) lead to the rapid emergence of new types of embodied interactions and joint agencies. While it is well established that humans readily assign human-like attributes to artificial others, less is known how the human embodiment affects human-artificial agents interactions. We conducted a study (n°43) looking at the relationship between Depersonalisation (DP) experiences and joint agency in human-virtual agent interactions. DP is condition that makes people feel detached from their self and body, with atypical sense of agency over one’s own actions, and distressing subjective feelings of "being a robot” or an “automatic pilot”. Specifically, we have created a VR environment where participants with low versus high levels of DP experiences perform the classic Joint Simon Task while embodying either a human or a humanoid robot avatar in tandem with either another human avatar or robotic avatar. Our findings suggest a significant effect of the DP experiences on the sense of joint agency as measured by the Joint Simon task. Specifically, participants with high levels of DP experiences displayed faster reaction times (RTs) when they embody the Human avatar as compared to when they embodied the robotic avatar. In addition, using the classic Intentional Binding task, we found that time estimations were shorter in high DP participants (but not in Low DP participants) when they embodied a robotic avatar as compared to a human avatar. Our study provides for the first time evidence that the human embodiment matters too in joint agency tasks in addition to the artificial embodiment. Our results pave the way towards more human-body centred design in creating interactions with artificial others, especially when these interactions permeate our daily lives.

articles.title: Gasliteracy: Lay People’s Understanding of Memory Conflicts in Relation to Gaslighting within Intimate Relationships
articles.authors: Yikang Zhang; Celine van Golde
articles.abstract: Gaslighting has been conceptualised as psychological abuse that often centres on challenges to a victim's memory, yet everyday memory disagreements are a normal feature of intimate relationships. This study examined how laypeople distinguish ordinary memory conflicts from gaslighting, and how this distinction relates to individual differences and relationship dynamics. Two hundred and fifty-two participants (134 women) recalled an incident in which their partner contradicted their memory, defined gaslighting in their own words, rated how gaslit they felt during the conflict, and completed measures of relationship quality and individual differences; independent coders also rated the incidents for gaslighting. Memory conflicts were common (62.84% of eligible participants), but only about a quarter of participants interpreted their conflict as gaslighting to any extent. Gaslighting ratings were negatively associated with relationship satisfaction, trust, and sense of power, and positively associated with dark traits. Third-party ratings showed moderate agreement with participants' ratings and similar associations with relationship quality, but not with dark traits. These findings highlight the role of relational climate and individual differences in whether memory disagreements are perceived as abusive gaslighting versus ordinary fallibility, underscoring the need to differentiate these phenomena in research and science communication.

articles.title: Educating Minds with Generative AI
articles.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo; Andy Clark; Thomas Wachter
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering education, framed as a tool for efficiency and personalisation. In this Perspective, we argue this obscures a deeper transformation. Schools are cognitive ecologies in which tools and social practices actively shape learning. GenAI restructures this ecology, redistributing epistemic labour, consolidating pedagogical functions, and reorganising how knowledge is accessed, produced, and evaluated. Unlike most educational technologies, it is active, persistent, and generalist. We identify two enduring misalignments: a pedagogical gap between learning sciences and AI design, and a goal gap between measurable performance and developmental aims. Both gaps reflect logics already embedded within existing educational systems organised around efficiency, standardisation, and control. GenAI does not introduce but risks entrenching and amplifying these gaps. Rather than accommodating GenAI through technical adjustments, we propose treating it as a diagnostic opportunity to redesign schooling for embodied, collaborative, and distinctly human forms of learning.

articles.title: Moralized Feeds, Stable Values: A Latent Class Growth Analysis of Adolescents’ Moral Values and Influencers’ and Celebrities’ Moral Content on Social Media
articles.authors: Anaëlle Gonzalez; Lindsay Hahn; Laura Vandenbosch
articles.abstract: Social media personalities (SMPs) increasingly function as moral exemplars in adolescents’ lives, yet little is known about how adolescents’ moral values relate to the moral content of their favorite social media accounts over time. This study combined three-wave panel data from 530 adolescents with a content analysis of their favorite influencers and celebrities (n = 305). Latent class growth analyses identified joint trajectories of adolescents’ moral foundation salience and exposure-weighted SMP moral content. Most profiles (71.1%) contained moral cues, particularly related to care, loyalty, and fairness. Across models, class membership was driven primarily by baseline differences in SMP moral content rather than divergent developmental trajectories. Parasocial relationships and age predicted membership in a “high-moralization class” but not in domain-specific trajectories. Overall, moral media processes on social media seem to be characterized more by the maintenance of stable, heterogeneous patterns of moralized engagement than by systematic changes in adolescents’ moral foundations.

articles.title: Beyond STEM versus humanities: Academic discipline shapes how students weigh AI- and human-attributed information
articles.authors: Michaela Svoboda; Katerina Chladkova
articles.abstract: Trust in AI has been widely studied; however, most evidence comes from explicit self-reported attitudes toward AI and AI-generated content. Here, we examined trust-related responses using a behavioural credibility-judgement paradigm in which university students evaluated the truthfulness of factual statements attributed either to an AI system or a human source. By avoiding explicit questions about AI, this approach allowed us to test whether source attribution influences credibility judgments beyond consciously reported attitudes. Overall, participants judged AI-attributed statements as less credible than identical statements attributed to a human source, demonstrating an AI-attribution bias. Crucially, this bias varied across fields of study: while humanities/social sciences and technical/mathematics students discounted AI-attributed information relative to identical human-attributed information, medical students showed substantially reduced sensitivity to source attribution. This difference could not be explained by greater use of AI: medical and technical/mathematics students reported comparable levels of AI use, yet only medical students showed a reduced AI-attribution bias. These findings provide behavioral evidence of algorithm scepticism and suggest that academic discipline shapes how students evaluate AI-generated information beyond differences in AI use. The findings further suggest that domain-specific educational practices or epistemic norms, rather than AI experience alone, may shape trust in AI-generated information, highlighting the importance of field-specific AI literacy education.

articles.title: Being who you are: phenotype-genotype congruency and wellbeing
articles.authors: A.J.M.R. Geijsen; René Pool; Meike Bartels
articles.abstract:
Background: Differences in wellbeing are shaped by genetic predispositions and environmental influences, yet recommendations for improving wellbeing are often framed as universally beneficial. We examined whether wellbeing is higher when individuals’ observed phenotypes correspond more closely to their genetic predispositions. 
Methods: We used data from 18,748 participants of the  Netherlands Twin Register. Phenotype-genotype congruency was examined across social, health, and lifestyle-related phenotypes using a triangulation approach with three complementary methods. First, cross-sectional generalized estimating equation models tested whether difference scores between phenotypes and corresponding polygenic scores were associated with wellbeing. Second, response surface analyses (RSA) modelling linear, non-linear, and interaction effects of phenotype and genotype. And third, longitudinal multi-level models using repeated measures of phenotype-genotype difference scores and wellbeing over time.
Results: Greater phenotype–genotype congruency was associated with higher wellbeing for BMI, neuroticism, sleep duration, and social interaction in cross-sectional analyses,. Longitudinal analyses showed similar associations for BMI, neuroticism, self-rated health, sleep duration, social interaction, and TV time. Effect sizes were small but generally consistent across models. In contrast, RSA did not support phenotype–genotype congruency effects. BMI, neuroticism, and social interaction showed partial congruency patterns, but neither satisfied the congruency criteria (Humberg et al., 2019). 
Conclusions: Across phenotypes, higher congruency between phenotypes and genetic predispositions was associated with higher wellbeing in difference score models, but were not confirmed by RSA. The findings suggest that phenotype–genotype congruency may be relevant for wellbeing in some domains, and that replication is needed to better understand the complexity of wellbeing.

articles.title: Visual Guidance of Pictorial Composition in the Absence of Figures: An Eye-Tracking Study
articles.authors: Sophia Kury; Xingyu Long; Jozsef Arato; Teresa Kamencek; Anna Miscenà; Raphael Rosenberg
articles.abstract: Art literature has long held that the composition of a painting guides the beholder's eye, which would imply that viewers perform similar eye movements when looking at the same picture. Recent eye-tracking work has supported this claim, but almost exclusively with figure-dominated paintings, in which depicted humans are strong attractors of attention—leaving open whether shared gaze reflects composition or merely the pull of figures. We tested compositional guidance in the absence of figures by recording the eye movements of 46 art-history students who viewed six still lifes (17th–18th c.) and six abstract paintings (20th c.) for one minute each and afterwards drew the most important compositional lines of each painting. Following Sancarlo et al. (2020), we quantified three kinds of similarity for each painting: between observers' saccades, between their compositional drawings, and between saccades and drawings, in each case contrasting within-painting (self) with between-painting (other) similarity. At the reference grid resolution, within-painting similarity exceeded between-painting similarity for the saccades of all twelve paintings, for the drawings of eleven, and between saccades and drawings for nine. Saccadic similarity decreased with rated visual complexity, whereas drawing similarity did not; no difference emerged between still lifes and abstract paintings. Pictorial composition therefore does shape the gaze even when no figure is present, at least for trained viewers.

articles.title: Beyond Labels: Data-Derived Profiles Better Describe Children and Young People’s Needs in Education
articles.authors: Jo Hutchinson; Emre Deniz; Megan Frith; Kathryn Asbury; Dianne Newbury; Umar Toseeb
articles.abstract: Background. Children and young people (CYP) with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) have poorer outcomes compared with those without SEND. It remains unclear how to best identify CYP with SEND. We examined whether profiles of CYP needs align with SEND identification and whether they discriminate young adult outcomes better than current SEND identification. Methods. We analysed data from three population-based cohorts in England: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (N = 15,645); Millennium Cohort Study (N = 18,827); Twins Early Development Study (N = 7,859). We fitted latent mixture models to data on social and behavioural, emotional, and cognitive functioning. We did this separately for each cohort at three developmental stages: early childhood (age 3-5 years); middle childhood (age 7-9 years); adolescence (age 13-18 years). We ran logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses to determine whether data-derived sub-groups discriminate young adult outcomes better than SEND identification. Results. There were CYP with similar profiles of strengths and challenges: typically developing; global difficulties; cognitive difficulties; and social, emotional, behavioural difficulties. Up to a third of CYP experienced difficulties at two or more developmental stages, indicating high levels of persistent educational need in England. SEND identification only partially overlapped with the data-derived sub-groups. Agreement was highest for global and cognitive difficulty sub-groups and lowest for emotional difficulties sub-groups. Difficulty sub-groups showed consistent associations across a range of young adult outcomes. Data-derived sub-groups discriminated university degree attainment, receipt of state benefits, anti-social behaviour, and mental health outcomes better than SEND identification, whereas SEND identification performed better only for GCSE attainment. Conclusions. Current SEND identification only partially captures underlying persistent educational need in England. Descriptive profiles of CYP’s strengths and challenges are likely to be a better alternative to the current SEND system for identifying CYP at risk of poor outcomes post compulsory education.

articles.title: Developmental variation from rational choice
articles.authors: Samuel David Jones; Dara Tan; Paul Rauwolf
articles.abstract: Rational choice theory offers a normative account of the allocation of bounded cognitive resources under constraints. This work has focused largely on static solutions, leaving the developmental implications of rational choice relatively under-researched. Conversely, developmental science has in general overlooked the role of an individual's choices, actions, and habits in shaping rather than merely reflecting developmental variation, from delay to psychopathology to expertise. The aim of this paper is to characterise the developmental implications of rational inattention, a leading framework within rational choice theory, and in doing so develop a normative account of how adaptive behaviour reciprocally shapes the emergence of diversity in intelligent behaviour. The thesis we develop is that rational choice – behaviour that is adaptive not only to the structure of the environment but to the constraints of the agent – shapes neurodevelopmental variation beyond the neurogenetic factors that promote that behaviour. We begin by presenting static solutions to rationally inattentive choice problems, before turning to adaptivity and learning over time. We demonstrate that adaptive behaviour contributes unique variance to developmental outcomes and predicts inertia in changing environments. Finally, we distil the key features of rationally inattentive behaviour and corresponding empirical support from the developmental science literature. The strength of this approach is to demonstrate that some of the signatures of diversity in intelligent behaviour across the lifespan can in principle fall out of a minimal set of rational assumptions. This has implications for how we think about and respond to individual differences in human development.

articles.title: Risks of Using Large Language Models in Grading: LLMs and Humans Prefer LLM-Generated Writing Over Human’s but LLMs Show a Stronger Systematic Bias
articles.authors: Matthew HC Mak
articles.abstract: Recent studies suggest that large language models (LLMs) can approximate human grading performance, raising the prospect of their use in educational assessment. However, an important question remains: can LLMs evaluate student work fairly? In Study 1, we examined whether LLM evaluators exhibit systematic preference when grading psychology dissertations from three sources: (a) dissertations authored by 1,426 undergraduate students, (b) the same dissertations rewritten by GPT-4 or GPT-5 (i.e., paraphrased), and (c) dissertations fully generated by GPT models using student-written abstracts as prompts. Across three families of evaluators (GPT, Gemma, Qwen), LLMs consistently assigned the lowest scores to student-authored dissertations, intermediate scores to GPT-rewritten dissertations, and the highest scores to fully GPT-generated dissertations (student-authored < GPT-rewritten < fully GPT-generated). In Study 2, we tested the generalisability of this pattern using abstracts rather than the entire dissertations and observed the same graded preference across three of the four LLM evaluators. To assess whether humans also demonstrate the same graded preference, we conducted a preregistered experiment with 300 human raters who scored student-authored, GPT-rewritten, or fully GPT-generated abstracts. Human raters scored student-authored and GPT-rewritten abstracts similarly, although both were rated significantly lower than the fully GPT-generated abstracts (student-authored ≈ GPT-rewritten < fully GPT-generated). Importantly, though, the effect size for the contrast between student vs. fully GPT-generated abstracts was considerably smaller in humans (Cohen’s d = 0.58) than in LLM evaluators, where Cohen’s ds > 0.85. These findings provide evidence that LLMs generally have a strong bias to favour LLM-generated content, more so than humans’, raising important concerns about the fairness of deploying LLMs as evaluators in educational settings.

articles.title: A Review of How Linguistic Context Shapes Incidental Word Learning During Reading and the Adaptive Binding of Context (ABC) Theoretical Framework
articles.authors: Matthew HC Mak; Kate Nation
articles.abstract: From mid-childhood onwards, much vocabulary growth occurs through independent reading. In this review, we examine how the linguistic contexts surrounding unfamiliar words influence incidental word learning, aligning with emerging perspectives that view word meanings as context-sensitive representations that are updated and refined across encounters. Specifically, we review evidence concerning six contextual characteristics: contextual presence, contextual informativeness, contextual valence, topic familiarity, topic interest, and contextual diversity. Two characteristics emerge as relatively consistent facilitators of learning: Words are learned more successfully when they occur in familiar topics and in texts that readers find interesting. In contrast, the effects of the remaining contextual characteristics are more conditional, and/or less evidenced. For example, contextual informativeness appears more beneficial for L2 than L1 readers, and more semantically diverse contexts tend to hamper initial meaning learning of abstract but no necessarily concrete words. We propose the Adaptive Binding of Context (ABC) Framework to unify these heterogenous and disparate findings. It assumes that unfamiliar words are initially encoded as part of the situation model constructed during reading and that linguistic context influences word learning through three interrelated pathways: constraining meaning inference, regulating attention, and linking new words to existing knowledge. Critically, the relative contribution of these pathways varies adaptively as a function of word characteristics, readers’ cognitive and linguistic resources, and the current state of word-specific knowledge. This perspective helps explain why the same contextual characteristic may facilitate learning under some conditions but not others. More broadly, we argue that contextual influences on word learning are best understood as adaptive rather than fixed, highlighting the need for research that moves beyond asking whether a particular contextual characteristic facilitates learning and instead asks when, for whom, and at what stage of learning it is most beneficial. We conclude by outlining priorities for future research.

articles.title: De la communication médiatisée par l’IA à l’usurpation d’authenticité : quels risques pour la confiance épistémique dans les relations intimes et thérapeutiques ?
articles.authors: Sophie Schmidt; Royce Anders; Benjamin PUTOIS
articles.abstract:
Contexte. L’essor rapide des systèmes d’intelligence artificielle générative a conduit à l’émergence de la communication médiatisée par l’IA (AI-mediated communication, AIMC), dans laquelle un système algorithmique intervient directement dans la production du langage et de l’expression affective. Si l’AIMC est de plus en plus utilisée dans les relations intimes et les contextes thérapeutiques, ses implications cliniques et éthiques demeurent largement sous-théorisées.
Méthode. Une recherche systématique de la littérature a été réalisée dans MEDLINE afin d’identifier les travaux empiriques et théoriques portant sur l’AIMC et ses effets interpersonnels, psychologiques et cliniques.
Résultats. La littérature existante met en évidence des résultats ambivalents. D’une part, l’assistance par l’IA peut améliorer l’efficacité communicationnelle dans des interactions instrumentales ou transactionnelles. D’autre part, lorsque la communication est censée véhiculer une présence subjective, un engagement personnel ou une responsabilité morale, l’AIMC peut fragiliser les perceptions d’authenticité et de confiance, en particulier lorsque son usage est implicite. Afin de conceptualiser ce risque spécifique, nous proposons la notion d’usurpation d’authenticité, distincte de l’usurpation d’identité, qui désigne le déplacement silencieux du travail subjectif, intentionnel et affectif par lequel une personne se rend présente à l’autre.
Implications cliniques. L’usurpation d’authenticité est susceptible d’affecter particulièrement les relations fondées sur la confiance épistémique, telles que les relations intimes et la psychothérapie, ainsi que les populations vulnérables (traumatismes complexes, trouble de l’attachement). En psychothérapie, l’AIMC non divulguée pourrait compromettre l’alliance thérapeutique.
Conclusion. Ces éléments plaident pour une posture de précaution, fondée sur la transparence, la prévention de la cyberviolence relationnelle et la clarification des usages de l’IA, ainsi que pour le développement de recherches empiriques visant à tester les hypothèses cliniques formulées.

articles.title: Source-Focused Inoculation Offers Protection Against Emotive AI-Generated Misinformation Featuring Deepfakes
articles.authors: Paul McIlhiney; Emily Rebecca Spearing; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: AI-generated content can emotionally manipulate audiences across multiple media formats. We examined how exposure to an emotive AI-generated article featuring a deepfake video influenced health-related beliefs and behavioural intentions, and evaluated the effectiveness of two pre-emptive interventions. Participants (N = 429) received either (i) a neutral article about a retiring science radio-show host (control), or (ii) an emotive misleading article claiming alleged health risks of nanoparticles in sunscreen, featuring a deepfake video of an individual providing an emotional testimonial about their own health consequences from nanoparticle-sunscreen use. The misleading article was preceded by either: a generic warning that AI can produce misleading content; a source-focused inoculation explaining how AI can be used deceptively, supported by a demonstrative example; or no intervention. The misleading article significantly influenced beliefs about the safety of nanoparticle sunscreen and increased the amount participants were willing to pay for non-nano sunscreen. The inoculation significantly reduced, but did not eliminate, effects on belief; however, it failed to attenuate effects on behavioural intention (i.e., willingness-to-pay). The AI warning was ineffective for both outcomes. These findings demonstrate that emotionally manipulative AI-generated misinformation can alter health-related beliefs and behavioural intentions, with a source-focused inoculation providing only partial protection.

articles.title: A two-timescale framework for gut–brain influences on arousal, motivation, and affect
articles.authors: Nikolina Birimac; Irene Perez-Montalvo; Soyoung Q Park; Ignacio Rebollo
articles.abstract: The same brain can think, feel, and perform differently from one hour to the next. Cognitive neuroscience has traditionally explained this variability through fluctuations in neural activity and network dynamics within the brain itself. Yet the brain continuously receives bodily signals that convey physiological state and energy availability. Here, we propose a two-timescale framework for gut–brain communication. We argue that the gut influences cognition, mood, and arousal through two partially distinct but interacting pathways operating at different temporal scales. On a fast timescale, rhythmic gastric activity, cycling approximately every 20 seconds, may bias neural excitability and large-scale brain dynamics. We propose that stomach–brain coupling functions as an “arousal dial,” biasing the brain towards internally oriented and metabolically efficient states. On a slower timescale, metabolic hormones such as ghrelin, GLP-1, insulin, and leptin fluctuate across minutes to hours, providing information about metabolic state. We hypothesise that these hormonal signals act as an “energy gauge,” tuning motivation, reward sensitivity, and affective state according to energy availability. We review evidence linking gastric rhythms and metabolic hormones to arousal, cognition, reward, and mood, and outline predictions for dense within-person neuroimaging, physiological, and endocrine studies of mental fluctuations.

articles.title: Retained Activity and Psychological Capital in Ukrainian Academic Populations, 2024
articles.authors: Volodymyr Evheniiovych Momot; Viktoriia Sokolova
articles.abstract:
Research on Ukrainian higher education under war has documented institutional adaptation in detail, but individual psychological resources remain largely unmeasured, and where activity appears as a coping factor, its content is rarely distinguished from its presence.

This study reports psychological capital (PCQ-24) across three independent Ukrainian academic collections in 2024 (N = 240): faculty at a private university in Dnipro (N = 76), students at the same university (N = 61), and students at two state universities in front-line Zaporizhzhia (N = 103).

Retained activity predicted psychological capital in every sample; geography and demography did not. The employment contrast replicated in two independent student collections under different assignment procedures (g = +0.62, 95% CI [+0.05,+1.23]; g = +1.43). Among faculty, self-rated research activity predicted psychological capital (b = +0.40, p < .0001, R² = 0.31). Location, displacement, gender and age showed no large effects, with Bayes factors weakly supporting the null (BF₀₁ = 2.4–2.9); displacement, available here at individual level, replicated a null reported in earlier work on this population.

Four structural analyses characterise the construct. Profile analysis shows samples differing in elevation rather than shape (variance ratio 58:1). Clustering, blind to all covariates, yields a stable partition (88%) falling along research activity (p = .0006) rather than demography. Network modelling identifies Hope as most central — robustly among students (96–99% of resamples), contested with self-efficacy among faculty (52%). Mokken scaling reveals a reproducible difficulty gradient (ρ = .67–.82) in which Resilience is retained longest and Optimism relinquished first, a possible early depletion marker.

A further claim, more tentative, concerns which activity qualifies. Conservation of Resources holds that investment implies return, predicting that only activity reproducing what was invested generates resource. Two contrasts support this: volunteering dropped out when controlled against research activity (p = .20), and among equally employed students those working in their field scored higher (g = 0.64, p = .023), though this did not survive multivariate control at n = 58. Students holding employment and a merit stipend scored lower than employed non-stipend holders (g = −0.48; BF₀₁ = 0.96), an effect absent among non-working students. These contrasts were formulated after inspecting the data and rest on the weakest links in the chain.

At the institutional level, a single case documents a university resuming teaching eighteen days after suspension in February 2022, enabled by organisational competence built for a different crisis. We propose a refinement to Hobfoll's resource caravan passageways: a passageway defines what is possible but does not itself produce passage through it.

Magnitudes varied across replications (g = 0.62–1.43); the pooled value should not be interpreted.

articles.title: Victimhood Narratives Increase Support for Opponents’ Political  Participation by Promoting Empathy
articles.authors: Emily Kubin; Daniel Revach; Shelley McKeown
articles.abstract: Research suggests that in increasingly polarized societies, individuals are often willing to restrict their political opponents’ political participation. Less is known, however, about the factors that may increase support for opponents’ political participation. Across two experiments conducted in the U.S., we tested whether reading victimhood narratives from political opponents increased both support for opponents’ political participation and participants’ own political action intentions, and whether these effects were driven by increased empathy toward political opponents. In Study 1, participants (N = 245) read about a gun-policy opponent whose position was framed as either rooted in a victimhood narrative or a non-victimhood narrative. Study 2 replicated this with a larger sample (N = 434), the addition of a factual information condition, and a political action intention measure. In both studies, victimhood narratives increased empathy toward the opponent, which in turn increased support for both the individual opponent’s and the broader outgroup’s political participation. In Study 2, the same indirect pattern emerged for participants’ political action intentions, measured via willingness to sign up for updates from a bipartisan organization. Together, the findings have important theoretical and practical implications suggesting that communicating political beliefs through narratives of suffering can foster empathy and in turn increase willingness to support opponents’ civic and political inclusion.

articles.title: A Systems Approach to Understanding Underserved Autistic Adults Experiences of Primary Healthcare: Development and Evaluation of Participatory Creative Systems Mapping
articles.authors: Victoria Newell; Neil Anderson; Ayman Eckford; Katie Needham; Maggie Scrivener; Alexandra Webster; Vyv Huddy; Rachael Hughson-Gill; Ian Kellar; Joe Langley
articles.abstract:
Autistic people who are racially minoritised, from areas of high economic deprivation, have co-occurring learning disabilities, or non- or minimally- speaking are systematically excluded from autism research, leaving critical gaps in evidence for service development. We addressed this by developing and evaluating “Participatory Creative Systems Mapping (PCSM)” – an emerging practice that combines Community-Based Participatory Research, Participatory Systems Mapping, and creative methods. The novelty arises from combining these approaches to systemically reduce barriers to underserved autistic adults’ participation and engagement in research.

We partnered with disability-focused and community organisations, and an autistic steering group to develop and deliver four accessible workshops. These workshops incorporated persona development, user journey mapping, storyboarding, and live artist visualisation to translate underserved autistic adults’ experiences of primary healthcare into system-level insights. 

Thirty-one participants took part across four individual workshops, including representation from Somali and Black African communities (35.5%) and areas of high neighbourhood deprivation. However, participants did not self-report learning disability. Evaluation indicated high satisfaction, with all respondents reporting they felt able to share their ideas and experiences in the workshops. As proof of concept for PCSM as a method, we successfully produced a causal loop diagram reflected on by the steering group – the "Misalignment-Invalidation Cycle", illustrating how communication barriers and clinician invalidation generate reinforcing loops of misunderstanding and disengagement from healthcare. 

Finally, we share key methodological lessons for trust-building, flexibility, and accessibility infrastructure. These offer a roadmap for researchers who are seeking to engage underserved autistic people in participatory, system-level inquiry.

articles.title: Digital implementation: Developing digital mental health skills in the psychological workforce using e-learning.
articles.authors: Helen Pote; Alesia Moulton-Perkins; Gemma Rides
articles.abstract:
Background: Digital mental health (DMH) delivery is expanding across psychological services, yet many practitioners lack the digital skills and confidence required for safe and effective online practice. In order to support digital implementation within mental health governmental and professional bodies emphasise the urgent need to develop digital competencies in the workforce and the need for scalable training solutions.

Aims: To develop and evaluate a national e-learning package designed to improve digital mental health competencies, confidence and attitudes among novice psychological practitioners in the UK.

Methods: A four-module e-learning package was produced using Sheth et al.’s five-phase e-learning development framework. Content aligned with the British Psychological Society’s Digital Competence Framework. First-year students from three clinical psychology doctoral training programmes participated in the e-learning and completed pre- and post-training measures of digital competence (Digital Competencies for Applied Psychological Practitioners, DCAPP), attitudes towards digital interventions and confidence. Quantitative data were analysed using paired t-tests. Qualitative user feedback was gathered and synthesised using deductive thematic analysis. 

Results: Eighty-three students completed the e-learning and 52 provided matched pre-post data. Overall digital competencies significantly improved, including students’ digital mental health knowledge and abilities. Attitudes towards digital interventions became more favourable and confidence in practising digitally increased. Qualitative findings indicated the modules were comprehensive, relevant and engaging, with valued interactive elements such as reflective exercises, quizzes and video content. Some students found modules lengthy and suggested shorter videos, improved time estimates, and downloadable summaries. Minor technical issues and diversity considerations were also identified.

Conclusions: The e-learning package effectively enhanced DMH competencies, attitudes and confidence among novice psychological practitioners. Embedding competence-based digital training into preregistration curricula supports workforce readiness and contributes to scaling digitally enabled care pathways.

articles.title: Risk-Free Study Designs Miss the Weak Trust–Behavior Link in Human–Automation Interaction: Evidence From Two Virtual Reality Experiments
articles.authors: Tobias Rieger; Steffen Hoesterey; Linda Onnasch
articles.abstract: Theories and practitioners alike assume that trust—a latent construct—causally predicts behavior. In human–automation and human–AI interaction, a system's characteristics (e.g., its reliability) are often thought to shape trust, which in turn supposedly predicts how much a human depends on the system. However, little evidence thus far supports this claim, particularly under risk, which theory treats as a precondition for a trust–dependence link. We addressed this gap in two laboratory experiments that used virtual reality to manipulate risk immersively, as part of the environment. In Experiment 1, we varied system reliability (low vs. high) and risk (absent vs. present) between subjects and tested whether several trust measures mediated the effect of reliability on dependence behavior. Trust mediated this effect only under risk, and only for a single-item measure. Thus, a standard no-risk design would have missed the link entirely. However, even the single-item trust measure explained little of the variance in behavior. In Experiment 2, conducted entirely under risk, we replicated the single-item trust mediation but found two further mediators: external regulation (the felt pressure to monitor the system) and one's perceived competence relative to the system. None of them, however, explained more than a small portion of variance within dependence behavior. Thus, even where trust predicted behavior, it did so weakly and non-uniquely. Subjective measures therefore cannot substitute for measuring behavior—whether or not trust theory is correct.

articles.title: Emotions and bodily sensations evoked by natural and urban environments
articles.authors: Heidi Laine; Katariina Pajuranta; Tuulia Malén; David Sander; Jarmo J. Ahonen; Lauri Nummenmaa
articles.abstract: While the affective benefits of nature are well documented, the underlying embodied mechanisms remain elusive. Here we mapped the emotional responses and bodily sensations associated with natural versus urban environments in two experiments with a total of 587 participants. In the first experiment, participants rated videos and images of natural and urban environments for emotions and sensory qualities. In the second experiment participants reported the bodily sensations evoked by viewing the environments using topographical self-report method (emBODY). Our findings highlight that the affective impact of the environment depends heavily on arousal, which aligns with the circumplex model of affect. Low-arousal natural stimuli were experienced as the most spacious and passive and had the strongest positive valence, while highly arousing natural environments were rated as the most unpleasant and unsafe. Viewing natural environments also elicited stronger and more widespread bodily sensations than urban environments and these embodied responses may underlie the positive emotions and the restorative powers of nature as well as the negative emotional reactions.

articles.title: The Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (GAILS): Development, Validation, and Measurement Invariance Across Sex and Occupational Status Groups
articles.authors: Yuchen Zhang; Jia Qi; Xinyi He; Zhe Feng; Feng Ji
articles.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools are rapidly reshaping how people seek information, learn, and work, while also raising concerns about misinformation, bias, privacy, and academic integrity across both educational and workplace contexts. However, many existing AI literacy scales targeted broad AI knowledge rather than GenAI-specific competencies (e.g., prompt formulation, evaluating generated outputs). Emerging GenAI literacy measures have also focused primarily on university students and non-North American samples, limiting their generalizability. We developed and validated a GenAI literacy scale (GAILS) in a diverse North American adult sample (N = 341; Mage = 39.00 years; 38.42% students, 61.58% workforce). The GAILS showed excellent internal consistency (α = 0.973, 95% CI [0.968, 0.978]). Exploratory factor analysis supported a three-factor solution (KMO = 0.959; Bartlett’s χ²(561) = 5784.58, p < .001), and confirmatory factor analysis further supported the model (CFI = 0.967, TLI = 0.965, SRMR = 0.058, RMSEA = 0.087). Items were designed to assess three domains: (a) Adaptive Operational Skills, (b) Responsible GenAI Literacy, and (c) Critical Evaluation & Autonomous Use. Measurement invariance analyses supported scalar invariance across sex (female vs. male) and occupational status (student vs. workforce) groups. Construct validity was supported by positive correlations with GenAI acceptance (r = 0.81) and GenAI trust (r = 0.47). Semantic embedding analysis further supported the conceptual structure of the scale by showing distinct semantic clustering for Responsible GenAI Literacy and meaningful conceptual proximity between Adaptive Operational Skills and Critical Evaluation & Autonomous Use. These results suggest that the GAILS is a psychometrically and conceptually supported tool for assessing GenAI literacy gaps and informing educational, workplace, and policy interventions.

articles.title: The Phenomenology of Advanced Meditation Experiences and Interpretation of the Nature of Human Consciousness
articles.authors: Patrizio Tressoldi; Fabio Mattiussi
articles.abstract:
