Forty-five long-term meditators with a minimum of five years of continuous daily practice were requested to describe their highest meditative experiences using the micro-phenomenological self-inquiry (MPSI) method and to provide their interpretation of the nature of human consciousness.
The first-person accounts of meditators consistently reported profound and stable experiences of body and identity transcendence, often describing non-dual states and a pervasive sense of unity. Most participants understood consciousness to be universal in nature and not reducible to a byproduct of the brain.
These first-person accounts offer novel insights into the characteristics of long-term meditation experiences and the fundamental nature of consciousness.

articles.title: A Pattern of Relatively Conserved Fluency Indicates Preclinical Minor Cognitive Decline
articles.authors: Rain Simons; Andrew R. A. Conway
articles.abstract:
Objective: When neuropsychological testing is used for medical assessment of cognition, individual differences in premorbid ability may not be accounted for, leaving some individuals at risk for under-detection of impairment. We investigated whether patterns of relative performance in different cognitive domains could be used to detect early-stage cognitive decline in the absence of baseline performance data and irrespective of individual differences in overall performance.
Method: In an exploratory secondary analysis of data from 200 older adults followed longitudinally, we used profile analysis to compare the domain-specific performance of those who experienced minor cognitive decline over a 12-to-18-month interval with those who did not experience decline.
Results: We found that having experienced minor cognitive decline in the preceding 12 to 18 months was associated with a pattern of higher performance in fluency relative to performance in six other cognitive domains. In our study, this pattern of relative performance could be used to identify recent decline with 79.5% accuracy, 95% CI [73.2%, 84.9%], even without knowledge of overall performance. However, individuals who performed in the top third at baseline could not be shown to exhibit the same pattern of cross-domain cognitive performance following decline.
Conclusions: A pattern of higher performance in fluency relative to other cognitive domains may indicate recent minor cognitive decline. Results suggest that knowledge of a patient’s baseline cognitive ability or intelligence can inform the interpretation of neuropsychological test results. This study should be replicated using a dataset for which early adulthood cognitive scores are available.

articles.title: A Systematic Review of Effects of Long-Term and Advanced Meditation on Mental Health: Psychiatric Symptoms, Stress, and Challenging Events
articles.authors: Terje Sparby; Jerron Chan; Oliver Andersson Hugemark; Vanessa Naughton; Matthew Sacchet
articles.abstract: Meditation research has grown considerably, yet its clinical implications for advanced and long-term practitioners remain poorly understood. Meditation’s mental health implications extend beyond benefit, encompassing psychiatric risk, adverse experiences, and differentiating between meditative progress and psychopathology. This review synthesizes evidence on how advanced and long-term meditation affects psychiatric symptomatology, stress, and challenging practice-related experiences. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search across PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Embase on April 5, 2026 identified 1,229 articles, of which 52 met inclusion criteria following rigorous screening. Although findings suggest advanced practice confers deeper mental health benefits than non-advanced practices, significant literature gaps remain. Terminology is inconsistent across studies, adverse event monitoring is largely absent, and no established frameworks exist for distinguishing between potentially transformative challenges and the onset of psychopathology. Addressing these gaps demands safety-centered research protocols, clear risk stratification criteria, and evidence-based clinical guidelines governing contraindications and appropriate practitioner support.

articles.title: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Variational Bayesian Inference in Diagnostic Classification Models
articles.authors: Kazuhiro Yamaguchi
articles.abstract: Variational Bayesian (VB) estimation is commonly used in diagnostic classification models (DCMs). However, VB estimation underestimates posterior variance, so confidence intervals (CIs) based on the VB posterior are not appropriate. To overcome this limitation, bootstrap methods can be used. This study introduced bootstrap methods for interval estimation and described how they improve CIs for the DCMs parameter estimation. A simple simulation study demonstrated that the bootstrap procedures often improved CI coverage, although their performance varied across methods and conditions. These results support considering bootstrap methods when evaluating estimation uncertainty in VB estimation, while recognizing their condition-dependent performance.

articles.title: Two separable axes of intervention in a dependency-ordered recovery geometry
articles.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles.abstract: Catatonia recovers through capacities returning in a fixed dependency order, and benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy work without a known target. On an evidence-coupled bistable cascade over that order we take three quantities to be externally accessible: the root capacity, the coupling between capacities, and accumulated evidence. Here we show that evidence has no external port and the other two act on disjoint regions. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so acute conversion needs an excursion, whereas an additive excitatory drive converts on its own. Above one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, propagation separates into immediate, metastable and confined. On the modelled branch coupling alone shifts the resting first stage, so a treatment effective in both states is predicted to have separable excursion and coupling components, identifiable in model coordinates.

articles.title: The Eight-Mode AI Engagement Typology: Differential Cognitive Signatures and a Self-Report–Behavior Gap
articles.authors: Mark Keith; David A. Wood; Clay Posey
articles.abstract: Generative AI can improve assisted performance with differing consequences for learning, motivation, agency, and reliance. We introduce an eight-mode AI Engagement Typology and test parallel self-report and turn-level behavioral measures in working adults (N = 359) and students (N = 203; 171 with classifiable paired profiles). The modes show different cognitive associations. Oracle has the broadest adverse adjusted pattern, whereas Verification is the only agency-tier mode with favorable associations surviving correction; the proposed tier ordering receives only partial support, but Verification's predicted uniqueness is supported. Seven modes correlate positively with both perceived productivity and perceived dependency, while Verification has near-zero and small negative correlations, respectively. These cross-sectional associations do not establish a temporal tradeoff. Self-reported and observed mode profiles show near-zero correspondence: no correlation survives false-discovery correction, stable across three coding-protocol generations. In the learning task, explanation-seeking turns accompany higher quiz scores (in-sample), and AI-proposed moves comprised roughly half of codeable learning-task turns. In working adults, the modes add R² = .23 in-sample (.20 cross-validated) beyond usage measures. The results support multidimensional engagement and a self-report-behavior gap while leaving causal mechanisms, temporal effects, and full eight-mode resolution for future tests.

articles.title: A Bayesian account of line bisection in spatial neglect
articles.authors: Tianwei Gong; Bonan Zhao; Neil R Bramley; Christopher G. Lucas; Robert D McIntosh
articles.abstract: Spatial neglect is a neuropsychological syndrome characterized by an asymmetry of attention and behavior away from one side of space, following unilateral brain damage. We develop a Bayesian framework for understanding a specific manifestation of spatial neglect: the characteristic pattern of responses observed on line bisection tasks. When asked to mark the middle of a horizontal line, patients with neglect often bisect lines away from the neglected side, but can also show paradoxical "cross-over" responses, deviating toward the neglected side under some stimulus conditions. We model bisection as perceptual inference under uncertainty, in which an observer combines noisy estimates of the line endpoints with prior expectations about line length. In this framework, increased uncertainty about the left endpoint reduces the constraining influence of sensory evidence from that side, increasing the role of a task-level prior expectation about line length in shaping the direction and magnitude of bisection errors, including crossover effects. Applied to patient and control data, we found that neglect patients showed greater estimated uncertainty for the left endpoint than healthy controls, whereas right-endpoint uncertainty was comparatively similar across groups. Model-derived parameters were also associated with established measures of neglect and distinguished previously classified neglect patients from controls. These findings suggest that Bayesian perceptual inference provides a useful quantitative account of line bisection behavior in neglect, enriching our understanding of spatial neglect through the lens of perceptual uncertainty and top-down influences on perception.

articles.title: The Cognitive Science of Maria Montessori.
articles.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo
articles.abstract: Maria Montessori is among the most globally influential figures in the history of education, yet she remains almost entirely absent from the history of science. This paper argues that her absence is unwarranted, and that her work is best understood not as pedagogy but as the empirical investigation of cognitive development by a scientist trained in the positivist and evolutionary milieu of late nineteenth-century Rome. Drawing on Italian-language sources and untranslated early publications, we reconstruct her scientific formation, in particular her relationships with the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi and the experimental psychologist Sante De Sanctis. We believe that these relationships gave her a theory of cognitive development structured around three irreducible and simultaneous dimensions: individual variation, the designed material environment, and the socio-cultural context. The prepared environment, the central contribution of her method, was designed to make these dimensions explicit and tractable, and maps with notable precision onto frameworks that cognitive science has formalised only recently. We then ask why this scientific dimension of her work has gone so consistently unseen, identifying three historical and contingent causes: a communicative style bent by financial and political necessity, systematic losses in translation, and the structural exclusion she faced as a woman in the scientific institutions of her time. We close with the case of Jean Piaget, whose sustained exposure to Montessori's method, and subsequent formalisation of a developmental theory that diverged from hers on precisely the points where later research has moved back in her direction, offers the sharpest illustration of what the misreading has cost.

articles.title: A Small and Fragile Effect: Four Conceptual Replications of Dwyer et al. (2007) on Evaluative Conditioning of Foods with Body Images, and the Consequences of Stimulus-Assignment Choices
articles.authors: Patrycja Uram; Robert Balas; Sebastian Binyamin Skalski-Bednarz; Joanna Wąsowicz
articles.abstract: Dwyer et al. (2007) reported that foods paired with images of obese bodies became devalued, and that the devaluation survived extinction. We revisited both claims across four conceptual replications (total N = 274), crossing presentation duration with stimulus assignment. Studies 1a (N = 59) and 1b (N = 91) used long (7000 ms) and short (2500 ms) presentations and fixed food-to-condition assignment, unlike the original Experiment 1, which counterbalanced CS and US assignments across participants; Studies 2a (N = 59) and 2b (N = 65) used the same timings but randomised assignment afresh for each participant. A random-effects meta-analysis of participant-level acquisition contrasts gave dz = –0.15, 95% CI [–0.27, –0.04], I² = 0%. The direction matches the original, but the magnitude is substantially smaller than the approximate original-study benchmark in absolute magnitude (dz ≈ 0.49). Significance depended on how the eight food images were treated: with images fixed the pooled effect was reliable, but with stimuli modelled as a random factor it was not, F(1, 4087) = 2.90, p = .089. The assignment scheme did not moderate the estimate, F(1, 4087) = 0.0001, p = .994, but governed precision within our studies: fixed assignment left six denominator degrees of freedom for the stimulus-aware test, versus 869 and 966 under randomisation. The original strong, extinction-resistant devaluation was not reproduced. Our fixed-assignment variants additionally show that permanently tying a small stimulus set to conditions can severely weaken stimulus-level inference.

articles.title: Polarity and the speed of scalar implicature processing
articles.authors: Michael Vrazitulis; J E Loy; Vera Demberg
articles.abstract: Scalar implicatures (SIs) such as the inference from 'some' to 'some but not all' are known to vary in processing cost. According to the Polarity Hypothesis (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some'). We tested this prediction in a sentence–picture verification experiment with 538 English-speaking participants. Each participant judged whether sentences containing weak or strong scalar terms matched a corresponding picture, allowing us to measure response times as an index of processing effort. Our results showed no clear evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis; specifically, we found it to not generalise across the different scales included in our experiment. We additionally conducted a meta-analysis pooling our estimate with all existing evidence so far: the pooled effect is small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely in magnitude. Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect (Bott & Noveck, 2004), i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect. Overall, we conclude that polarity may influence the speed of scalar implicature processing, but that this effect is not robust across all types of scales.

articles.title: Day in the life: Mapping speech sound development from 2,000+ days of children’s everyday lives
articles.authors: Meg Cychosz; Sonia Patrizi; Daisy Ye; Julianna Gross; Emma Montilla; Jihyun Stephans; Rachel R Romeo; Dylan Chan
articles.abstract: A central question in human development is how biological maturation and experience combine to produce complex behavior. Child speech development is ideal for examining this question: it depends on species-specific anatomy and neural circuitry, yet experience strongly shapes its emergence. However, determining what drives the timeline of speech development has been difficult (1) theoretically, because anatomical growth and experience are confounded in typical human development, and (2) methodologically, because child speech is typically captured via structured assessments that provide only a limited snapshot of a child's abilities. Here, we apply automatic speech recognition to child-centered recordings, captured via wearable technology, that span 2,219 days from 660 typically-hearing and deaf/hard-of-hearing children (3–90 months). We show that speech milestones from babbling through consonant mastery are measurable from a single day of recording and predict clinical speech-language assessments. In deaf/hard-of-hearing children, babbling is graded by accumulated listening experience across hearing devices and degrees of hearing loss rather than strictly by biological age. By demonstrating that this aspect of child development is observable from everyday behavior, we offer a scalable pathway toward earlier detection of speech and language delays.

articles.title: Measuring Face Recognition Ability: Identifying Individuals at the Extremes of Performance
articles.authors: Joe DeGutis; Alison Campbell
articles.abstract: This chapter reviews contemporary approaches to measuring and classifying extremes of face recognition ability, with a focus on developmental prosopagnosia and super-recognizers, and considers whether these extremes reflect discrete categories or the tails of a continuous ability distribution. It traces the evolution of face memory and face perception tests, highlighting the strengths and limitations of widely used measures such as the Cambridge Face Memory Test, famous face memory tests, and modern face matching paradigms. The chapter critically evaluates dominant classification frameworks, including highly conservative “classic” criteria, symptom-first self-report approaches, and recently proposed multi-test expanded threshold frameworks inspired by neuropsychological and DSM-5 conventions. Particular emphasis is placed on methodological challenges that complicate extreme group identification, including variability in normative samples, reliance on single tests, limited insight and potential bias in self-report, and the statistical consequences of combining multiple thresholds. Drawing on evidence from both basic and applied research, the chapter argues that progress will depend on convergent, multi-measure classification strategies supported by transparent reporting, shared normative data, and continued refinement of objective tests. Together, these advances promise to improve the validity, reproducibility, and theoretical interpretability of research aimed at identifying and characterizing the extremes of face recognition ability.

articles.title: The “Feeling” of Inattention: ADHD Symptoms and Mind Wandering Beyond Remembered Thought Content
articles.authors: Liam Yeo; Emma Fernando; Nicholaus P. Brosowsky
articles.abstract: Mind wandering is frequently associated with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms in adults, yet the precise nature of this relationship remains unclear. The current study applied an approach from mind-wandering research to the context of ADHD by distinguishing between remembered mind wandering, defined as explicitly recalling off-task thought content, and subjective feelings of inattention, defined as sensing that one’s attention was off task without recalling specific thoughts. We investigated how these distinct aspects of off-task experience relate to ADHD symptomatology, well-being, impairment, and sustained-attention performance. Participants from university and online ADHD communities completed the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) with thought probes assessing remembered mind wandering and subjective inattention, along with measures of ADHD symptoms, well-being, and impairment. Results showed partially separable patterns of association: subjective feelings of inattention were associated with inattentive symptoms, well-being, impairment, and poorer SART performance, whereas remembered mind wandering was associated primarily with hyperactive–impulsive symptoms. These findings suggest that the association between mind wandering and ADHD depends on how off-task experience is defined and measured. More broadly, they highlight the importance of distinguishing metacognitive judgments about attentional state from reports of thought content when evaluating mind wandering, because reports of being off task may not always imply access to identifiable task-unrelated thoughts. By separating attentional state from accessible thought content, the present study helps clarify the complex relationship between mind wandering and ADHD and points to a broader measurement issue in research on inattention and off-task thought.

articles.title: The Mood-Attention Feedback Loop: Bidirectional Effects of Affect and Mind Wandering
articles.authors: Eniola Odeleye; Liam Yeo; Stephanie Lauren Souliere; Nicholas Daniel Evans; Nicholaus P. Brosowsky
articles.abstract: In the present study, we examined whether experimentally induced mood states causally influence mind wandering and sustained attention performance. Across three experiments, participants completed a positive, neutral, or negative mood induction followed by a sustained attention to response task. Mind wandering was assessed using probe‑caught thought reports in all experiments and retrospective reports in Experiments 2 and 3. Although the mood inductions reliably shifted self‑reported affect, we observed no direct effects of mood induction on probe‑caught mind wandering, retrospective mind wandering, or behavioral performance. We further explored the relationship between mood, mind wandering, and attention by fitting a series of structural equation models pooling data across all three experiments. These analyses indicated that mood inductions influenced mind wandering and performance indirectly through changes in experienced affect. Negative affect reliably predicted poorer attentional performance, whereas both positive and negative affect predicted changes in mind wandering. In addition, mind wandering during the task predicted subsequent reductions in mood, indicating a bidirectional relationship between mood and attention. Together, these findings suggest that mood induction does not directly alter mind wandering or sustained attention performance. Instead, mood and attention appear to interact dynamically through indirect and reciprocal pathways that unfold over time, underscoring the importance of modeling affect as a continuous, within‑person process rather than as a purely categorical experimental manipulation.

articles.title: The Morality-Fairness Split of Revenge Judgments
articles.authors: Xiao Min Chang; Ruth Speidel; Tina Malti
articles.abstract:
Revenge is among the most universal of human responses to harm, yet it is widely condemned.
Philosophers have long held that this reflects a dual conceptual space: revenge is morally wrong
because it inflicts harm, yet can appear "fair" from a retributive standpoint because it delivers
what the transgressor deserves. Although theorized across disciplines, these two distinct
elements have typically been conflated in developmental psychology. Across an ethnically
diverse sample of children, adolescents, and adults, we examined evaluations and justifications
of revenge on two dimensions: moral acceptability and fairness. The dimensions were distinct as
expected. Revenge was condemned more harshly as a moral matter than as a fairness issue, and
the two judgments were justified through distinct reasoning: fairness through concrete
reciprocity; moral acceptability through broader moral principle. Crucially, the dimensions
differed not only in degree but in consensus. Participants broadly agreed that revenge in
response to a single provocation is morally wrong, but diverged on whether it was fair, and this
moral consensus dissolved when transgressions were repeated. Justifications evolved with
development while evaluations remained stable. These findings suggest that condemning
revenge as morally wrong and deeming it unfair are separable judgments — the perceived
fairness of revenge, unlike its moral wrongness, is a contested — with implications for how
justice systems weigh punishment and desert.

articles.title: Expert Forecasts and Public Expectations of Future Global Warming
articles.authors: Danielle Goldwert; Madalina Vlasceanu
articles.abstract: Expert communities vary in projections of future global warming, raising the question of how forecasting sources  influence  public  expectations  of  climate  change.   Here,  we  examined  how  people  revise  predictions of  global  warming  by  2100  following  forecasts  from  different  expert  sources.    Participants  (N  =  1,996)were  randomly  assigned  to  nine  conditions,  receiving  projections  from  academics,  policymakers,  business leaders, innovators, researchers and reformers, artificial intelligence (AI), all expert sources simultaneously, as elf-selected source, or no information.  Participants initially underestimated warming relative to most experts. AI forecasts produced the largest increase in expected warming, despite academics and researchers being the most  trusted  sources  and  business  leaders  projecting  the  highest  temperature  increases.   Participants  showed greater Bayesian updating when they trusted the source.  Moreover, Republicans were three times more likely than Democrats to select AI as their information source. Finally, forecast updating did not increase climate policy support, which remained strongly associated with political ideology.

articles.title: Into the blue: A qualitative study of the acceptability of Wizso™ pellets for saving water by reducing toilet-flushing at home
articles.authors: Benjamin Gardner; Sophia Shaw-Brown; Pablo Pereira-Doel
articles.abstract: Water scarcity is increasing globally, creating a need for behavioural approaches to reduce domestic water demand. Reducing toilet-flushing after urination presents an opportunity to achieve substantial household water savings, but there is currently limited understanding about the acceptability of interventions designed to support this behaviour. This study examined public responses to a trial of commercially available, dissolvable toilet pellets that are designed to turn toilet water blue, so masking the sight and smell of unflushed urine and thereby facilitating reduced flushing. Twenty participants, recruited from southeast England, were given a free pack of 70 pellets to trial, and one week later completed semi-structured interviews regarding the acceptability of the pellets. Data were analysed using thematic analysis. Five themes were constructed relating to: practical facilitators and barriers to use, perceived aesthetic and sensory effectiveness of the pellets, social concerns around non-flushing behaviour, environmental motivations for water conservation and flushing as a socially grounded practice. Participants generally viewed the pellets as acceptable and easy to integrate into existing routines. However, acceptability was constrained by cleanliness norms, concerns about social judgement and discomfort with persistent disgust-related cues indicating toilet use. Although our participants appeared particularly environmentally conscious, our findings suggest that toilet pellets offer a potentially acceptable and promising opportunity to support water efficiency initiatives in the UK.

articles.title: Neither human nor rational:  how artificial intelligence reshapes conflict
articles.authors: Angelo Romano; Emanuele Bastianelli; Fernando P. Santos; I. Malavolta
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become pervasive decision-making tools in daily life, defense, and economic competition, critical questions arise: how do machines behave under conflict? how do they compare with human behavior? And ultimately, how does conflict change when machines replace humans? We address these questions through a large-scale behavioral experiment combining game theory with over 17,000 decisions from 20 Large Language Models (LLMs) and more than 500,000 decisions from 12,813 human participants across 51 societies. We compare human and LLM behavior in asymmetric incentivized attacker–defender contests, where agents can invest in conflict to exploit or protect resources. LLMs invest substantially less in conflict than humans, particularly in attack, yet we observe substantial heterogeneity across models. LLM decisions diverge systematically from both human patterns and game-theoretic predictions, positioning them as a distinct class of decision-making agents. To assess the consequences of a conflict dominated by AI agents, in a complementary study, we paired LLMs with human participants (N = 409) who knew their decisions might be replaced by those of an AI assistant. When acting on behalf of humans, LLMs largely outperformed human players in defense, yet performed worse in attack. This reveals a pronounced behavioral asymmetry: artificial agents do not simply mimic human strategy, but fundamentally reshape it. Our findings expose a tension between human competitive tendencies and the strategic logic of machines, raising urgent questions about responsibility, alignment, and the governance of conflict in human–AI systems.

articles.title: Domain-general object encoding ability explains shared variance between perception and memory factors
articles.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson; Andrew Tomarken; Isabel Gauthier
articles.abstract:
Domain-general object recognition ability (o) is an individual’s capacity to tell apart
similar objects. O has been measured using tasks that make strong demands on either
perception or memory. Both types of tasks ought to require precise encoding of high-level visual
details. However, the assumption that each task type measures perception and memory to a
differing extent has not been tested, nor has the critical assumption that they both tap into the
same high-level visual ability when other relevant abilities are controlled. An online sample (n =
275) completed a battery of perceptual and memory type object recognition tests alongside
tests of low-level perception, working memory, and general intelligence. Preregistered
structural equation models were used to examine the overlap among abilities. Perception and
memory o tests loaded onto two separable factors, with the perceptual o factor relating to low-
level visual perception and the memory o factor relating to working memory. Both o factors
were strongly correlated, and remained so when general intelligence, low-level perception and
working memory abilities were controlled. These results are consistent with the view that both
types of tasks measure the same o ability in addition to either perception or memory ability.
General intelligence explained a large share of the ability to make high-level visual
discriminations, but a substantial proportion of variance remained independent. The results
may be taken to suggest that both perception and memory o tests measure a domain-general,
high-level encoding ability.

articles.title: “Like a double-edged sword”: How ADHD and non-ADHD people perceive ADHD emotions
articles.authors: Sara Mae; Fay Sweeting; Emily Arden-Close; Rachel L Moseley-Braund
articles.abstract: Differences in emotion-related processes and experiences impact ADHD people’s wellbeing, but have historically been framed through a deficit-based lens, without sufficient recognition of interpersonal and environmental influences. We explored positive and challenging aspects of ADHD emotions, how these emotions were perceived by others and their impacts on relationships, eliciting perspectives from 15 ADHD people and 15 non-ADHD people (with ADHD loved ones) through semi-structured interviews and the Grid Elaboration Method respectively. Data were analysed using interpretative phenomenological analysis  and Reflexive Thematic Analysis respectively. Both groups reported that ADHD emotions co-existed as disabling and sustaining, strength and weakness. Societal pressures appeared to shape both how ADHD people experienced and expressed their emotions, which added to dysregulation; and how they were perceived by non-ADHD people, contributing to frustration. Emotion-related differences in ADHD impact the lives of ADHD and non-ADHD people, and are influenced by societal and systemic inequalities, though the extent to which this is the case is not yet fully understood.

articles.title: Distributed Brain Hypothesis: A Brain, Maybe, Bigger than We Though
articles.authors: Arash Javanbakht
articles.abstract: The dominant view in neuroscience treats the brain as the primary computational organ of cognition and emotion, with the peripheral nervous system supplying sensory input and executing motor and autonomic commands. Embodied and interoceptive theories acknowledge the role of bodily states, but they retain the brain as the sole site of computation, treating peripheral signals as something the brain interprets. This paper proposes the Distributed Brain Hypothesis: that specific extracranial neural networks, most plausibly the enteric and intrinsic cardiac nervous systems, perform local computation that is non-redundant with central processing, such that selectively disrupting peripheral activity produces deficits not explained by degraded input alone. I make the claim precise by contrasting two architectures, a centralized model in which the brain holds the only posterior over body states and a distributed model in which peripheral networks maintain their own local estimates. I review the neuroanatomical substrate that makes local computation possible, synthesize indirect functional evidence, and propose falsifiable predictions with experimental signatures, including a worked closed-loop gastric experiment, designed to separate non-redundant local computation from relay and modulation. I end with exploring clinical and research implications of these possibilities.

articles.title: Sharing Good Times and Recovering from Difficult Moments: Development and Validation of the Parenting Joy Scale
articles.authors: Jason W. Payne; Sebastian Dys; Kristen Anna; Patti Ranahan; Janet Mainland; Marlene Moretti
articles.abstract: Existing parenting measures primarily focus on the challenges and negative feelings of parenting, however there is a growing interest in developing scales that capture positive experiences. Two distinctly positive aspects of parenting are feelings of joy and happiness in the good times, and renewed closeness, comfort, and security when difficult moments are repaired. The Parenting Joy Scale (PJS; Moretti et al., 2026) was developed as a 16-item caregiver-report measure that captures two dimensions of positive experiences of parenting: Mutual Fun/Enjoyment (8 items) and Repair/Reunion (8 items). Across a clinical (N = 306) and a community sample (N = 152), confirmatory factor analyses supported this two-factor structure. Further, scalar invariance held across samples. Associations with attachment insecurity, parenting, and youth mental health situated the scale within a coherent nomological network. The PJS provides a foundation for testing developmentally contextualized and theoretically driven questions about what promotes the emergence of each parenting facet alone or in combination and their impacts on parent and child wellbeing and the quality of parent–child relationships.

articles.title: What drives early helping? Motor and social skills shape infant prosocial development across cultures.
articles.authors: Georgia Tuohy; Carlo Vreden; Herbert Ainamani; Prima Ainembabazi; Ellie Donnelly; Brenda Kakai; Precious Katusiime; Julia Landstedt; Eunice Ndyareeba; Josephine Paricia
articles.abstract: By their second year of life, infants across the globe reliably help others. Despite this apparent universality, little is known about the developmental mechanisms underlying early helping, including the role of the socio-cultural environment, as previous research has been heavily biased towards minority-world samples. To address this gap, we longitudinally examined multiple predictors of helping in a large cohort of infants from rural and urban Uganda (N=256), and the UK (N=59). At 10 months, we tested infants’ understanding of others’ needs using an eyetracking paradigm. At 16 months, we then assessed their spontaneous helping, maternal scaffolding, motor development, and social skills. Results showed that infants across all sites showed evidence of understanding others’ needs at 10 months, indicating cultural robustness in early prosocial cognition. Yet, by 16 months, cultural differences in helping emerged: Ugandan infants were more likely to help than UK infants, and Ugandan mothers used more assertive socialisation than UK mothers, who showed more deliberate scaffolding of helping. However, our findings showed that motor and social skills, rather than needs understanding or maternal socialisation, were the strongest drivers of early helping. By testing the influence of cognitive, social, motor and socialisation factors within a large diverse sample in a longitudinal cross-cultural design, our study provides the first developmental systems evidence of early helping with a large Majority-world sample beyond standard lab-settings and advances our understanding of prosocial development while promoting more inclusive developmental science.

articles.title: Modeling Environmental Behavior: Lessons from Social Computational Neuroscience
articles.authors: Veronika Wendler; Anne Saulin; Tony Craig; Caroline Moraes; Yansong Li; Chunliang Feng; Lei Zhang
articles.abstract: Addressing climate change requires a better understanding of environmental behavior. Yet environmental-behavior research has largely focused on single observed outcomes, with limited use of computational models to identify the processes through which these behaviors emerge. Many environmental decisions are also socially interdependent, meaning individuals often must weigh personal costs against benefits for others, future generations, and collective outcomes. Social computational neuroscience provides formal models for examining precisely such value-based and social decisions, making it a useful foundation for environmental research. However, environmental decisions also have distinctive features, as their consequences are often delayed, uncertain, and difficult to observe directly. We therefore propose that repeated, computationally structured tasks can complement conventional environmental experimental designs by estimating latent decision processes rather than only measuring behavioral outcomes. We introduce computational frameworks from social computational neuroscience, focusing on subjective-value, reinforcement-learning, drift-diffusion, and agent-based models, and discuss how to adapt them to study environmental behavior. We illustrate this approach with an eco-product choice task integrating product design, learning from feedback, visual attention, and choice. Overall, we propose social computational neuroscience as a framework for linking individual decision mechanisms to socially situated and collective environmental behavior, contributing to the emerging field of environmental social neuroscience.

articles.title: Keep It in Sight: Reward Function Compression Through Goal Visibility
articles.authors: Xitong Chen; Chaofan Li; Gaia Molinaro; Anne Collins
articles.abstract:
Humans often learn from outcomes defined by abstract goals rather than explicit rewards. This flexibility supports real-world behavior but typically causes slower and less efficient learning compared to directly observable rewards. The reward function compression hypothesis proposes that this inefficiency arises because evaluating abstract goal outcomes burdens limited cognitive resources otherwise directed toward learning, and that this cognitive cost can decrease over iterations when a specialized reward function over a compressed goal feature space is learned. Alternatively, this cost could simply arise from an immediate dual-task effect, where goal maintenance imposes a cost on decisions. 
To arbitrate between these two hypotheses, we extended a goal-based learning protocol to offload goal or non-goal information to a visible reminder. While the dual-task hypothesis predicts that this manipulation should immediately rescue goal-based learning, the reward compression hypothesis predicts a gradually acquired benefit proportional to the compressibility of the match/mismatch rule. Our results (N = 61)  supported the reward compression hypothesis. Visible goals gradually reduced learning efficiency costs, eventually approaching the point-based learning performance. An equivalent decrease in memory load (visible non-goals) did not boost learning as much, highlighting the role of outcome evaluation in goal-directed learning. Computational modeling revealed that outcome evaluation efficiency, proxied by participants' ``reward collection'' response time, specifically influenced participants' learning processes, rather than decision noise. These results show that learning from goals depends on our ability to train efficient estimators of outcome values, which is facilitated by keeping goals in sight.

articles.title: Translation and Validation of a Japanese Version of the Short General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (Short GAAIS-10): The GAAIS-10-J
articles.authors: Yu Kanno; Rina Kagawa
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes widespread, brief instruments measuring general attitudes toward AI are needed. We translated the Short General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (Schepman & Rodway, 2026) into Japanese (GAAIS-10-J) and evaluated its psychometric properties. Among 468 Japanese adults (in their 20s to 60s), we examined the factor structure, item characteristics, internal consistency, and associations with external variables. A retest one month later (N = 429) assessed temporal stability. Confirmatory factor analysis generally supported the original two-factor structure (Positive and Negative), although not all preregistered fit criteria were met. Item-level analyses were largely acceptable, and both subscales showed good internal consistency and adequate test–retest reliability. Positive and reverse-scored negative subscales showed expected associations with perceived usefulness, ease of use, AI usage intention, and comfortableness with hypothetical AI applications. The GAAIS-10-J appears to be a brief, reliable measure of general attitudes toward AI among Japanese-speaking adults.

articles.title: AI-driven interventions correct misinformation, but their effectiveness fades from text to images to video
articles.authors: Mihir Pandey; Shail Shankar
articles.abstract:
AI-driven interventions promise rapid, scalable correction of misinformation, but most evidence
for their effectiveness comes from text-based falsehoods, even though misinformation
increasingly spreads through images and video. In an experiment with 259 participants, we
tested how well an AI-driven intervention corrected false claims presented in each of these formats.
Effectiveness declined steadily across modalities: strongest for text, moderate for photos,
and weakest for video. AI-driven interventions are a useful tool, but they need to be honed for
the visual formats where misinformation now thrives.

articles.title: This Is Not the ex-Gaussian Model You Are Looking For: On the Default Parameterization of Bayesian ex-Gaussian Models in brms
articles.authors: Jason Geller; Bernhard Angele; Dominique Makowski
articles.abstract:
The ex-Gaussian distribution is a popular mathematical model for analyzing response time
  (RT) data because it separates the central portion of the distribution,
  captured by the Gaussian parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$, from the positively
  skewed tail, captured by the exponential parameter $\tau$. Researchers often use these
  parameters to make inferences about underlying cognitive processes. As Bayesian methods
  have become increasingly accessible, complex ex-Gaussian models can now be fit
  with relative ease, and in R, the {brms} package makes this especially
  straightforward. However, it is important to recognize that the default
  parameterization offered by {brms} does not map onto the classical
  parameterization familiar to many researchers in experimental psychology in the
  default model, $\mu$ indexes the mean of the full ex-Gaussian distribution rather
  than the location of the Gaussian component alone. This distinction matters
  because changes in the Gaussian location and changes in the exponential tail
  can offset one another at the level of the overall mean, so some published
  studies may have drawn incorrect inferences from effects estimated on the
  default $\mu$ parameter. Using simulated data and a published finding we highlight 
  how using the default parameterization can lead to misleading inferences. We then demonstrate 
  how to fit the classical parameterization directly using the {cogmod} package, with the aim of helping researchers 
  and reviewers align ex-Gaussian model parameters with their theoretical questions.

articles.title: Disentangling declarative and procedural working memory: Sensorimotor electroencephalography activity distinguishes unknown and known potential actions
articles.authors: Isabel Courage; Freek van Ede; Gidon T. Frischkorn
articles.abstract: Working memory (WM) encompasses information for tasks at hand as well as how to act on this information. Researchers have distinguished between declarative and procedural WM, the declarative part being WM’s content information while the procedural part includes how to execute actions. Procedural WM representations are theoretically distinguished from declarative representations by being configured for direct execution in a prepared reflex format. However, past evidence is mixed on how to delineate these representation formats based on this prepared reflex property. In parallel, neurophysiological studies examined how action preparations unfold when future actions are known at encoding. A direct comparison between neural activity linked to putative action plans when future actions are unknown at encoding (declarative allegedly) versus known (procedural allegedly) is still lacking. Here, we sought evidence for the theoretical proposed distinction between declarative and procedural WM by tracking action engagement through attenuations of sensorimotor mu-alpha and mu-beta electroencephalography (EEG) activity. To additionally assess possible long-term memory (LTM) contributions to WM performance due to repetition, we tracked action planning separately for repeated and unrepeated WM representations. Results show greater attenuations in sensorimotor mu-alpha and mu-beta activity for representations with known actions relative to unknown actions, both when unrepeated and repeated. Thus, EEG markers associated with action plans provide evidence for a distinction between declarative and procedural WM representations. Moreover, sensorimotor attenuations for procedural unrepeated relative to repeated representations did not differ warranting future studies examining the influence of potential LTM contributions beyond current boundary conditions.

articles.title: Predicting and Interpreting Psychological Distress and Mental Health Treatment Experience from Life Experiences and Everyday Behaviors
articles.authors: Takumi Kitahara; Masashi Mizuno
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to examine whether psychological distress and treatment experience among university students can be predicted using machine learning models based on daily experiences and behaviors. Participants were university students who completed a web-based survey assessing psychological distress (K10 scores), treatment experience, and various life and behavioral factors. To reduce self-report bias, behaviorally specific and concrete variables were selected as predictors. Multiple models, including linear/logistic regression, Random Forest, and CatBoost, were trained and evaluated using nested five-fold cross-validation. The models explained approximately 30% of the variance in K10 scores, and classification performance reached an AUC of .77. Across both studies, key predictors consistently included seeking mental health information, persistent rumination over minor issues, and perceived lack of parental respect. Additional predictors included satisfaction with university entrance exam results and drinking frequency for distress, and experiences of bullying and family history of mental illness for treatment experience. These findings suggest that everyday experiences and behaviors may serve as useful indicators of psychological distress and help-seeking among university students.

articles.title: Theory-guided passive sensing in mental health: interpretable indices before prediction
articles.authors: Yufei Wang; Markus Bühner; Maximilian Hagspiel; Yannik Terhorst
articles.abstract: Passive sensing via smartphones and wearables is increasingly used to predict mental health outcomes, yet the predictive accuracy of these models remains highly variable. Performance obtained in small, homogeneous samples often drops in larger and more diverse ones, and individual features can reverse their association with symptoms between studies. These issues may share a root: behavioral data are used as raw predictors, optimizing black-box models for prediction accuracy, without asking whether these predictors are meaningful or stable. We suggest that the field could benefit from a paradigm shift to a theory-driven, interpretable representation of behavioral data. We propose theory-guided passive sensing, in which theoretically related features are grouped into behavioral indices, validated against structured clinical assessment, before entering any predictive model. This reframing, from optimizing algorithms to validating indices, would make results comparable across studies and give clinicians interpretable, actionable inputs for monitoring and intervention. Cardiology, sleep medicine and affective computing each made this transition. We set out what it would look like in mental health and what the field stands to gain.

articles.title: A Bayesian Linear Mixed Model for Estimating Optimal Dynamic Treatment Regimes from Multisite Data
articles.authors: Hangil Noah Hong; Kazuya Fujita
articles.abstract: Dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) are sequences of decision rules that take an individual's covariates and intervention history as input and output recommended interventions. To gather large, representative samples to estimate optimal DTRs, data are often collected in multisite settings. However, many existing methods for estimating optimal DTRs assume independent and identically distributed observations. This assumption ignores site heterogeneity and may result in suboptimal treatment strategies. Here, we build upon the Bayesian Machine Learning framework and propose a Bayesian Machine Learning Linear Mixed Model (BML-LMM) for multisite data. The proposed approach shares information across sites and models between-site heterogeneity. We conduct simulation studies to compare the proposed approach with other DTR models. The simulation results show that the proposed approach outperforms non-hierarchical models in the presence of site heterogeneity while performing comparably in the absence of heterogeneity. The paper concludes with a discussion of the proposed approach and its limitations.

articles.title: INDIVIDUAL VARIATION IN INFANT SPEECH PROCESSING: IMPLICATIONS FOR LANGUAGE ACQUISITION THEORIES
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: To what extent does language acquisition recruit domain-general processing mechanisms? In this dissertation, evidence concerning this question is garnered from the study of individual differences in infant speech perception and their predictive value with respect to language development in early childhood. In the first experiment, variation in the processing of a linguistic unit at six months was found to predict vocabulary development at around 2 years of age, whereas processing of a non-unit did not. In the second experiment, one possible source for that variation in linguistic performance was assessed, namely information processing abilities. Infants were tested on the same linguistic task as in Experiment 1, and on a well-researched task that yields a measure of information processing in infancy. No covariance was found between measures gathered in the linguistic and the information processing tasks. In a third experiment, the impact of variation in the infants’ input on their speech processing was investigated. Correlations between infants’ performance in a speech sound discrimination task and acoustic characteristics of their primary caregivers’ speech were investigated. Two types of acoustic characteristics were measured; some were not relevant to the speech sound being tested, but are known to influence infants’ attention and learning (pitch and pitch modulations); others were specific to the contrast tested. Results suggested that only those characteristics relevant to the contrast being tested affected infants’ speech processing. In sum, these three experiments and extensive literature reviews suggest specific ways in which domain-general factors (such as attentional mechanisms) are involved in infants’ development of linguistic knowledge. While these factors appear to play a role in the learning of phonological units, their influence may not be evident once linguistic categories are already established.

articles.title: An Object’s Motion, but not its Sound, Influences its Perceived Similarity to Other Object Shapes
articles.authors: Martina Andrea Seveso; Rebecca Hirst; Alan O'Dowd; Fiona Nora Newell
articles.abstract: The perceived similarity between object shapes can act as an organisation principle for categorisation: objects with similar shape features are more likely to be grouped together into a meaningful object category. However, objects can be represented based on multiple featural dimensions, including across modalities, rendering object categorisation a more complex process. Inter-item similarity may be determined by an integrated combination of cues or by each featural dimension separately. Here we investigated whether motion and sound influence inter-item similarity judgements of novel objects based on shape alone. In Experiment 1, we found that object shapes with similar motion patterns were perceived as more similar than shapes with mis-matched or no motion. However, the addition of (movement-correlated) sounds did not further influence perceived shape similarity. In Experiment 2 we used a Garner Interference task (i.e., shapes are classified based on one relevant dimension while ignoring an irrelevant one) to determine the nature of the influence of motion. The results indicated that object motion is integrated into the representation of object shape in memory. Our findings suggest that modality specific cues can be integrated into an object’s representation and have implications for understanding how novel object categories are formed from multisensory featural information.

articles.title: Speech sound categories in language acquisition and learning (2006 Master's thesis)
articles.authors: Alejandrina Cristia; Alex Eguiluz
articles.abstract: Phonological processes and patterns in spoken languages often involve groups of sounds. It has been assumed that this is because the primitives on which phonology operates are abstract features shared by a group of sounds. There are two opposing views as to how features arise. One view ascribes them to a Universal Grammar that is part of the genetic endowment of humans (the linguistic hypothesis), while the other proposes that language users induce features from their linguistic experience (the phonetic hypothesis). This thesis tests the predictions that these views make on language learning using an artificial grammar paradigm to test learning of a linguistic set of sounds and a phonetic set of sounds by three groups of subjects: seven month-old infants, fourteen-month-old infants and adults. The results of these experiments suggest that learning of phonological patterns involving groups of sounds through a perceptual task is possible only in the youngest age. These results seem to support the linguistic hypothesis, since only the linguistically-based grouping was learned. Further, a developmental trend is suggested, such that younger infants group sounds into phonological classes, while fourteen-month-old infants, like adults, tend not to rely on phonological classes when learning phonotactic constraints.

articles.title: Linking Eyewitness Recognition Memory to Identification Accuracy using Item Response Theory
articles.authors: Paul Riesthuis; Henry Otgaar; Renan Benigno Saraiva; Charlotte A Bücken
articles.abstract:
Objective(s): Eyewitness testimony plays an important role in legal proceedings, particularly when other evidence is limited. Although extensive research has examined factors that influence eyewitness memory and eyewitness identification, the relationship between these two aspects of eyewitness evidence remains poorly understood. In the present study, we examined the relationship between eyewitness memory and identification accuracy using an item response theory (IRT) framework.
Hypotheses: We predicted that participants who accurately identified the perpetrator would demonstrate higher recognition memory performance on both memory for persons and memory for the witnessed event  than participants who identified a filler or made no identification.
Method: In a pilot study (N = 175) and a preregistered main study (N = 794), participants watched a mock crime video including two perpetrators from the Jena Eyewitness Research Stimuli (Kruse & Schweinberger, 2023). Participants then completed a 40-item two-alternative forced-choice recognition memory task and made identification decisions from two simultaneous eight-person lineups.
Results: The IRT model identified two latent dimensions of eyewitness memory: Person memory and Event memory. Interval-based hypothesis testing indicated a meaningful association between eyewitness identification accuracy and Person memory: The estimated difference in recognition performance exceeded our smallest effect size of interest (1 detail). In contrast, identification accuracy was not meaningfully associated with Event memory.
Conclusions: Eyewitness memory and identification are related, but their association depends on the type of memory assessed. Person memory (e.g., perpetrator, victim), but not Event memory (e.g., a theft), was meaningfully associated with identification accuracy. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing different dimensions of eyewitness memory and considering the psychometric properties of memory measures when examining factors that may undermine eyewitness memory. In particular, researchers should carefully consider which aspect of eyewitness memory their measures assess when drawing conclusions about factors that may affect eyewitness identification accuracy.

articles.title: Modeling Digit Span Test Performance in Cancer Patients: Working Memory Capacity, Attention & Executive Function
articles.authors: Ruben Daniel Potthoff; Sanne Schagen; Joost Agelink van Rentergem
articles.abstract:
Cancer survivors often exhibit problems in attention, working memory, and executive function. Digit span forward and backward tests are widely used to assess these cognitive  domains but do not isolate specific cognitive processes.
We compared 260 breast cancer patients diagnosed with metastatic disease —of which 151 (58%) had previously received treatment (hormonal N=141, 54%, chemotherapy N=126, 48%, targeted N=3, 1%), with most receiving more than one treatment (N=116, 45%)— to 130 non-cancer controls using a digital version of the digit span test. Traditional analysis showed patients performed significantly worse on backward digit span for maximum span and total correct (d=0.38, p < .001; d=0.37, p < .001), while no differences emerged in forward digit span (p = .09, p = .08). Results did not depend on treatment type, reported fatigue or psychological distress.
Using a novel hierarchical Bayesian cognitive process model, we disentangled three processes: working memory capacity, attentional decay, and executive decay. Working memory capacity and attentional decay contribute to both digit span tests, while executive decay affects only backward digit span. The cancer patients showed worse working memory capacity compared to controls (d=0.37, CI [0.13, 0.59]), with no significant differences in attentional (d=0.23, CI [-0.08, 0.55]) or executive decay (d=0.18, CI [-0.37, 0.74]).
Working memory capacity, attentional decay, and executive decay processes provide a more detailed understanding of digit span performance. This process-level analysis shows that lowered digit span test performance in cancer patients may reflect deficits of working memory rather than deficits of attention or executive function.

articles.title: The Price of Speaking Fluently: How the Sublexical Bottleneck Makes Speech Far from Perfect
articles.authors: Marina Laganaro; Marco Sala
articles.abstract: Speaking is a highly practiced activity in humans’ life, with about two hours of speech production, corresponding to ~16’000 words produced per day. In spite of such high practice, speaking is far from being perfect: all speakers produce at least one slip of the tongue every few minutes. Such error rate indicates that the speech production system is imperfect, but is good-enough for human communication. The non-optimality of the language production system has been attributed mainly to lexical selection. However, a large proportion of slips of the tongue involves phonological/sublexical errors (e.g. “this fiece is beautiful” for “this piece is beautiful”), meaning that the current hypothesis of non-optimal lexical selection cannot provide an explanation for those highly frequent types of errors. Here we present the arguments for an alternative hypothesis, namely that sublexical encoding processes are not fast enough relative to conceptual, syntactic and lexical encoding, causing a bottleneck. We will first remind the current claims of the non-optimal but good-enough language production system before reviewing empirical evidence in favor of a sublexical bottleneck: (i) high occurrence of sublexical errors in slips of the tongue corpora across languages, (ii) the mechanisms that have been proposed for the production of sublexical errors, (iii) the span and flexibility of phonological advance planning and its relation to control of co-activation and error monitoring. Based on the review we will conclude on a detailed proposal of the sublexical bottleneck and argue that it largely contributes to the imperfect but good-enough language system.

articles.title: Where do disfluencies come from? Towards a mechanistic account
articles.authors: Aurélie Pistono; Robert Hartsuiker
articles.abstract:
Naturalistic speech is strewn with disfluencies, such as repetitions (the the ball), filled pauses
(the um ball), or self-corrections (the pall..ball). Understanding where these phenomena come
from is important because disfluencies provide a window into the interaction between speech
planning, execution, and monitoring, while also influencing how interlocutors interpret
speakers and their messages. Focusing on neurotypical adult speech production, this review
examines accounts that attribute disfluencies to errors, planning delays, or communicative
signaling, together with evidence linking difficulties at different production stages to partly
distinct but overlapping disfluency patterns. We then propose MONET (MONitoring for Error
and Time), a mechanistic framework that explains how the interplay between speech
planning, execution, and monitoring may lead speakers to pause, repeat, interrupt, or repair
their speech. We outline its empirical grounding, derive testable predictions, and identify
directions for computational implementation.

articles.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of stress assessment in young people’s daily lives
articles.authors: Laura Elisabeth Meine; Paula Philippi; Björn Schlier; Aleksandra Kaurin
articles.abstract: Stress is a major risk factor for mental disorders, many of which first emerge during adolescence. Given the proliferation of studies of stress in daily life, we systematically reviewed how stress is conceptualised, operationalised, and quantified in youths’ everyday lives (preregistration: https://osf.io/cxpmw). Two independent reviewers screened PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Embase, and preprint servers for intensive longitudinal assessment studies of stress (≥1 measurement/day for ≥5 days) in participants aged ≤25 years. Design, measures, sampling, and risk of bias (adapted NIH tool) were extracted, and comparable results evaluated using multilevel random-effects meta-analysis. Across 180 identified studies (N=27,515), designs and stress measurement approaches showed substantial heterogeneity. Despite this, daily stress was robustly associated with depression (r=0.30-0.35, 95% CI 0.21-0.45) and anxiety (r=0.36-0.55, 95% CI 0.28-0.60). Emerging best practices and key literature gaps are highlighted.

articles.title: Strategic learning of people's names as a function of expected utility in young and older adults
articles.authors: Christel Devue; Marie Badolle; Serge Brédart
articles.abstract: People’s names are notoriously challenging to learn at all ages, more so than semantic information. Because people are somewhat aware of memory limitations and of their own difficulty of learning names, they might spontaneously use cost-efficient encoding strategies whereby they devote more memory resources to the names of people that are most likely to be useful to learn than others. To test this hypothesis, we told young and older participants that they would judge excerpts of a new TV series about a group of twelve musicians and that they could first review information about the characters to facilitate the upcoming viewing, which consisted of face-name-instrument triplets. Further, the probability of appearance of each character was specified via an importance label (main or secondary characters, bit parts). Participants then performed a surprise cued recall test and recalled names, instruments and importance labels associated with pictures. Unsurprisingly, young adults had better memory performance than older ones and semantic information was better recalled than names. In line with a cost-efficient encoding strategy, participants in both groups recalled names and semantic information of the most important characters better, suggesting they had prioritised encoding information about those characters to the detriment of others. Interestingly, there were individual differences in spontaneous encoding strategies used. People who reported using cost-efficient strategies had better memory performance than others and individuals who remembered more semantic information about main characters than about bit parts also did so with names, suggesting that cost-efficient strategies improves the encoding of two types of information.

articles.title: Ready and Willing? Psychological Conditions for Demand-Side Climate Policy in a High-Income Country
articles.authors: Alaa Aldoh; Jan Michael Bauer; Joachim Peter Tilsted; Mads Ejsing; Cameron Brick; Kristian Steensen Nielsen
articles.abstract: Climate policy in high-income countries disproportionately prioritizes supply-side solutions over demand-side solutions that often require behavioral change among citizens. One reason for this skewed prioritization may be policymakers’ skepticism about citizens’ readiness and capacity for behavior change. Yet, it remains unclear whether this skepticism reflects the actual conditions around demand-side engagement in the population, how climate-relevant perceptions interrelate as a system, and which factors predict perceived feasibility of changing high-impact behaviors. We address these questions using a nationally representative survey of 2,005 adults in Denmark—a high-income, climate-progressive country where supply-side solutions dominate despite ambitious mitigation targets. We map the structure of climate-relevant perceptions using psychological network analysis and estimate associations with perceived behavioral plasticity across eight high-impact behaviors using Bayesian ordinal regression. Results show that the Danish public is highly concerned about climate change and expresses a strong personal responsibility for mitigation. Perceived behavioral plasticity closely tracked perceived (but not objective) climate footprints of behaviors. Carbon footprint literacy was generally low, with participants overestimating the footprints of low-impact behaviors (e.g., waste sorting) and underestimating high-impact ones (e.g., dietary change). Network analysis revealed a dense interconnected system with personal responsibility as the most central node; perceived behavioral plasticity clustered with psychological factors (descriptive norms, efficacy, climate change concern, personal responsibility, and responsibility of households in reducing climate change), suggesting these constructs form a mutually reinforcing system. Regression models indicate that personal responsibility, climate change concern, perceived behavioral impact, and social norms consistently relate to the plasticity of eight impactful climate-relevant behaviors, and higher-income households reported lower plasticity of several behaviors. Together, these findings challenge the dismissal of demand-side solutions. The psychological conditions for behavioral engagement are favorable, and realizing this potential will require pairing communication strategies that strengthen norms and correct misperceptions of behavioral impact with structural policies that make high-impact change affordable and accessible.

articles.title: Causal inference with Bayesian regression modeling: A tutorial
articles.authors: Lena Holzwarth; Michael Franke
articles.abstract: This tutorial provides a first general introduction to causal inference with the do-calculus, as introduced in the work of Judea Pearl and a hands-on programming example in R for an artificial data set instantiating Simpson's paradox, showcasing the use of Bayesian regression modeling to obtain causal effect estimates with quantified uncertainty.

articles.title: Envisioning the Future of Social Robots in Education: Perceptions, Applications, and AI Literacy for the Public Good
articles.authors: Luca M. Leisten
articles.abstract: This thesis investigates alternative social robot designs and deployment strategies to support children’s learning and equip them with the necessary Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy to interact safely and responsibly with AI. Social robots offer significant promise as embodied learning partners, yet their integration into K-12 classrooms is hindered by high costs, technical complexity, and limited stakeholder involvement. To address these barriers, this thesis evaluates how alternative robot designs and deployment strategies, such as soft robots and “do-it-yourself” (DIY) robotic toolkits, could create more transparent and accessible tools. By exploring children’s baseline knowledge, educator perceptions, and the impact of robot assembly on learning outcomes, this work seeks to move beyond expensive, black-box systems toward accessible, community-driven, and pedagogically grounded social robots designed for the public good. Across four mixed-methods studies, this thesis captures the perspectives of 660 children, parents, teachers, and principals, using surveys, focus groups, interviews, and an active control group design. The results indicate that while these alternative designs could effectively support children’s learning in some contexts, the technology seems more ready than the system around it. Children lack the foundational literacy to engage with AI safely and critically; stakeholders across the educational ecosystem have legitimate and largely unaddressed concerns about equity, governance, and pedagogical control; and teachers hold perceptual biases that limit their ability to deploy different robots effectively. To bridge these gaps, I propose “The Four C’s for Educational Social Robotics”, a visionary roadmap that moves from the minimally designed robot itself (C1: Conscious Design), to the child who builds and personalizes it (C2: Co-Evolving Companions), to the curriculum that embeds it across subjects and age groups (C3: Cross-Curricular Integration), to the community that governs and sustains it (C4: Community Governance). Ultimately, this thesis contributes evidence-based guidelines for a more accessible, realistic, and pedagogically grounded deployment of social robots as community-driven tools, through which children may develop the knowledge, critical awareness, and agency to navigate an AI-shaped world.

articles.title: Experience with odors matters for mental simulation of odor and taste: comparing acquired and congenital anosmia
articles.authors: Bea van den Berg; Robert Pellegrino; Laura Jane Speed; Ilja Croijmans
articles.abstract: Reading a description of a simmering curry can conjure the mental representation of the smell of toasted spices, but this might be difficult for someone who has never smelled it before. Grounded theories of language posit that experiential history correlates with the ability to mentally simulate sensations. However, how sensory history affects this process in individuals with olfactory deficits remains unclear. This study investigated whether losing the sense of smell reshapes the simulation of food, and whether the timing of that loss matters. People with congenital anosmia (no smell across the lifespan), acquired anosmia (smell lost later in life), and a normal sense of smell rated the extent to which they could imagine the odor, taste/flavor, and texture evoked by neutral and sensory-rich food descriptions, then reported how much they desired each food. Odor simulation was most impaired in congenital anosmia and intermediate in acquired anosmia, a gradient showing that experience supports imagined smell. Taste/flavor simulation further dissociated the two groups: acquired anosmics simulated taste less than normosmics, whereas congenital anosmics did not differ, plausibly because they never formed flavor as a fusion of taste and smell in the first place. Texture simulation was preserved across all groups. Critically, following the onset of smell loss, acquired anosmics increasingly simulated the remaining modalities of taste and texture, and this heightened simulation predicted greater desire for the food. Together these findings ground food simulation in sensory history and show that, when one sense is lost, simulation reorganizes around the modalities that remain.

articles.title: A computational model of infant lexical stress preferences: Is the trochaic bias in English an emergent property of chunk learning?
articles.authors: Andrew Jessop; Fernand Gobet; Julian Pine
articles.abstract: From early in development, children acquiring English as their first language show a preference for words with trochaic stress (strong-weak: doctor, candy, broken) compared to words with iambic stress (weak-strong: giraffe, police, forgot). Since children develop this trochaic bias as they become more familiar with English, it could be an emergent property of the statistical learning mechanisms that allow infants to discover words embedded in their continuous input. We tested this hypothesis using simulations with the CIPAL architecture, which represents the patterns it encounters by learning a diverse collection of chunks. The model was trained with samples of English child-directed speech, then presented with 24 trochaic and 24 frequency-matched iambic words. CIPAL showed a consistent preference for the trochaic items; they were more likely to be represented with single chunks in long-term memory, they were processed using fewer chunks, and they had faster processing times compared to the iambic items. CIPAL also demonstrated an iambic bias when the phonemes in the training samples were presented in reverse order, consistent with evidence that children’s stress preferences reflect the prosodic structure of their input. These results suggest that the trochaic bias in English can emerge through an incremental chunking process, which favours trochaic sequences because they are the most efficient way of processing English input.

articles.title: The Impact of Long-term Interactions with a Digital Voice Agent on Trust and Roles Within a Household
articles.authors: Aline Moore Lorusso; Ghislaine Lex van den Boogerd; Melissa Jansen; Ann Hogenhuis; Ruud Hortensius
articles.abstract: Digital voice assistants (DVAs) provide information and support to users in a household across a wide variety of tasks. While they are part of a social system in the household, earlier research has largely ignored how DVAs impact this system. This study investigates how long-term DVA usage affects trust and roles of the users and their household. Using a multi-methods approach, we measured behavioural and self-reported trust, mapped the dynamic position of a DVA in the household, and the impact on the roles of household members over time across three experiments (combined n > 250; all DVA owners). In Experiment 1 and 2, participants completed an Information Dilemma Task, ranking whom they would be more likely to approach from their household (including their DVA) for dilemmas across domains (entertainment, social, domestic, and knowledge). They rated how much they trust the agents’ responses (Experiment 1) or indicated their general trust of the agent (Experiment 2). Results showed that the DVA was predominantly approached and trusted in the knowledge, but not social domain regardless of DVA ownership duration. However, we observed a decrease in trust in the DVA over time. We also found that approaching behaviour of other roommates changed across ownership-time: a first indication of changing dynamics in the household with the presence of a DVA. In Experiment 3, we interviewed short- and long-term users of DVAs. This qualitative approach provided converging evidence that DVA-owners, although occasionally personifying the device, use and trust it mainly in a functional manner and not a social one, with a small indication of prolonged usage impacting the dynamics in the household. While task measures did not point directly at an objective impact of ownership time, the interview data suggested a subjective experience of ownership time. In sum, while DVAs are mainly used for utilitarian reasons, their effect on household dynamics suggests its potential of reshaping roles in the household in the future.

articles.title: Beyond verbal irony: Nonliteral evaluative stance in Mandarin-speaking family interaction with preschool children
articles.authors: Jiayi Zhong; Yibin Zhang
