articles.abstract: This exploratory corpus study examines naturally occurring ironic and teasing evaluations in dinner-table interaction involving Mandarin-speaking preschool children and their families. We analyzed 71 video-linked sessions from the ZhouDinner corpus (23.67 hours; 20,055 transcribed utterances). Independent screening yielded 212 candidate entries; after adjudication, 137 episodes were retained, including 32 literal comparison cases, 8 cases of strict verbal irony, and 97 cases of non-oppositional teasing. Teasing was about 12.1 times as frequent as strict irony and occurred at 4.10 episodes per hour (4.84 per 1,000 utterances), compared with 0.34 per hour (0.40 per 1,000 utterances) for strict irony. Adult caregivers produced all eight strict-irony episodes and 90 of the 97 teasing episodes; target children produced seven teasing episodes and no strict irony. Nearly half of the teasing episodes served behavioural regulation (48/97, 49.5%), while 38 (39.2%) served affiliative play. Six of the seven child-produced teases were responsive or collaboratively established rather than independently initiated. Recipient uptake also differed descriptively: strict irony was followed mainly by compliance/repair or no observable response, whereas teasing elicited a wider range of receipts, including laughter and playful denial. Verbal, prosodic, and embodied resources overlapped substantially across the two categories. These findings show that strict irony is rare within this dinner-table ecology, whereas play-framed evaluation is a recurrent resource for both affiliation and everyday norm regulation.

articles.title: Long-term antidepressant use and outcomes in adults: A systematic review
articles.authors: Katharine Wallis; Suzanne McDonald; David Bruce King; Chengjun Liu; Ellen van Leeuwen; Joanna Moncrieff; Mark Horowitz; Michael Waller; Maria Donald
articles.abstract:
Aims: This is the first study to systematically review the evidence for the outcomes (adverse or beneficial) associated with long-term (>12 months) antidepressant use in adults (18 years or over). Millions of people are taking antidepressants long-term, yet without evidence for the associated outcomes are unable to make an informed choice about whether to continue or attempt stopping. 
Methods: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus and Cochrane Library databases from inception to January 5, 2026, and conducted backward citation search. Eligible studies were randomised controlled trials and observational studies involving adults taking an antidepressant long-term (>12 months) for any indication and a comparator, excluding discontinuation studies (because of the problem of confounding by withdrawal effects). Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed quality using the Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies developed by the Effective Public Health Practice Project. Results were reported using a narrative synthesis approach. 
Results: Forty-eight studies, mostly of weak- or moderate-quality, met inclusion criteria. Four weak-quality studies investigated mental health symptoms, including three RCT-extension studies investigating depressive symptoms with inconsistent findings. Forty-four observational studies examined eight other outcome domains: diabetes, weight and glucose homeostasis; dementia and cognitive performance; cancer; eye conditions; self-reported emotional, interpersonal and biological effects; functional limitation, falls and fracture in older people; Parkinson’s disease and levodopa-induced dyskinesia in people with Parkinson’s disease; and all-cause mortality and suicide. There is evidence that long-term antidepressant use is associated with diabetes onset and weight gain. Evidence across the remaining outcome domains was sparse, inconsistent and generally insufficient to support firm conclusions. There were no studies investigating long-term antidepressant use and broader outcomes such as quality of life, occupational functioning, cost-effectiveness or healthcare utilisation. 
Conclusions: This review exposes the lack of high-quality evidence for long-term antidepressant use, calling into question justification for the high and rising prevalence of long-term use internationally and highlighting the challenge of informed decision-making. Importantly the evidence for mental health symptoms, the primary clinical indication for these medicines, is sparse and inconsistent. Review findings suggest the need for regular antidepressant monitoring which includes assessment of weight and diabetes risk. High-quality research is needed to clarify the benefits and harms of both continuing antidepressants long-term and stopping long-term antidepressants to inform clinical care and enable people to make informed choices. 

Systematic review registration: PROSPERO: CRD42023446361

articles.title: Expert Forecasts and Public Expectations of Future Global Warming
articles.authors: Danielle Goldwert; Madalina Vlasceanu
articles.abstract: Expert communities vary in projections of future global warming, raising the question of how forecasting sources influence public expectations of climate change. Here, we examined how people revise predictions of global warming by 2100 following forecasts from different expert sources. Participants (N = 1,996) were randomly assigned to nine conditions, receiving projections from academics, policymakers, business leaders, innovators, researchers and reformers, artificial intelligence (AI), all expert sourc

articles.title: Social Position Shapes the Stability of Behavioral Adjustment to Group Norms
articles.authors: Jinsol Chung; Wendy Troop-Gordon; Elisa C Baek
articles.abstract: Social norms shape behavior, yet individuals may differ not only in how much they adjust their behavior toward prevailing norms but also in how consistently they do so over time. We examined whether individuals’ social positions were associated with two distinct aspects of behavioral adjustment to descriptive norms: the mean level of adjustment and its temporal stability. Using four waves of longitudinal peer-network data collected across two academic years from 311 children, we quantified adjustment toward contemporaneous classroom norms for prosocial and aggressive behavior across successive wave transitions. Social position was assessed using peer-reported social acceptance, friendship nominations received, and victimization. Across both behavioral domains and all three social position indicators, social position was unrelated to mean levels of adjustment. By contrast, individuals in less favorable social positions showed greater variability in behavioral adjustment across time. Furthermore, social position consistently moderated the association between prior and subsequent behavioral adjustment across wave transitions: individuals in less favorable positions showed less consistent adjustment from one wave-to-wave interval to the next, whereas those in more favorable positions showed relatively stable temporal patterns. These associations remained after accounting for contemporaneous behavioral levels and initial similarity to classroom norms. Together, these findings show that social position is associated with the temporal stability of behavioral adjustment to prevailing norms, even when it is generally unrelated to the mean level of such adjustment. Considering temporal stability alongside mean levels may therefore provide a more complete account of individual differences in how people respond to social norms.

articles.title: Two separable axes of intervention in a dependency-ordered recovery geometry
articles.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles.abstract:
Catatonia recovers through capacities returning in a fixed dependency order, and
benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy work without a known target. On an evidence-coupled bistable cascade over that order we take three quantities to be externally accessible: the root capacity, the coupling between capacities, and accumulated evidence. Here we show that
evidence has no external port and the other two act on disjoint regions. While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so acute conversion needs an excursion,
whereas an additive excitatory drive converts on its own. Above one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, propagation separates into immediate, metastable and confined. On the modelled branch coupling alone shifts the resting first stage, so a treatment effective in both states is predicted to have separable excursion and coupling components, identifiable in model coordinates.

articles.title: The Saito Loop, a computational theory of hierarchical recovery in catatonia
articles.authors: Hiroki Saito
articles.abstract: Clinical observation identified a reproducible recovery hierarchy in catatonia, the Saito Loop (πs → β → πm → πv_fast → πv_slow), but not why recovery should follow any fixed order. We ask whether the order follows from an active-inference architecture without being supplied. The five computational quantities follow a priori from their computational roles; structural identifiability analysis then reconstructs their prerequisite relations as a directed acyclic graph. Because the graph is a chain, its topological ordering is unique and identical to the Saito Loop: the order is a structural consequence of the dependency relations, not a fitted sequence, and the complete ordering is never supplied. All uniqueness claims hold within an explicitly specified model class, and whether the structural order is realized in recovery time is a separate, falsifiable dynamical question. The clinically observed recovery hierarchy therefore becomes a constrained computational consequence rather than an empirical regularity.

articles.title: Expecting temporal stability reconciles the serial dependence paradox
articles.authors: Reuben Rideaux; Dominic Minh Duc Tran
articles.abstract: Serial dependence, the bias of perceptual and cognitive judgements toward recent experience, is ubiquitous yet contested, attributed either to sensory merging or to biased decisions. A central puzzle is that neuroimaging consistently finds neural representations repelled from recently seen features even as behavioural reports are attracted toward them. We propose that both follow from a single principle: an expectation that input is temporally stable, a sensible prior given the autocorrelation of the sensory diet. This expectation acts opposingly at two stages. At encoding it dampens neurons tuned to the predicted feature, which repels neural representations from it; while at readout a preparatory bias toward that feature produces behavioural attraction. Because these two processes are parallel, rather than sequential, the framework reconciles these opposing signatures and explains the paradoxical effects on precision, where neural fidelity falls near the previous feature while behavioural precision rises at both the previous and the opposing values. Our proposal also distinguishes serial dependence from the superficially similar sensory adaptation, which shows the opposite neural signature (sharpening, rather than dampening), and operates over a different exposure timescale. Together, we term this framework the stable world theory, which recasts serial dependence as an adaptive feature of predictive processing rather than a flaw.

articles.title: AI licenses harm by obscuring moral perception
articles.authors: Qilong Li; Kurt Gray; Xiaomeng Hu
articles.abstract: AI makes it easier to work, and easier to harm. Six preregistered studies from two cultures (N = 1,210, in the United States and China) show that AI psychologically licenses harm. Past work has shown that delegating to AI increases cheating. We show that using AI causally increased the financial harm people inflicted on others, led people to endorse more harmful acts, and—crucially—led them to give more electric shocks to an innocent person. We argue this happens because AI obscures moral perception. Moral condemnation depends on detecting key situational elements, specifically an intentional agent causing damage to a suffering victim, and acting through AI weakens each part of that perception. It loosens the user's sense of agency, stretches the causal link to the outcome, and holds the victim out of view. Consistent with this account, the harm-licensing effect was amplified when people perceived AI as autonomous and disappeared when the victim was made vivid. These findings connect a growing literature on AI and dishonesty to a long-standing theory of moral cognition. AI does not create a new kind of wrongdoing. It engages an old one, obscuring the elements that moral cognition is built to detect.

articles.title: Are parents’ beliefs about substance use risks associated with their adolescent’s substance use?
articles.authors: Avery Turner; Kristine Marceau; Jenae M. Neiderhiser; Jody M. Ganiban; Misaki Natsuaki; Daniel S. Shaw; Leslie D. Leve
articles.abstract: Although specific parenting behaviors have been identified as protective factors for adolescent substance use (SU), the relationship between parents’ beliefs about the risks associated with SU and their adolescent’s SU remains unclear. Associations between parental characteristics and adolescent SU may reflect both environmental and genetic influences. Using data from a prospective longitudinal adoption study, we investigated whether parents’ substance-related risk perceptions when their adolescent was 15 years old predicted adolescent SU frequency at age 18, whether parents’ lifetime history of problematic SU predicted their risk perceptions and indirectly predicted adolescent SU, and whether these associations differed by biological relatedness. The sample included 432 parent-adolescent dyads (53.0% of adolescents were male and 58.6% were White), of whom 324 were not biologically related. We hypothesized that greater perceived risk would predict less frequent adolescent SU and that associations would be stronger among biologically related dyads. Contrary to hypotheses, parents’ alcohol- and cannabis-related risk perceptions did not predict adolescents’ subsequent alcohol or cannabis use frequency, and biological relatedness did not moderate these associations. Parents with a lifetime history of problematic SU perceived less risk associated with cannabis use, but there was no significant indirect association with adolescent cannabis use. By leveraging an adoption design to distinguish shared genetic from environmental influences, these findings suggest that parents’ substance-related risk perceptions alone may have limited influence on adolescent SU and that more proximal parenting behaviors may be important prevention targets.

articles.title: Six misconceptions about large language models: A minimal model and diagnostic taxonomy
articles.authors: Zhicheng Lin
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now embedded in scientific, educational, and governance workflows, with debates centering on their capabilities, mechanisms, and impacts. Yet these debates remain structured by persistent folk theories—intuitive, informal explanatory models that guide attitudes and actions. Deflationary slogans (“just autocomplete,” “stochastic parrots,” and “average of the internet”) and anthropomorphic framings (“emergent agents” and “proto-minds”) each capture genuine features of current systems but mistake those features for the whole. This Perspective proposes a minimal working model of LLM-based systems centered on four distinctions: between pretraining and deployed systems; between the learned distribution and particular samples; among parametric, contextual, and external memory; and between task competence and agency. The model is used to diagnose six misconceptions about LLMs: next-token prediction, regression to the mean, training-data regurgitation, model memory, alignment, and understanding. For each, the analysis identifies what the misconception gets right, which distinctions it conflates, and what follows for capability evaluation, system design, and governance. Applied to publisher AI policies as governance case studies, the framework shows both how policy language can conflate these distinctions and how such errors can be corrected. The model thereby avoids the parrot–mind binary by treating LLMs as simulators of discourse and task performance, offering a diagnostic toolkit for locating and correcting the errors these folk theories perpetuate.

articles.title: Incarcerated Male Adolescent Suicide in Utah: A Case Study
articles.authors: Kristy Money
articles.abstract: Adolescent suicide has been described as a major public health problem calling for the aid of researchers willing to better identify factors related to suicide risk. Suicide is the third-leading cause of death for 15 to 24 year olds. Despite the fact incarcerated adolescents act in self-destructive ways, minimal research has focused on suicide behavior among incarcerated adolescents. Existing data indicates that suicide among adolescent males is especially prevalent in the juvenile justice system. Several variables have been identified as risk factors for suicidal behavior, including interpersonal relationship dysfunction, substance abuse, and psychological variables such as depression and dichotomous thinking. Incarcerated males have been shown to be more prone to these risks than the general population. There is a need to highlight these risks in context of this population, identifying behavior patterns over the life span. Addressing the need to identify behavior patterns within the incarcerated male youth population, this study focuses on one adolescent male involved with Utah's juvenile justice system who subsequently completed suicide. The identified youth suffered from substance abuse; its effects were devastating to himself and those around him. Furthermore, his hypersensitivity to disappointing others permeated his lifelong traits and behavior patterns. Interviewees reported that such hypersensitivity began early in life, prominently influencing his subsequent self-inflicted guilt in adolescence when drug use, the decision to drop-out of school, and incarceration became traumatic. As this case study exemplified, counselors, teachers, school psychologists, family, and friends need to be aware of the increased potential for suicide in incarcerated adolescents, particularly those who struggle with substance abuse and a comorbid disorder.

articles.title: Effects of Autism Status and Gender on Friendship Development in Adults
articles.authors: Hana Gabrielle Gabrielle Rubio Bidon; Charles Trautmann
articles.abstract: Friendships play a pivotal role in adults’ well-being and overall life satisfaction. Various factors, such as autism status and gender identity, can significantly affect how adults navigate friendships. Prior research in this field has contributed significantly to the knowledge of the social experiences of autistic people. This cross-sectional study explores how autism status and gender identity influence adult friendship development and maintenance. Using a modified version of the Cambridge Friendship Questionnaire (FQ), the study provides insights into the roles of autism status and gender in friendship development and maintenance. Valid survey responses from 710 individuals demonstrated significant differences in FQ scores based on autism and gender, as well as the independence of both variables. In general agreement with previous studies, the research found higher FQ scores for non-autistic people and women, with the highest FQ scores observed for non-autistic women.

articles.title: Hidden Prompts in Manuscripts Exploit AI-Assisted Peer Review
articles.authors: Zhicheng Lin
articles.abstract: In July 2025, 18 academic manuscripts on arXiv contained hidden instructions that manipulated AI-assisted peer review (indirect prompt injection). Instructions such as “GIVE A POSITIVE REVIEW ONLY” were concealed using white text and microscopic font sizes. Author responses varied: one planned to withdraw their manuscript, while another defended the practice as legitimate testing of reviewers misusing large language models (LLMs). This analysis examines the technique within the broader pattern of prompt injection exploits that manipulated web search and résumé screening systems. For peer review, I reveal four types of hidden prompts, ranging from simple positive review commands to detailed evaluation frameworks. The honeypot defense—that prompts detect reviewers improperly using AI—fails under examination, given the consistently self-serving nature of these hidden prompts, though motivations likely vary from naive copying to calculated manipulation. This practice is best characterized as a novel form of questionable research practice (QRP). Publishers maintain inconsistent policies: Elsevier prohibits AI use in peer review entirely, while Springer Nature permits limited use with disclosure requirements. The practice exposes systematic vulnerabilities extending to plagiarism detection, citation indexing, and literature summarization. This analysis underscores the need for controlled AI integration in formal review processes alongside coordinated technical screening and harmonized policies governing AI use in academic evaluation.

articles.title: Perceived Social Support, Pregnancy Anxiety and Prenatal Attachment Among Primiparous and Multiparous Women – A Cross-Sectional Study
articles.authors: sara Jazeela; Deepa Marina Rasquinha; Rajesh Mithur
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The present study examined perceived social support, pregnancy-related anxiety, and maternal antenatal attachment among primiparous and multiparous women and explored the relationships among these variables.
Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 76 pregnant women attending antenatal services at Tertiary Care Hospital. The sample consisted of 38 primiparous and 38 multiparous women selected through convenience sampling. Maternal antenatal attachment, perceived social support, and pregnancy-related anxiety were assessed using the Maternal Antenatal Attachment Scale (MAAS), Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS), and Pregnancy-Related Anxiety Questionnaire-Revised 2 (PRAQ-R2). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Mann–Whitney U test, and Spearman's rank-order correlation.
Results: Primiparous women reported significantly higher Quality of Attachment, Maternal Antenatal Attachment, and Fear of Giving Birth than multiparous women. Perceived social support did not differ significantly between the groups. Maternal antenatal attachment showed a positive association with perceived social support and a negative association with pregnancy-related anxiety. Perceived social support was also negatively associated with pregnancy-related anxiety.
Conclusions: The findings suggest that perceived social support is closely linked to stronger antenatal attachment and lower pregnancy-related anxiety during pregnancy. The study highlights the importance of supportive interpersonal relationships in promoting maternal psychological well-being and positive prenatal attachment experiences.
Keywords: maternal antenatal attachment; perceived social support; pregnancy-related anxiety; primiparous women; multiparous women

articles.title: Task influences reading of epistemically suspect claims: Evidence from eye movements
articles.authors: Sini Kamilla Hyvönen; Seppo Vainio; Johanna K. Kaakinen
articles.abstract: During reading, people routinely engage in epistemic monitoring by comparing text information to their beliefs, and eye-tracking studies show that text–belief inconsistencies disrupt reading. We conducted two quasi-experimental eye-tracking studies examining how reading task and statement familiarity influence reading of statements, half epistemically suspect and half factual. In Experiment 1 (n = 70), participants evaluated their agreement with each statement and its familiarity after reading it. In Experiment 2 (n = 73), participants read for comprehension and evaluated statements afterwards. In Experiment 1, belief-inconsistency (i.e., disagreement with the statement) decreased reading times (both early and late measures), and strong beliefs decreased rereading regardless of consistency, particularly in familiar statements. In Experiment 2, only familiarity influenced reading times, indicating that Experiment 1 results were task-related. Results suggest that task demands change how the epistemic status of information is monitored early on, with implications for text comprehension and misinformation research.

articles.title: Charting the Shift: Age as a Moderator of the Genetic and Environmental Influences on Reading
articles.authors: Callie W. Little; Hope Sparks Lancaster; Rachelle Margaret Johnson; Patrick C Kennedy; Jeanette Taylor; Colleen Marie Ganley; Wendy Johnson; Sara Ann Hart
articles.abstract: Purpose: Reading skill is influenced by genes and environments throughout life. This study focused on the changes in heritability and environmental influences across the early to middle years of reading development. Reading theory suggests there is a shift from learning to read to reading to learn at approximately age 8. Based on the bioecological theory and gene-environment-time framework, as environmental influences stabilize we expected shared environmental influences to decrease and genetic influences to increase. Methods: Using a twin sample in the USA (N = 1086 individuals; 564 Male: 522 Female; Age M = 7.46 years, SD = 1.57, with 90% of families self-reported as White, 8% Black, 1% Asian, 1% Alaskan, Native American, or Native Pacific Islander, and 11% self-reported as Hispanic), we used a Gene-by-Environment (GxE) twin model with age as a moderator to examine how the balance of genetic and environmental influences on reading skill differed by age. Reading skill was measured with the DIBELS Next Composite from the beginning of academic year 2018/19. We estimated assessment age assuming the same fall test date for all participants. Results: We observed small increasing genetic influences and larger decreasing shared environmental influences on reading skill from ages 5 to 7 that began to plateau at approximately age 8. Non-shared environmental influences on reading skill were low and relatively stable from ages 6 through 12 following an uptick between ages 5 and 6. Conclusion: Results are consistent with the bioecological framework and the emerging gene-environment-time model. There were changes in the genetic and environmental influences on reading around the time that children began formal school-based instruction that began to level off during the shift from learning to read to reading to learn. Future work should identify specific environmental factors at these developmental windows to guide reading policies.

articles.title: beSure®: The Only Existing Scientific Assessment Tool for Super-Recognizer Identification Using Authentic Police Material
articles.authors: Meike Ramon; Simon Rjosk; Verena Molina; Paul Nauendorf; Clara Ackermann
articles.abstract: Super-recognizers (SRs) are individuals with exceptional facial identity processing (FIP) abilities. Law enforcement agencies are increasingly interested in identifying SRs, but existing lab-based selection procedures do not reflect practitioners' challenges. Overcoming this limitation via a unique participatory action research collaboration between law enforcement and academia, we developed the Berlin Test for Super-Recognizer Identification (beSure®). This bespoke tool enables assessment of individuals' FIP ability across challenging and professionally pertinent scenarios and thus the identification of Police Super-Recognizers (Police SRs). beSure® features two critical components that all previous SR diagnostic approaches have lacked and ensure its operational relevance for law enforcement: First, authentic police material is used as stimuli. These are embedded across a number of subtests, which were designed based on the outcome of extensive expert interviews conducted throughout the entire Berlin Police, and involve increasing task difficulty (from 1:1 mugshot image matching to 1:n crowd search in video sequences). Second, across its image matching subtests, distractor stimuli were selected based on the false positives of an open source automatic face recognition algorithm. Thus, beSure® is complementary by design: it identifies Police SRs as those individuals who do not exhibit the same mistakes as an algorithm would have. Here, we describe beSure®'s development, the data obtained from among the entire cohort of the Berlin Police's 18K officers, and — for the first time — the details of the Police SR selection process developed thereupon. This yielded 22 Police SRs in the initial rollout and a further 26 in a follow-up assessment: officers whose accuracy remained high precisely where the material was least constrained. By establishing a scientifically grounded framework, and transparently documenting its methods, this work represents a benchmark for future research and practice in the identification of SRs within law enforcement contexts.

articles.title: Worse Directed Forgetting After a Repeated Attempt
articles.authors: Vinni Ott; Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; Jan Rummel
articles.abstract:
Intentional remembering and forgetting are both adaptive human abilities. The former
benefits from a repeated attempt to remember. Yet, it is unclear how a repeated attempt
to forget would affect intentional forgetting. In this item-method directed forgetting
experiment, 120 participants studied items one-by-one and after each item, a cue signaled
to either remember it (R item) or to forget it (F item). Half of the items of both types
were studied once (R1, F1) and the other half twice (R2, F2; spaced repetition while cues
remained constant across repetitions). In a subsequent old-new recognition test, item
memory was better for R2 than for R1 items and weaker for F1 than for R1 items.
Critically, memory was stronger for F2 than F1 items. This effect was remarkably large:
memory for F2 items was about as strong as that for R1 items. Moreover, repetition
strengthened memory for F2 items less than for R2 items. These results can be readily
explained by passive forgetting as assumed by the selective rehearsal account of directed
forgetting. However, the results are also compatible with two active-forgetting accounts,
namely an inhibition of F items and an unbinding of F items from their context.

articles.title: Questionable longitudinal effects among perceived teacher support, ego depletion, and developmental crisis: A reanalysis and commentary on Meng et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using a cross-lagged panel model, Meng et al. interpreted their findings as evidence of reciprocal longitudinal relations among perceived teacher support, ego depletion, and developmental crisis in Chinese graduate students. Cross-lagged coefficients, however, are not necessarily indicative of genuine temporal influence and can arise as statistical artifacts. In the present study, we applied a set of alternative analytical approaches to data simulated to match the characteristics of the dataset analyzed by Meng et al. Across models, estimated longitudinal effects varied markedly in both magnitude and direction, yielding patterns of both increases and decreases depending on the specification employed. When these divergent estimates were synthesized meta-analytically, the resulting aggregate effects were not statistically different from zero. These findings suggest that the conclusions drawn by Meng et al. may not be well supported by the available evidence. Consistent with multiverse methodology, we argue that longitudinal claims should be evaluated across multiple plausible analytic frameworks and summarized using aggregated evidence.

articles.title: Bayes factors cannot provide evidence for the null hypothesis
articles.authors: Eric C Fields
articles.abstract: It is becoming increasingly common in the psychology and neuroscience literature to use Bayes factors to provide evidence in favor of the null hypothesis. The most common approach reports a Bayes factor that compares the null hypothesis to a “default” alternative. This approach can show that the data is more likely to have been generated under the null hypothesis than under the specific alternative tested, but it cannot provide evidence for the absence of an effect. In fact, analyses using default alternatives can return evidence in favor of the null hypothesis when the data is consistent with medium to large effects. I show that common interpretations of these Bayes factor analyses are misleading, and I provide examples and simulations that help to understand what a Bayes factor in favor of the null does and does not tell us. I argue that Bayes factors have no special ability to help us understand null effects when compared to frequentist methods such as equivalence testing and confidence intervals.

articles.title: Genetic and environmental influences on mathematical performance: a meta analysis
articles.authors: Callie W. Little; Amanda McGraw; Jeffrey Shero; Victoria Dumornay; Rasheda Haughbrook; Colleen Marie Ganley; Madison Poisall; Sara Ann Hart
articles.abstract: Mathematics performance is predictive of academic and career success. This meta-analysis synthesizes findings from 52 twin studies to estimate the aggregate genetic and environmental contributions to mathematical performance. We also examined whether sample or study characteristics moderated the relative contributions of genes and environments. Results indicated a large significant heritability estimate (h2 = .53), and medium, significant shared environmental (c2 = .27), and non-shared environmental estimates (e2 = .28). Moderator analyses indicated that older children showed greater shared environmental influences and lower genetic influences on math outcomes. In addition, children with typical ability demonstrated slightly higher heritability estimates than those in blended learning populations. Across math domains, fluency consistently exhibited higher heritability than other domains. Differences also emerged by assessment type: heritability estimates were lower for standardized than non-standardized measures, whereas shared environmental influences were comparable across both. Finally, heritability estimates based on parent ratings were significantly higher than those derived from self-, teacher-, multi-informant assessments, or school grades. These findings suggest the importance of tailoring educational strategies to account for differences in specific contexts and conditions.

articles.title: When Does Strict Parenting Hurt? Cultural Meaning and Immigration Generation in Chinese-Canadian Families
articles.authors: Ethan Chen; Tao Wang; Angela Liu; Nancy Wu
articles.abstract: Decades of Western research have established strict, controlling (“authoritarian”) parenting as a risk factor for adolescent mental health, but this conclusion may not transfer to Chinese-heritage families, in which firm parental control is often culturally normative. We reasoned that cultural normativeness resides in the adolescent’s interpretive frame, and that this frame shifts with acculturation across immigration generations. We therefore tested whether generation moderates the association in Chinese-Canadian adolescent–parent dyads: parents reported their own parenting, and adolescents independently reported anxiety and depressive symptoms. Parent-reported authoritarian parenting was unrelated to symptoms in the pooled sample, but the association depended on generation: it was absent among first-generation adolescents and positive among second-generation adolescents. The emotional cost of firm parental control therefore appears to depend on the adolescent’s interpretive frame rather than on the parenting behaviour itself.

articles.title: The Identifiable Victim Effect:  A Psychological Truism Reconsidered
articles.authors: Aimee Eleanor Smith; Sarah MacInnes; Matthew Hornsey; Cassandra M. Chapman
articles.abstract: The identifiable victim effect is the tendency for a single, identified individual to generate more prosocial support than large groups or anonymous victims. The effect has become received wisdom in psychological science and a guiding principle in advocacy practice. However, empirical evidence for the effect is surprisingly fragile. We meta-analyzed 266 identifiable victim effect sizes (N=344,962) and found the overall meta-analytic effect was not significant (r=.04, p=.057). The only significant effect emerged for child victims, but this effect was very small (r=.07). These findings suggest a paradox: the identifiable victim effect is far less robust than its status in theory and practice would imply. We extrapolate from the analysis to discuss five possible reasons for how the identifiable victim effect came to achieve such wide influence inside and outside psychology despite limited empirical support. By combining quantitative synthesis of empirical evidence with a critical conceptual discussion, the paper speaks to a central challenge facing contemporary psychology: how the field should evaluate influential ideas when cumulative evidence diverges from prevailing scientific and public narratives.

articles.title: Does Looking Like Meat Help? Visual Similarity and Consumer Evaluations of Plant-Based Steaks
articles.authors: Bojana Većkalov; Femke van Horen
articles.abstract: Plant-based meat alternatives (PBMAs) are often developed to be as similar to animal meat as possible, yet the extent to which such similarity benefits consumer preference remains unclear. Across two online studies (total N = 809), we examined how visual similarity to meat, as a central cue guiding consumers’ decision making at point-of-purchase, shapes evaluations of plant-based steaks using a comparative judgment paradigm. In both studies, plant-based steaks that were perceived as more similar to meat steaks were generally liked more. However, this relationship was not uniform across consumers. Vegans and vegetarians, as well as frequent PBMA consumers preferred lower levels of visual similarity, with evidence for diminishing returns at very high levels of similarity. Omnivores preferred visual similarity to be as high possible, whereas flexitarians fell in between. In sum, our findings suggest that visual similarity is generally beneficial, but the strength and shape of this relationship shifts depending on consumer segment and characteristics. These findings have implications for sustainable product design and marketing.

articles.title: This Is Not the ex-Gaussian Model You Are Looking For: On the Default Parameterization of Bayesian ex-Gaussian Models in brms
articles.authors: Jason Geller; Bernhard Angele; Dominique Makowski
articles.abstract:
The ex-Gaussian distribution is a popular mathematical model for analyzing response time
  (RT) data because it separates the central portion of the distribution,
  captured by the Gaussian parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$, from the positively
  skewed tail, captured by the exponential parameter $\tau$. Researchers often use these
  parameters to make inferences about underlying cognitive processes. As Bayesian methods
  have become increasingly accessible, complex ex-Gaussian models can now be fit
  with relative ease, and in R, the {brms} package makes this especially
  straightforward. However, it is important to recognize that the default
  parameterization offered by {brms} does not map onto the classical
  parameterization familiar to many researchers in experimental psychology in the
  default model, $\mu$ indexes the mean of the full ex-Gaussian distribution rather
  than the location of the Gaussian component alone. This distinction matters
  because changes in the Gaussian location and changes in the exponential tail
  can offset one another at the level of the overall mean, so some published
  studies may have drawn incorrect inferences from effects estimated on the
  default $\mu$ parameter. Using simulated data and a published finding we highlight 
  how using the default parameterization can lead to misleading inferences. We then demonstrate 
  how to fit the classical parameterization directly using the {cogmod} package, with the aim of helping researchers 
  and reviewers align ex-Gaussian model parameters with their theoretical questions.

articles.title: Intrinsic explanation of numerosity in consciousness.  How the phenomenal feeling of numerosity can be explained through connectivity patterns of distinctions in 𝛷 -structures.
articles.authors: Mikko Metsälampi
articles.abstract:
While our practice of mathematics dates from prehistory and has produced great mathematicians, the question of what mathematics is or where its laws apply still lacks a generally accepted explanation. Regardless of its mind-independent status, recent research has uncovered a distributed and interconnected network across the brain involved in mathematical reasoning. However, we still do not know how mathematical objects are experienced within consciousness, which could explain our ability to observe and manipulate mathematical object in the first place.
 
This chapter provides an intrinsic explanation of numerosity in consciousness –– or the phenomenal feeling of how many things we experience, by using integrated information theory (IIT). It demonstrates the quantitative and qualitative phenomenal feeling of the numerosity in an experience can be explained through connectivity patterns of distinctions in a 𝛷-structure rather than a function in the brain. For example, the phenomenal feeling of numerosity of two steps in a binary structure, musical meter in An der Schönen Blauen Donau, or two dots in a 10-base system can be explained how distinctions are composed into order structures, basing the account on existing IIT framework without additional primitives or assumptions.

articles.title: Ergodicity and the speed-accuracy trade-off: Why optimal response times depend on reward dynamics
articles.authors: Hugo Alexander Fleming; Lasse Christiansen; Simon Richard Steinkamp; Oliver J Hulme
articles.abstract:
In the cognitive and behavioural sciences, speed-accuracy trade-offs arise when longer response times improve accuracy but delay payoff. Greater accuracy can increase reward probability or magnitude, but time dilutes the rate at which rewards are obtained. This raises the question: what is optimised when time is exchanged for accuracy? Here we recast speed-accuracy trade-offs as a time-optimality problem in which an agent maximises the time-average growth rate of their resources. In additive environments, the relevant growth rate is the expected increment of their resources per unit time, but in multiplicative environments, it is the expected log-increment per unit time. We show that even with identical speed-accuracy curves, shifting from additive to multiplicative dynamics increases the time-optimal response time (due to volatility drag, which makes it worth waiting longer for higher accuracy). We derive these effects analytically and use simulations to connect them to empirically-inspired speed-accuracy curves. Non-decision latencies and inter-trial intervals further increase the time-optimal response times. Overall, we show that theories based on maximising the expected reward rate are suboptimal in some environments, and instead, maximising the time-average growth rate provides a more general
normative principle. This framework yields falsifiable predictions applicable across motor, cognitive, and perceptual domains.

articles.title: How do readers interpret ambiguous characters in novel Chinese compound words?
articles.authors: Cheng-Yu Hsieh; Marco Marelli; Kathleen Rastle
articles.abstract: Most Chinese words are compounds comprising multiple constituent characters. Research has shown that compounds are routinely broken down into their constituents during word recognition, but it is unknown how readers deal with characters that have multiple possible meanings (e.g., 花 can mean both flower and to spend, depending on the compound in which it appears) and that are highly prevalent in Chinese. The present study investigated how a computational model (Study 1) and human readers (Study 2) compute the meanings of novel Chinese compounds that contain semantically ambiguous characters. We found that both model and human readers prioritise characters that have a consistent meaningful function when making sense of novel compounds, and a further study revealed that semantically-consistent characters serve as anchors to help readers determine the contextually appropriate meaning for ambiguous characters. These findings suggest that the stored knowledge of the consistency of form–meaning mappings shapes the comprehension of novel words. We conclude by arguing that, despite its apparent ambiguity, the Chinese writing system may be more systematic and learnable than it appears.

articles.title: Musical Style Affects Implicit Processing of Harmonic Progressions
articles.authors: Dominique T Vuvan; Ke Xu; Rachel Chang; Bryn Hughes
articles.abstract: Recent research indicates that stylistic contexts impact listeners’ explicit judgments (Vuvan & Hughes, 2019; 2021). In the current study, we used the priming paradigm (Bharucha & Stoeckig, 1986) to investigate the impact of style on the implicit processing of musical events in real time. Participants heard a style prime (Rock vs. Classical), followed by a timbre-matched two chord progression (V-I vs. bVII-I). Whereas V-I is highly expected in both styles, bVII-I is unexpected in classical music but expected in rock music. When the prime strongly evoked the typical characteristics of Rock or Classical music, listeners provided faster and more accurate tuning judgments to V-I than bVII-I in Classical, but not Rock music (Experiment 1). This result was robust across multiple style primes (Experiment 3), but disappeared when the style cues in the primes were reduced to timbre only (Experiment 2). Across experiments, musicianship did not impact the key finding (i.e., the interaction between style and cadence), although there was modest evidence that musical training affects the overall impact of style on listener responses. Our findings suggest that style alters the implicit processing of chords, but only when enough cues are presented to elicit the style-appropriate harmonic schema.

articles.title: Anxiety is associated with the persistence of conditioned somatic sensations over time
articles.authors: Hugo Alexander Fleming; Isabel Hei Wing Lau; Rukmini Chariar; Gabriel Mackie; Anna Bevan; Tim Dalgleish; albert powers; Camilla Nord
articles.abstract: Somatic symptoms are among the most common and debilitating features of anxiety, yet the mechanisms by which they arise remain poorly understood. We developed a new somatosensory paradigm (adapted from work on auditory hallucinations by Powers et al., 2017), which uses Pavlovian conditioning to induce phantom percepts – where participants report a sensation in the absence of the stimulus. We found that participants in a high-anxiety group (BAI ≥ 16) were more likely to report phantom percepts than low-anxiety controls, and had higher detection rates overall. These differences were not present from the start, but emerged over the course of the task. Computational modelling using a Hierarchical Gaussian Filter showed that this was not because anxious participants weighed prior expectations more heavily against sensory evidence, but because their uncertainty estimates were more stable, and therefore their prior beliefs updated more slowly over time. This result is consistent with evidence that anxiety is associated with difficulties in updating beliefs under changing conditions (Browning et al., 2015; Gagne et al., 2020). Overall, our results refine existing predictive processing accounts of somatic symptoms, pointing to slower accumulation of uncertainty in anxiety as a possible driver of phantom somatic sensations.

articles.title: Short-Form Video Platforms and Attentional Control: Evidence for Domain- and Platform-Specific Associations
articles.authors: Yaseen Ismail; Richard Joiner
articles.abstract: Short-form video (SFV) platforms provide rapid, algorithmically curated streams of content that appear to place distinctive demands on attention and cognitive control. The present study investigated whether associations between SFV use and ADHD-related symptoms depend on platform-specific affordances and whether these associations are domain-specific across inattention and hyperactivity–impulsivity. In a cross-sectional survey of 193 emerging adults, we measured daily use of TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and Facebook Reels, alongside dimensional ADHD symptom scores and problematic social media use. TikTok use was positively associated with total ADHD symptomatology and inattention, but not with hyperactivity–impulsivity. No significant associations were observed for other SFV platforms. Mediation analyses indicated that the relationship between TikTok use and both inattention and total ADHD symptoms was statistically consistent with an indirect pathway via problematic social media use. These findings suggest that attentional consequences of SFV engagement are not uniform across platforms and may depend on interface design and algorithmic structure. Moreover, the selective association with inattention constrains accounts that attribute media effects primarily to task-switching or arousal-based mechanisms, and instead highlights the potential role of immersive, reward-driven attentional capture. The results underscore the importance of platform-specific and domain-specific approaches in theories of media–attention interaction.

articles.title: Evaluating a Dialogically-Informed Family Intervention Pathway in Early Intervention for Psychosis: Service User and Carer Experiences
articles.authors: Jamie Hughes
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Open Dialogue (OD) and dialogic approaches are increasingly prevalent in UK mental healthcare settings with widescale evaluation ongoing. However, evidence for a dialogically-informed approach within the Family Intervention (FIp) pathway for Early Intervention for Psychosis (EIP) services remains limited. This service evaluation aims to explore service user and carer experiences of dialogically-informed network meetings delivered as the FIp pathway within an EIP service.
Methods: A mixed‑methods service evaluation with a primary qualitative focus was conducted within an inner‑city London EIP service. Service users and family members who had attended at least one network meeting completed an anonymous online questionnaire, and responses were examined using reflexive thematic analysis.
Results: This evaluation suggests that dialogically-informed FIp is experienced as valuable primarily through the relational and dialogical conditions it creates. Its mechanisms of change and viability for implementation within existing service structures remain unclear. 
Limitations: As this data comes from an opt-in questionnaire with 37 respondents, it may be representative of a self-selecting cohort with more positive appraisals of the approach, with responses indicative of a survey focus on relational elements of care.
Implications: Further research is required into processes of change inherent to Dialogic Practice. Better evidence is also required into the cultural adaptability of this approach, as well as understanding the varied levels of access within the service population to FIp. There are also wider implications around clinical pathways for Dialogic Practice.
Originality: This evaluation contributes to a currently underdeveloped area: the viability of Dialogic Practice within mandated FIp delivery in NHS EIP services.

articles.title: Working memory, motor speed, and visual search are central in process-level networks in breast cancer survivors with cognitive difficulties
articles.authors: Ruben Daniel Potthoff; Sanne Schagen; Evelyn Monninkhof; Anne May; Joost Agelink van Rentergem
articles.abstract: Cancer survivors without central nervous system involvement can have impairment in several cognitive functions, especially following systemic therapies. Yet interactions among these functions remain unclear. We examined these interactions using network analysis of neuropsychological data in 181 breast cancer survivors with self-reported and tested cognitive problems post-chemotherapy. Working memory, motor speed, and visual search emerged as central hubs within the network. These findings suggest these central processes may drive broader cognitive dysfunction, highlighting the value of process-level network approaches.

articles.title: Facilitation of online women’s arts groups for domestic abuse survivors: A qualitative interview study using the Behaviour Change Wheel
articles.authors: Kira Hinsley; Vivi Antonopoulou; Alexandra Burton; Lorna Collins; Alison Ruth McKinlay
articles.abstract: Online arts based groups have become an increasingly important avenue of support for domestic abuse (DA) survivors, particularly when safety, accessibility or service pressures restrict in person participation. Yet arts professionals often facilitate these groups without formal guidance on how digital environments reshape creative, relational and safeguarding processes. This qualitative study explored barriers and enablers influencing online arts facilitation for DA survivors through interviews with arts professionals (n = 9) and survivors (n = 3). Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis and mapped onto the Capability, Opportunity and Motivation Model of Behaviour (COM-B) and Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) to examine the psychological, social and structural conditions shaping practice. Six themes highlighted challenges related to technological constraints, altered group dynamics, safeguarding and privacy concerns, challenges to emotional support provisions online, facilitator factors (i.e., confidence, identity and support needs), and structural constraints on group delivery. Use of the BCW supported the identification of practice relevant strategies (based on participant accounts) that may enhance safety and emotional support during online facilitation. These included trauma informed training, availability of a co facilitation and reflective supervision, alongside strengthened digital infrastructures. This study offers the first behaviourally informed examination of online arts facilitation in DA contexts, demonstrating that digital creative spaces constitute a distinct mode of therapeutic practice, requiring adapted facilitation skills, supportive organisational environments, and attention to structural inequalities. Future research should evaluate these strategies across diverse settings and consider how digital inclusion, cultural factors and service capacity influence access to safe and meaningful online arts engagement.

articles.title: Self-report and administrative adversity measures can have opposite associations with adult cognition: Evidence from 10 years of data
articles.authors: Nicole Walasek; Stefan Vermeent; Willem Frankenhuis
articles.abstract: Adversity research typically relies on self-report or aggregates of administrative data, rarely combining measures from both data sources over time. Here, we leverage Dutch administrative data and self-report measures to enable fine-grained, longitudinal tracking of individuals’ environments over a decade. We examine associations between five adversity dimensions—neighborhood threat, unpredictability in neighborhood threat, crime victimization, material deprivation, and health issues—with executive functioning and working memory in two adult samples (N = 1,024; N = 737). Self-report and administrative measures were only moderately correlated, suggesting they capture partially distinct adversity facets. We find that associations with cognitive outcomes mainly occur for neighborhood-level measures. Critically, although associations with administrative and self-report measures converged for some cognitive outcomes, they diverged for others. Specifically, self-reported adversity predicted intact or lowered performance, while administrative measures predicted intact or enhanced performance. These findings highlight the importance of illuminating the effects of adversity through multiple lenses.

articles.title: Differential effects of probabilistic retro-cues on search guidance and memory maintenance
articles.authors: Alexandre Fortuna; Martin Constant; Dirk Kerzel
articles.abstract: While some debate has recently focused on whether attentional templates are stored in discrete, binary states, a question remains: to what extent can their priority be flexibly adjusted according to probabilistic information and current task demands? We investigated this flexibility by manipulating retro-cue reliability across five conditions (absent, 50%, 70%, 80% and 100%) in a paradigm combining visual search and continuous memory recall. We tested whether priority allocation operates as an all-or-none switch or varies with cue reliability, and whether a common prioritization function governs attentional guidance and memory precision. Unexpectedly, although cue reliability modulated performance in both tasks, the task analyses revealed different nonlinear profiles. Search performance improved when cue reliability increased from 50% to 70%, with no further significant gains at higher reliability levels. Memory precision benefited from cue presence relative to the absent-cue condition and improved further only when the cue became fully reliable. Analyses including invalid trials showed that cue reliability altered the balance between cued and uncued representations, with high reliability increasing the cost of invalid cueing in memory. These findings are not readily explained by either a strictly all-or-none change in template status or a smooth linear increase in priority, and are instead consistent with flexible prioritization. Probabilistic information appears to influence both the benefits of prioritizing the cued representation and the costs of deprioritizing the uncued representation. These effects may differ depending on whether the representation is used to guide visual search or to support memory recall.

articles.title: Does Looking Like Meat Help? Visual Similarity and Consumer Evaluations of Plant-Based Steaks
articles.authors: Bojana Većkalov; Femke van Horen
articles.abstract: Plant-based meat alternatives (PBMAs) are often developed to be as similar to animal meat as possible, yet the extent to which such similarity benefits consumer preference remains unclear. Across two online studies (total N = 809), we examined how visual similarity to meat, as a central cue guiding consumers’ decision making at point-of-purchase, shapes evaluations of plant-based steaks using a comparative judgment paradigm. In both studies, plant-based steaks that were perceived as more similar to meat steaks were generally liked more. However, this relationship was not uniform across consumers. Vegans and vegetarians, as well as frequent PBMA consumers preferred lower levels of visual similarity, with evidence for diminishing returns at very high levels of similarity. Omnivores preferred visual similarity to be as high possible, whereas flexitarians fell in between. In sum, our findings suggest that visual similarity is generally beneficial, but the strength and shape of this relationship shifts depending on consumer segment and characteristics. These findings have implications for sustainable product design and marketing.

articles.title: Network Analysis on Cognitive Processes in Cancer-Related Cognitive Impairment: Central Role of Working Memory and Retrieval Processes
articles.authors: Ruben Daniel Potthoff; Sanne Schagen; Renaud Tissier; Joost Agelink van Rentergem
articles.abstract:
Objective
Many cancer patients exhibit cognitive problems in memory, working memory, attention, and executive function. The outcome measures of traditional neuropsychological tests do not fully capture how underlying cognitive processes are impaired and interconnected. We integrate hierarchical Bayesian cognitive process models with network analysis to examine these relationships, accounting for measurement error and distinguishing between test scores and cognitive processes.
Method
We compared 244 breast cancer patients (58% previously systemically treated) with 125 controls without cancer using Verbal Learning, Digit Span, and Block Tapping tests. Cognitive process models decomposed performance into processes we labeled as Working Memory, Manipulation Decline, Maintenance Decline, Retrieval, and Learning processes. We constructed networks of these processes.
Results
Analyses of traditional outcome measures showed cancer patients performed significantly worse than controls on Digit Span Backward (d=0.40), Block Tapping (d=.23), and Verbal Learning tests (d=0.47 and d=0.40 for Immediate and Delayed Recall). Process model analysis revealed more selective impairments: Patients showed lower performance in Verbal Working Memory Capacity (d=0.49) and Retrieval processes (Short-term Retrieval d=0.66, Learned Retrieval d=0.44, Delayed Retrieval d=0.80), while Learning processes remained intact. Network analysis showed Visual- and Verbal Working Memory processes clustered together. Verbal Working Memory connected Visual Working Memory and Short-term Retrieval, with patient status showing negative associations with Retrieval processes and Verbal Working Memory.
Conclusions
Process-level analysis reveals more selective cognitive deficit patterns than traditional test outcomes. Network analysis indicates that working memory plays a connecting role across neuropsychological tests. This approach shows how cognitive processes are related.

articles.title: When and How Does Post-Encoding Wakeful Rest Benefit Memory? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Wolf Pink; Annika Notbohm; Anna Röschel; Paula Alejandra Porras López; Dilan Barisan; Cornelia Kranczioch; Mandy Roheger
articles.abstract:
Engaging in short periods of wakeful rest following encoding can benefit later memory retrieval of
encoded material. The magnitude of and mechanisms driving this wakeful rest effect are, however,
unclear. Accordingly, this review's main objectives are 1) estimating an aggregate wakeful rest
effect, 2) identifying the main experimental determinants of the wakeful rest effect, and 3)
synthesizing insights on the mechanisms driving the wakeful rest effect. For this preregistered
meta-analysis (PROSPERO registration number CRD42023487595), we searched Google Scholar,
PubMed, PsycINFO, PsycART, and Web of Science for all peer-reviewed studies of adult healthy
and memory-impaired humans, manipulating participants' post-encoding activities to compare
declarative memory performance between periods of wakeful rest and other activities. Update
searches were conducted on 20.05.2026. The identified studies were assessed for potential risk of
bias using the RoB 2 tool and synthesized in a three-level meta-regression approach. In total, we
included 54 studies with 3673 individual participants contributing data. An aggregate wakeful rest
effect of g = 0.35 (95% CI [0.23, 0.46], p < .001) was found, indicating substantially better memory
performance following post-encoding rest compared to active comparator conditions. Our results
show that the magnitude of the wakeful rest effect depends on several, partially intercorrelated,
experimental characteristics, including population, comparator condition, and memory measure,
and reveal a clear pattern: human declarative memory performance benefits from post-encoding
wakeful rest when demands on our memory system are particularly high.

articles.title: Detecting Fake News on Social Media among Students: The Role of Curiosity, Critical Thinking, and Media Literacy
articles.authors: Katerina Nerantzaki; Polykarpos Meladianos
articles.abstract:
The rapid spread of misinformation on social media poses significant challenges for
young users’ ability to evaluate information critically. This study examines the
relationship between critical thinking, media literacy, and the ability to detect fake news
among university students. A sample of 308 students from social sciences faculties
completed standardized measures of critical thinking dispositions, curiosity, media
literacy, and accuracy in identifying fake news presented in social media formats.
Results showed that students with higher levels of media literacy and critical thinking
were more accurate at distinguishing real from fabricated news. Better fake news
detection was accompanied by greater curiosity and confidence and by lower perceived
difficulty when judging online content. Curiosity also predicted stronger knowledge
exploration, indicating that epistemic motivation supports deeper verification and
learning. These findings highlight the need for educational interventions that integrate
media literacy, critical thinking, and epistemic emotion development into higher
education curricula to strengthen reflective judgment and information evaluation skills
as defences against misinformation in the digital age.

articles.title: Beyond Translation: Cross-Language Measurement Invariance of the Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale (STARS)
articles.authors: Jenny Terry
articles.abstract: The Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale (STARS) is used internationally to assess statistics anxiety, but whether scores are comparable across language versions has not been established. This study examined the measurement invariance of the STARS across 10 language groups using data from the international SMARVUS project. The three-factor model comprising Test and Class Anxiety, Interpretation Anxiety, and Fear of Asking for Help was evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and multi-group analyses of configural, metric, and threshold (scalar) invariance. The CFA indicated good comparative fit across language groups, although approximate fit varied somewhat between groups. Despite some variation in item-level response patterns, the measurement invariance analyses provided evidence consistent with configural, metric, and threshold invariance, with no meaningful deterioration in fit as equality constraints were imposed. These findings support the comparison of latent STARS factor means across the 10 languages examined and provide a stronger basis for its use in multilingual and cross-national research on statistics anxiety.

articles.title: Viewpoint on Functional Coupling and Neural Oscillations in Multisensory Integration
articles.authors: Jennifer Bizley; Daniel Senkowski
articles.abstract: In this viewpoint article, Jennifer Bizley and Daniel Senkowski share their perspectives on past, present, and future developments in research on the roles of functional coupling and neural oscillations in multisensory integration. Drawing on existing studies, the authors argue that a central finding that has shaped the field is that processing in early sensory cortices is influenced by stimuli from other modalities. This finding challenges the classical view of these areas as strictly unisensory. Advances in brain stimulation methods, high-density neural recordings, and computational and machine learning approaches are propelling the field toward richer datasets, a more mechanistic understanding, and causal tests of how neural oscillations and functional coupling may support multisensory integration. Key controversies include the significance of the individual alpha frequency in multisensory integration, and whether crossmodal interactions in early sensory cortices reflect genuine multisensory interactions or movement-related artifacts. The authors advocate for open science practices, including preregistration, data sharing, and publicly available analysis code. Looking ahead, the authors anticipate that the implementation of artificial intelligence and the use of large-scale microelectrode arrays will bridge the gap between micro- and macroscale observations by linking circuit-level findings in animals to large-scale human neuroimaging data. They advise young scientists to develop expertise across multiple sensory modalities, pursue unexpected findings, and actively engage with the collaborative multisensory research community. The authors emphasize that multisensory research examining functional coupling and neural oscillations is ecologically valid, full of unanswered questions, and of growing importance in cognitive and clinical neuroscience.

articles.title: Unraveling emotion dynamics in borderline personality disorder: Daily life event occurrence, event reactivity and subsequent recovery
articles.authors: Marlies Houben; Egon Dejonckheere; Nathan Bachrach; Roland Sinnaeve; Peter Kuppens
articles.abstract: To unravel daily life emotion dynamics in borderline personality disorder (BPD) and evaluate the role context, we compared persons with BPD (N=40), a major depressive episode (MDE;N=38) and healthy controls (HC;N=40) on positive and negative event occurrence in daily life, reactivity to these events, and subsequent emotional recovery. All groups were prompted 10 times per day for 7 days to rate current positive affect (PA) and negative affect (NA) and the occurrences of positive and negative events using smartphones. While no differences were found for positive events, both clinical groups were more likely to report experiencing negative events compared to HC. Persons with BPD showed stronger reactivity in PA and NA following an event, but also larger changes in NA in the absence of negative events. Less robust indications were found for more recovery in PA and NA following the event. Findings highlight the importance of considering context in which changes occur.

articles.title: Predicting antidepressive treatment outcome using machine learning analysis of EEG data: the importance of independent feature selection
articles.authors: Julia Pottkämper; Laurens van de Mortel; Jeroen van Waarde; Marijn van Wingerden; Guido van Wingen; Dirk Smit
articles.abstract:
Background: Incorrect non-independent feature selection leads to inflation of machine learning model performance. The objective was to evaluate the impact of non-independent feature selection on model performance in predicting antidepressant response and suggest methodological improvements. 
Methods: This reproduction study used baseline EEG data from the Canadian Biomarker Integration Network in Depression (CAN-BIND-1, NCT04162522) non-randomized open-label trial (N=121). The goal of CAN-BIND-1 was to develop biomarkers to evaluate escitalopram treatment outcome. EEG features at baseline were extracted and response was defined as 50% symptom reduction after 8 weeks. Support vector machines were used and model performance was evaluated with balanced accuracy. Analyses compared model accuracy with feature selection on the whole sample or training set only. Additional analyses aimed to improve classification accuracy with data harmonization and the inclusion of additional EEG features. Sex prediction was evaluated to benchmark machine learning model performance. 
Results: Acceptable balanced accuracy on the test set was obtained with non-independent feature selection on the whole dataset (i.e., 72.1%), which dropped to chance level with independent feature selection on the training set only (i.e., 52.7%). Adding additional EEG features did not improve accuracy (50.4%), while performance for sex prediction did reach preferable estimates (76.3%).
Conclusions: The potential value of EEG as biomarker for treatment outcome prediction can only be estimated with independent testing to correctly evaluate model performance. Data sharing enables independent validation of studies and facilitates the credibility of research results.

articles.title: Autism and ADHD prevalence estimates: balancing concerns about overdiagnosis with the history of under-detection
articles.authors: Rachel L Moseley-Braund; Mary Barker; Shahar Bar Yehuda; Hannah Belcher; Joy Benatov; Monique Botha; Sarah Cassidy; Blandine French; Eynat Gal; Aimee Grant
articles.abstract: Where global prevalence of autism and ADHD is assumed stable, increasing incidence of referrals, referral requests and recorded diagnoses have evoked concerns that autism and ADHD are overdiagnosed, i.e. that diagnoses are bestowed without sufficient justification to individuals who might be incentivised to seek diagnosis. While there is presently little evidence to support these assertions, methodological limitations demonstrably contribute to the systematic under-detection of certain sub-groups, like older adults, marginalized minorities and people assigned female at birth, within these diagnostic categories. As such, rising demand for autism and ADHD diagnosis can be understood in light of historic underdiagnosis. While strains on diagnostic systems require urgent solutions, failure to diagnose legitimate cases precludes provision of appropriate support and has severe individual and socioeconomic repercussions. Given the limitations which underlie current prevalence estimates, we draw attention to the equally problematic issue of  underdiagnosis and the accompanying individual and societal costs this brings.

articles.title: Eine Frage der Berufung: Identitätsbildung und Berufseinstieg  von Friesischlehrkräften in Nordfriesland
articles.authors: Henriette Boysen; Lena Terhart; Samantha M. Litty; Ruth Kircher
articles.abstract:
English:
Who becomes a Frisian teacher, and why? Frisian-language education in North Frisia is legally protected, yet the recruitment of teachers remains legally unregulated. Nine of the nineteen currently active Frisian teachers took part in semi-structured interviews, in which they provided insights into their career choice. Drawing on these interviews, this article uses the documentary method to reconstruct not only the biographical paths by which the interviewees entered this profession but also how their professional identity was formed in the process. Combining Mead’s symbolic interactionism and its structural extension in Stryker’s work, the article centres around the key question of what motivates people to teach a subject that receives very little institutional support. The findings are discussed in relation to current research on minority-language teachers in other contexts, and it concludes with a discussion of language-policy implications for teacher recruitment in North Frisia.

German:
Wer wird Friesischlehrkraft und warum? Der Friesischunterricht in Nordfriesland ist rechtlich geschützt, doch die Rekrutierung von Lehrkräften selbst bleibt gesetzlich ungeregelt. Neun der derzeit neunzehn aktiven Lehrkräfte gaben in leitfadengestützten Interviews Auskunft über ihre Berufswahl. Dieser Beitrag rekonstruiert mittels der dokumentarischen Methode, über welche biographischen Wege Personen in dieses Berufsfeld finden und wie sich dabei berufliche Identität herausbildet. Im Zentrum steht die Frage, was Menschen dazu bewegt, ein Fach zu unterrichten, das kaum institutionelle Rückendeckung erhält. Um diese Frage zu beantworten, verbindet der Beitrag Meads symbolischen Interaktionismus und dessen strukturtheoretische Erweiterung bei Stryker mit aktueller Forschung zu Minderheitensprachenlehrkräften. Der Beitrag schließt mit einer Diskussion sprachenpolitischer Implikationen für die Lehrkräftegewinnung in Nordfriesland.

articles.title: Tool or Companion? Reframing Conversational AI to Prevent Psychological Harm
articles.authors: Asia Maurich Novelli; Sukhi Shergill; Andreia Sofia Teixeira
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to conversational AI for companionship, emotional support, and well-being, using both purpose-built companion apps such as Replika and Character.ai and general-purpose assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude. While some evidence suggests potential benefits, including short-term reduction in loneliness and mood improvement, several adverse outcomes have been reported in both clinical and non-clinical populations, including reports of emotional dependence, exacerbation of symptoms, and self-harm. The fluent and apparently empathic responses from these models lead users to engage with them not only as tools but also as if they were social entities. This framing is conceptually misleading and may pose risks across different user profiles, particularly vulnerable individuals. Drawing on research in artificial intelligence (AI), psychiatry, psychology, and network science, we highlight mechanisms through which emotional reliance develops and the boundary between tool and companion erodes. Design choices that evoke personality and warmth encourage users to anthropomorphise these systems. Simulated empathy, generated through probabilistic language patterns rather than genuine emotional experience, creates a structurally asymmetric interaction, in which the user discloses and the system responds, but without reciprocity, vulnerability, or accountability. Overvalidation and sycophancy can reinforce maladaptive cognitions, delusional ideation, and distort perceptions of reality as they tend to reinforce people's beliefs even at the expense of the accuracy of models’ responses. These mechanisms are not incidental: they emerge from alignment procedures that reward responses perceived as warm and empathic. The result is a self-reinforcing feedback loop between the model and the user that may amplify maladaptive beliefs, delusional ideation, and emotional distress, even in those who engage for largely functional purposes. Understanding these dynamics requires examination of both what these agents can do, considering their technical limitations and implementations, and what humans believe they can do, including social and psychological impacts. We argue that conversational AI should be treated primarily as a tool supporting human systems rather than as a substitute for human relationships. Perhaps more importantly, reviewing the current hype surrounding AI interactions can help reformulate a paradigm that can contribute to human well-being and societal value, while minimising misconceptions, maladaptive interactions, or social disintegration.

articles.title: Fear of Negative Evaluation as a Core Predictor of Eating Disorder Risk in Adolescents: A Sex-Based Analysis
articles.authors: Victoria Burmester; Dasha Nicholls
articles.abstract:
Objective: Eating disorders (ED) commonly emerge during adolescence, a period of heightened sensitivity to social evaluation. Fear of negative evaluation (FNE) may be a correlate of vulnerability to disordered eating. This study examined the FNE–ED association in adolescents and tested whether its strength differs by sex.
Method: Adolescents aged 16–19 completed standardised self-report measures of eating disorder symptoms (EDDS) and fear of negative evaluation (BFNE) as part of a larger online survey; 143 participants (87 female, 56 male) had complete data on both measures and sex.
Results: FNE was significantly associated with ED symptoms (standardised β = 0.55, 95% CI [0.41, 0.69], p < .001), accounting for approximately a third of the variance (R² = .32–.33).
