Females scored significantly higher than males on both FNE and ED symptoms (medium effect sizes). This association was not significantly moderated by sex (β = −.08, p = .255).
Conclusions: FNE is significantly associated with ED psychopathology in adolescents, with no significant sex difference in this association. Given the cross-sectional design, causality cannot be established; prospective and experimental research is needed to test whether reducing FNE could lower ED risk.

articles.title: Learning Dynamic Neural Evidence Representations for Time-Adaptive Brain--Computer Interfaces
articles.authors: Beining Cao; Ziyi Zhao; Xiaowei Jiang; Daniel Leong; Yingtao Ren; Thomas Do; Yu-Cheng Chang; Chin-Teng Lin
articles.abstract: Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) decode neural activity into commands, yet most existing systems rely on fixed-window decoding that may result in redundant observation or unreliable predictions due to insufficient evidence. Adaptive temporal decision-making (ATDM) addresses this accuracy–time trade-off by progressively accumulating EEG evidence and deciding when to stop. However, existing EEG encoders are mainly designed for fixed-window decoding and may not provide reliable state representations under variable observation lengths. In addition, current ATDM-oriented encoders are typically tailored to specific EEG paradigms, limiting their applicability across different BCI tasks. To address these limitations, we propose ProtoTrigger, a two-stage prototype learning-based EEG state encoder for ATDM. ProtoTrigger uses prototype matching to extract stable local EEG embeddings and prototype-based attention to aggregate decision-relevant temporal evidence during progressive observation. Offline evaluations across three EEG paradigms demonstrated state-of-the-art accuracy-time trade-offs and strong generalizability across different EEG paradigms. An online human-in-the-loop augmented reality-based BCI experiment further demonstrated its real-time feasibility. These results suggest that ProtoTrigger provides a general EEG state encoding framework for efficient ATDM-based BCI systems.

articles.title: The Link between Family-Supportive Supervisor Behavior and Work-Family Enrichment: Results of Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Tadas Vadvilavicius; Giedrė Genevičiūtė-Janonė
articles.abstract: The mere presence of resources does not automatically lead to work-family enrichment. The current study aims to explore the mediating roles of work-family enrichment self-efficacy and leader-member exchange in the relationship between family-supportive supervisor behavior and work-family enrichment. A sample of 218 Lithuanian employees (166 women) participated in the study. Scales measuring family-supportive supervisor behavior, work-family enrichment, work-family enrichment self-efficacy, and leader-member exchange were utilized alongside demographic questions. The results confirmed that work–family enrichment self-efficacy and leader–member exchange fully mediate the relationship between family-supportive supervisor behavior and work-family enrichment. Additional analyses were performed at the dimensional level of family-supportive supervisor behavior. Paper discusses that merely having contextual resources, such as family-supportive supervisor behavior, may not by itself fully explain work-family enrichment. Further studies are needed to better understand the relationship between resources and work-family enrichment.

articles.title: How Sense of Coherence and Job Crafting Are Associated with Momentary Job Performance Among Employees With and Without Current Mental Health Issues
articles.authors: Anja I. Lehmann; Georg F. Bauer
articles.abstract: This study examined how Sense of Coherence (SOC) and job crafting relate to momentary job performance, using an ecological momentary assessment (EMA) design. We also investigated whether these relationships differ between employees with and without current mental health issues (MHI). Data were collected from 362 employees over 6 working days within 14 days, yielding 4,789 observations nested in 1,792 days. Multilevel analyses revealed that SOC positively predicted momentary job performance, with this effect mediated by general (between-level) job crafting: employees with stronger SOC engaged more frequently in job crafting behaviours, which in turn enhanced their performance. Among employees with current MHI, SOC and momentary (within-level) job crafting showed a compensatory function: SOC had a stronger positive effect on momentary performance, and the performance-enhancing effect of momentary job crafting was more pronounced. These findings highlight SOC and job crafting as key salutogenic factors that were linked to better momentary performance overall, with SOC and momentary job crafting showing an additional compensatory role for employees with current MHI.

articles.title: Validity and Heritability of the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology
articles.authors: Jeggan Tiego; Toby Constable; Kane Pavlovich; Samuel Brown; Jessica Tyler; Sue Malta; John Hopper; Kristian Eric Markon; Bree Hartshorn; Jessica Kwee
articles.abstract: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) model is an empirically based dimensional alternative to current consensus based diagnostic classification systems. It was developed through the synthesis of decades of empirical studies, but its construct and structural validity have never been comprehensively evaluated within a single sample using a confirmatory modeling approach. We assessed 108 psychopathology phenotypes, incorporating 37 novel components, in 542 monozygotic and 155 dizygotic twin pairs with diverse mental health histories to validate the hierarchical dimensional structure of psychopathology and quantify its genetic and environmental influences. Analyses largely replicated the theorized dimensional structure at lower, but not upper, tiers of the model. Heritability was lower and more variable at lower (median h2 = 43.5) than upper (median h2 = 57.1) tiers. Our findings provide partial construct and structural validation for the HiTOP model while identifying novel psychopathological phenotypes and heritability estimates to guide future biological studies.

articles.title: Social Diversity is Associated with Diversified Visual Attention in Infancy
articles.authors: Dean D'Souza; Sarah Josephine Rajendra; Leher Singh
articles.abstract: Perceptual narrowing of speech in infancy is often characterized as a maturational process driven by domain-specific experience with language. However, relatively little is known about the role of domain-general attentional mechanisms in this process. In the present study, we examined whether variability in infants’ everyday social environments is associated with attentional disengagement and whether disengagement, in turn, relates to perceptual narrowing. Seventy-nine Singaporean infants aged 9–11 months with varied exposure to multiple languages completed a visual attentional disengagement task and an auditory discrimination task assessing sensitivity to a non-native Hindi dental–retroflex phonemic contrast. Infants’ social diversity was quantified as the proportion of lifetime exposure to caregivers of other racial backgrounds. Results revealed that infants who disengaged attention more efficiently showed greater discrimination of the non-native phonemic contrast. Greater exposure to racially diverse social partners predicted more efficient attentional disengagement but was not directly associated with phoneme discrimination. Mediation analyses indicated that social diversity was indirectly related to non-native discrimination via attentional disengagement. Together, these findings support a developmental cascade in which variability in infants’ social environments is associated with adaptations in domain-general attention that, in turn, relate to perceptual sensitivity. The results highlight attentional disengagement as a potential mechanism linking environmental diversity and perceptual specialization and underscore the importance of considering infants’ everyday social ecologies in theories of early learning.

articles.title: The WEIRDest Theories in the World: The Narrow Intellectual Foundations of a Global Science of Mind
articles.authors: Leher Singh; Megan Pham
articles.abstract: Modern psychology has attended closely to the limits of WEIRD samples. At the same time, the field has paid far less attention to the foundational narrative which preceded and contributed to a WEIRD sampling bias. This paper connects Modern psychology has attended closely to the limits of WEIRD samples. At the same time, the field has paid far less attention to the foundational narrative that preceded and contributed to WEIRD sampling bias. This paper traces these patterns to two interconnected canons: an institutional canon that has traditionally centered Euro-American laboratory psychology and a philosophical canon that has framed foundational questions about mind primarily through a Western intellectual lineage. We conceptualize this pattern as disciplinary selectionism, whereby the privileging of particular intellectual traditions constrains the theories, constructs, methods, and ultimately the populations through which psychological knowledge is generated. Drawing on transregional histories of psychological science and philosophies of mind, the paper formulates a broader institutional and philosophical canon and discusses the contributions of scholars, traditions, and intellectual lineages often left outside psychology’s standard narrative. The aim is to broaden the historical and conceptual foundations of psychological science and thereby expand the areas of inquiry and explanatory frameworks available to the field. From this perspective, the WEIRD sampling problem is not merely a methodological consideration but one visible expression of a centuries-long process of disciplinary selectionism that has shaped the contours of modern psychological science.skews sampling to a WEIRD philosophy of mind, expressed through two interconnected canons: an institutional canon that centers Euro-American laboratory psychology and a philosophical canon that incorrectly represents questions of mind as emerging primarily from a Western intellectual lineage. Drawing on transregional histories of psychological science and philosophies of mind, the paper formulates a broader institutional and philosophical canon and discusses the contributions of scholars, traditions, and intellectual lineages often left outside psychology’s standard narrative. The aim of this paper is to broaden the historical and conceptual foundations of psychological science and thus expand areas of inquiry and explanatory frameworks available to the field.

articles.title: Operational Closure, Predictive Coding, and Psychosis: An Evolutionary Framework for Delusion, Hallucination, and Social Cognition
articles.authors: Leonel Gómez-Sena
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Predictive coding is an influential framework for psychosis, but most accounts begin at cortical inference and leave implicit the problem that makes prediction necessary: organisms must act in real time while operating only on internally generated states.

Methods: This theoretical review integrates theoretical biology, predictive processing, computational psychiatry, the cognitive neuropsychiatry of delusions and social cognition.

Results: Nervous systems evolved to coordinate action, not to reconstruct the world. Because perturbations become organism-specific neural states, the nervous system is operationally closed and causally open, and requires an anticipatory model constraining perception, action and belief. Self-monitoring follows as the generic solution for any closed system that acts, grounding comparator accounts. The model is updated in content and calibrated in confidence through two routes of correction: direct sensorimotor coupling, and interpersonal exchange, which operates only on what can be shared. As an appraisal accumulates structural load it becomes less shareable, and so beyond interpersonal correction.

Conclusions: Hallucinations, delusions and social-cognitive disturbances appear as disruptions at different levels of a single system that updates and calibrates the model of the world. The account accommodates domain-general updating abnormalities, predicts that structural centrality explains additional variance in resistance to revision, and grounds psychosocial intervention.

articles.title: The costs and benefits of mind-wandering: 13 years on
articles.authors: Shivang Shelat; Jonathan Schooler
articles.abstract: An abundance of evidence suggests that mind-wandering, or task-unrelated thought, poses significant detriments to performance. In 2013, however, Mooneyham & Schooler broadened mind-wandering’s impact by reviewing emerging literature on both its costs and benefits. Research has now expanded enough that mind-wandering can no longer be treated as a simple failure of attention. In this sequel, we synthesize key findings from the past 13 years on when mind-wandering harms and when it helps. On the cost side, mind-wandering can reduce sensitivity to others’ pain, spread lapses across peers in learning contexts, disrupt fine motor control, and weaken memory encoding. On the benefit side, mind-wandering is linked with improved memory consolidation, especially when thoughts return to recently learned material. Additional work suggests that mind-wandering can facilitate extraction of hidden probabilistic structure during statistical learning, support low-stakes decisions with less deliberative effort, and reduce semantic satiation during highly repetitive tasks. We also revisit mind-wandering’s relation to mood, emphasizing that affective outcomes depend on more than just task-relatedness alone. This article outlines future directions to cultivate a sharper scientific understanding of how mind-wandering shapes different kinds of behavior.

articles.title: Revealing implicit social bias through EEG-informed generative AI.
articles.authors: Aotong Li; Tuukka Ruotsalo; Christian Montag; Michiel Marten Spape
articles.abstract: Our first impression of others is commonly defined by our emotions and attitudes towards perceived group identities, which can influence how we judge their competence and trustworthiness. Investigating this remains challenging as social desirability and lack of awareness obscure attitudinal measures of first impressions. Although behavioural, computerised tests can provide an alternative, indirect means for assessing bias, such measures are not easily interpretable and may not be individually diagnostic. Rather than relying on questionnaires or reaction times, we suggest EEG evoked by faces can be used to infer how social bias affects first impressions. Participants (N=38) viewed AI-generated faces while their EEG was recorded. Brain responses to these faces were then used to train classifiers to predict which candidates each individual would later vote for in a fictional leadership contest. These predictions were used as implicit “BrainVotes” to recalibrate the generative neural network to produce new images that aligned with individual leadership perceptions. Two months later, participants from the original sample took part in a mock election: BrainVote-generated images were 2.67 times more likely to win than matched controls. Visual analysis of the BrainVote images gave evidence for a common senior, masculine leader stereotype, especially for those participants who scored high in gender-career implicit association tests. Thus, using brain-responses in interaction with generative AI can project individual impressions of what constitutes leadership, and in so doing, reveal our implicit social biases.

articles.title: Artists Can Design Memory, and AI Can Predict It
articles.authors: Trent Davis; Yifei Evie Chen; Wilma A. Bainbridge
articles.abstract: Can artists deliberately design artworks to be remembered—or forgotten? Prior research has shown that artwork memorability is consistent across viewers and can be predicted by deep neural networks, yet it remains unclear whether memorability can be intentionally manipulated. Across three complementary experiments, we tested whether visual memory outcomes can be shaped through artistic design, and how well such outcomes are predicted by artists, laypeople, and artificial intelligence. We launched a nationwide art contest in which artists submitted works explicitly intended to be either memorable or forgettable. Using both online and in-gallery recognition tasks, we found that artist intent significantly influenced memory performance, with memorable and forgettable artworks diverging reliably across individuals and contexts. Yet when comparing predictions, a deep neural network (ResMem) consistently outperformed both human observers and artists in forecasting which artworks would be remembered. Moreover, clustering and regression analyses revealed a reduced set of psychologically interpretable features that accounted for nearly half of the variance in memory performance and aligned with ResMem’s predictions, but not with human judgments. Together, these findings suggest that visual memorability is not only a stable and generalizable construct but also one that can be deliberately crafted, though often in ways that elude human intuition and are better captured by computational models.

articles.title: Measurement Reliability of Individual Differences in Naturalistic Reading
articles.authors: Cui Ding; Lena A. Jäger
articles.abstract: Research on individual differences in reading often links participant-specific effects of linguistic predictors to reader characteristics such as cognitive abilities. Such analyses require that these effects be measured reliably, yet reported reliabilities (operationalized as correlations across measurement contexts) vary widely, raising concerns about the suitability of these effects for individual-differences research. We argue that reliability should first be understood as a measurement outcome shaped by experimental design and estimation method before drawing conclusions about the inherent reliability of a specific linguistic predictor, task, or paradigm. Using formal derivations and simulations, we show that, under conventional correlation estimation methods, reliability is attenuated by measurement noise, limited trial counts, low predictor variability, and weak between-subject variance, while participant count primarily determines estimation uncertainty. By comparing five estimation methods, we identify Bayesian two-task hierarchical models that estimate the latent correlation as providing the most accurate estimates and the best-calibrated uncertainty. We validate these findings using cross-session eye-tracking data from the German Individual Differences Corpus (InDiCo), focusing on individual effects of word length, lexical frequency, and surprisal on gaze duration. Empirical reliability estimates increase with trial count, participant count, predictor variability, and the ratio of between-subject variance to measurement noise, with the Bayesian latent-correlation approach performing the best overall. These findings provide a principled framework for interpreting observed reliability, evaluating estimation methods, and improving the planning and designing of studies on individual differences in naturalistic reading.

articles.title: Attribute-guided attention is an adaptive mechanism for efficient search during naturalistic decision-making
articles.authors: Xiaozhi Taro Yang; Wenjia Joyce Zhao; Alexandre Filipowicz; Laura Ayres Zaneski; M. Kathleen Caulfield; Hilke Plassmann; Joe Kable
articles.abstract: Many real-world decisions require selecting from large displays of options that vary along multiple attributes, as when choosing a product from a store shelf. Here, we examine how decision-makers navigate such displays and how search strategies vary as the number of options increases. In a large-scale mobile eye-tracking study (n > 200), participants shopped in a controlled mock grocery store and chose among varying set sizes of products across categories. Our descriptive analysis showed that participants used perceptually accessible attributes, particularly brand, to guide search. This attribute-based search increased in larger choice sets and was strongest in categories where brand was most visually distinct, and among individuals who rated brand as more important. Using an efficient search model based on Bayesian updating, we show that relying on accessible attributes is consistent with an adaptive strategy. Together, these results provide novel insight into how attribute-guided search supports naturalistic multi-option decision making.

articles.title: Characterizing actors in online research: Authenticity checking is more than bot detection
articles.authors: Greg Jensen; Megan Bruun; Elizabeth A. Velkoff
articles.abstract: Alongside the growing prevalence and flexibility of AI tools, there has been corresponding concern that data collected using online recruitment platforms may increasingly be compromised by “bots.” We tested a variety of countermeasures intended to detect bad-faith behavior on the part of online participants recruited from a Prolific sample (N = 372) and tested using both the Qualtrics and Gorilla research task platforms. Our test suggest that although fully automated bots likely remain rare on Prolific, a substantial minority (21.5%) of participants exhibited patterns of behavior that we characterized as suspicious. Our results suggest that many patterns of behavior that pose a threat to the integrity of data collected online arise not from bots, but from humans who disregard task instructions and make intermittent use of AI and other tools as shortcuts. This renders traditional “attention checks” insufficient to verify good-faith adherence to task instructions. We provide recommendations and next steps for the development of both visible and invisible assays of participant behavior, intended not only to verify their attention to instructions, but also the good-faith authenticity of their responses.

articles.title: How Large Language Model Benchmarks Are Built: A Measurement-Oriented Tutorial and Empirical Demonstration with IRT-Viz-Eval
articles.authors: PRESTON DAVID BOTTER
articles.abstract:
Benchmark construction differs from developing an educational or psychological
assessment. This tutorial introduces LLM benchmark development to social-science
readers, especially those working in psychological and educational measurement, through
eight stages from intended use to maintenance. IRT-Viz-Eval illustrates the process
with 84 generated psychometric plots and 198 tasks. Five vision-language systems were
administered through Hugging Face Inference Providers and scored against program-
matic ground truth. Mean task-normalized scores ranged from .600 to .719; task profiles,
output validity, latency, and aggregation differed. The demonstration shows why in-
terpretation requires more than a leaderboard total. Validity and scale-development
scholarship disciplines benchmark claims, but benchmark scores are not treated as
psychological traits, and the paper does not assume that every benchmark requires a
human-test psychometric model.

articles.title: Interpretable Symbolic Regression for Psychological Questionnaire Data: Prediction, Descriptor Discovery, and Nonlinear Interaction Analysis
articles.authors: Kyung-Ran Yu; Seong-Hoon Jang
articles.abstract: Psychological researchers increasingly use machine-learning methods to improve prediction, yet many high-performing models require post-hoc explanation and provide limited insight into how predictors combine to shape outcomes. We present an application-oriented workflow for GoodRegressor, a hierarchical, depth-controlled symbolic-regression framework, using psychological questionnaire data. The workflow was demonstrated with independent datasets of middle-aged wives from Japan (n = 201) and South Korea (n = 220), with marital satisfaction predicted from demographic variables, family viewpoints, conflict-resolution strategies, and derived descriptors. The datasets were analyzed separately because the family-viewpoint measure was not sufficiently invariant across countries. Nine regression methods were evaluated using identical deterministic five-fold test partitions. In five-fold held-out testing, GoodRegressor showed the strongest predictive performance in Japan (5 = .441, 5 = 0.220, 5 = .178). In South Korea, GoodRegressor remained competitive (5 = .338, 5 = 0.199, 5 = .155), although Elastic Net, Ridge, and Random Forest performed somewhat better overall. Among equation-oriented methods, GoodRegressor substantially outperformed PhySO and EQL. Full-data GoodRegressor ensembles identified husband’s age, assertion, and age-difference-by-assertion structure in Japan, and avoidance, husband’s age, and family-priority-by-avoidance structure in South Korea. These findings support symbolic regression as a practical approach for combining competitive prediction with directly inspectable nonlinear and interaction structure, facilitating interpretable hypothesis generation in psychological research.

articles.title: A Framework for Ongoing Psychotherapy Case Review
articles.authors: Juan P. Quintanilla
articles.abstract: Psychotherapy is a complex clinical task prone to biases and overlooked factors, requiring ongoing case evaluation. This paper proposes a structured set of questions designed to support systematic case review, addressing risk assessment, case formulation, relational dynamics, and therapeutic progress. The framework is intended to facilitate continuous self-supervision in clinical practice and may be useful for both early-career and experienced therapists, as well as in formal supervision contexts. The rationale and clinical relevance of each component are discussed.

articles.title: Artificial-Intelligence-Mediated Contamination in Online Research: Taxonomy, Risk Gradient, and Recommendations
articles.authors: Zhicheng Lin
articles.abstract: For 2 decades, online research has relied on a quality heuristic: Careful, coherent responding is good data. That heuristic is no longer reliable. Autonomous artificial-intelligence (AI) agents can now pass nearly all conventional quality checks, and in text-rich crowd-work tasks, reported use of large language models approaches one third. When such consultation shapes the response process itself—not just its surface expression—the resulting data appear human-generated while embedding systematic, model-shaped distortions. I synthesize emerging evidence on how AI-mediated contamination varies across research settings in prevalence, mechanism, and inferential consequence; and distinguish three contamination pathways (full delegation, partial mediation, and spillover) and three vulnerability zones (text-rich tasks at highest risk, browser-based cognitive paradigms as an emerging vulnerability, and supervised or identity-vetted settings at lower risk). Even modest contamination can shift estimated public opinion, compress attitudinal extremes, and, over time, feed back into the training data for future models. Current platform countermeasures may raise the cost of contamination but have not been independently validated under adversarial conditions. I argue for a shift from ad hoc detection to infrastructure redesign: contamination-aware sensitivity analyses, explicit stratification of data collection by evidential role, transparency norms that balance open science with adversarial robustness, and a minimum reporting checklist for online studies in vulnerable settings. I close by asking when AI mediation should be treated not as contamination but as part of the ecological baseline of human responding—a question that requires the field to specify the target cognitive system in any given study.

articles.title: Sensory Processing Sensitivity and cognitive performance: A systematic review and theoretical framework through the lens of hot and cold cognition
articles.authors: Jessica O'Brien; Sophie Cronin; Tadgh Connery; Christian Ryan; Francesca Lionetti; Fiadhnait O'Keeffe; Jason Chan; Heleen A Slagter; Annalisa Setti
articles.abstract: Sensory Processing Sensitivity (SPS) reflects stable individual differences in sensitivity and responsivity to social, emotional, and physical environments. It is associated with negative and positive outcomes, such as mental health issues and responsivity to interventions respectively. Core tenets of the trait are differences in cognitive processing, particularly environmental awareness, allocation of attention and depth of processing; however, whether and how SPS actually modulates cognitive processing remains poorly understood. This understanding is necessary to better define the trait and its interplay with environmental features. This systematic review evaluated evidence for the influence of SPS on cognitive processing. Comprehensive searches of PubMed, EBSCO, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar and grey literature yielded 51 articles comprising 62 studies. Narrative synthesis revealed evidence of modulation in perception, attention and inhibition, specifically when emotions are involved (stimuli or context). Social cognition was a consistent association with SPS. Situating these findings within the theoretical framework of hot and cold cognition, we propose that SPS-related cognitive differences are most evident in tasks requiring hot (emotion-dependent) cognition (e.g. social cognition and tasks with emotional/motivational elements) rather than cold (emotion-independent) cognition (e.g. attention, problem solving) or in situations where the context has emotional or social relevance. This pattern is consistent with existing neuroimaging evidence. We propose testable hypotheses on the interplay between the trait, contextual variables, and task characteristics in determining cognitive performance, and the potential mechanisms behind it, particularly predictive coding, possibly modulated by arousal.

articles.title: The Meaning of "I": Semantic Self-Representation Tracks Internalizing Symptoms Within and Across Persons in Psychotherapy
articles.authors: Steven Mesquiti; Elizabeth Cameron Stade; Thomas Hull; Erik C Nook
articles.abstract: How we see ourselves, whether it be as good or bad, capable or helpless, is central to psychological well-being, and many forms of psychotherapy aim to change these exact self-representations. Could signatures of these beliefs emerge in how people talk about themselves? If so, linguistic assessments of self-representation could provide passive and scalable tools for tracking if and how self-concept changes over psychotherapy. Here, we develop such tools and demonstrate their relationship with psychological symptoms and treatment response in a large naturalistic dataset of message-based psychotherapy (N = 6,229). Using word embeddings, we measured where clients’ representation of self (operationalized as first-person pronoun embeddings) fell along semantic axes spanning ‘good–bad’ and ‘able–unable’ poles over the course of therapy. All analyses were first conducted in an exploratory subset of the data and replicated in a holdout validation subset following preregistration. In both datasets, first-person pronoun representations shifted toward the positive poles of both axes (i.e., ‘good’ and ‘able’) over treatment, and more positive representations were associated with greater reductions in symptoms. Control analyses suggested these results were specific to first-person pronouns and were not attributable to sentiment or the frequency of words used to compute embedding scores. A complementary analysis identified short phrases associated with each pole, revealing themes of apology, parents, and emotional preoccupation at the negative ends and themes of progress, social relationships, and activity at the positive ends. Together, these findings demonstrate that psycholinguistic measures can automatically and unobtrusively assess self-representational processes thought to underlie effective psychotherapy.

articles.title: MODELS AND SIZE: A QUALITATIVE TEXTBOOK ANALYSIS OF DIAGRAMMATIC BIAS IN COGNITIVE MODELS USING THE CODA METHOD
articles.authors: Mohsen Dolatabadi
articles.abstract: This qualitative textbook analysis employs the CODA (Conditions, Operations, Distortions, Actions) method to systematically examine the systematic biases embedded in diagrammatic representations of cognitive models. Through comparative analysis across three domains—linguistic image schemas derived from embodied cognition theory, Baddeley's working memory model as a paradigmatic cognitive diagram, and spectroscopic instrumentation diagrams as a contrast case with physical constraints—this investigation identifies a persistent "pen-model bias" wherein abstract-uncountable processes are consistently represented as small, bounded, discrete objects. This bias directly contradicts both linguistic image schemas that map abstract concepts to large/diffuse spatial configurations and neural evidence demonstrating that executive functions are distributed across extensive prefrontal networks. The analysis reveals that this bias constitutes a structural category error: the imposition of countable-object ontology onto uncountable processes, arising from the material constraints of two-dimensional diagrammatic representation, historical anchoring in computational and information-processing metaphors, and institutional perpetuation through textbook conventions. Drawing on Lakoff and Johnson's (1980, 1999) theory of embodied cognition, Johnson's (1987) image schema theory, and Baddeley's (1986, 2000) working memory framework, this study demonstrates that diagrams are not neutral illustrations but first-order theoretical commitments that systematically shape experimental design, data interpretation, and theory construction. A principled remodelling framework is proposed based on five principles: countability determines boundedness; scale should be annotated and defended; arrows should be replaced by gradients of influence; multi-page representation is honest representation; and legends should include ontological status. The remodelled working memory model presented here replaces the central executive box with a large, translucent, gradient region, maintains bounded forms only for countable components, and substitutes uniform arrows with graded influence fields. This work contributes to the emerging field of cognitive cartography and argues that representational choices require explicit bias auditing, interdisciplinary constraint integration from linguistics and neuroscience, and a commitment to scientific honesty over visual aesthetic. The analysis concludes by identifying a meta-blind spot: that replacing boxes with gradients merely substitutes one metaphor (discrete-object) for another (continuous-fluid), suggesting that static two-dimensional representations inherently distort dynamic neural processes and that the path forward lies in dynamic, time-animated representations.

articles.title: Self-regulation shapes who benefits from large language models
articles.authors: Xiangbin Teng; Sirui Ren
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) promise to broaden access to expertise, yet their benefits are uneven: the same model can scaffold a novice, accelerate an expert, or produce polished work that masks shallow understanding. We apply the established framework of self-regulated learning to human–LLM interaction and argue that loop quality emerges from the user–task–interface system rather than residing in the user alone. Productive loops involve three observable moves: steering sets goals and standards; monitoring evaluates fluent but fallible output; and repair tests, critiques, and revises it. Weak loops can create a synthesis trap in which users offload comparison and integration, producing false mastery—better assisted performance without corresponding transfer, confidence calibration, or error detection—and accumulating verification debt. The framework predicts that LLMs will widen differences between users when verification burden is high and regulatory support is weak, but narrow them when tasks are verifiable and interfaces externalize standards, evidence, and checks. We propose constraint density, monitoring calibration, and repair depth as process markers linking interaction traces to independent outcomes. This account turns divergent findings into testable predictions and motivates cognitive workbenches designed to preserve verification, agency, and transfer.

articles.title: Evidentiality, time, and inference in the New Guinea Highlands
articles.authors: Lila San Roque
articles.abstract:
Certain languages of New Guinea show a close attention to time and evidence within their evidential systems.
These languages position the moment that one apprehends an event, either directly or through other signs, as
something not only worth talking about, but worth contrasting in grammar. The paper presents examples from
these languages and identifies that even within this small area there is a range of semantic and structural
possibilities for evidential time reference. Perhaps this points to speakers’ creative responses to communicative
needs once evidence becomes of grammatical concern; how to convey not only the time something happens, but
also the time or place that one learned of it, and even how this implicates features of the addressee’s access to
knowledge. Discussion focuses on situations of inference about past events and on independent declarative
clauses, but extends to examples concerning direct evidence, future events and non-verbal predicates.

articles.title: Systematic theory–method dependencies in consciousness research
articles.authors: Morten Overgaard; Martin Dietz; Peter Thestrup Waade
articles.abstract: Scientific theories of consciousness are typically evaluated by comparing empirical findings across experimental paradigms. Such comparisons implicitly assume that different paradigms provide commensurable evidence and do not systematically favour particular theoretical interpretations. Here, we test this assumption using the updated ConTraSt database, comprising 518 published consciousness experiments, and Bayesian regression models relating methodological characteristics to theoretical interpretations. We find decisive evidence that experimental methodology predicts whether studies support, challenge, or do not mention major theories of consciousness. These associations are robust across multiple Bayesian model comparison approaches and remain evident across a range of prior specifications. Methodological effects differ substantially across theories, indicating that theories occupy partially distinct methodological niches rather than a common empirical space. While these findings do not imply that any individual theory is more or less valid, they suggest that empirical support is systematically shaped by methodological tradition. Ultimately, it can be challenged if neural correlates of consciousness are “studying the same things” – and if not, what they in that case are actually about. Consequently, direct comparisons between theories may be more constrained than generally assumed. Our results highlight the need for greater methodological diversity in theory testing and suggest that future progress in consciousness science may require approaches that explicitly address the relationship between experimental methodology and theoretical interpretation.

articles.title: Read Between the Li(n)es: Lateral Reading Training Promotes Information Discernment, Analytic Thinking, and Persuasion Knowledge
articles.authors: Marvin Fendt; Christian Scheibenzuber; Peter Adriaan Edelsbrunner; Nicolae Nistor
articles.abstract: In the current digital ecosystem, teaching individuals to critically evaluate sources is crucial for combating misinformation. Lateral reading is a cognitive strategy that can help people judge source credibility before reading an article. This preregistered randomized controlled study (N = 344) examined the effectiveness of two lateral reading interventions, a one-hour, cognitive apprenticeship-based training and one-page self-guided learning materials, on participants’ ability to judge information credibility and process it analytically. Using Bayesian regression analyses, we found that both interventions increased credibility judgments. While participants’ analytic thinking increased in both intervention conditions, it decreased in the control condition. Higher analytic thinking was also associated with more accurate credibility judgments. This study is among the first to measure persuasion knowledge as an outcome of interventions against misinformation, indicating that the interventions enhanced participants’ awareness of tactics used by unreliable information sources. Both interventions shifted participants’ focus away from content toward source evaluation, which was associated with more accurate credibility judgments. These findings confirm that lateral reading interventions are effective tools for fostering critical evaluation skills, that they enhance analytic thinking, shift assessment strategies, and bolster persuasion knowledge. Future research should explore long-term outcomes, motivational factors, and the role of persuasion knowledge in diverse populations.

articles.title: When Does the Body Bias the World? A Bayesian Causal Inference Model of Embodied Spatial Perception
articles.authors: Wenbo Luo; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: Bodily states can bias spatial judgments, yet the mechanisms underlying such effects remain contested. Using the backpack effect in hill-slant perception as a motivating case, the present study formalized a multisensory-integration account of embodied spatial perception within a Bayesian causal inference (BCI) framework. The model treats visual information specifying hill slant and bodily information associated with anticipated climbing effort as noisy signals that may arise from either a common cause or two independent causes. Deterministic parameter-space simulations examined how predicted perceptual bias varied with cue discrepancy, visual uncertainty, bodily uncertainty, and the prior probability of a common cause. Bodily bias emerged when the bodily signal received sufficient reliability weight and the two signals were inferred to share a common cause. Bias was suppressed when visual information was highly reliable, bodily information received little effective weight, or the common-cause prior was low. Cue discrepancy and bodily uncertainty produced nonlinear effects. The standard BCI model predicted a transition from attraction toward the bodily signal to near-zero bias under extreme discrepancy, but not repulsion. An exploratory extension showed that repulsion can emerge when causal segregation is supplemented by a conflict-sensitive contrastive-correction process. By translating a qualitative multisensory proposal into a formal computational model, we provide a mathematical basis for formulating and testing hypotheses about embodied spatial perception and, more specifically, explicit computational boundary conditions for bodily bias.

articles.title: EVALUATING THE BIOLOGICAL RELEVANCE OF THE RELATIVISTIC THEORY OF CONSCIOUSNESS
articles.authors: Wolfgang Kromer
articles.abstract: According to the Relativistic Theory of Consciousness by Lahav and Neemeh, consciousness is not an absolute feature but a relativistic one that depends on the reference system of the observer. The theory offers a new, thought-provoking view on consciousness, but also raises critical issues. First: What is the fundamental precondition of consciousness which the Relativistic Theory may be based upon? Although this aspect does not question the relativistic principle as such, it still remains open. Therefore, a Comparator Model of consciousness will be discussed in relation to the Relativistic Theory of Consciousness. Second: What is the Relativistic Theory’s biological relevance? This solely depends on the theory’s real-world applicability because this is it what the authors fundamentally envisage by their statement that we just need to move to the appropriate frame of reference in order to measure phenomenal properties. Although the mathematical formulation of changing from a third-person to a first-person frame of reference is possible when based on suitable premises, and may well be internally consistent, this does not per se prove any corresponding biological reality. Thus, the technological requirements for such a transition are a most critical issue. The obstacles in real-life will be addressed.

articles.title: Quantifying the rate and amplitude of cultural change in populations of AI agents
articles.authors: Alberto Acerbi; Simon Carrignon; Joseph Michael Stubbersfield
articles.abstract:
Researchers in cultural evolution have developed a wide range of models which quantify the rate and amplitude of cultural change across diverse contexts, from the spread of technology in prehistoric societies to the diﬀusion of ideas and changes in musical content. These models provide insights into how behavioural and psychological factors influence population level dynamics in humans and other animals. In this paper, we use these models to analyse the rate and amplitude of cultural change in a population of artificial agents producing health advice. The content is generated using an evolutionary algorithm in
which groups of Large Language Models (LLMs) are prompted to generate and select textual content generated by other LLMs. We then fit a series of cultural evolution models using Approximate Bayesian Computation to estimate the factors influencing LLMs' content creation and selection, and the population dynamics such behaviours produce. By employing standard methods already widely used to examine human behaviour, we provide a framework where cultural evolution driven by both human and artificial agents can be analysed and compared, with relevance to the potential dynamics of hybrid environments.

articles.title: A Diagnostic-Guided Hierarchical Bayesian Framework for Meta-Analytic Correlation Matrices: From Cellwise Estimation to Latent Co-Moderation
articles.authors: Piers Steel; Hadi Fariborzi
articles.abstract: Meta-analytic syntheses of correlation matrices typically estimate each cell independently and then repair the assembled matrix. That ordering creates compounding problems: cellwise heterogeneity estimates are least stable exactly where evidence is thinnest, independently generated cells routinely violate positive-definiteness, and the tendency of correlations to rise and fall together across studies is ignored entirely. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework that reverses the derivation: each study’s population correlation matrix is parameterized natively on the positive-definite manifold, cellwise means and heterogeneity are derived from the joint posterior, and the between-study covariance of cells receives a low-rank factor-analytic structure: co-heterogeneity — regularized by increasing shrinkage, with effective rank assessed from posterior eigenvalues and sensitivity refits. A tiered ladder of models with accompanying diagnostics recommends the simplest structure a given dataset supports. Across 1,225 simulation replications in 13 conditions, coverage of 95% credible intervals was generally near nominal across conditions (.920–.985), central-matrix recovery correlates .99 with truth, and on data with no co-heterogeneity the estimated between-study covariance is nearly structureless (mean absolute off-diagonal correlation .08, versus .25 under genuine structure). A preliminary sensitivity study quantifies the cost of ignoring within-study sampling covariance. Applied to a cross-cultural meta-analysis of the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (113 samples), between-study variation among the 36 directly reported matrices concentrates overwhelmingly on a single dimension (.83 of Fisher-z between-study variance; .76 under an Olkin–Siotani-corrected sensitivity fit, the two specifications bracketing the estimand); including the 77 matrices reconstructed from published factor loadings dilutes the share to .63 and exposes matrix provenance as the dataset’s largest structural moderator. Directly reported and reconstructed matrices should not be treated as exchangeable when the estimand is between-study matrix variation.

articles.title: Restructuring scientific papers for human and AI readers
articles.authors: Zhicheng Lin
articles.abstract: Scientific communication faces a dual crisis: exponential publication growth—now accelerated by AI-assisted writing—overwhelms human readers and reviewers, while fragmented research practices block automated synthesis. The behavioral and social sciences in particular suffer from incomparable stimulus databases, jingle–jangle measurement fallacies (same label, distinct constructs; different labels, same construct), and contextual blindness that conceals effect heterogeneity. Current AI tools can summarize papers but cannot synthesize findings across incommensurable studies; they also risk amplifying biases when trained on unstructured, unverified text. I propose restructuring scientific papers for dual audiences: front-loaded narratives for time-pressed human readers, paired with research-object packages containing executable code, semantic annotations, and tidy trial-level data. This design makes papers queryable research environments: readers can interrogate data and probe analytic choices in real time, while research-object packages enable automated verification and AI-assisted peer review grounded in executable evidence rather than narrative claims. Such papers become nodes in continuously updated evidence networks: each publication automatically contributes effect sizes to living, versioned meta-analyses, with corrections and retractions propagating through dependent analyses. Widespread adoption will require institutional recognition of structured documentation as essential scholarly output and computational infrastructure that serves both human comprehension and machine analysis.

articles.title: The View from Among: a Relational Epistemology for Structural Approaches
articles.authors: Francesco Ellia; Naotsugu Tsuchiya
articles.abstract: Consciousness science remains caught between a first-person approach that cannot independently corroborate its data and a third-person approach that excludes its target of explanation. We argue that this is a false dichotomy, and propose a third option, the first-person plural perspective (FPP): the position that the primary route of epistemic access to the structure of experience is the plural “we”, the field of structural features recoverable across perspectives, rather than the singular “I” or the observer’s “them”. FPP is an epistemic position, not an ontological one; it posits no group mind, and it is a modest, deflationary realist about the relational structure of experiences as they are had. We show that this is the epistemology already implicit in the Qualia Structure paradigm, and illustrate it with a free-report paradigm.

articles.title: Dissociable Influences of Positive and Negative Incentives on Psychophysiological States During Mental Effort Allocation
articles.authors: Ziwei Cheng; Zhiyuan Liu; Jieni Zhou; Amitai Shenhav; wendy berry mendes
articles.abstract: Potential positive and negative outcomes can drive effort and motivation, but the affective and physiological responses associated with these motivational states are less examined. To examine whether affective experiences directly drive effort adjustments or if affective experiences and effort adjustments are independent responses to incentives, the current study investigated the relationships between incentives, psychophysiological states, and behavioral responses. Participants (Study 1, n=144; Study 2, n=101) played a cognitively demanding task under varying positive incentives (monetary reward per correct response) and negative incentives (monetary loss per error). We found that potential rewards led to faster responses and increased approach motivation and challenge states, whereas potential penalties led to slower and more accurate responses, and increased avoidance motivation and threat states. We also found an affect-behavior link such that greater avoidance motivation and threat states were associated with more cautious behavioral patterns. Furthermore, by manipulating participants' stress states in Study 2, we found that individuals in a threat state showed attenuated behavioral, subjective, and physiological reactivity to potential penalties relative to those in a challenge state. Together, the findings suggest that affective representations of incentives, specifically the subjective experience of threat, avoidance motivation, and sympathetic arousal, are closely linked to adjustments in mental effort allocation.

articles.title: A validity-guided workflow for robust large language model research in psychology
articles.authors: Zhicheng Lin
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly being integrated into psychological and behavioral research as research tools, evaluation targets, human simulators, and cognitive models. Yet recent evidence reveals severe measurement unreliability: personality assessments degenerate under factor analysis, moral preferences reverse with punctuation changes, and theory-of-mind accuracy varies widely with trivial rephrasing. These “measurement phantoms”—statistical artifacts masquerading as psychological phenomena—threaten the validity of a growing body of research. Guided by the dual-validity framework that integrates psychometrics with causal inference, we present a six-stage workflow that scales validity requirements to research ambition—using LLMs to code text requires basic reliability and accuracy, whereas claims about psychological properties demand comprehensive construct validation. Researchers must (1) explicitly define their research goal and corresponding validity requirements, (2) develop and validate computational instruments through psychometric testing, (3) design experiments that control for computational confounds, (4) execute protocols transparently, (5) analyze data with methods appropriate for non-independent observations, and (6) report findings within boundaries and use results to refine theory. We illustrate the workflow through an example of model evaluation—“LLM selfhood”—showing how systematic validation can distinguish genuine computational phenomena from measurement artifacts. By establishing validated computational instruments and transparent practices, this workflow provides a path toward building a robust empirical foundation for AI psychology research.

articles.title: Can AI Be Morally Wise? Evidence of a Systematic Alignment Artifact from a Validated Human Baseline
articles.authors: Sweta Kaman; Ankita Sharma; Romi Banerjee
articles.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in ethically sensitive roles - therapeutic support, clinical decision assistance, and legal analysis, raises the question of whether these systems possess genuine moral wisdom or merely simulate it. This study introduces a dual-layer computational psychometrics pipeline that combines lexical-emotional profiling with a five-dimension, behaviorally anchored wisdom rubric (Cognitive Integration, Contextual Adaptability, Reflective Empathic Action, Social-Emotional Equilibrium, and Ethical Flexibility) and validates it against an independent human expert baseline before using it to benchmark artificial intelligence. Free-text responses from 100 participants (1,300 vignette-level observations) to thirteen pictorial moral dilemmas were scored by five trained human raters, establishing a human-human inter-rater reliability benchmark (ICC = .764) prior to any AI comparison. Three architecturally distinct LLMs were then validated as automated raters against this human baseline, and a self-serving-bias check confirmed rater impartiality. Five state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Claude Sonnet, and Hy3) were subsequently benchmarked against the validated human baseline. All five systematically overrated their own moral reasoning relative to humans across every wisdom dimension, an alignment artifact further characterized by a cross-vignette variance paradox and scenario-insensitive moral differentiation consistent with reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback-style training; a sixth model, the small language model Llama-3.1-8B, was subsequently evaluated post hoc to test whether this pattern depended on model scale and showed the identical inflation pattern despite being an order of magnitude smaller. Cross-layer analyses linked this artifact to a structurally asymmetric human affective architecture in which disgust suppresses, and anticipation and trust amplify, wisdom-relevant cognition. These findings suggest that LLM moral response distributions differ systematically from validated human moral cognition baselines across multiple independent measurement layers. Critically, automated raters exhibited high internal consistency and no self-serving bias toward AI-generated text yet achieved only Poor agreement with independent human experts (ICC = .505 and .551), while agreeing more with each other (ICC = .585),  a finding with direct implications for LLM-as-judge evaluation frameworks across AI ethics, psychometric assessment, and behavioral research. These results carry implications for AI ethics governance and the responsible deployment of LLMs in emotionally consequential contexts.

articles.title: From Prompts to Constructs: A Dual-Validity Framework for Large Language Model Research in Psychology
articles.authors: Zhicheng Lin
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are entering psychological research both as tools and as objects of inquiry. Yet many studies apply human instruments to LLMs without establishing that the outputs are reliable or interpretable, raising the risk of measurement phantoms—statistical regularities mistaken for genuine psychological phenomena. This review argues that robust AI psychological research requires integrating two methodological traditions: psychometric validation of what a score means and causal inference standards for what the results warrant. It develops a dual-validity framework in which evidentiary demands scale with scientific ambition: from tool use through behavioral characterization and human simulation to cognitive modeling. Classifying text may require only accuracy and reliability; claiming that an LLM simulates anxiety or illuminates cognitive mechanisms requires additional evidence, including construct validity evidence and experimental controls. Progress depends on developing computational analogs of psychological constructs rather than assuming human measures automatically apply to language models.

articles.title: “He did not want to tell me and so I did not push”: Researchers' experiences of navigating ethnographic data collection in a special school
articles.authors: Astrid Bowen; Laura Fox; Kayleigh Doyle; Kathryn Asbury
articles.abstract: Learning-disabled children and young people experience systemic barriers to their inclusion in research, and researcher expertise and experience can either act as one of those barriers or as a facilitator. Researcher accounts of conducting research with learning-disabled children and young people can provide useful insights into practices that facilitate inclusion, yet such accounts are scarce. This study presents a secondary analysis of ethnographic data collected by four researchers during a study exploring the communication preferences of learning-disabled students in a special school setting in the North of England. It focuses on the researchers’ reflections on their own experiences of data collection, as captured in their fieldnotes.  Four themes were developed using thematic analysis: (1) Moving beyond a "one size fits all" approach; (2) The importance of relationships; (3) Researching as an outsider/insider; (4) Why it matters who does the research. Findings highlight the positive, yet sometimes challenging, experiences of working with learning-disabled students in a special school setting, and contribute to the knowledge base on supporting inclusive practices for qualitative research with learning-disabled participants. Suggestions for how researchers can develop strategies to navigate the challenges they may encounter during data collection are discussed.

articles.title: Psychological mechanisms mediating the effect of gamified digital interventions on physical activity: A randomized controlled trial
articles.authors: Alexandre Mazéas; Martin S Hagger; Martine Duclos; Aïna Chalabaev
articles.abstract:
Background: Despite the promising efficacy of gamified digital interventions in promoting physical activity, we currently have limited evidence on the theory-based mechanisms responsible for effects of these interventions on behavior change. 
Objectives: As part of the DIPPAO intervention randomized controlled trial, we examined the effects of a digital, gamified adapted physical activity program (KiplinTM) on autonomous motivation and weight stigma processes among obese patients with type 2 diabetes and tested candidate psychological mechanisms underlying these effects based on self-determination theory and the social identity approach.
Methods: Participants (N = 50, M age = 47.90 years, SD = 12.49; 74% female) were randomized to either the KiplinTM digital intervention program or a usual care control group and followed the program for three months. Outcome measures of device-assessed physical activity and psychological variables (motivation, need satisfaction, in-group identification, weight stigma) were assessed at baseline and 6-month follow-up. Data were analyzed using mixed-effects models and partial least squares structural equation modeling.
Results: Autonomous motivation increased significantly in both groups, but with no significant between-group differences. Structural equation modeling did not support the proposed theory-based mechanisms for intervention effects.
Conclusion: Current data do not support motivation and weight stigma changes as potential mechanisms for the efficacy of the digital intervention over traditional programs. Future research should investigate additional candidate psychological mechanisms that account for program effects using designs with adequate statistical power and sufficiently sensitive measures, consider psychological mediators representing reflective and automatic behavioral determinants, and employ appropriate control or comparison groups.
Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04887077; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04887077

articles.title: Neuroinflammation and Oxidative Stress in Methamphetamine-Induced Psychosis: Mechanisms and the Therapeutic Potential of Melatonin as a Neuroprotective Agent
articles.authors: Anh Ngoc Tran; Michael Maes; George Anderson; Rasmon Kalayasiri
articles.abstract: Methamphetamine-induced psychosis (MAP) is a prevalent and severe complication among methamphetamine (MA) users. Although current treatment follows antipsychotic-based strategies mirroring schizophrenia (SCZ) management, a substantial proportion of patients experience treatment failure, disease progression, or adverse effects, highlighting the need for novel treatment options. Emerging evidence suggests that MAP pathophysiology extends beyond neurotransmitter dysregulation to encompass immune disturbances and oxidant/antioxidant imbalance. MAP is characterized by a significant decrease across all immunological profiles, with the compensatory immune-regulatory reflex system (CIRS) being particularly depleted, thereby contributing to a selective upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1α, CCL5, and IL-12p70, reflecting an aberrant immune-inflammatory response system (IRS)/CIRS imbalance that is distinct from patterns observed in SCZ, major depressive disorder, and bipolar disorder. MAP development is also associated with reduced antioxidant defense, increased advanced glycation end products (AGEs) and its soluble receptor sRAGE, circadian and mitochondrial dysregulation, and an increased oxidant/antioxidant ratio that correlates with psychosis severity. This narrative review is among the first to synthesize these two complementary pathways – IRS/CIRS imbalance and AGE/RAGE axis stress – within a unified neuroimmune-oxidative-circadian-mitochondrial framework of MAP pathophysiology. Building on this framework, melatonin, given its anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, circadian and mitochondria-optimizing properties, emerges as a promising adjunctive neuroprotective candidate. However, there is a lack of clinical evidence to establish the efficacy of melatonin in MAP patients. Future research priorities include randomized controlled trials of melatonin in MAP, investigation of mirtazapine and other adjunctive candidates, and exploration of metabolic disturbances as an additional etiological pathway in MAP.

articles.title: Surpassed by Nature: A Qualitative Exploration of Ehrfurcht (Awe) in German Context
articles.authors: Tini L. C. Katz; Jonathan R. Hicks
articles.abstract: To investigate awe in a culture-sensitive manner, we wanted to understand the nuances of its German translation, ehrfurcht. This study explores the current meaning, perception, and contexts of ehrfurcht in nature. We conducted N = 21 semi-structured interviews with 11 female and 10 male German-speaking participants, who had an affinity for nature. Qualitative content analysis revealed that ehrfurcht is a rarely used term that encompasses respectfully marveling at nature, being humble, and accepting one’s smaller significance. Two types of the ehrfurcht perception emerged: temporary (i.e., short-term) and attitudinal (i.e., longer-lasting). Temporary Ehrfurcht involved the themes Extraordinary Qualities of Perception, Interacting with Nature as Counterpart, and Religiosity, Spirituality, and Mindfulness, and Accommodation of Outlook on Life. Attitudinal Ehrfurcht involved Companionship with Nature, Considering oneself to be Integrated into Nature, Being Limited as Human Compared to Nature, and Acknowledging Nature’s Transcendence. Contexts of Temporary Ehrfurcht were linked to Diverse Perceptions of Nature, Being Physically Surrounded by Nature, and Sufficient Attention for Nature. Contexts of Attitudinal Ehrfurcht were embedded in multiple areas of life, such as consumption, behavior towards other living beings or education. This study provides a foundation for further ehrfurcht research and cross-cultural comparisons.

articles.title: Prior width, test dimensionality, and power: reassessing Ballinger and Crocker's (2021) Bayes-factor evidence on Whites' reactions to multicultural policies
articles.authors: Lukas Wallrich
articles.abstract: Pooled and tested as one composite, identity threat shows a small effect (d = 0.17); exclusion and valuation nulls hold only when pooled or under a prior wider than field effects.

articles.title: No convincing evidence for prospective effects between internet gaming disorder and sleep problems: A reanalysis and comment on Peng et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using results from a cross-lagged panel model, Peng et al. argued that internet gaming disorder (IGD) and sleep problems exert reciprocal longitudinal influences on one another during adolescence. However, statistically significant cross-lagged associations do not necessarily indicate genuine prospective effects and may instead arise as artifacts of the underlying data structure. We fitted several alternative models to data simulated to reproduce the correlation structure reported by Peng et al. The analyses yielded conflicting results, with some models indicating increasing effects and others suggesting decreasing effects between IGD and sleep problems. Furthermore, a model assuming spurious longitudinal associations provided an adequate representation of the data without requiring direct effects between the constructs over time. Consequently, the findings reported by Peng et al. may reflect statistical artifacts rather than true prospective influences. Consistent with multiverse methodology, we recommend evaluating competing models and drawing conclusions from the collective pattern of evidence rather than from a single analytic approach.

articles.title: Dissociable Roles of Reward Prediction Error in the Contrasting Mood Dynamics of Depression and Anxiety
articles.authors: Zhihao Wang; Ting Wang; Tian Nan; Jiahua Xu; Andre Aleman; Yue-jia Luo; Bastien Blain; Yunzhe Liu; Pengfei Xu
articles.abstract: Mood fluctuations, central to human experience, are profoundly influenced by reward prediction errors (RPE). Although depression and anxiety traditionally exhibit contrasting mood fluctuations, their interrelated nature has made it challenging to pinpoint their specific roles in RPE-induced mood variations. In this study, we employed a computational model of momentary mood within a gambling task, involving 2,043 participants across five experiments. Participants also completed a battery of questionnaires designed to allow us to dissociate anxiety- and depression-specific traits through bifactor modelling. Results showed that depression was associated with dampened mood fluctuations due to mood hyposensitivity to RPE. Importantly, this pattern was also found in patients with affective disorders. In contrast, anxiety correlated with heightened mood fluctuations stemming from mood hypersensitivity to RPE in non-clinical participants. Moreover, the shared depression/anxiety component was linked to lower affective baseline and greater risk aversion. Collectively, our results uncover computational dissociation of depression vs. anxiety using RPE-based mood modeling and present multi-dimensional computational signatures for these symptoms, with clinical relevance for management of mood disorders.

articles.title: Post-Error Slowing May Not Be Proactive: Electrophysiological evidence favours a disorienting account
articles.authors: Nathan Beu; Nicholas Burns; Irina Baetu
articles.abstract: Post-error slowing (PES) is widely assumed to reflect strategic response caution, but this assumption is based primarily on computational modelling rather than direct neural evidence. Dutilh and colleagues (2012b) compared five accounts of PES and concluded that slowing results from widened response boundaries reflecting increased caution. We used EEG to test predictions derived from three of the five accounts modelled by Dutilh and colleagues, as well as Notebaert and colleagues' (2009) orienting account. In a Go/No-Go task administered to healthy young adults (N = 94, 24.3 ± 4.8 yrs), ERPs provided temporally specific indices of the cognitive operations implied by these accounts, including stimulus evaluation, attentional processing, and error appraisal. A response-caution account would predict a larger N2 after errors and correlation between N2 amplitude and PES magnitude. Neither prediction was supported. Instead, the results favoured a disorienting account in which errors disrupt ongoing attentional processing. The anterior N1 was significantly attenuated after errors (p = .012), and a less negative post-error N1 was positively correlated with PES magnitude (p = .027). PES in this task was therefore more closely associated with attenuation of early attentional processing than with strategic response caution or the magnitude of error appraisal. This pattern is more consistent with attentional vulnerability than deliberate cognitive control.

articles.title: Music behind bars: Observing musical abilities of people in prison improves social attitudes towards them
articles.authors: Tanushree Agrawal; Adena Schachner
articles.abstract: Intergroup contact is often effective at reducing prejudice; however, it is less effective for groups that people find threatening (e.g. people in prison). We test whether a novel form of parasocial contact, a brief video demonstrating the musicality of a person experiencing incarceration, reduces negative attitudes towards incarcerated people. Participants from across the U.S. (N=720) made social judgments about people in prison before and after watching a real video of an incarcerated person (<2 minutes; from documentary 16 Bars). Across randomly-assigned conditions, we manipulated whether matched-length videos demonstrated musicality, or overt prosocial behavior without music. Pre-intervention attitudes towards people in prison were more negative than other comparison groups (immigrants, people experiencing homelessness). Videos depicting musicality significantly increased feelings of warmth, reduced blatant dehumanization, and improved judgments about the beauty, goodness, pleasantness, honesty, and niceness of people in prison. These videos were as effective at improving social attitudes as videos that showed overtly prosocial behavior. Brief video interventions showing others’ musicality hold promise as a tool to change attitudes and behavior toward marginalized people at a large scale, with applications for policy, education, and the value of music in the public sphere.

articles.title: Within-Person Physiologic State Transitions in Burnout-Like Functional Collapse Across Autistic and High-Ability Phenotypes: A Retrospective Longitudinal Case Series
articles.authors: Simone Hauck; Luciana Terra de Oliveira
articles.abstract:
Background. Autistic adults and others with high processing cost describe burnout-like functional collapse as predominantly physical, with extreme fatigue, sensory amplification and loss of executive throughput. Quantitative within-person descriptions of collapse and re-engagement are scarce. We examined whether these transitions coincided with coordinated neuroendocrine, osmotic and iron-handling changes against a low acute-phase inflammatory background.

Methods. This retrospective observational mechanistic case series used routine-care records from one private practice. Four deliberately selected, non-consecutive adults contributed paired containment/collapse and reopening/re-engagement windows; a fifth contributed three draws at 72-h intervals. States were anchored in contemporaneous function and context, not biomarker direction. The corpus comprised 182 dated collections and 3,523 non-empty data cells, treated as correlated observations rather than independent replicates. A separate single-case exercise assessed feasibility of a low-cost within-person monitoring workflow and did not define states or enter the cross-case analysis. Ethics approval: CAAE 99556626.7.0000.5327.

Results. Paired comparisons showed recurrent but heterogeneous patterns: reduced HPA dynamic range, state-sensitive osmotic regulation, altered iron availability in elevated- and low-ferritin configurations, and predominantly low acute-phase inflammatory markers. Functional reopening accompanied expansion of dynamic range following load reduction, circadian/metabolic recalibration and clinically supervised withdrawal of non-targeted pharmacologic burden. At available sampling times, first coordinated axis changes occurred 10-18 days after documented turning points in three participants; in one, peak transferrin saturation preceded the first observed HPA change by 18 days. The 144-h exhibit showed reversible leukocyte reconfiguration, including eosinophils 380 → 0 → 750/µL, against low sampled acute-phase inflammation. The feasibility exercise yielded 78 entries across 53 days in a 103-day window, retaining a 29-day gap without interpolation.

Conclusions. These selected observations generate a testable framework in which burnout-like transitions are more consistent with multisystem regulatory decoupling than simple depletion. They do not establish mechanism, diagnostic thresholds or treatment effects. Prospective, high-frequency, independently replicated within-person studies are required. The separate monitoring exercise demonstrates workflow feasibility only and does not validate diagnostic, clinical-monitoring or medication-management use.

articles.title: The inversion-induced size illusion in letters and the role of the contour-based centroid
articles.authors: Karin Hasegawa; Hiroyuki Muto
articles.abstract: Inverting a visual stimulus can alter its perceived size. Recent studies have shown that upright letters are perceived as larger than inverted letters, an effect opposite in direction to the inversion-induced size illusion reported for faces. However, previous studies have primarily examined the average illusion across letters, leaving unclear whether the effect depends on letter-specific processing and whether it varies systematically with visual properties of individual letters. In Experiment 1, we measured the point of subjective equality (PSE) for 17 Latin letters. Upright letters were perceived as larger than inverted letters on average, replicating the previously reported inversion-induced size illusion, although the magnitude and direction of the effect varied across letters. A post hoc exploratory analysis further revealed a strong positive association between the illusion effect and the vertical position of the contour-based centroid. In Experiment 2, we therefore examined non-letter polygons corresponding to the convex hulls of the letters from Experiment 1, thereby preserving their contour-based centroids while eliminating letter identity. The polygons showed no inversion-induced size illusion on average, but the strong association between contour-based centroid position and illusion magnitude was replicated. Across both stimulus categories, stimuli with higher contour-based centroids tended to produce larger positive illusion effects. These findings suggest that the contour-based centroid is associated with perceived size across different visual shapes but cannot fully account for the average inversion-induced size illusion observed for letters. The illusion in letters may therefore depend on interactions between orientation-dependent shape properties and other visual or orthographic characteristics.

articles.title: Modular Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) Adaptations for Symptom-Level and Past-Week Depression Assessment in Clinical and Nonclinical Adults
articles.authors: Dawson Haddox; Eiko I Fried; Ricarda K. K. Proppert; Carlotta Rieble; Zachary Daniel Cohen
articles.abstract: The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and its shorter forms are widely used measures of depression symptoms. We evaluated three modular adaptations: (1) separating four double-barreled items into eight single-barreled items (sad mood/hopelessness, insomnia/hypersomnia, poor appetite/overeating, and psychomotor agitation/retardation), (2) adding irritability and low libido items, and (3) revising the instructions and response options to assess symptoms over one week rather than two. We tested these adaptations across six studies (N = 2,467). The single-barreled format showed excellent total score and screening classification agreement with the original format, as well as comparable internal consistency, temporal stability, and convergent validity.
