It also captured greater symptom-level information: the separated items showed stronger correlations with matched criterion measures, distinct endorsement patterns, and non-redundant inter-correlations. The irritability and libido items correlated moderately to strongly with established measures of these constructs. The one-week versions showed moderate-to-strong internal consistency, convergent validity, and temporal stability. We conclude that these adaptations can be adopted individually or together for symptom-level or past-week assessment.

articles.title: Digital Transformation Capabilities and Supply Chain Finance Resilience: An Integrated AI–Blockchain–Analytics Framework
articles.authors: Jainish Bhagat
articles.abstract:
Supply chain finance (SCF) plays a pivotal role in maintaining liquidity and operational continuity across global value networks. However, systemic supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic volatility, and information asymmetry frequently expose SCF programs to severe friction and default risks. While digital transformation is widely touted as a catalyst for supply chain resilience, empirical evidence regarding the explicit mechanisms through which distinct digital transformation capabilities enhance Supply Chain Finance Resilience (SCFR) remains fragmented. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), and Information Processing Theory (IPT), this study develops and tests an integrated framework evaluating the direct and indirect impacts of Artificial Intelligence Capability (AIC), Blockchain Capability (BC), and Data Analytics Capability (DAC) on SCFR, mediated by Digital Trust in SCF Platforms (DT).
Using a computational research simulation methodology, a respondent-level dataset (N=500) representing supply chain, finance, operations, and IT decision-makers across international enterprises was algorithmically generated under a defensible latent-variable covariance structure. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was executed to evaluate the measurement and structural models. The structural analysis reveals that AIC (β=0.241,p<.001), BC (β=0.312,p<.001), and DAC (β=0.284,p<.001) significantly and positively drive Digital Trust in SCF Platforms, explaining 54.2% of its variance (R^2=0.542). Digital Trust, in turn, exerts a substantial direct effect on SCFR (β=0.385,p<.001). Furthermore, direct effects on SCFR were confirmed for DAC (β=0.218,p<.001) and AIC (β=0.152,p=.002), whereas the direct link from BC to SCFR was non-significant (β=0.071,p=.158). Formal mediation testing using percentile bootstrapping confirmed that Digital Trust fully mediates the relationship between Blockchain Capability and SCFR, while partially mediating the relationships for AIC and DAC. The overall structural model accounts for 58.6% of the variance in Supply Chain Finance Resilience (R^2=0.586,Q_"predict" ^2=0.412).
This methodological prototype advances theoretical understanding by unpacking the granular capability configurations necessary to foster digital trust and financial resilience in supply networks. For practitioners and policymakers, the findings highlight that investing in blockchain technology yields minimal resilience benefits unless coupled with platform-wide digital trust mechanisms, whereas AI and analytics offer dual-pathway benefits across operational and relational domains.

articles.title: La reserva de plazas de PDI permanente para personas con discapacidad
articles.authors: Francisco J Plaza Martín
articles.abstract: Este trabajo analiza la aplicación de la reserva legal de plazas para personas con discapacidad en el acceso al PDI permanente de las universidades públicas españolas entre 2016 y 2025. El artículo 59 del Estatuto Básico del Empleado Público protege y desarrolla, entre otros derechos,  el acceso en condiciones de igualdad a las funciones públicas (artículo 23.2 de la Constitución Española). A partir de solicitudes de información pública dirigidas a las universidades, se observa el incumplimiento generalizado de este deber de reserva, así como déficits de trazabilidad, información homogénea y control institucional. El problema detectado no debe describirse únicamente como una suma de omisiones administrativas universitarias, sino como un déficit de implementación de una política pública legalmente obligatoria.

articles.title: Estimating Regional Industry Employment from Economic Location Mechanisms: A Constrained Spatial Disaggregation for European Geographies
articles.authors: Riccardo Boero
articles.abstract: Fine-scale employment by industry is largely unavailable across European municipalities, yet it underpins regional economic analysis, environmental-economic extensions, and the regionalization of input--output accounts. This paper presents a mechanism-driven, constrained spatial disaggregation framework that estimates industry employment down to the Local Administrative Unit level while preserving official totals exactly at every geographical level. The economic mechanisms that shape where activity locates --- settlement, infrastructure and accessibility, natural-resource endowments, and inter-industry co-location --- are represented as a reproducible input dataset assembled from official and remote-sensing sources; a family of constrained allocation models, combined by a cross-validated convex ensemble, is trained on data-rich United States geographies and transferred to Europe under official Eurostat totals as constraints. Validated against independent national statistics in Italy, France, Germany, and Spain, the estimates reproduce the observed spatial distribution of employment within the held-out uncertainty of the models themselves, and the error does not inflate down the four-step disaggregation. The framework is open, inspectable, and reproducible, providing internally consistent fine-scale employment estimates wherever sub-national industry data are sparse.

articles.title: The Paperwork of Grief: Administrative Burden as a Defence Against Death Exposure in Clinical Care
articles.authors: Chukwudi Egbuonu
articles.abstract: Administrative work (documentation, the electronic record, the proliferation of meetings, the referral of distress onward to specialists) is treated almost universally in the clinician-wellbeing literature as a cause of burnout to be measured and reduced. This paper argues that in the most death-saturated settings of medicine (the cancer ward, the intensive care unit, the palliative service) that same burden may also do something the literature has not noticed: function as a social defence against sustained exposure to dying, offering clinicians a bounded, completable, finite task to retreat into when the bedside offers only problems that often end in death. The argument revives Isabel Menzies Lyth’s 1959 account of hospital routine as a collective defence against anxiety and brings it forward to the era of the electronic record, joining four literatures (on documentation burden, on death exposure and numbing, on terror management, and on the social defences of institutions) that have not previously been read together. If the conjecture holds, the prevailing prescription to strip administration away on efficiency grounds alone risks removing an unrecognised container without supplying a deliberate one, and the proper task is not to reduce paperwork but to distinguish what merely numbs from what genuinely contains, and to design containment for those who work among the dead. The claim is interpretive and bounded to high-mortality settings; the paper sets out how it could be tested and the competing explanations it complements rather than displaces.

articles.title: When Does Generative AI Become a Developmental Resource? A Multilevel Taxonomy of Enactment Conditions
articles.authors: Andreea Nicolau; Sonja Rispens; Pascale Marie Le Blanc; Kees Maton; Piet J. R. van Gool; Ad Kleingeld
articles.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) creates a developmental ambiguity for organizations: it can support learning, reflection, and judgment, but it can also accelerate task completion while reducing engagement with the cognitive and social processes through which capabilities develop. This study asks which multilevel conditions shape whether GenAI is enacted as a resource for learning and continuous development or as a shortcut for task completion. Drawing on an inductive, multi-stakeholder qualitative study with 41 organizational actors, we use thematic analysis to identify empirical categories and morphological principles to organize them into a multidimensional taxonomy of GenAI enactment. The taxonomy identifies four interrelated dimensions: Organizational Conditions, Capability Conditions, Decision Drivers, and GenAI Enactment. Interpreting these findings through the automation–augmentation paradox, we show that automation- and augmentation-oriented uses are not fixed properties of technologies or tasks but contextually produced orientations shaped by an iterative system of societal/institutional, organizational, and individual-related conditions. The study contributes to AI and management research by specifying the condition architecture through which GenAI becomes more or less developmental in practice. We argue that learning-oriented GenAI integration requires attention to the multilevel conditions that preserve verification, reflection, feedback, and accountable judgment when task completion no longer necessarily develops capability.

articles.title: Climate policy is domestic politics: Mechanisms shaping the political feasibility of mitigation
articles.authors: E. Keith Smith; Christina Eder; Sarah Gomm; Gabriele Spilker; Isabelle Stadelmann-Steffen
articles.abstract: The Paris Agreement shifted the central challenge of climate mitigation from international burden-sharing to domestic politics. In high-emitting countries, the binding constraint on near-term emissions cuts is no longer the absence of effective policy instruments, but their political feasibility, that is, governments' capacity and willingness to adopt, implement, and sustain mitigation policy over time. We review the political feasibility of climate mitigation along four dimensions: stakeholder interests and influence, public opinion and social norms, political-economic context and institutional constraints, and distributional effects and inequality. Using the policymaking process as our analytical lens, we trace how these dimensions hinder or enable mitigation at successive stages of agenda-setting, formulation, and implementation. We synthesise this literature into a practical framework for making mitigation politically feasible, identify a set of persistent misconceptions that obstruct progress, and outline near-term actions that the evidence supports. The central challenge of mitigation is no longer identifying effective instruments, but making them politically feasible under real-world conditions.

articles.title: Statistischer Quartalsbericht 2/2021
articles.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles.abstract: Regelmäßige vierteljährliche Veröffentlichung: Textbeiträge zu ausgewählten Themen (Teil 1) und statistische Daten (Teil 2)

articles.title: Leveraging LLMs to assist tourists at destinations – The opportunities and risks of deploying open-source humanoid robots
articles.authors: Yash Pandey; Spencer Kayser; Marius Portmann; Siamak Layeghy; Sara Dolnicar
articles.abstract: LLMs are transforming tourist search behaviour. Tourists currently access LLMs on phones, tablets, and laptops. Open-source humanoid robots change this: the LLM becomes embodied and physically situated at the destination. This conceptual paper develops a framework for understanding the consequences of deploying open-source humanoid robots in tourism. The framework rests on two constructs. Embodied authority transfer describes how tourists reattribute LLM output from a private planning tool to the destination's official service infrastructure when delivered by a robot hosted in a tourism setting. Capability asymmetry describes the gap between what an embodied LLM can fluently discuss and what it can accurately know or actually do. The article discusses deployment scenarios and risk, and offers a detailed research agenda.

articles.title: Corruption in Nepal's Local Governments: A Case Study of Institutional Weaknesses and Citizen Outcomes
articles.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles.abstract: This case study deals with corruption in public procurement at the local government level in Nepal. Nepal established 753 local governments with substantial responsibility for public spending, including procurement of goods, works and services, following the adoption of the Constitution in 2015. Mostly today, public spending is the responsibility of local governments, especially on capital investment in infrastructure, such as roads, schools, health facilities and water supply systems. But the speed of devolution of responsibilities has not been matched by adequate systems of transparency, accountability and integrity. This paper explores the nature and extent of corruption in local government procurement in Nepal, drawing on publicly available data from the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority, Transparency International, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and government audit reports. The analysis shows that procurement is a high-risk area for corruption at the local level. Corrupt practices are many and include bid-rigging, inflated costs, shoddy work, kickbacks, collusion among bidders, political interference with contract awards, etc. The data show that many local governments do not follow procurement rules well, publish limited information and have weak oversight. Audit reports frequently find irregularities in procurement by local government. The paper investigates factors leading to procurement corruption including weak institutional capacity, political interference, lack of transparency, limited oversight by citizens and poor enforcement. The report ends with recommendations for improving procurement integrity, including better procurement rules, more transparency, capacity building, stronger oversight, more citizen participation, and accountability enforcement.

articles.title: Beyond Blame: School Violence, Youth Despair, and the Failure of Containment in Recent Philippine Shootings
articles.authors: Rhine Lesther Tague
articles.abstract: Recent school-related shootings in the Philippines, especially the June 2026 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban and the August 2026 shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, generated public pressure to locate a single cause: a teacher, a game, a security failure, a disturbed child, a family failure. This paper argues that such explanations are emotionally understandable but causally insufficient. Drawing on incident reporting, official and reported-official statements, verified WHO Global School-based Student Health Survey data, DepEd Region VIII memoranda, public-health and threat-assessment literature, and C. G. Jung's Modern Man in Search of a Soul, the paper proposes a different representation: recent Philippine school violence should be understood as a failed ecology of containment. In this frame, adolescent grievance, despair, humiliation, or rupture become dangerous when they converge with firearm access, missed warning signs, weak disclosure pathways, digital scripts or grooming environments, livestream/notoriety affordances, and institutions that are not yet able to metabolize distress before it turns into public violence. The argument does not claim that Jungian "spiritual crisis" is a forensic motive. Rather, Jung helps name the meaning-layer of youth collapse: psychic pain, futurelessness, shame, and disconnection are real in their effects even when they cannot be reduced to one external cause. The paper concludes that prevention must move beyond blame toward containment: firearm accountability, threat assessment, confidential reporting, anti-bullying systems, psychosocial support, digital-platform safeguards, and living forms of youth meaning and belonging.

articles.title: Staying Long Enough to Stop Seeing: Autoethnography, Long-Term Immersion, and Tourism Research
articles.authors: Rob Burton
articles.abstract: Autoethnographic tourism research has typically been based on discrete journeys or bounded periods of fieldwork, leaving the epistemological implications of long-term residential immersion comparatively underexamined. This article argues that sustained residence produces a distinctive form of knowledge grounded not simply in prolonged observation but in the transformation of perception over time. Drawing on more than a decade of living and working across Nanjing, Hangzhou, and Wenzhou, China, it proposes a three-stage framework of estrangement, normalisation, and critical re-estrangement. Initial unfamiliarity heightens attention; repeated exposure subsequently renders once-remarkable features ordinary and increasingly invisible; disciplined analytical attention can then return the researcher to these normalised environments with a capacity to recognise recurrence, pattern, and institutional continuity. Through examples of everyday urban landscapes and the seasonal infrastructure underlying Hangzhou's elevated-highway flower displays, the article demonstrates how long-term immersion makes visible processes that shorter encounters may register only as isolated events or spectacles. Critical re-estrangement therefore offers a methodological means of converting habituation from an apparent limitation of long-term residence into an analytical resource.

articles.title: Detention as a disabling institution: Age-related health disparities in the US immigration detention system
articles.authors: Caitlin Patler
articles.abstract: From 2008 to 2018, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement apprehended over two million noncitizens in the US interior. However, data on detained immigrants' health is limited, with a particular lack of research on older detained immigrants, despite the distinct vulnerabilities aging individuals confront within and outside carceral settings. Immigrants face diverse structural challenges as they age, and incarcerated individuals experience accelerated aging and have worse health relative to non-incarcerated individuals, due to exposure to structural disadvantage, coupled with the health harms of incarceration itself. Using data from the Immigrant Detention Survey (n=495) and the National Health Interview Survey (n=8,383), and drawing on theories of aging in carceral settings, immigrant health and aging, and immigration policies as structural determinants of health, I address two critical and unresolved questions: What is the health profile of older detained adults, relative to younger adults? How do age-related health disparities among detained immigrants compare to those of non-detained immigrants? My findings reveal age-related health disparities in detained and non-detained populations. I also find much higher rates of poor health among detained immigrants than in the non-detained population, regardless of age. Results suggest immigration detention may be considered a mass disabling institution linked to poor health across the life course and may exacerbate age-related disparities, highlighting the need for more humane and equitable immigration and health policies.

articles.title: The Credibility Revolution in Political Science
articles.authors: Carolina Torreblanca; William Dinneen; Guy Grossman; Yiqing Xu
articles.abstract: How far has the credibility revolution spread through political science? We address this question by classifying 91,632 articles published between 2003 and 2023 across 156 political science journals using large language models, focusing on research design, credibility-enhancing practices, and citation patterns. We find that design-based studies, those leveraging plausibly exogenous variation to justify causal claims, have become increasingly common. In contrast, model-based approaches that rely more heavily on modeling assumptions have declined. Yet the rise of design-based work is uneven: it is concentrated in top journals and among authors at highly ranked institutions, and it is driven primarily by the growth of survey experiments. Other credibility-enhancing practices that help reduce false positives and false negatives, such as placebo tests and power calculations, remain rare. Taken together, our findings point to substantial but selective change, more consistent with a partial reform than a revolution.

articles.title: Sense of place based on shared imaginaries for caring for the chinampa socio‑ecosystem
articles.authors: Ana Paula Margain Leon; Lakshmi Charli Joseph; Jesús Mario Siqueiros-Garcia
articles.abstract: Sense of place refers to the meaningful connection that people establish with a space, which can either motivate or inhibit environmental care. Understanding the mechanisms that strengthen this connection is central to promoting sustainable ways of cohabiting a place. This study proposes imagining desired futures as a mechanism to mobilise a sense of place among young people from Xochimilco in Mexico City and to catalyse new forms of care. Drawing on a qualitative methodology, the study shows that this connection became a conscious, deliberate act that enabled reflection and collective visibility of bonds with place. The findings suggest that imagining futures expands the possibilities for collective care.

articles.title: You Have My Attention: Offline Events and the Temporal Dynamics of Online Harassment in Politics
articles.authors: Sabrina Kreyzerman; Inessa De Angelis
articles.abstract: The online harassment of politicians has become a defining feature of contemporary digital politics. While existing research has documented the forms and consequences of online harassment, less attention has been paid to how salient offline events shape its temporal dynamics. This study examines the relationship between salient offline events, such as wildfires and political resignations, and online harassment directed at Canadian federal Members of Parliament (MPs) on YouTube throughout 2024. We find that while a baseline level of harassment is consistently present, salient offline events are associated with short-term fluctuations in harassment, with comments increasing in the few days following an event. However, enduring structural factors, particularly MPs' gender and political party affiliation, are stronger predictors of harassment than offline events. By foregrounding time as an analytical dimension, this research advances our understanding of how offline events shape the temporal dynamics of online harassment while highlighting the structural factors that sustain it.

articles.title: Differences in Gender Pension Gaps in public and private pensions in West Germany: An Analysis Sensitive to Interdependencies across the Life-Course
articles.authors: Carla Rowold
articles.abstract:
Gender Pension Gaps (GPG) surpass Gender Wage Gaps in most European countries. Research has largely relied on single-factor, employment-centred explanations, and we know less about how GPGs emerge from an interdependent life-course perspective. 
This study contributes by applying a life-course-sensitive decomposition to linked survey-register data for Germany (SHARE-RV), comparing gender gaps in public and private pensions based on common work-family life courses, including relative earnings positions, relevant due to pension privatization in Europe. It considers the interdependencies of employment, family life, and earnings over the life course.
GPGs occur because privileged life courses yielding high pensions are almost exclusively accessible to fathers, while female-typical life-course patterns characterised by care work and part-time employment yield low pensions. Gendered access to high-income careers drives the GPG in private pensions more strongly than in public pensions, underscoring the future risk of high GPGs given persistent gender wage inequalities and pension privatization in Germany.

articles.title: A Foot in the Door: Ethnic Employment Quotas and Democratic Attitudes in Uruguay
articles.authors: Jorge Soler-Lopez
articles.abstract: Does bringing a marginalized group into the state raise its members' trust in democratic institutions? Uruguay's 2013 Ley 19.122, reserving eight percent of public-sector hires for Afro-descendant citizens, offers a rare test on the dimension representation theory names. Using the Uruguayan household survey and eight waves of the Latinobarómetro, we document a genuine but small first stage, Afro-Uruguayan public employment rose about 1.3 percentage points, a composition shift rather than a net gain, against a target the state met only fractionally. In addition, as second stage delivered a precise attitudinal null, with equivalence tests rejecting effects larger than roughly 0.15–0.20 standard deviations. The result establishes a scope condition rather than a refutation: at this level of exposure, bureaucratic inclusion produces no measurable attitudinal return. How much inclusion is required before the representation mechanism fires remains an open and newly quantifiable question.

articles.title: The development of patriotism among youth in the EU
articles.authors: Vladislav Medintsev
articles.abstract: The article separates patriotism from nationalism and blind allegiance while examining the developmental trajectory of patriotism among young people in the European Union. Integrating identity status theory, social identity theory, and political socialization models, it constructs a developmental account of how patriotism matures from childhood through emerging adulthood. The review defines mature patriotism through four properties: differentiation, integration, criticality, and self-authorship. It identifies a shift from uncritical, affective attachment in childhood to a potential for “constructive patriotism”—characterized by critical loyalty and dual national-European identification—in later stages. Key mechanisms facilitating this maturation include open classroom climates, cross-border mobility programs like Erasmus, and digital engagement, though the article notes these opportunities are often stratified by class and education. Conversely, significant obstacles are analyzed, including populist mobilization, economic precarity, and East-West asymmetries in historical memory. The article concludes by proposing an integrative developmental-contextual model comprising three levels (substrate, elaboration, consolidation) and four moderating conditions. It argues that while a historically novel, reflexive form of patriotism is emerging among European youth, its full realization remains contingent on specific ecological conditions and faces ongoing threats from social stratification and political polarization.

articles.title: El hombre que resiseñó la racionalidad
articles.authors: Jorge Zazueta
articles.abstract:
Herbert Simon (1916–2001) es uno de los científicos sociales más influyentes del siglo XX. Premio Nobel
de Economía en 1978 y Premio Turing en 1975, sus aportaciones van desde la psicología hasta la
inteligencia artificial pasando por la teoría de la administración con una visión centrada en el concepto de
racionalidad limitada: la idea de que los seres humanos hacemos decisiones con información incompleta,
capacidad cognitiva finita y aspiraciones flexibles. Buscando soluciones suficientemente buenas en lugar
de óptimas. Este capítulo examina los tres dominios principales del legado simoniano — la teoría de
decisiones, la inteligencia artificial y las ciencias sociales computacionales — y comenta sobre su recepción
en América Latina, donde sus ideas llegaron fragmentadas y con retraso, adoptadas selectivamente por la
administración pública y la teoría organizacional, pero escasamente exploradas en su dimensión
computacional.

articles.title: Ambiguity-Robust Dictionaries using Contextualized Embeddings
articles.authors: Jamil Civitarese; Sylvan Zheng
articles.abstract: Keyword dictionaries remain widely used in text analysis for their simplicity, transparency, and replicability. However, sensitivity to keyword selection and inability to account for context introduce measurement error that attenuates estimates and obscures real relationships. We introduce ambiguity-robust dictionaries, a text-as-data method that leverages contextual word embeddings to produce more precise measures while preserving the key advantages of dictionary approaches. Our method generates contextualized embeddings for all keyword instances, then applies constrained fuzzy clustering to determine the degree of each instance's membership in a target cluster defined by a small set of researcher-identified anchor words. This approach allows the construction of ambiguity-robust document level word counts, increasing precision and reducing sensitivity to keyword selection. We demonstrate the method using three applications:  UN environmental discourse, ethnic bias in Kenyan judicial politics, and moral language in US Congressional speech. In each application, our method yields substantively more robust and precise estimates than conventional approaches.

articles.title: The Rise and (Partial) Retreat of DEI Claims in Recruiting
articles.authors: Janet Xu; Reuben Hurst; Shanshan Liu
articles.abstract: In recent years, and especially after the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, U.S. employers increasingly affirmed commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Donald Trump's second administration has sought to reverse this shift. Yet how far pro-diversity language actually rose in employers' recruiting, and how much of that rise has since been undone, has not been established. Drawing on the near-universe of U.S. online job postings between January 2016 and February 2026—371.1 million postings from 2.7 million employers—we find that pro-diversity claims appeared in 7–12% of job postings until mid-2020, then rose 152% to a peak of 25.4% postings on the eve of the 2024 election. They fell 21% thereafter, to 19.9% by February 2026. Declines were sharper among federal contractors but proportionally similar for Democratic- and Republican-leaning employers. The reversal is unprecedented, yet partial: it has undone roughly a third of the post-2020 rise, but pro-diversity claims remain twice as common as in June 2020.

articles.title: Ageism by Default: Representational Ageism as an Upstream Risk in Medical AI
articles.authors: Alexander Seifert
articles.abstract: Age bias in medical AI is often treated as a performance problem, a perspective that fails to recognize an already existing risk: Generative systems may produce narrow, default representations of later life that enter health communication, patient personas, training materials, and care documentation. Because these representations potentially determine the needs, risks, and forms of support that take priority before clinical decisions are made, representational ageism should be addressed in bias audits, design documentation, procurement, and participatory review.

articles.title: Generational Warfare Online? Social Media Use and Intergroup Attitudes in a National Survey
articles.authors: Andrew Micah Lindner
articles.abstract: Content analyses document vitriolic generational discourse across social media platforms, yet surveys reveal moderate attitudes among the public. Does social media exposure create extreme generational attitudes? Using nationally representative survey data (n=1,221), this study examines whether total social media use and platform-specific usage patterns correlate with generational self-identification and intergroup attitudes among American adults. Results reveal limited associations with even frequent users not exhibiting greater generational antagonism. Platform-specific analyses reveal few significant effects, though YouTube use is associated with more favorable attitudes toward other generations. These largely null findings suggest extreme online discourse does not reflect typical users’ attitudes, implying that reasons for extreme discourse are connected to visibility mechanisms, such as algorithmic amplification and creators’ strategic performance. The study also demonstrates the risks of inferring population attitudes from content analysis.

articles.title: Dynamic Savings with Adaptive Adjustment in the Solow–Swan Model: Bistability and Escape from a Poverty Trap
articles.authors: Jorge Zazueta; Leobardo Plata
articles.abstract:
We extend the Solow–Swan growth model by replacing the constant savings rate with a
savings rate that adjusts gradually toward a capital-dependent target of Hill form. The savings
rate becomes a state variable, turning the model into a two-dimensional dynamical system. For
a sufficiently savings steep target, the system admits a poverty-trap regime with three equilibria:
the origin, a saddle, and a stable high-capital equilibrium. We characterize the stability of every
positive equilibrium by the elasticity of the savings target; in the bistable phase portrait, the
saddle’s stable manifold provides the natural separatrix between the two observed attraction
regions. We then study escape by a temporary public-investment flow. A direct geometric
argument identifies an upper forward-invariant region from which the uncontrolled system
converges to the high-capital equilibrium. If the investment flow satisfies a sufficient condition,
the policy drives capital above a buffer level in finite time; savings then catches up through
adaptive adjustment, after which the stimulus can be removed permanently. The model therefore
converts the one-dimensional threshold of a static savings specification into a two-dimensional
basin problem, where both the level of capital and the speed of savings adjustment are necessary
for escape.

articles.title: Humility in Journalism: The epistemic virtue that allows journalists to learn from experiences of others
articles.authors: Gregory P Perreault; Claudia Mellado
articles.abstract: Journalists have long been associated with a strong ego and the hubris necessary to share the news as “the way it is.” But overlooked, and perhaps more important, is the humility required by journalists to gather new knowledge in the first place. Through the lens of joy and journalistic epistemology, the present study explores interviews with 27 journalists in Chile and the United States in regards to their experiences with humility. Journalists broadly believed that their work could be done without humility, but that good journalism necessitated humility. The best journalists, across these national contexts, were considered to be those who were humble: which journalists defined as being willing to listen, to learn, to be corrected and to apologize for mistakes.

articles.title: Do Large Language Models Reproduce Question-Wording Effects? A Type-Level Map from Published Split-Ballot Experiments
articles.authors: Howard Kim
articles.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can stand in for human survey respondents is contested: some studies report striking correspondence with human data, others report systematic failure. We argue the question is mis-posed as a binary and answer it instead with a type-level map. We assembled 56 experiment pairs from published split-ballot experiments in the Time-sharing Experiments for the Social Sciences (TESS) archive - verbatim condition wordings with condition-level response distributions computed from public raw data - spanning ten classic questionnaire-design manipulations in the Schuman-Presser tradition. LLM respondents were conditioned on demographic profiles sampled from each original study's own probability-sample respondents and answered one condition each (n = 300 per condition, three seeds), in a preregistered design with a fully disclosed pilot, same-item internal replication on new seeds, and a hash-locked corpus. Reproduction divided by effect type. Semantics-based effects - lexical wording, question form, and equivalency framing - moved in the human direction on 7 of 8 significant pairs; because those pairs cluster in four studies, cluster-robust tests leave this as a consistent pattern rather than a confirmed one (study-level permutation p = .13). On a common, range-standardized effect scale the semantic-family correlation is r = .32 (cluster-bootstrap CI [.05, .79]; Spearman rho = .58), with magnitudes attenuated to roughly one-fifth to one-third of the human effects. Cognitive-burden-based effects failed as mechanism predicts: forced-choice response-order effects were at chance (1 of 4), and a recall-instruction effect was flat. Two model-specific signatures emerged, each anchored in a single item pair: acquiescence to a socially undesirable assertion vanished (human effect +.39; LLM -.00; z = -7.8), a pattern consistent with alignment training, and the models over-acquiesced to contradictory generic assertions (agreement sum 1.82 vs. .81 in humans). On six pilot-unexposed extension pairs, significant-pair signs matched in 5 of 6 model-pair evaluations across two models, which weakens simple literature-memorization accounts but cannot exclude pretraining exposure. We also document a mid-study behavioral discontinuity of a commercially served model under a stable model name, consistent with serving-version drift. Overall, the evidence supports an exploratory, direction-oriented use of LLM panels for pretesting semantic wording manipulations, and cautions against any use as a general-purpose effect estimator.

articles.title: Hype as a Critique of Communication: What Exaggeration Costs, Seen Through Five Lenses
articles.authors: Maximilian Roßmann
articles.abstract: Calling something hype is a charge against communication. Yet it rarely specifies the fault. Was the claim inaccurate, oversold, over-promised, or crowding out something more deserving? Different lenses of communication theory show different faults, and different remedies. Exaggeration buys reach, assent, uptake, frame dominance, and resonance, often several at once. What differs is the cost. Read as information transfer, exaggeration spends the discriminating power of language; as rhetoric, the credibility of the speaker and their peers; as a speech act, the coordinating force of commitment and assertion; as discourse, the space in which opposing views can be uttered and acknowledged; as a pattern of reception, the contestability of a social representation held in common. These are over-generalization, over-selling, over-commitment, over-shadowing, and over-resonance. None requires intention. A field can overshoot through contributions that are individually calibrated and sincere, and where speakers relinquish control over reception, hype becomes a matter of platform design and power. Each lens is blind to what the others register, and a remedy reaches only those positioned to apply it.

articles.title: Backlash and the Limits of Immigrant Solidarity
articles.authors: Priyanka Sethy; Marco M. Aviña
articles.abstract: Does anti-immigrant backlash unite the people it targets? Using Cooperative Election Study data from 2010--2025, we track the pro-immigration attitudinal gradient, from third-generation US-born respondents to noncitizens, through Donald Trump's rise. The gradient contracted and remained smaller afterward; the fully adjusted 2010--2024 estimate is a 0.133-SD reduction from third-generation US-born respondents to noncitizens. Recurring items show why: third-generation respondents liberalized more, while naturalized citizens moved modestly toward restriction on conditional legalization. The contraction appears both on policies governing new immigration and on policies affecting immigrants already present, survives timing, measurement, composition, local-context, and unrelated-outcome checks, and is smaller among immigrants with longer residential tenure, homeownership, and higher income. Republican and conservative immigrants also shift less---not more---than simple cue-taking predicts. Backlash can make a category politically salient without making the people associated with it more politically aligned.

articles.title: Exploring socioeconomic inequalities in healthy and sustainable diets using big data: An observational analysis of loyalty card data from a UK Retailer, 2022.
articles.authors: Mark Alan Green; Emma Wilkins; Mark S Gilthorpe; Thomas Sawczuk; Charlotte Hardman; Hannah Greatwood; Rebecca Ann Stone; Alexandra Johnstone; Michelle Morris
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Promoting healthier and more sustainable diets is needed to improve population and planetary health. However, limited evidence has described how these intersecting issues vary together by socioeconomic position. Our study uses novel large-scale retailer consumer purchase data, adjusted for known biases, to explore socioeconomic inequalities in health and environmental impacts of food and beverage purchases.

Methods: Data were household-level loyalty card records from a major UK supermarket retailer between 24th July and 31st December 2022 (n = 117 710). The health-related outcome was proportion of purchases that were ‘High in Fat, Salt or Sugar’ (HFSS), determined using the UK nutrient profile model. We estimated three environmental outcomes: total greenhouse gas emissions, total land use footprint, and total water use from food purchases. Multilevel regression with post-stratification was used to estimate each outcome measure by level of neighbourhood socioeconomic deprivation, adjusted for age, household size, distance to nearest supermarket, and urbanicity. We also described environmental outcomes by food category across level of deprivation. 

Results: Households residing in the most deprived 10% of areas purchased a larger proportion of HFSS items than households in the least deprived 10% of areas. Households in the least deprived 10% of areas had a greater absolute environmental impact. However, when considered per weight of items, households in the most deprived 10% of areas purchased items that contributed to higher greenhouse emissions per kg but had lower impacts for land use. Soft drinks, ready meals, pasta, and pastry products were identified as key food categories for targeted ‘food swaps’ to reduce environmental inequalities. 

Conclusions: Our novel application of retailer loyalty card data shows how these data can offer valuable insights for informing strategies to promote healthy, sustainable, and equitable diets. Tackling environmental inequalities in food purchases requires tailoring approaches to different population groups.

articles.title: Additional evidence on Madagascar's tourism-led growth hypothesis
articles.authors: Franck Maminirina Ramaharo
articles.abstract: We evaluate the validity of the tourism-led growth (TLG) hypothesis for Madagascar through an examination of the asymmetric relationships among economic growth, tourism activity, and financial development over the period 2007Q1-2024Q4. Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag (NARDL) modeling reveals a statistically significant long-run asymmetric effect, wherein negative shocks to tourist arrivals exert a stronger adverse impact on economic growth than the expansionary effect of equivalent increases. With respect to causal dynamics, bivariate symmetric Granger causality testing first uncovers empirical support for the TLG hypothesis. Subsequent short-run asymmetric causality then supports the conservation hypothesis, wherein negative economic growth shocks trigger positive tourist inflows. This dynamic suggests that tourism functions as a counter-cyclical shock absorber during domestic downturns. Consequently, our analysis highlights the need to pivot strategy away from mere tourist volume toward high-yield retention and investment in a resilient tourism sector.

articles.title: Do Large Language Models Reproduce Question-Wording Effects? A Type-Level Map from Published Split-Ballot Experiments
articles.authors: Howard Kim
articles.abstract: Whether large language models (LLMs) can stand in for human survey respondents is contested: some studies report striking correspondence with human data, others systematic failure. We argue the question is mis-posed as a binary and answer it with a type-level map. We assembled 56 experiment pairs from published split-ballot experiments in the TESS archive (verbatim condition wordings; condition-level distributions computed from public raw data), spanning ten classic questionnaire-design manipulations in the Schuman-Presser tradition. LLM respondents were conditioned on demographic profiles sampled from each original study's own probability-sample respondents (n = 300 per condition, three seeds), in a preregistered confirmatory design with a fully disclosed pilot, new-seed confirmation, and a hash-locked corpus. Reproduction divided sharply by effect type. Semantics-based effects (lexical wording, question form, equivalency framing) were reproduced in direction (7 of 8 significant pairs; r = .72), with magnitudes systematically shrunk (slope = .52). Cognitive-burden-based effects failed as mechanism predicts: forced-choice response-order effects were at chance and a recall-instruction effect was flat. Alignment training suppressed acquiescence to a socially undesirable assertion (human effect +.39; LLM -.00; z = -7.8), and models over-acquiesced to contradictory assertions (agreement sum 1.82 vs. .81 in humans). Results held on six pilot-unexposed extension pairs (5/6 significant-pair sign matches across two models), disfavoring contamination explanations. We also document mid-study behavioral drift of a commercially served model under a stable model name. LLM pretesting of survey questions is defensible as a conditional, direction-oriented screen within the semantic domain, not as a general-purpose effect estimator.

articles.title: Cognitive Degradation: The Reconfiguration of the Labor Process and Knowledge Authority in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
articles.authors: 王本杰
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering knowledge-intensive work, including programming, writing, design, analysis, and management. Unlike earlier forms of automation that were often concentrated on physical operations or clearly defined executional tasks, generative AI can produce text, code, classifications, and proposals within the workflow itself. Its significance therefore lies not simply in the displacement of particular tasks, but in the possibility that activities once associated with professional judgment become increasingly mediated by corporate technological systems. This paper examines that possibility through the concept of “cognitive degradation.” Drawing on Marx’s analysis of machinery and fixed capital, Braverman’s account of labor-process control and deskilling (Braverman, 1974), and Burawoy’s emphasis on worker agency and consent (Burawoy, 1978; 1979), the paper defines cognitive degradation narrowly. It occurs when AI takes over cognitive tasks previously performed by workers, workers’ effective authority over the criteria and application of judgment declines, and that shift is stabilized through organizational rules, technological systems, or labor institutions. The concept therefore should not be treated as synonymous with deskilling, declining productivity, or algorithmic management. To explore the mechanism, the paper examines three ideal types rather than three directly comparable causal cases: boundary-setting in the Writers Guild of America (WGA), internalization in AI-assisted software development, and institutional mediation through German co-determination. The cases show that AI can increase productivity without necessarily reducing workers’ skills, while still altering how knowledge and judgment are organized. The paper argues that the central issue in AI-mediated labor is therefore not whether machines replace workers, but whether workers retain meaningful authority over the definition, evaluation, and application of knowledge. The paper further proposes that sustained changes in such authority may affect occupational autonomy, skill formation, and bargaining power. Claims about macro-level class restructuring, however, remain propositions for future empirical research rather than conclusions established by the cases examined here.

articles.title: Creative offloading and creative agency in AI-assisted educational game design: A thematic analysis of student reflection essays
articles.authors: Eemeli Eiste; Antti Koskinen; Muhterem Dindar; Kristian Kiili
articles.abstract: Generative AI has raised growing educational concerns regarding cognitive offloading and the preservation of students’ creative agency in creative learning tasks. This study examined how higher education students reflected on their creative agency when using generative AI as a design partner during the ideation and initiation phase of an educational game design assignment. Using a qualitative case study approach, we thematically analysed reflection essays written by 26 students following an AI-supported game design activity in a university course. The analysis identified a spectrum of reflected creative agency patterns related to how students described delegating, evaluating, and directing creative work with generative AI. Students’ reflections described strategic forms of offloading in which AI was positioned as a complementary support tool while evaluative judgment and authorial direction were retained. At the same time, reflections also revealed more unregulated forms of offloading characterised by overreliance on AI, unclear interaction strategies, and diminished ownership of creative decisions. These patterns sometimes coexisted within individual reflections, suggesting that creative agency may vary across offloading decisions rather than represent fixed student characteristics. The study introduces the concept of creative offloading as a lens for understanding student-AI interaction in creative educational tasks.

articles.title: Are environmental and climate worries connected to individual feelings of anomie? Evidence from the German Socio-Economic Panel Study
articles.authors: Talea Bruns; Stefanie Kley
articles.abstract: Feelings of anomie manifest themselves in perceptions of meaninglessness and disorientation that are expected to arise in response to rapid social change and threatening social conditions. We analyze whether and how concerns about environmental protection and the impacts of climate change (“environmental worries”) contribute to individual feelings of anomie, based on theoretically informed hypotheses about distinct relationships across social class. Fixed-effects panel regression and random intercept cross-lagged models are used, based on data from the German Socioeconomic Panel study (GSOEP; years 2008–2023). We find that environmental worries contribute to feelings of anomie but are trumped by adverse events in individual’s life course. The contribution of environmental worries to feelings of anomie is weak compared to worries about one’s own economic situation and health. Levels of both, feelings of anomie and environmental worries, are relatively stable within individuals across the years, whereas spill-over effects between the two are seldom observed. Exclusively in the social class of lower-grade professionals a positive spill-over effect of anomie on environmental worries is observed, whereas among blue-collar workers a negative connection is found. The findings are discussed regarding their contribution to a theory-driven explanation of how climate change and environmental degradation might promote social disintegration.

articles.title: Beyond the Deepfake: Synthetic Persuasion and the Infrastructural Transformation of Political Communication
articles.authors: Daniele Battista
articles.abstract: Political communication research has approached deepfakes primarily as deceptive audiovisual artifacts whose democratic relevance depends on realism, detection, and the possibility of misleading citizens. This perspective remains necessary but is increasingly insufficient. Generative artificial intelligence now enables political actors and intermediaries to produce, adapt, personalize, and recirculate persuasive text, image, audio, video, and conversational content at a scale that exceeds the conventional deepfake problem. This article develops the concept of synthetic persuasion to describe political influence processes in which AI-generated, AI-transformed, or AI-assisted symbolic content is deliberately embedded in communicative strategies designed to shape attention, interpretation, evaluation, identity, trust, or behavior. Building on a focused theory-building synthesis of research on deepfakes, political persuasion, platformization, algorithmic visibility, fact-checking, and AI governance, the article proposes the Synthetic Persuasion Infrastructure (SPI) model. The model distinguishes four analytically connected stages: production, platform embedding, amplification, and reception-recirculation. It argues that the political power of synthetic content cannot be reduced to successful deception: persuasion may also operate through narrative congruence, repetition, identity reinforcement, uncertainty, strategic disclosure, and hybrid-media amplification. Six propositions translate the model into falsifiable expectations for future comparative and experimental research. The article concludes that the democratic challenge posed by generative AI lies less in the existence of isolated synthetic objects than in the emergence of infrastructures capable of producing and circulating persuasive variants continuously across platforms and publics.

articles.title: NursingWave: entry, exit, and market concentration of home-visit nursing providers across Japan's secondary medical zones, 2020–2026
articles.authors: Kunihisa Ohno
articles.abstract:
Background: Japan's home-visit nursing workforce faces the most acute shortage of any nursing field, and national policy deliberations moved in July 2026 from prefecture-level to secondary-medical-zone-level data. Existing evidence, however, consists of static cross-sections; the dynamics of the provider market have never been measured at zone level.
Methods: We constructed a semiannual panel of all home-visit nursing providers listed in the national long-term care information disclosure registry across 12 waves (December 2020 to June 2026), linked providers by insurance provider number, and assigned them to 330 secondary medical zones using a bitemporal municipality-to-zone crosswalk. We computed supply density per population aged 75+, cumulative entry/exit rates, turnover, corporate-group market concentration (HHI), and physician-issued home-visit nursing instructions (NDB item C007) per zone, with Theil decomposition of inequality. All sources are open data; the dataset, code, and an interactive viewer are released under CC BY 4.0.
Results: Providers grew 41.5% nationally (13,032 to 18,436), with designated stations up 48.4% and deemed medical institutions down 16.7%. Yet 43 of 330 zones (13.0%) experienced net decline, concentrated in small zones (24.3% of zones with <25,000 residents aged 75+ vs. 1.7% of large zones), which also showed 12-fold higher market concentration (median HHI 0.125 vs. 0.010). Within-prefecture disparities accounted for 38.4% of total inequality. Same-name re-registrations explained only 2.1% of 5,729 observed exits.
Conclusions: Behind aggregate growth, small zones face a triple disadvantage — lower density, net provider retreat, and single-provider dependence — invisible in prefecture statistics. Zone-level dynamic monitoring is feasible with open data alone.

articles.title: Closing The Domestic Peace Gap Applying the Domestic Peace Deficit Framework to SDG 5, SDG 16, and the Women, Peace and Security Agenda
articles.authors: Ijeoma Ezeukwu
articles.abstract: Over the past three decades, the international community has adopted an unprecedented set of legal, policy, and institutional commitments to advance gender equality, protect women and girls from violence, and promote peaceful and inclusive societies, most notably through Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 5 and 16 and the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda. Yet global monitoring confirms that progress on the relevant targets remains off track, and everyday realities inside households continue to diverge sharply from these commitments. This paper argues that the principal barrier is not the absence of formal commitments but the limited capacity of institutions to translate those commitments into lived domestic security, a pattern it terms the domestic peace gap. It applies the Domestic Peace Deficit (DPD) framework, developed in a companion conceptual paper (Ezeukwu, 2026), as an implementation lens for SDG 5, SDG 16, and the four WPS pillars of Prevention, Protection, Participation, and Relief and Recovery. The paper maps DPD's three pillars against relevant SDG targets and WPS commitments, and closes with practical recommendations for governments, United Nations agencies and development partners, and civil society organisations. Its central contribution is diagnostic and practical rather than theoretical: it shows how an institutional-performance lens, rather than an institutional-presence lens, can be used to evaluate whether global commitments are producing safer households.

articles.title: Fugitive Statistics: A Verification-Chain Protocol for Preserving Policy Numbers That Exist Only Inside Documents
articles.authors: Kunihisa Ohno
articles.abstract: A growing share of policy-critical statistics is published only as tables embedded in advisory-committee documents — ad hoc tabulations produced for a single meeting, carried exclusively by PDF, with no versioned machine-readable release, no persistent identifier, and no documented reproduction path. We term these fugitive statistics, by analogy with the fugitive documents of library science — government publications that fall within the scope of a depository system yet escape its collection net. Fugitive statistics are load-bearing: they inform national workforce projections, capacity planning, and crisis-response policy, yet they are exposed to link rot, silent revision, format death, and provenance loss. Crucially, ex-post policy evaluation is possible only if the numbers used ex-ante survive: Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) could score its 7th nursing workforce projection against realized outcomes (deviations of 2.98% and 2.36% for demand and supply) only because the original projection documents remained retrievable. We present a lightweight verification-chain protocol — capture, SHA-256 hashing, independent witnessing via the Internet Archive, semantic extraction with cell-level provenance, bitemporal cataloguing, DOI deposit, and revision monitoring — and demonstrate it end-to-end on the document set of the 4th meeting of MHLW’s 2040 nursing workforce committee, in which prefecture-supplied municipal microdata were re-tabulated into secondary-medical-area statistics that exist nowhere else. All nine artifacts were captured, hashed, and independently witnessed (8/8 PDFs byte-identical to Internet Archive copies), and the embedded tables extracted under two-tier quality control (row-sum checks passed 60/60; double-entry cross-verification matched 916/916 cells), yielding a DOI-bearing dataset within one operator-day on commodity hardware. We position preservation as the precondition of accountability, and fugitive statistics as a measurable site of institutional debt: the divergence between the statistics a policy decision consumed and the statistics later available to evaluate it.

articles.title: Two Ways of Being Misled: Composition Bias, Weak Within-Municipality Progress, and a Fixed Size Gradient in Japan's Individual Evacuation Plan Statistics, 2022–2026
articles.authors: Kunihisa Ohno
articles.abstract:
Japan requires every municipality to maintain a registry of residents who cannot evacuate unaided (2013 amendment to the Disaster Countermeasures Basic Act) and, since 2021, to make best efforts to prepare an individual evacuation plan for each person listed. Progress is monitored through annual national surveys published as municipality-level tables in PDF format. We reconstruct these tables into a machine-readable panel of 1,741 municipalities across five survey waves (2022–2026; 10 source documents, plan and registry series), with documented recovery of 74 rows lost to table-rendering defects, external reconciliation of ambiguous column semantics against published national aggregates, and a complete provenance registry of corrections and known gaps.
Three findings follow, and they cut in different directions. First, the pooled statistics are misleading about direction: the median creation rate across all responding municipalities falls from 19.0% to 17.8%, whereas every continuously observed subset improves, because late-entering municipalities start low and are added faster than incumbents advance. Second, and against our own initial reading, composition control does not reveal robust progress. Within the 423 municipalities observed in all five waves, the median change is only +0.77 points over four years, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval reaching down to zero (+0.00 to +1.80; mean +3.79, CI +0.81 to +6.82; Wilcoxon p = 0.0006), and only 54.6% improved at all. The +8.3-point rise in the panel median is a shift in the position of the distribution driven by strong gains in its upper part, not the experience of a typical municipality. Third, plan creation is steeply graded by registry size in levels—the smallest quartile reaches a median of 43.3% against 9.9% for the largest—but not in growth: within-municipality change does not differ across size quartiles (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.47; municipality-fixed-effects interactions all p > 0.55). Small municipalities are ahead, not faster, and the gap shows no tendency to close.
The published series is thus misleading twice over: it reports a decline where continuously observed municipalities do not decline, and it invites the inference that composition control would reveal healthy progress, which the panel does not support. We interpret this within an institutional-debt framework: the statistical encoding of an institution (survey composition, question definitions, item discontinuation) drifts away from the institutional reality it is meant to measure, and the divergence is itself measurable—but correcting the encoding does not, here, rescue the institution's performance. The panel, extraction code, and provenance registry are archived for reuse.

articles.title: The Geography of Green Deficits: Creating a 3-30-300 Measure for all UPRNs in Great Britain
articles.authors: Alex Singleton; Mark Alan Green; Meilin Shi
articles.abstract:
The 3-30-300 rule has emerged as an influential benchmark for equitable urban green space provision, specifying that every
home should have visibility of 3 trees, 30% neighbourhood tree canopy cover, and access to public green space within 300
metres. Despite growing international application, there is no GB-wide assessment of how households meet the rule. This
paper presents the first nationally consistent operationalisation of the framework at the highest possible spatial resolution,
calculating indicators for approximately 40 million Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs) using high-resolution
tree mapping, open green space data, and network-based pedestrian routing. We generate the 3-30-300 indicators as contin-
uous measures, enabling assessment under canonical and alternative threshold specifications. Results reveal a substantial
national green deficit: only 0.7% of urban UPRNs satisfy all three thresholds, with the 30% canopy criterion the binding
constraint. The three components decouple both spatially and socio-economically. Tree visibility and canopy cover concen-
trate in affluent southern suburbs and exhibit steep positive deprivation gradients, whereas proximity to formal green space
marginally favours the most deprived urban neighbourhoods, reflecting inherited civic park provision in dense industrial-
era cities. Composite compliance is nine times higher in the least deprived decile than the most deprived, a pattern robust to
threshold relaxation. We argue the framework is best understood as three distinct policy levers rather than a single standard,
and that place-sensitive, component-specific targeting is required to avoid widening the inequalities the rule seeks to ad-
dress.

articles.title: Advancing open research information: exploring the persistence of proprietary bibliographic databases
articles.authors: Tanya Lee; Kathleen Gregory; Alexander Rushforth
articles.abstract:
Purpose – “Research information”, which informs how research is searched,
conducted, monitored, and evaluated, is usually made available in proprietary
databases in ways which often restrict its use. Recently, there has been a movement
towards opening research information through the creation of systems such as
OpenAlex, but their adoption remains inconsistent. In this study, we explore challenges
which university stakeholders face in switching from proprietary to open databases for
research information.

Design/methodology/approach – We conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with
university stakeholders in the Netherlands, a particularly proactive environment in the
Open Research Information movement. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic
analysis and informed by literature in platform capitalism and infrastructure studies.

Findings – The analysis shows that even in seemingly progressive environments,
systemic change remains challenging. Longstanding routines, technical dependencies,
and embedded practices present challenges for universities to disengage from
proprietary databases and their complementary services. Concerns about the viability
and further development of open databases became apparent through the context of
collective action dilemmas perceived by interviewees. Importantly, we find that platform
capitalism, a framework often employed in analyzing proprietary companies, is not
sufficient to explain these hesitancies. 

Originality/Value – Our findings highlight the challenges faced in an under-researched
area of open science: the adoption of open research information. Our study is relevant
to open science advocates and for institutions struggling with similar challenges. Our
analysis makes a conceptual contribution through treating claims about the platform
dominance of proprietary databases as empirical questions and highlighting the
importance of stakeholder agency, contingency and variation.

articles.title: Building a Sustainable Educational System in an Era of Declining Birthrate ―A Theory of School Education Reform―
articles.authors: Shigenori Tanaka
articles.abstract: This paper proposes a reconstruction of Japan’s school education system in the context of a declining-birthrate society, using the QDT (Quatro Dynamic Thinking) model as its analytical foundation. The QDT model is a four-dimensional thinking framework comprising Diving (deep thinking), Expanding (expansive thinking), Networking (network thinking), and Flowing (fluid thinking), and offers a method for multilayered, dynamic, and holistic analysis of educational reform. The educational crisis precipitated by demographic decline is understood here not merely as a problem of quantitative contraction, but as a phenomenon that exposes the structural obsolescence of an education system originally built to align with an industrialized society. The paper first clarifies the nature of the problem through a three-layer Diving Thinking analysis (surface, intermediate, and deep levels), then develops multidirectional solutions through Expanding Thinking. It further constructs a pentagonal collaboration model through Networking Thinking, and outlines a hypothetical phased implementation roadmap spanning 2026 to 2036 through Flowing Thinking. Building on this foundation, the paper introduces the paradigm of a “learning ecosystem,” and through concepts designed to innovate conventional education — fractal transformation, the living curriculum, and the QDT model itself — sketches a blueprint for a next-generation education system that Japan or other countries could pioneer on the global stage. Finally, the paper draws on an actual regional case to illustrate the proposed direction for educational reform. What this paper ultimately presents is not merely a logic of institutional change, but a reform vision grounded in the evolving consciousness of all stakeholders involved in education.

articles.title: Beyond Whitechapel: A Transnational Forensic Reassessment of the Jack the Ripper Murders
articles.authors: Tina Jacobs; Alicia V. Donaldson
articles.abstract: This study presents the transnational Whitechapel linkage hypothesis, an integrated retrospective hypothesis examining whether evidence traditionally treated as unrelated may be better understood within a mobile, cross-jurisdictional offender framework. The analysis brings together the canonical Whitechapel murders of 1888, reported Rotterdam dockside killings and contemporary “Whitechapel-like” comparisons, the 1890 Mary Eleanor Wheeler Pearcey case, the testimony and subsequent archival disappearance of John Charles Pearcey, Mary Pearcey’s unusual final communications preserved in Spanish-language Fabra/Havas dispatches, the later confession attributed to a sailor using the name John Anderson, the South American voyage of the Annie Speer, and the incompletely identified 1895 Iquique death registration of Evaristo Vergara. Rather than treating any single item as dispositive, the theory uses modern forensic-psychological reasoning, behavioral case-linkage principles, temporal and geographic reconstruction, victimology, maritime mobility analysis, forensic linguistics, identity reconstruction, and alternative-hypothesis testing to ask whether the combined pattern is consistent with a mobile offender or offender network operating across port environments. The evidence presently supports a historically plausible and investigatively testable linkage model, but it does not establish a definitive identity for the Whitechapel offender. The contribution of the theory is therefore not a declaration that the case has been solved; it is a structured model explaining why the Rotterdam-London maritime corridor, the Pearcey evidence, the Anderson confession, and the Iquique records warrant examination together rather than in isolation.

articles.title: Measuring and Repairing Document Conversion Errors in the Michigan Child Welfare Policy Manual
articles.authors: Nanyi Deng
articles.abstract:
Author Note (August 18, 2026): This preprint is currently undergoing systematic review and revision. An updated version will be posted upon completion. Readers are encouraged to consult the latest version of the manuscript.
Child welfare practice is governed by documents written for people to read. A state policy manual specifies how quickly a caseworker must see a child after the child returns home, and it does so in a PDF laid out for the eye. Any system that answers questions from such a manual must first convert it into text, and that conversion step is rarely measured. This study measures it. Five test documents were constructed to replicate the layout of the Michigan Children’s Protective Services Manual, with identifiers replacing its words. The identifiers run consecutively, so that a loss reads as a gap in a counted run and a person can see it without tooling, and each one ends in a check code, so that a converter driven by a language model cannot supply a convincing replacement for whatever it dropped. The same artifact is therefore verifiable by a person reading it and by a script counting it, and the tool under test cannot repair the evidence before either of them looks at it.
Four converters were evaluated on the test documents, and the two generations of the commercial service were evaluated on the manual itself, for a total of 31 documents and 328 pages. No converter was adequate for every property required by a retrieval corpus. The older generation invented 43 section headings that appear nowhere in the source, and the corpus assembled from it labels a column in a contact-standards table with the wrong requirement, so it lists three contacts with each child at intensive risk, where the manual states one. The current generation’s cheapest tier deletes the opening line of every paragraph beginning Exception:, which is how this manual marks the cases a rule does not cover. None of these failures garbles the text. Each produces fluent prose that reads as policy and states a rule the manual does not contain. The study then reports a repair procedure that derives document structure from the PDF’s geometry, and fifteen checks that halt conversion if any fail. Every check passes across all 31 documents, measured against the same documents from which the repair rules were derived. A fourth failure property emerged only after presence, level, and order had all reached their best values: 380 paragraph boundaries across 200 of the 328 pages were marked in the source by vertical spacing that the converter does not read.

articles.title: Unifying Interpretations of Probability Through Popper’s Propensity View
articles.authors: Gang Xie
articles.abstract: Confusion surrounding the foundations of probability often arises from conflating its definition with its methods of estimation or use. Statistical practice tends to mix axiomatic, frequentist, classical, and subjective perspectives without clarifying their philosophical status. This note argues that Karl Popper’s propensity interpretation offers a coherent foundational concept that underlies and unifies these approaches. Interpreting probability as an inherent dispositional property of systems aligns naturally with Kolmogorov’s probability‐space formalism and reframes frequentist long-run frequencies as practical approximations of propensities. Bayesian statistics, understood simply as a mathematical framework for updating probabilities via Bayes’ theorem, can incorporate either frequentist or subjective estimates; subjective probability is therefore not intrinsic to the Bayesian approach, despite common misconceptions. Examples from engineering reliability, scientific experimentation, and classical statistical tests illustrate the intuitive strength of the propensity view. Recognizing propensities as fundamental helps clarify the nature of uncertainty and reduces long-standing interpretive confusion.

articles.title: El poseedor que no existe: la reivindicación contra el ocupante material y la regla de cierre del artículo 915 del Código Civil (comentario a la sentencia de la Corte Suprema de 29 de julio de 2026, rol N° 34.734-2026)
articles.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles.abstract:
La Primera Sala de la Corte Suprema, en sentencia de 29 de julio de 2026 (rol N°

34.734-2026), declaró inadmisible por falta de preparación el recurso de casación en la forma y

rechazó por manifiesta falta de fundamento el de fondo, deducidos contra la sentencia de la Corte

de Apelaciones de Chillán que, confirmando el fallo de primer grado, acogió la acción

reivindicatoria dirigida por la dueña y poseedora inscrita de un inmueble contra sus ocupantes

materiales. El recurso planteaba la objeción clásica del sistema registral: si conforme a los artículos

724 y 728 del Código Civil nadie adquiere la posesión de un inmueble inscrito sin inscripción, el

ocupante material no es poseedor, y la reivindicatoria del artículo 889 —acción del dueño no

poseedor contra el poseedor no dueño— se queda, en rigor, sin demandado. La Corte responde con

dos movimientos: constata que el dueño inscrito privado de la tenencia material carece de la

posesión «cabal e íntegra» que exige el artículo 700, y convoca el artículo 915 como regla de cierre

—siguiendo a Alcalde— que integra los supuestos de legitimación pasiva de la acción, de modo

que los artículos 889 y 915 cumplen una misma función y se tratan unitariamente. El fallo

consolida una línea de cinco pronunciamientos en trece meses y la blinda procesalmente con el

artículo 782 del Código de Procedimiento Civil. Este comentario reconstruye el caso, sitúa la

decisión en la disputa centenaria entre inscripción-ficción e inscripción-garantía, examina la

legitimación pasiva resultante y sus consecuencias prácticas frente al precario, extrae la lección

procesal del recurso de forma no preparado y cierra con un decálogo de litigación. La tesis: el

sistema registral define al poseedor, pero la tutela restitutoria persigue al que ocupa; entre el papel

y el suelo, el artículo 915 tiende el puente.

articles.title: Why Workers Use AI Less Often: Reasons for Declining Workplace AI Use in Germany
articles.authors: Marco Lünich
articles.abstract: This short report summarizes recent findings on the extent and the change in the professional use of artificial intelligence (AI) among workers in Germany. It is based on a quota-based online survey of 2,585 workers, conducted from 29 April 2026 to 11 May 2026. The focus is on how professional AI use has changed over the past three months, what reasons are cited for reduced use, and how an increase or decrease is related to individual and organizational characteristics. The majority report that their use has remained unchanged. Overall, increases predominate, while a decrease affects only a small proportion of the workforce. A decline in usage is associated with a more critical attitude toward AI, lower perceived competence and organizational support, as well as a perceived lack of added value, unreliable results, and data privacy concerns. At the same time, social differences are evident: higher-skilled workers are more likely to increase their usage, while lower-skilled workers are comparatively more likely to reduce it. This raises the question of whether AI reduces or exacerbates existing inequalities in the workplace.

articles.title: Unionization in Higher Education: An Industry-Level View
articles.authors: Joseph van der Naald
articles.abstract: This research note presents estimates of union membership and collective bargaining coverage in the higher education industry using data from the Current Population Survey. The paper analyzes the extent of union membership and collective bargaining coverage from 1983-2025, both in the industry and among faculty specifically, and estimates of the variation in union membership by employment sector, race and gender for 2024. Using a 10-year span of data, the paper also estimates union wage premiums in the industry and among faculty. This note finds union membership and bargaining coverage has remained stable over the past four decades, but documents notable gendered and ethnoracial disparities in both measures in 2024. Faculty and industry collective bargaining results in earnings premiums ranging between 4% and 5%. The findings present quantitative estimates of unionism and its material effects for higher education workers that complement recent research published by the National Center for the Study of Collective Bargaining in Higher Education and the Professions.
