articles.title: HIERARCHICAL METHODOLOGY OF DMYTRO KRIVENKO: THE LIMITS OF DIALECTICS AND LEVELS OF PHYSICAL KNOWLEDGE
articles.authors: Yaroslav Dmytrovych Kivenko-Emetov
articles.abstract:
This article reconstructs the philosophical and methodological programme of Dmytro T. Krivenko (1941–1994) as a level-sensitive approach to scientific and philosophical thought. Its historical basis comprises his publications of 1973–1988 on quantitative concepts, informational levels, rational inheritance, and the coarse-graining of complex systems; his 1991 formulation of a “hierarchical model of human cognition”; and manuscripts completed during his lifetime and published posthumously as Prynat i prynatyka (1996).

The article argues that Krivenko did not merely add the notion of levels to a universal dialectical scheme. He distinguished the functions of general-philosophical, logical-methodological, and discipline-specific scientific levels. General philosophy could orient inquiry, but it could not replace measurement, mathematical constructions, models, limiting transitions, or empirical testing. Dialectics thereby ceased to operate as a self-sufficient algorithm of cognition and became one possible heuristic instrument within a broader hierarchical methodology.

Five central elements of this programme are examined: the formation of physical quantities, informational levels, the growth of informativeness, rational inheritance, and coarse-graining. Scientific development is understood neither as the simple accumulation of facts nor as a universal movement through thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. A successor theory selectively preserves confirmed observations, relations, procedures, and limiting results while changing the ontology and structure of explanation. Coarse-graining shows how knowledge may advance through a controlled loss of detail.

The anthropological and political dimension is reconstructed through the concepts of the Prynat and Prynatics. The Prynat is a holistic configuration of three levels of human Nature—the biological, the social or “sociumal,” and the spiritual—together with the individual forms through which they are expressed. All three levels are necessary, but the spiritual has the highest normative status because it integrates biological and social existence with freedom, dignity, and responsibility. Krivenko associates the absolutization of the biological with extreme nationalism and Nazism, the absolutization of the sociumal with communism, and the integrative spiritual level with democracy.

Finally, Krivenko’s programme is compared with contemporary discussions of emergence, effective theories, multilevel ontology, and later applications to quark and exploratory preon models. These comparisons are not retrospective attributions, but tests of his central principle: a deeper description is scientifically meaningful only when it preserves validated knowledge, defines its domain of applicability, constructs explicit transitions between levels, yields independent consequences, and remains open to empirical falsification.

articles.title: Great Expectations? Researchers in Germany are Optimistic about the Potential of Grant Lotteries.
articles.authors: Christophe Heger
articles.abstract: In this study I investigate researchers’ expectations towards the potential advantages of grant lotteries in a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions provided by the Scientists Survey of the German Centre for Higher Education Research and Science Studies (DZHW). I describe the saliency of the two debates on bias in grant peer review and on grant lotteries, as well as researchers’ levels of experience with grant peer review. I use both descriptive statistics and analytical models to investigate which characteristics shape scientists’ relative grant lottery optimism. I find that experienced and more senior scientists are significantly less optimistic about grant lotteries. Saliency and reviewer workload are positively associated with optimism. I conclude that, even though saliency of the issue remains sparse, researchers are generally optimistic about grant lotteries, yet also aware of some of their potential disadvantages.

articles.title: Individual perception of bias in grant peer review strongly associated with openness towards the introduction of lotteries.
articles.authors: Christophe Heger
articles.abstract: This study of a representative sample of scientists at German universities and higher education institutions investigates researchers’ individual perception of bias in grant peer review and their openness towards the potential introduction of grant lotteries, as well as the potential link between the two concepts. Indeed, bias in peer review is often cited in the theoretical debate on grant lotteries. But even though researchers are both very involved in and strongly affected by grant decision-making, there is not enough empirical evidence on their perspective. I find that bias perception is very prevalent, openness is generally rare and researchers who perceive more bias in grant peer review are more open towards grant lotteries in a substantial and statistically significant way.

articles.title: ¿Cómo se trabaja la intervención en masculinidades en las Universidades?
articles.authors: Camila Stipo Lara; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Rocío Gallardo; Daniela Lillo; Andrea Vera Gajardo; Antonieta Vera; Tamara Vidaurrazaga
articles.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo presenta resultados intermedios del proyecto Anillo ATE220009 "Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista" (2022-2025), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID) de Chile. A partir de un grupo de discusión realizado en Santiago en 2024 con profesionales —mayoritariamente psicólogos y trabajadores sociales— que coordinan dispositivos de intervención en masculinidades en universidades chilenas, el texto examina quiénes realizan este trabajo y cómo lo hacen, y cómo la demanda institucional tiende a reducir la intervención en masculinidades al problema de la violencia de género, privilegiando un enfoque terapéutico e individual por sobre uno comunitario. Se analiza también cómo esta labor se concentra predominantemente en la atención a estudiantes "funados" y sancionados, respondiendo a una lógica reactiva antes que preventiva, y se documentan las frustraciones de quienes ejercen este rol por la falta de enfoque comunitario, la escasez de espacios de conversación entre varones, y la posición ambigua que ocupan al ser percibidos como "defensores" de los acusados. El cuaderno concluye señalando el lugar de los varones y las masculinidades como uno de los nudos críticos en la institucionalización de la política de género en las universidades chilenas tras la revuelta feminista de 2018.

articles.title: ¿Cuáles son los balances del Mayo Feminista de 2018?
articles.authors: Valentina Lastra; Camila Stipo Lara; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Tamara Vidaurrazaga; Rocío Gallardo
articles.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo presenta resultados intermedios del proyecto Anillo ATE220009 "Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista" (2022-2025), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID) de Chile. A partir de 21 entrevistas realizadas entre abril y diciembre de 2024 a (ex)estudiantes universitarias de La Serena, Antofagasta, Santiago, Valparaíso, Concepción y Valdivia que participaron activamente en las movilizaciones feministas de mayo de 2018, el texto examina las expectativas que motivaron dichos procesos, las percepciones sobre los avances logrados a nivel institucional, social y personal, y las limitantes que enfrentaron las estudiantes, incluyendo obstáculos normativos, represalias institucionales y la instalación de sentidos comunes punitivistas. El cuaderno cierra con reflexiones emergentes sobre el rol de las funas, la tensión entre lo sancionatorio y lo transformador, y los desafíos pendientes para los feminismos universitarios.

articles.title: ¿Cómo se entiende la Educación No Sexista en las universidades?
articles.authors: Carolina Muñoz; Lelya Troncoso Pérez; Rocío Gallardo; Cecilia Loaiza; Daniela Lillo; Karina Pinto; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Camila Stipo Lara; Tamara Vidaurrazaga
articles.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo presenta resultados intermedios del proyecto Anillo ATE220009 "Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista" (2022-2025), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID) de Chile, en colaboración con el Núcleo de I+D+i "Diversidad y género: abordajes feministas interseccionales" del Departamento de Trabajo Social de la Universidad de Chile. A partir de entrevistas cualitativas realizadas en 2023 y 2024 a profesionales que trabajan en direcciones o unidades de género en universidades de seis ciudades de las zonas norte, centro y sur del país, el texto examina cómo se reconoce el sexismo en las instituciones de educación superior y qué significados se atribuyen a la educación no sexista (ENS). Se analiza además cómo se operacionaliza la ENS mediante acciones heterogéneas —modelos educativos, manuales, talleres y promoción del lenguaje no sexista— y se identifican las tensiones y resistencias que limitan su avance, incluyendo la falta de obligatoriedad curricular, las resistencias del profesorado y la percepción de la ENS como una demanda radical o inviable. El cuaderno concluye que sexismo y educación no sexista son categorías mutuamente constitutivas, cuya definición se co-produce institucionalmente en un contexto de importantes limitaciones estructurales.

articles.title: ¿Cómo son las denuncias por acoso sexual, violencia y discriminación de género en las Universidades?
articles.authors: Sandra Vera Gajardo; Rocío Gallardo; Daniela Lillo; Cecilia Loaiza; Karina Pinto; Camila Stipo Lara; Tamara Vidaurrazaga; Oriana Miranda
articles.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo describe el recorrido que sigue una denuncia por acoso sexual, violencia o discriminación de género al interior de las instituciones universitarias chilenas, a partir del relato de profesionales que trabajan en unidades de género. El documento aborda las actorías y herramientas institucionales involucradas en las denuncias formales (unidades de género, comisiones técnicas, protocolos, comisiones investigadoras), los desenlaces y efectos de estos procesos en las partes implicadas, la caracterización de los casos recibidos, y las tensiones que surgen entre la jurisdicción interna de las universidades y los organismos judiciales externos. Se cierra con un resumen de los principales problemas identificados en los procesos de denuncia y sanción, entre ellos la duplicidad de procesos, la falta de recursos institucionales y los vacíos en la legislación vigente. Las entrevistas que sustentan este cuaderno fueron realizadas en 2023 y 2024 en universidades de seis ciudades de las zonas norte, centro y sur de Chile. El documento forma parte de la serie Cuadernos de Trabajo Disonantes, resultado del proyecto Anillo Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista (ATE220009), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID).

articles.title: Domestic Peace Deficit: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Gender-Based Violence through Institutional, Relational, and Structural Peace Failures
articles.authors: Ijeoma Ezeukwu
articles.abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) continues to persist at high levels despite decades of legal reform, policy intervention, and scholarly attention. Existing approaches, drawn from criminology, public health, sociology, psychology, and law, have generated important insights into individual acts, risk factors, and immediate responses. Yet they remain less equipped to explain the cumulative institutional conditions that allow harm within domestic and intimate life to endure across the life course. This paper introduces the Domestic Peace Deficit (DPD) as a conceptual framework that addresses this gap. DPD explains how cumulative institutional failures undermine peace within domestic life by shaping exposure to violence, access to protection, and recognition of harm. Its central contribution is to treat the household as a peace system rather than merely a private social space or a site of interpersonal violence. Drawing on and extending insights from structural violence, positive peace, feminist peace research, human security, the ecological model of GBV, and intersectionality, the framework organises analysis around three pillars: the Violence and Coercion Deficit, the Agency and Relational Peace Deficit, and the Institutional and Structural Support Deficit. The paper defines domestic peace, formalises the deficit concept, outlines core principles, describes how the framework was developed, sketches pathways of accumulation, a future measurement agenda, and states the framework's principal limitations. DPD does not replace existing theories; it integrates and extends them into a coherent architecture centred on the domestic sphere. In doing so, it offers researchers, policymakers, and practitioners a tool for understanding why formal protections so often fail to produce lived safety, and for designing responses that address institutional recognition, accountability, and the intergenerational transmission of harm.

articles.title: Identity Claims in Political Speech
articles.authors: Asli Ceren Cinar; Mirya Holman; Tyler Simko
articles.abstract: Social identities shape political behavior, but when, how, and why do people talk about these identities? We introduce the concept of identity claiming: publicly identifying oneself as a member of a social group to establish standing and strengthen political appeals. Drawing on five corpora of political communication, including congressional newsletters, campaign biographies, social media, and public comments at school board and city council meetings, we show that elites and members of the public regularly make identity claims. The identities they invoke are not random: claims match the setting, deserving reference groups are used more frequently, and identity claims associated with increased vocal pitch. Experimental and social media evidence shows that speech with identity claims prompts engagement from the audience. Our work shows how ordinary people and political elites strategically and frequently engage in identity politics in their public communication.

articles.title: Das gelesene Buch. Lesen und Geschmackspräferenzen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz
articles.authors: Carolin Amlinger; Luca Keiser; Oliver Nachtwey; Jörg Rössel
articles.abstract:
This preprint presents descriptive findings from a standardised online survey on book reading conducted in Germany, Austria and Switzerland in May and June 2026 (N = 6,427; quota-sampled by gender, age, region and education). It asks how reading practices and literary preferences are socially distributed across the German-speaking countries.
The findings suggest that what divides the reading public is not how much is read but whether people read at all: the share of avid readers varies only between 5 and 13 per cent across social groups, whereas the share of non-readers ranges from 7 to 30 per cent. Education marks the sharpest boundary, with the decisive break falling between the highly educated and everyone else rather than along a continuous gradient. Gender and having been read to in childhood operate as independent axes, while age structures taste more than volume. Evaluative criteria follow the same logic: immersion and involvement dominate across all groups, but formal criteria such as stylistic quality and complexity gain weight with education. At the same time, the cultural legitimacy of the book remains broadly acknowledged, including among those who barely read.
The analysis is deliberately descriptive and serves as a first step towards subsequent multivariate analyses of the social and literary space.

articles.title: ¿Cómo son las funas en las Universidades? Descripciones desde las Unidades de Género universitarias
articles.authors: Rocío Gallardo; Cecilia Loaiza; Karina Pinto; Sandra Vera Gajardo; Oriana Miranda; Camila Stipo Lara; Tamara Vidaurrazaga
articles.abstract: Este cuaderno de trabajo describe cómo ocurren las funas en las universidades chilenas, entendidas como acusaciones públicas sobre violencia de género que se producen por canales no formalizados (redes sociales, afiches, páginas web, entre otros). A partir de entrevistas realizadas en 2023 y 2024 a personas que trabajan o coordinan unidades de género en universidades de seis ciudades de las zonas norte, centro y sur del país, el documento organiza los relatos en torno a cuatro ejes: quiénes se implican en las funas y para quiénes tienen efecto, cuándo ocurren, qué posiciones existen frente a ellas, y qué tensiones enfrentan las universidades al abordarlas. Se presentan también los efectos individuales y colectivos identificados por las entrevistadas. El cuaderno forma parte de la serie Cuadernos de Trabajo Disonantes, resultado del proyecto Anillo Disonancias: Comunidad, Universidad e Irrupción Feminista (ATE220009), financiado por la Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo (ANID).

articles.title: Support and contestation under the radar:  How states promote and undermine the international fight against corruption
articles.authors: Hortense Jongen; Kristina Sabrina Weißmüller
articles.abstract: This article investigates hidden forms of support for and contestation of international norms. Existing research largely focuses on publicly visible behavioural forms of contestation, such as member states’ exit from international organizations (IOs). However, less visible practices can also effectively undermine and sabotage international norms, or, conversely, strengthen them. We explore this phenomenon by researching a prominent IO in the global fight against corruption, the Group of States against Corruption (GRECO), by means of interviews with delegates to GRECO and members of the Council of Europe secretariat, complemented with an analysis of policy documents. The empirical evidence reveals five distinct types of hidden contestation and two types of hidden support. Contestation typically originates from the political macro-level rather than from the involved expert community. Member states contest GRECO’s authority through ineffective implementation, delays, obstructive voting, and by negotiating review outcomes. Conversely, peer pressure and peer support emerge as meaningful micro-level practices of norm support that counteract contestation. This study’s insights advance research on contestation and support of international norms and inform research, theory, and practice on how to strengthen the global fight against corruption.

articles.title: Coding choices and short-sequence artefacts undermine claims of a conventional Palaeolithic sign system – a comment on Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026)
articles.authors: Alexander Koplenig
articles.abstract: In this comment, I show that methodological and statistical flaws undermine the central conclusions of Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026).

articles.title: Educating Physicians in Clinical Healthy Longevity Medicine: A Comprehensive Training Framework from an Academic Hospital
articles.authors: Evelyne Bischof; Sara Bonnes; Dominika Wilczok; Abigail Goshen; Chaim Haber; Tzipi Strauss
articles.abstract: Healthy longevity medicine is expanding rapidly, yet no standardized, hospital-based pathways exist for training physicians. This paper presents the first validated training framework within a dedicated hospital department. The model uniquely spans all stages of medical formation and integrates key elements of healthy longevity medicine into routine clinical workflows. It demonstrates how longevity training can be formally incorporated into approved specialty pathways while remaining fully embedded within curative medicine.

articles.title: A Healthier Start Abroad? The health at birth of the children of migrants and of those born at origin
articles.authors: Alessandro Ferrara; Marco Cozzani
articles.abstract: The health of migrants is mostly studied in relation to destination-country natives, Origin-country comparisons are rarely pursued, even though they provide a more convincing counterfactual, allowing us to (a) measure “health gains” from migration, (b) disentangle mechanisms including selectivity, cultural factors and contextual change, (c) elucidate the relationship between migration and global health inequality. We address this gap by comparing the health at birth of children born in Spain to migrant parents from 15 origin countries with that of children born in those same origin countries, using Spanish vital statistics linked to Demographic and Health Surveys and other origin-country sources. We find that, for most groups, the children of migrants are healthier at birth (measured via low birth weight) than children in their parents' origin countries. This is also true among groups disadvantaged relative to Spanish natives, and is more pronounced for non-Western and, especially, Asian-origin groups. We find limited support for cultural explanations and stronger support for both migrant selectivity and improved contextual conditions at destination. Though the latter two are not fully separable, our evidence favors the effect of the change in contextual conditions. These results suggest migration can function as an equalizing force, narrowing birthplace-based health inequalities.

articles.title: When Resources Are Scarce: Formal Mentoring as a Compensatory Resource for Sustainable Performance Expectations
articles.authors: Andreea Nicolau; Ad Kleingeld
articles.abstract: Drawing on Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) theory, this study conceptualizes formal mentoring as a resource system and examines how mentoring functions, job resources and demands, self-empowerment, and organizational support relate to mentoring program effectiveness and sustainable performance expectations. Using cross-sectional self-report data from 71 participants in a formal peer mentoring program, we found that perceived program effectiveness was positively associated with sustainable performance expectations, defined as participants’ beliefs about their ability to sustain performance and well-being over time. Mentoring functions were positively related to program effectiveness and, indirectly, to sustainable performance expectations via perceived mentoring effectiveness. In addition, job cognitive resources, self-empowerment, and organizational support moderated the relationship between mentoring functions and program effectiveness, such that mentoring functions were most strongly associated with perceived effectiveness when these resources were lower. These findings suggest that mentoring functions may operate as compensatory resources in resource-constrained contexts. Employment status was also relevant, with full-time employed participants reporting higher program effectiveness than solopreneurs. Overall, the findings extend JD-R theory by positioning mentoring not only as a developmental intervention but also as a resource that supports sustainable human performance.

articles.title: Standardising Access to Digital Platform Data: A Taxonomy for Social Research
articles.authors: Futoon Abushaqra; Damiano Spina; Amanda Lawrence; Daniel Angus; Robert Glasgow
articles.abstract:
[This manuscript has been submitted for peer review]
Abstract: Recent regulations granting individuals the right to access their personal data stored on digital platforms have reshaped the landscape of data collection. Under frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union and the 2019 New York SHIELD Act, platforms are now required to provide users with mechanisms to retrieve and inspect their own data; commonly referred to as Data Download Packages (DDPs). These developments have enabled new forms of data collection through data donation, where users voluntarily share their DDPs for research purposes. However, the structure, format, and granularity of DDPs vary significantly across platforms and over time, posing challenges for researchers, especially those without technical expertise. Responding to these challenges, this paper contributes to the Australian Internet Observatory's broader agenda of building national research infrastructure for independent, public-interest platform research. We propose a taxonomy for categorising DDPs across different platforms, alongside a schema repository that systematically describes the content of each DDP, including its structure, data types, and formats. These contributions support a more consistent and comprehensive understanding of DDPs across diverse platforms, with a particular focus on social media and digital services, and enable their effective use in both academic and applied research contexts.

articles.title: An Open Two-Corpus Dataset of Animal Harm Incidents and Criminal Judgments in China (AHID-CN)
articles.authors: Nanyi Deng
articles.abstract:
Author Note (August 18, 2026): This preprint is currently undergoing systematic review and revision. An updated version will be posted upon completion. Readers are encouraged to consult the latest version of the manuscript.
China has no anti-cruelty statute, so there is no offense category, court statistic, or government database that records harm to animals. AHID-CN makes this harm countable through two deliberately separate sub-corpora. An incident corpus documents 30 publicly reported animal-harm events through archived sources, extracted claims, and coded institutional responses. A judgment census identifies 490 animal-harm criminal judgments (about 409 unique cases) from CAIL2018, a frozen corpus of 2.68 million Chinese criminal judgments published up to 2018, using a documented search protocol in which every automated exclusion was manually re-examined. The dataset ships as five CSV tables with full field documentation under CC BY-SA 4.0 on Zenodo. It supports research on how existing criminal law stretches to cover harms it was not written for, on the co-occurrence of animal abuse with interpersonal violence, and on what public reporting captures that the judicial record misses.

articles.title: Tracking Change, Informing Policy: Longitudinal Evidence of Shifting Political Affiliations and Public Attitudes Toward Higher Education
articles.authors: Stephen M Gavazzi; Suzanne Bartle-Haring; E. Gordon Gee
articles.abstract: This longitudinal study examines how public attitudes toward U.S. public higher education shifted between 2021 and 2025 across five policy-relevant domains: funding priorities, rural-urban engagement, global-local emphasis, financial aid preferences, and the perceived importance of national rankings. Using data from panel respondents across nine states, results show growing support for balanced approaches to geographic engagement, financial aid, and global-local activities, alongside increased prioritization of teaching and declining support for community engagement. Nearly 30 percent of participants changed their political affiliation over the four year period, and these shifts were strongly associated with changes in funding preferences, especially allocations to teaching. Cross lag analyses further indicate that changes in funding priorities, engagement emphases, and ideological self-placement help explain trust in state universities. Findings underscore the importance of longitudinal designs for understanding how individual-level political dynamics shape public expectations for, and confidence in, higher education.

articles.title: New alternatives, same orders: modern alternative proteins did not replace meat purchases in restaurants
articles.authors: Jared Winslow; Jacob Robert Peacock; Jayisha Dhargawe; Hailey Sherman; Seth Ariel Green; Maya B Mathur
articles.abstract: Plant-based alternative proteins are widely expected to displace meat consumption and, in turn, reorient the global food system away from the externalities of animal agriculture, but little empirical work has assessed these presumed substitution effects in naturalistic settings. Here, we use a dataset of 1.2 million transactions across seven restaurants and eight years to investigate whether introducing modern alternative proteins to restaurant menus reduces purchases of meat-containing dishes. We analyzed effects on total meat purchases and on category-matched purchases, pairing each alternative protein with the meat it emulates; we also estimate individual (within-customer) purchasing changes. Our results from 40 preregistered outcome-exposure pairings are overwhelmingly null, whether pooled across restaurants or stratified by restaurant. These findings challenge the widespread belief that alternative proteins displace meat purchases.

articles.title: Digital state capacity: a conceptualization approach
articles.authors: Yago Paiva
articles.abstract: Digital technologies matter more and more for state affairs, yet few formulations define what digital is for the continuous structure of the state after decades of digitalization. This article argues that digital has become an essential dimension of state capacity. Drawing on an ontological-semantic approach to concept building, it constructs the concept of digital capacity around three necessary dimensions: digital apparatus, digital space control and digital interaction. It then develops the Digital Capacity Index, covering the 193 United Nations members from 2001 to 2022. Validity tests show a consistent concept-measure relationship and support comparative policy analysis of the digital state.

articles.title: Two Cycles, Not One: A Continuous-Time Point-Process Analysis of Reciprocal Violence in the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict
articles.authors: Carlin Percha
articles.abstract: Whether violence in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict is reciprocal — each side's lethal action provoking the other's — has been studied largely through vector-autoregression on time-binned counts, an approach that obscures the timing, branching structure, and directionality of response. We model lethal violence in the two directions as a bivariate Hawkes process, a continuous-time self- and mutually-exciting point process, using individual-incident fatality records from the Second Intifada through October 2023. Reciprocal excitation is genuine but profoundly asymmetric: a single Palestinian-to-Israeli event triggers on the order of one subsequent Israeli lethal event, nearly thirty times the reverse coupling. The asymmetry survives placebo, regime-detection, and flexible-baseline checks designed to rule out a common-driver confound, and goodness-of-fit testing confirms the models describe the data adequately. Allowing the couplings to take either sign, we find no evidence of deterrence in either direction. The strength of the Israeli response is statistically indistinguishable across the conflict's two main eras, but its speed is not: the characteristic response lag roughly halves between the Intifada and the later Gaza-war period, a temporal change binned methods cannot represent. Resolving the Israeli-to-Palestinian direction into its Gaza and West Bank theaters reveals that they operate as nearly independent systems: violence within each is strongly self-exciting while cross-theater coupling is negligible, and the reciprocal dynamic that dominates the pooled analysis is localized almost entirely to the West Bank, whereas Gaza's violence is driven by internal escalation. What appears in aggregate as a single cycle is, spatially, two barely-interacting logics — a separation we argue reflects the differential governance of the two territories rather than any natural division of the conflict. A three-stream extension shows settler violence to be a distinct channel: reactive to Palestinian action, increasingly self-exciting, and temporally preceding rather than following state violence. All findings replicate on an independently constructed event dataset. We document these regularities for 2000–2023 and set out why we do not extend them through the subsequent war: individual-incident records for that period exist, but not on a footing commensurable with the present analysis.

articles.title: The reach of violence: Infant health among diasporas in the United States during the onset of the 2023 Gaza War
articles.authors: Jasmin Abdel Ghany; Emma Romell; Joshua Wilde
articles.abstract: A large body of research documents the harm that armed conflict inflicts on the health of populations in conflict zones. Yet if violence injures collectivities rather than only those who experience it directly, its health consequences should extend to those who identify with affected populations wherever they reside. We test this hypothesis by examining the effects of the October 7, 2023, attacks in Israel and the ensuing onset of the Gaza War on infant health in the United States among mothers born in Israel, the West Bank, and neighboring, Arab, and Muslim-majority countries. In a novel application of the event-study design, we trace month-by-month changes in preterm birth and low birthweight – outcomes that shape health and socioeconomic attainment throughout the life course. Our analyses show that the Israel-born diaspora experienced an immediate, short-lived reversal in their previously substantial infant health advantage after the October 7 attacks. Infant health also deteriorated among mothers born in neighboring, other Arab, and other Muslim-majority countries. These findings indicate that the health consequences of violence are not confined to the conflict zone but extend to geographically distant diaspora communities who are connected to the affected populations by shared national and ethnic origin and religion.

articles.title: Technology–Based Rehabilitation Interventions for Children with Cerebral Palsy in Low- and Lower-Middle-Income Countries (LMICs): A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Zahra Lalani; Salena Aggerwal; Jennifer O'Neil
articles.abstract:
Background: 
Cerebral palsy (CP) affects approximately 1.6 per 1,000 children globally. In Low- and Lower-Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), children with CP face significant barriers to rehabilitation. Emerging technology-based interventions such as 3D printing, virtual reality (VR), and telerehabilitation offer innovative, cost-effective solutions for resource-constrained settings.

Objective: 
This scoping review explored technology-based motor rehabilitation interventions for children with CP in LMICs, identifying implementation locations, challenges, and opportunities.

Methods: 
A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus (2015–2026) identified studies on technology-based motor rehabilitation for children with CP in World Bank–defined LMICs. Following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework, two independent reviewers screened studies and extracted data on intervention types, outcomes, and LMIC implementation factors, resolving discrepancies by consensus.

Results: 
From 2,046 screened titles, 18 studies were included across Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh. Interventions featured Kinect® therapy, augmented reality, Wii® exergaming, robotic-assisted gait training, biosensor-driven mechatronic devices with 3D-printed parts, and community-led telerehabilitation. Key challenges included high equipment costs, rural poverty, hardware instability, and caregiver technological unfamiliarity or overstimulation concerns. Opportunities included heightened patient motivation, objective progress monitoring to reduce reporting bias, and reduced physical burden on staff. The SMART-CP model demonstrated that integrated telerehabilitation increases service uptake, overcoming geographical and financial barriers.

Conclusions: 
Technology-based interventions, specifically VR, augmented reality, exergames, and telerehabilitation, show strong promise for improving motor function and engagement in children with CP in LMICs. Despite cost and accessibility hurdles, these tools represent viable, scalable solutions for expanding rehabilitation services in low-resource environments.

articles.title: Rethinking Social Sustainability Metrics in Chile’s Lithium Sociotechnical Transition: Numbers, Policies and Knowledge
articles.authors: Sebastián Herrera-León; Iván Ojeda-Pereira; Fernando Campos-Medina; Rodrigo Molina-Richardson
articles.abstract: Social sustainability indicators are central decision-support tools in mining, used to evaluate social performance and guide policy and investment. However, these indicators do not merely describe reality; they actively shape it by defining what is measured, reported, and governed. In the context of lithium extraction from brines, this performative role becomes particularly relevant as expanding production and technological changes reconfigure water use, territorial relations, and community livelihoods in sensitive ecosystems such as the high-Andean salt flats of Chile, which host some of the world's largest lithium reserves and production sites. This paper analyses how social sustainability is currently measured in the lithium industry and identifies the opportunities and limitations of existing indicator frameworks. Using a systematic analysis of sustainability reports and international reporting standards, combined with insights from stakeholder interviews, we examine the indicators commonly used to assess lithium extraction activities. The results show that existing indicator systems are structured by global reporting standards and compliance-oriented metrics, whilst territorial dynamics and relational aspects of social sustainability remain partially captured. Based on these results, the paper discusses implications for the design of social sustainability indicators in critical mineral extraction. We argue that improving sustainability assessment requires incorporating territorially situated perspectives, ecosystem-based knowledge, and broader participation of communities, universities, public institutions, and firms. In this sense, redesigning sustainability indicators as more reflexive and participatory tools may support more socially robust pathways in the sociotechnical transition of the lithium industry in Chile.

articles.title: Migration as Labor Governance: Empire, Replaceability, and Worker Power
articles.authors: Armando Ibarra
articles.abstract: Why does substantial worker mobilization generate effective leverage in some settings but not in others? This article argues that the answer depends partly on labor governance: the institutions through which labor is recruited, legally differentiated, disciplined, and rendered replaceable. Extending the Empire Theory of Migration (ETM), I distinguish the imperial production of migrant labor from its subsequent organization as labor supply. I develop the argument through three historically connected farmworker campaigns: the National Farm Labor Union’s struggle against the DiGiorgio Fruit Corporation, the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee, and the United Farm Workers. Their divergent outcomes—failed recognition, incomplete institutionalization, and contingent bargaining success—show that mobilization generates leverage only when workers and their allies can raise the costs of employer resistance despite employers’ access to alternative labor supplies. Drawing on Ernesto Galarza’s political economy of the Bracero Program, undocumented recruitment, deportation, and labor contracting, the article identifies recruitment, regulation, and legitimation as interconnected dimensions of labor governance. Empire produces migrant labor; labor governance organizes that labor as labor supply; replaceability conditions worker power.

articles.title: A History of Macroeconomics
articles.authors: Francesco Sergi; Beatrice Cherrier; Aurélien Saïdi; Pedro Duarte; Aurélien Goutsmedt; Matthieu Renault; Juan Acosta
articles.abstract: This book offers a history of macroeconomics (the study of “the economy” as a whole) from its inception in the interwar period to today. Its novelty is twofold: it goes beyond a history of theories to cover a wider range of macroeconomists’ practices; it relies on a growing body of historical research, challenging misconceptions commonly disseminated in macroeconomics textbooks. This is not “yet another history of macroeconomics”. It is one that should strike scholars and students in macroeconomics as novel. Such a history is needed because macroeconomics textbooks project a particular “identity” of the field, derived from a specific historical narrative, in which the field evolved through theoretical “revolutions” and “battles” between “schools of thought” initiated by “great men”. We argue that this misrepresents the actual dynamics of macroeconomics. Our history conveys a different perspective, highlighting a more diverse set of characteristics (what macroeconomics is about) and practices (what macroeconomists do). We emphasise how macroeconomics has always relied on the combination of research agendas (theoretical, mathematical, empirical, and computational); how the interaction with other fields (notably microeconomics and econometrics) has been constant; and how the field has been shaped by a cast of researchers with diverse geographical and institutional origins (some working within academia, others in policymaking institutions and private organisations). We bring these many dimensions together through a simple chronology outlining four periods: birth (1920s-1940s), bridges (1950s-1960s), frictions (1970s-1980s), and constellations (1990s-2000s).

articles.title: Moving targets?  Life-course dynamics in intergenerational mobility
articles.authors: Roujman Shahbazian; Erik Bihagen; Edvin Syk
articles.abstract: Research on intergenerational mobility assumes that individuals reach occupational maturity, typically around age 35, allowing occupational positions to be treated as stable destinations and mobility to be summarized by a single estimate. We argue that this assumption is difficult to reconcile with contemporary occupational careers. If occupational positions continue to evolve throughout adulthood, intergenerational mobility may itself be a life-course process rather than a fixed parameter. Using retrospective occupational histories from 27 European countries and the United States, we first show that occupational mobility commonly extends well beyond the age conventionally assumed to mark occupational maturity. We then analyze Swedish population register data, estimating parent–offspring associations across every combination of parental and offspring ages between 27 and 56. Rather than converging to a stable value, intergenerational associations vary systematically over the life course, peaking in mid-adulthood before declining. These findings challenge the view that age-related variation primarily reflects measurement error. Instead, they suggest that intergenerational mobility is continuously reshaped by intragenerational mobility over the life course, raising the more fundamental question of whether there exists a single intergenerational mobility parameter to recover.

articles.title: The Stratification Engine: A Recurrent Mechanism of Compound Exclusion
articles.authors: Jie Li
articles.abstract: Resource deprivation cuts two ways. It blocks access to new technologies, and scarcity can narrow the cognitive bandwidth needed to use them. I formalise this as the Resource–Technology–Cognitive (RTC) chain, in which disadvantage compounds at the interfaces between layers, so that exclusion multiplies rather than adds. Cognitive inheritance, reconstituted each generation through early-life conditions rather than genetically transmitted, is posited to carry this compound disadvantage across generations unless those conditions change. I trace the chain across eight technological transitions as an illustrative basis, and derive three falsifiable propositions about sequential causation, super-additive amplification, and intergenerational moderation. The AI transition restructures access and skill demands simultaneously, and the next cohort's starting conditions are already forming.

articles.title: Earning more but less secure: Unpaid carers, paid work, and a cliff edge in the design of a cash allowance
articles.authors: Gabriele Mari
articles.abstract:
Unpaid carers often experience economic insecurity despite having paid work. Dubbed a ‘new’ social risk, related social policies and research have focused on promoting employment and bolstering the public safety net when insufficient or absent. Yet the design of existing benefit programs might also have ‘new’ perverse effects. Here I ask how large, for how long, among whom, and why, by analysing the UK’s Carer’s Allowance and its earnings limit.
I rely on survey interviews from fifteen waves of Understanding Society (2009-2024). Economic insecurity is examined by combining material indicators (arrears, income losses, savings) as well as perceptions (financial worry, satisfaction with incomes). I compare carers with a history of Carer’s Allowance receipt to those without as their earnings progress in an event-study design.
Insecurity declines as earnings increase, but not homogeneously among carers. Past the earnings limit, carers with a history of Carer’s Allowance receipt report relatively more arrears with bills and housing, less regular savings, heightened financial worries, and more dissatisfaction with income. The relative gap in insecurity is large, persistent over time, and extends to the whole household. Although findings are generally mixed across socio-economic groups, renters drive estimates for arrears and middle- and working-class carers experience the most worries and dissatisfaction. Changes in insecurity appear unrelated to variation in caregiving involvement. Rather, differences in incomes, employment, and benefit receipt widen past the limit.
By foregrounding the role of policy design, findings speak to studies on social risks and economic insecurity, broadening the case for reforms aimed at carers mixing paid and unpaid work.

articles.title: Younger Adults’ Nuclear and Extended Family Relationships in Europe: A Latent Class Analysis
articles.authors: Bettina Hünteler; Karsten Hank; Diego Alburez-Gutierrez; Thomas Leopold
articles.abstract: The present study identifies and compares typical classes of relationship qualities in the nuclear and extended family ties of younger adults across nine European countries (Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, the United Kingdom, as well as the Nordic countries Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden). We used KINMATRIX data that were collected online in 2022-23 from an ego-centric perspective of 7,375 respondents aged 25–35. Employing latent class analysis and multinomial logistic regression models, we identified five distinct types of relationship qualities, labelled as ‘tight-knit’, ‘connected-but-autonomous’, ‘disharmonious-but-supportive’, ‘intimate-but-distant’, and ‘detached’. The prevalence of these relationship types varied across the family system, showing a clear gradient from tight-knit relations being most prevalent in the nuclear family to distant-extended relations being dominated by detachment. This resulted in a high overall proportion of relatively ‘weak’ relationships within young adults’ family networks. The distribution of classes across countries confirmed the existence of a North-South gradient of increasingly close nuclear and extended family ties in Europe: ‘Weaker’ relationships were more (and ‘stronger’ ties less) common in the Nordic countries, compared to an ‘intermediate’ cluster of countries consisting of the Netherlands, Germany, Poland, as well as the United Kingdom, and – especially – compared to Italy. Our study demonstrates the applicability of common typologies of relationship qualities to assess kin relations beyond the nuclear family and it highlights the relevance of accounting for extended kin relations across a range of European countries.

articles.title: Public Attitudes Toward National Border Controls
articles.authors: Korinna O. Lindemann; Lucas Schramm
articles.abstract: How do citizens evaluate national border controls? In this paper, we argue that while public attitudes toward national border controls are not necessarily fixed, they are primarily interpreted through the lens of migration. To test this argument, we conduct an original survey in Germany and combine open-ended questions with a conjoint and an information experiment. The findings show that migration is not only strongly associated with national border controls, but that the reduction of irregular immigration is also the most important dimension when evaluating these controls. Nonetheless, the findings provide evidence that attitudes toward these controls are not fully fixed: Information on the benefits of the Schengen free travel agreement modestly increases support for border-free travel and reduces support for national border controls. The results have important implications for how the public assesses national border controls in the European context.

articles.title: Exploring the impact of inference method, character coding scheme, and cognacy criterion on phylolinguistic inference: The case of the Japonic language family
articles.authors: Thomas Pellard; Kenan Celik; Reiko Aso; Yosuke Igarashi; Masatoshi Matsunami
articles.abstract: The application of phylogenetic methods to linguistic data requires several critical methodological choices, yet their relative influence on the resulting trees remains poorly understood. This study conducts a systematic sensitivity analysis to evaluate the impact of three key factors: (1) the phylogenetic inference method (neighbor-joining, maximum parsimony, and Bayesian inference), (2) the character coding scheme (binary vs. multistate), and (3) the cognacy (i.e. homology) criterion (root-based vs. stem-based cognacy). Using the Japonic language family as a model, we generated a diverse set of phylogenetic trees and compared them using multiple tree metrics and distance measures between trees. Variance partitioning through distance-based redundancy analysis reveals a clear hierarchy of influence: the choice of inference method is the primary driver of variation between trees, followed by the character coding scheme, while the cognacy criterion exerts a comparatively minor effect. Specifically, we show that the choice of inference method fundamentally shapes tree topology, whereas the character coding scheme impacts branch lengths and evolutionary tempo. While maintaining a consistent and transparent definition of cognacy remains good practice, our results indicate that the choice of one definition over another does not always lead to a significant loss of phylogenetic signal. Therefore, phylolinguistic research should prioritize first and foremost the rigorous selection of inference method.

articles.title: When statistics outlive their geography: asynchronous propagation of a secondary medical area redefinition across Japan's national health data infrastructure — a measurable instance of institutional debt
articles.authors: Kunihisa Ohno
articles.abstract: Health-system geographies are periodically redefined, but the national statistical products that encode them are updated on independent schedules. We report a natural experiment in how such a redefinition propagates. Effective 1 April 2024, Akita Prefecture consolidated its secondary medical areas (SMAs) from eight to three — the only SMA reorganization under Japan’s 8th Medical Plan cycle — reducing the national SMA count from 335 to 330. We examined how three national data products required for SMA-level analysis of the same reference year (2024) encoded the change, by comparing their SMA code sets and validating municipal re-aggregations against published totals. The Physician, Dentist and Pharmacist Statistics 2024 (census date 31 December 2024; released December 2025) and the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare’s municipality–SMA correspondence table (version dated April 2026) encode the new three-SMA definition. The 11th NDB Open Data, released June 2026, tabulates fiscal-year 2024 claims — all generated after the redefinition took effect — in the superseded eight-SMA geography. No product declares the vintage of its zone definition as metadata; the divergence surfaces only as unexplained code mismatches — and, for three zone codes reused across definitions, as silent mis-joins — observable from published artifacts alone. We interpret this as a measurable instance of institutional debt — the divergence between legally effective definitions and those encoded in infrastructure, with reconciliation labor externalized to analysts — quantifiable along three axes (lag, affected population, repairability). Contrasting England’s centrally remapped response to its 2022 commissioning-geography transition, we propose that zone-level statistics be published as versioned views over stable unit identifiers with mandatory definition-vintage metadata.

articles.title: Geodemographic Inequalities in Battery Electric Vehicle Adoption across UK Neighbourhoods
articles.authors: Alex Singleton; Ian Philips; Jillian Anable
articles.abstract: Battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption is an important contributor to the decarbonisation of road transport in the UK and other OECD countries, yet uptake remains highly uneven between places. This paper examines the geography of privately kept battery electric vehicles across UK small areas using quarterly DVLA vehicle licensing records, linked geodemographically to the 2021/22 UK Output Area Classification. The analysis measures observed private vehicle ownership at neighbourhood scale, enabling within local authority variation to be examined directly. The results show that BEV penetration is strongly right-skewed, with adoption concentrated in affluent professional neighbourhoods, prosperous suburban and rural areas, and dense urban cores with relatively small but rapidly electrifying private fleets. Lower uptake is associated with neighbourhoods characterised by rented tenure, terraced housing and flats, where access to private off-street charging is likely to be more constrained. Partitioning the national time series by geodemographic type reveals that the aggregate adoption curve is composed of distinct trajectories, with some early-adopting neighbourhood types showing signs of slower recent growth while later-adopting groups continue to accelerate. Residuals from the geodemographic baseline are spatially clustered, indicating that neighbourhood composition alone does not explain the geography of adoption. The paper demonstrates the value of combining administrative vehicle records with geodemographic classification to identify where BEV adoption is leading, lagging and diverging from demographic expectation, with implications for a more equitable rollout of charging infrastructure and transport decarbonisation policy.

articles.title: Cultures of Civil Crisis Preparedness
articles.authors: Lærke Høgenhaven; Jonas Toubøl
articles.abstract: Recent crises, including pandemics, extreme weather events, and humanitarian crises, have demonstrated informal civil society’s role as a crucial first responder to crisis situations. Yet crisis management research and policy have largely treated informal civil society as a spontaneous resource activated only during response and recovery and lack a conceptual understanding of informal civil society in the crisis preparation phase. This article develops a theoretical framework for understanding cultures of civil crisis preparedness: shared repertoires of perceived responsibilities and preparedness strategies through which civil society anticipates and prepares for future crises. The framework specifies how a community's crisis perceptions shape both responsibilities and strategies, how trust networks enable mutual coordination, and how institutional crisis management approaches, geographical exposure, and authorities' crisis communication shape informal civil society's role in preparedness. It thereby enables analysis of how people come to imagine their own and others' responsibilities before crises occur, and why cultures of civil crisis preparedness vary across national and local contexts.

articles.title: Beyond single-destination access: a tour-based analysis of proximity-based planning in Melbourne
articles.authors: Afshin Jafari; Billie Giles-Corti
articles.abstract: Proximity-based planning has become an influential framework in urban policy, typically framed around the idea that daily needs should be reachable within short walking or cycling distances from home. However, research and policy evaluation have largely focused on access to single destinations, while paying much less attention to the tours through which daily life is actually organised. This matters because many daily activities are linked within sequences of trips, and the feasibility of completing those tours without a car depends on whether urban accessibility and transport options are supportive. This paper examines that gap through a tour-based analysis of Greater Melbourne, using inner, middle, and outer areas as proxies for high, medium, and lower accessibility contexts. Using full-day travel diary data, we construct home-based tours, identify common weekday and weekend tour types using latent class analysis, and compare how those tour patterns vary across the metropolitan rings. The results show that broad tour patterns are relatively similar across rings, but the distances travelled to complete those tours and car dependence increase substantially from inner to outer Melbourne. Car-dominated tours increase from 49.5% in the inner ring to 79.9% in the outer ring, while walk-dominated tours fall from 27.4% to 12.2%. More importantly, patterns that are common across the city are completed over longer distances and increasingly by car in outer areas. This suggests that identifying the tours and behavioural patterns people commonly undertake can help reorient proximity-based planning from a narrow focus on nearby individual destinations toward supporting the everyday combinations of activities people actually need to complete.

articles.title: Prospective Travel Diary in Tourist Decision-Making
articles.authors: Elodie Manthé
articles.abstract: This research note introduces a new image-based tool that integrates inspiration and co-creation in tourist decision-making. Grounded in prospective memory – a concept developed in psychology literature- the tool enables participants to mentally simulate and visualize a future trip, constructing a fictitious travel diary through illustrated cards. This approach serves as both a research method for studying decision-making processes and a practical tool for tourism professionals. We explore its theoretical foundations, applications, and potential to enhance tourist engagement and travel booking experiences.

articles.title: Deliberative, affective, and experiential risk in crisis response: Fears of responders and people in crisis
articles.authors: Andrew David Eaton; Megan Wheeler Rowe; Claire Ryder; Amanda Mathew; Sandra Kwan; Jenny Angela Hui; Brandon Barksdale; Leyna Lowe
articles.abstract: Mental health crisis response is diverse and evolving, with ongoing debate about outcomes for people in crisis, the appropriateness of different responses, and the role of police. Crisis encounters combine three forms of risk assessment: reasoned judgments (deliberative), emotional responses (affective), and gut feelings (experiential). This qualitative knowledge-to-action study consisted of interviews with 33 Canadian and American key informants in crisis response (e.g., responders and people with lived experience of crisis encounters). Interpretive phenomenological analysis was employed by a large and diverse coding team on data pertaining to shifting dynamics and experiences of risk. Findings address: a) the governing logic of risk in crisis response, as risks are triaged and translated yet remain subjective and uncertain; b) constant perceptions of risk in crisis encounters that shift based on the scene and mental health discourses; and c) a double-bind to police involvement, where responders fear risks to themselves and others on scene and seek security and stability in police but people in crisis fear police involvement. Risk moves from deliberative to experiential via affective emotions on the scene. This study identified sustained reliance on police by responders, even within civilian-led, non-police alternative crisis response teams. Police remain a form of first response, co-response, and backup or escalation support, heightening risk for people in crisis, despite focused efforts to de-task police from crisis calls.

articles.title: Documentation Gap Analysis: Independent Audit of TGA COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Monitoring Plan
articles.authors: Paul Rekaris
articles.abstract:
This independent audit evaluates the TGA COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Monitoring Plan (February 2021). The Plan operationalised National Cabinet's commitment to enhanced pharmacovigilance accompanying provisional approval, covering 68.4 million doses, 91.2% of Australia's rollout. Enhanced monitoring claims cannot be independently verified when the underlying processes are undocumented. This audit tests whether that verification is possible.

The audit finds a systematic failure to demonstrate the enhanced monitoring underpinning Australia's largest provisional medicine rollout. Only 3 of 19 audited outputs (16%) are fully documented; 16 (84%) are partially or not documented. This is despite the TGA organising 2,218+ pages by Plan objectives for the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) in September 2024. The TGA reports 148 signals investigated and 57 regulatory actions taken (updated to 150 and 93 respectively in the subsequent Question on Notice 559). No audit trail links signals to actions, and 91 signals have no documented disposition in the record. The OAIC found that the implementation records could "not be located or do not exist".  

Senior TGA officials told the Senate (9 October 2025) that monitoring occurred through "day-to-day processes," without systematic tracking against Plan objectives.  The TGA cannot demonstrate documented implementation of its own Safety Monitoring Plan. This is a potential failure of regulatory accountability for the largest provisional medicine rollout in Australia's history.

The audit's open-source methodology applies ISO 19011:2018, ANAO guidance, and OSINT principles to public and FOI records, providing evidence for independent investigation and pharmacovigilance reform aligned with international standards and recognised good practice, including ICH E2E and CIOMS.  It is published under CC BY 4.0: open access and independently replicable.

The audit repository, containing the supporting evidence, primary sources, methodology, version history, and replication resources, is maintained at: https://github.com/paulrekaris/TGA-COVID19-Vaccine-Safety-Monitoring-Audit

Updated versions of this paper are available on SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6333058

Version note: This revised version incorporates substantial additional documentary evidence and analysis that became available after the original version, including strengthened analysis of the pharmacovigilance statutory and regulatory framework and clarification of the relationship between provisional approval, enhanced safety monitoring and the regulator’s documented implementation of its monitoring commitments.

articles.title: Religiosity or Religious Identity? Measuring Muslim Identity in the Study of Anti-Americanism
articles.authors: Azat Rakhmanberdiev
articles.abstract: Theories of anti-Americanism in the Arab world imply that hostility towards the United States stems from religious identity, yet individual-level findings from empirical studies remain mixed. I argue that this inconsistency may partly reflect how religious identity is measured in the literature—as religiosity, denomination, or identity salience. I derive two main constraints that the existing framework faces: conceptual mismatch with the identity-based explanations suggested by theoretical literature and limited variation in predominantly Muslim populations. I use two waves of Arab Barometer data (N = 2,336) to show how these constraints specifically apply to the case of Iraq and the region in general. The findings suggest that religious identity is not a self-interpreting individual attribute and cannot be treated as a portable predictor of anti-Americanism. In Iraq, anti-Americanism is associated with sectarian identity; however, that relationship only becomes interpretable once Iraq’s Sunni-Shia sectarian cleavage is understood.

articles.title: STEMming Opportunity: How High-School Majors Preserve Sorting and Educational Stratification
articles.authors: Brian Holzman; Shuyu Wang; Bethany Lewis; Hao Ma
articles.abstract:
Purpose--Texas House Bill 5 (2013) introduced the Foundation High School Program, requiring students to select an endorsement—a curricular concentration similar to a major. Although intended to expand flexibility and align coursework with college and workforce pathways, the STEM endorsement may function as a new form of tracking. Guided by Oakes and colleagues’ work on tracking and detracking and by Domina et al.’s application of categorical inequality theory to education, this study examines which students complete a STEM endorsement and how this choice shapes college enrollment outcomes.

Research Methods--We combine a content analysis of Texas college-admissions requirements with administrative data from the Houston Independent School District. Logistic and multinomial models estimate predictors of STEM endorsement completion and college choice, and nonlinear variance decomposition analyses assess how STEM–non-STEM differences in college enrollment are explained by background characteristics.

Findings--The STEM endorsement aligns closely with selective college admissions. Academic factors strongly predict STEM completion, and while the endorsement is associated with enrollment at selective colleges, this relationship is largely explained by prior academic achievement. High-achieving students are more likely to pursue the STEM endorsement, which accounts for its link to selective college enrollment.

Implications--The STEM endorsement operates less as a pathway for broadening opportunity and more as a marker of academic prestige. As a surface-level policy reform, the endorsement system reconstitutes familiar tracking dynamics under a new label, reinforcing educational stratification by privileging students with stronger preparation.

articles.title: Violent Backlash to Political Reform: Evidence from Anti-Jewish Pogroms in the 1905 Russian Revolution
articles.authors: Paul Castañeda Dower; Scott Gehlbach; Dmitrii Kofanov; Steven Nafziger; Vladimir Novikov
articles.abstract: Local violence often accompanies momentous political change. We examine this phenomenon during the 1905 Russian Revolution, when backlash to reform contributed to a spike in anti-Jewish pogroms. Adjudicating between work tying conflict to ethno-religious polarization, and historical accounts of a simpler relationship between group size and violence, we show that the increase in pogroms after the October Manifesto was smaller where Jews were relatively numerous. We rationalize this empirical pattern with Esteban and Ray's (2008) model of diversity and conflict, demonstrating that a group adversely affected by reform is less likely to resort to violence when comparatively small.

articles.title: Cumulative Advantage in Job Quality: Career Trajectories and Inequality in Sweden, 1968–2022
articles.authors: Edvin Syk
articles.abstract: Cumulative (dis)advantage is well documented for wages and occupational prestige, but whether similar patterns characterize non-monetary working conditions remains unclear. This study examines career trajectories in job quality—job complexity, physical demands, negative stress, and flexibility—using Swedish Level-of-Living Survey panel data from 1968 to 2022 (5,042 respondents; 14,857 observations). We ask whether inequalities in job quality widen or narrow across career stages, whether social groups differ in within-career change, and whether workers who begin from more favorable positions subsequently gain more or less. We estimate adjusted inequalities across career stages using random-slope growth curve models and differences in within-career change using individual fixed-effects models. Job quality generally improved over the first 20–25 career years among cohorts born from the 1940s onward. Educational inequality was large and persistent: workers with more education held better jobs throughout and gained more within their careers. Gender inequality emerged over time: men and women began near parity, but men gained more. Within social groups, however, workers who started with better job quality improved less, indicating convergence. Adjusting for occupation reduced career-stage inequalities more than differences in within-career change. Thus, inequalities may widen between social groups even as differences within groups narrow over the career.

articles.title: SOBRE LA PERSONALIDAD AUTORITARIA DE LOS MEXICANOS (2021-2024)
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: Este artículo analiza la evolución de la personalidad autoritaria en México entre 2021 y 2024 utilizando una versión adaptada de la Escala F de Adorno et al. (1950). A través de un diseño de tendencia con muestras probabilísticas independientes, se evalúan variables sociodemográficas, ideológicas e institucionales. Los hallazgos revelan un incremento significativo en el autoritarismo de la población mexicana al finalizar el periodo estudiado. Si bien se confirman determinantes clásicos como la educación, la religiosidad y la ideología, el análisis multivariado mediante regresión logística ordinal sugiere una reconfiguración: el autoritarismo ha mutado hacia una versión más cultural e identitaria, menos ligada a la estructura social tradicional. El estudio concluye que el fenómeno persiste y se adapta, impulsado por la polarización política y crisis normativas, rechazando la hipótesis de estabilidad y reafirmando la relevancia de instrumentos psicométricos refinados para auditar la cultura política en contextos democráticos contemporáneos.

articles.title: The cultural politics of risk: egalitarian civil society opposition to solar radiation modification
articles.authors: Julia S. Guivant; María Inés Carabajal; Eduardo J. Viola; Timothy Robert Silberg
articles.abstract: Solar radiation modification (SRM) has become a focus of climate research and governance debate. While much of the governance literature addresses scientific assessment, responsible research, participation, and multilateral oversight, less attention has been paid to how civil society actors shape what counts as legitimate governance. This article examines how the ETC Group and allied actors construct opposition to SRM. Drawing on Cultural Theory of Risk, sociotechnical imaginaries, and interpretive discourse analysis of public materials from 2008 to 2025, it reconstructs a predominantly egalitarian repertoire organized around the vulnerability of nature and affected communities, distrust of concentrated expertise and corporate power, and claims concerning consent, sovereignty, and environmental justice. Hierarchical, individualist, and fatalist registers are incorporated into this repertoire in distinct ways: authority is aﬀirmed when it supports limits, private initiative marks the adversary, and lock-in supplies the warning scenario. Three practices give this politics of refusal coherence: translating soft law into non-use, contesting field experiments as steps toward normalization, and constructing counter-expertise. The analysis shows that this position has political force because it exposes risks of normalization and concentrated authority. It also has crucial governance limits, narrowing the space in which research, assessment, participation, and Southern agency can be distinguished and debated.

articles.title: Reversal of the Educational Gender Gap and Assortative Mating: Increasing Educational Hypogamy amid Persistent Age Sorting in Latin America
articles.authors: Adriana Robles
articles.abstract: Previous research has revealed a positive association between female educational advantage and the prevalence of educational hypogamy. However, age assortative mating, as a relevant feature in the process of union formation, has been overlooked. This study analyzes the effect of the decrease of the educational gender gap on the likelihood of being married and age and educational assortative mating among Latin American women. Data come from the harmonized microdata samples from the census rounds of eight Latin American countries from 1970 to 2010, available in the Integrated Public Use of Microdata Series International database. Binomial and multinomial logistic regressions were used to evaluate the effects of changes in the educational gender gap on the odds of being single and being assortatively mated in terms of age and education. Results suggest that changes of the educational gender gap had a negative effect on the probabilities of being married and they were associated with higher levels of educational hypogamy, whereas the patterns of age sorting were more rigid than the patterns of educational sorting.

articles.title: Seguros complementarios y gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección de Fonasa: ¿riesgo moral o sesgo de selección? Análisis con microdatos administrativos, Chile, 2022 a 2025
articles.authors: Matias Goyenechea; Alberto Aylwin
articles.abstract:
Introducción. La crisis del sistema de Isapres, la migración de cotizantes hacia el seguro público y la expansión de la oferta de seguros complementarios han modificado los incentivos de gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección de Fonasa. No es claro si el mayor gasto de los beneficiarios asegurados refleja riesgo moral o sesgo de selección.
Objetivos. Estimar, desde la perspectiva del asegurador público, el gasto adicional en la Modalidad de Libre Elección atribuible a la tenencia de un seguro complementario, y descomponerlo en sesgo de selección y riesgo moral, entre 2022 y 2025.
Métodos. Estudio observacional analítico sobre microdatos administrativos individuales (enero 2022 a mayo 2025).El aseguramiento se identificó a partir de su uso efectivo. Se construyó un contrafactual mediante emparejamiento[MG1.1] de vecino más cercano (k = 1, sin reemplazo) sobre covariables observables y se corrigió el error de clasificación con un modelo no lineal de decaimiento por tamaño del hogar. El resultado fue la diferencia porcentual de gasto FAM en la Modalidad de Libre Elección por beneficiario, en unidades reajustables por inflación (unidades de fomento).
Resultados. La brecha bruta de gasto per cápita fue 57,6% mayor en los asegurados; se redujo a 44,2% tras el emparejamiento y convergió a un efecto promedio sobre los tratados de 30,2% (28,8 a 31,3% anual) tras corregir el error de clasificación. 
Conclusiones. El mayor gasto asociado a seguros complementarios combina selección de riesgo y riesgo moral; al menos unos 13 puntos porcentuales corresponden a diferencias de composición de la población que contrata seguros complementarios. Los seguros complementarios se asocian a un aumento del gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección del orden de 30% una vez controlados los sesgos observables y de clasificación.

articles.title: Comparing Information Disorder Policy: The Global Disinformation Policy Database, 2000–2023
articles.authors: Ryan Williams
articles.abstract: Comparative research on information disorder policy faces a dependent-variable problem: policies sharing a label differ in what they regulate, and policies regulating the same conduct carry different labels. The Global Disinformation Policy Database (GDPD) addresses this problem, coding 364 policies from 132 countries, 2000–2023, and decomposing each into label, information quality, regulated behavior, and intent standard. The decomposition shows that 57.7% of “disinformation” policies specify no intent standard, that policy growth predates the literature’s 2016 watershed, and that instruments have diversified away from criminal sanction along regional lines. The GDPD enables researchers to compare how governments conceptualize contested information.

articles.title: Increases in national origin disparities in ICE Arrests, 2025-26
articles.authors: Caitlin C Patler; Claire Morton; Avi Feller
articles.abstract: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has rapidly expanded operations since the January 2025 US presidential inauguration, raising concerns about profiling based on national origin or ethnicity. We assess this issue using administrative records on nearly 500,000 ICE arrests from November 2023 to March 2026, comparing per-capita arrest rates for unauthorized residents from Europe, Canada, and Oceania (EUCA) with those from all other regions (non-EUCA) in 2025-2026, relative to 2023-2024. We document two patterns that are inconsistent with claims of neutral enforcement. First, non-EUCA per-capita arrest rates rose substantially more than EUCA rates in the 14 months following the inauguration, both nationally as well as in every state and ICE jurisdiction with sufficient data. We estimate 217,000 excess non-EUCA arrests relative to a baseline scenario in which non-EUCA and EUCA arrest rates rose equally. Second, the largest disparities occurred among individuals without convictions apprehended in the community rather than via transfers from criminal custody, contrary to claims of targeting people with criminal records. Together, our findings document pervasive national origin differences in ICE enforcement at a time of acute legal and policy contention, raising new questions about the causes and consequences of these broad disparities.

articles.title: Perspectives from older adults with hearing loss on the link between hearing loss and dementia
articles.authors: Sarah Bobbitt; Signe Lund Mathiesen; Amanda Grenier; Bjorn Herrmann
articles.abstract:
Objective: Research and public messaging increasingly highlights a potential link between hearing loss and cognitive decline. This study explores how older adults interpret, evaluate, and act upon messages linking hearing and cognition.
Design: Data were collected using semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis followed the framework outlined by Braun and Clarke.
Study Sample: Twenty-five adults aged 56–97 participated. Participants were Canadian residents with self-reported hearing difficulties. 
Results: Four themes were identified. Participants constructed meaning about the hearing loss–dementia link by integrating lived experience, personal theorizing, and interpretations of scientific or professional information (Theme 1: Making Sense of the Message). They evaluated the need for action, the modifiability of hearing and cognition, and the link’s personal relevance (Theme 2: Weighing the Need for Action). These interpretations influenced hearing health behaviours, including initial help-seeking, persistence with treatment, and disengagement (Theme 3: Impacts on Hearing Health Behaviours).
