Certainty and trust in evidence, clinicians, and the hearing healthcare system shaped participants’ interpretations and mediated their willingness to act (Theme 4: Certainty and Trust). 
Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that public messages about hearing and cognition are filtered through personal and experiential frameworks, underscoring the importance of clear, balanced, and patient-centered communication when discussing hearing health and cognition.

articles.title: Spatial mobility and the risk of dropping out of vocational education and training in Germany: Costs, resources, and returns
articles.authors: Linda Hoffmann; Alexandra Wicht
articles.abstract: Vocational education and training (VET) dropout disrupts school-to-work transitions. While spatial mobility is an important strategy for accessing VET, little is known about how it relates to subsequent dropout. Drawing on a cost-benefit perspective, this study examines whether first-year VET dropout differs by spatial mobility and whether these differences vary with resources available to bear mobility-related costs and returns that may offset them. We use representative longitudinal data from the German National Educational Panel Study linked to administrative geospatial data. Logistic regression models distinguish non-mobile students from those mobile within and between regional labor markets (RLMs) and assess heterogeneity by parental socioeconomic status (SES), VET wages, realized occupational aspirations, regional attractiveness, and regional person-environment match. Predicted dropout probabilities are approximately three percentage points higher for mobility within RLMs and four points higher for mobility between RLMs than for no mobility. These mobility-related differences decrease with increasing parental SES for both mobility types. Higher VET wages correspond to smaller dropout differences for mobility within RLMs, whereas greater realization of occupational aspirations corresponds to smaller differences for mobility between RLMs. Higher regional attractiveness shows a similar pattern only for mobility within RLMs, while higher regional person-environment match coincides with smaller dropout differences for both mobility types. Overall, mobility-related dropout differences vary with available resources and realized returns. The social patterning of mobility-related dropout differences may contribute to inequalities in school-to-work transitions, underscoring the importance of considering spatial mobility and regional contexts in research on youths’ educational decision-making.

articles.title: Delisting without co-migration: author communities before and after removal from Scopus
articles.authors: Marek Deja
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Delisting removes a journal from an index but not its authors. This study asks whether cohorts disperse or share destinations and whether concentrated inflow is associated with receiving journals’ subsequent delisting.
Design/methodology/approach: The analysis reconstructs interval-valued delisting dates from successive Scopus lists, assigns delisted-journal event clocks to matched cohorts, and compares destination overlap with margin-preserving, opportunity-structured, and matched-observed benchmarks. A six-month-landmark discrete-time hazard model handles right censoring and administrative coverage-change exits. Findings: Across 136 stacks, delisted-journal output averaged 66.7% below the post-event reference path. For 121 cohorts, median observed-to-expected overlap was 2.40 under the opportunity-structured benchmark. Across 55 matched sets, delisted cohorts overlapped 10.6 percentage points less that references (95% CI [-0.14, -0.07]), a difference that predated delisting. The highest inflow quartile had 4.66 times the adjusted hazard of the lowest (95% CI [2.04, 10.64]), based on 78 events and 99.3% censoring.
Research limitations: Delisting is non-random, so estimates are descriptive contrasts, benchmark deviations, and conditional in-sample associations.
Practical implications: Synthetic benchmarks establish residual cohort structure; matched observed cohorts test whether it distinguishes the event-defined population.
Originality/value: The study provides a two-stage design for event-specific concentration claims. Pairing a constrained randomisation with matched observed cohorts reversed the substantive conclusion

articles.title: European and US companies communicate less about diversity post-Trump election
articles.authors: A.I. Loureiro Lopes; João Gonçalves
articles.abstract:
We analyzed the social media posts of top 20 European and US companies for their Diversity related content before (2024) and after (2025) the election of Donald Trump. We find that there was a decline in diversity related content in 2025 both in the US and in Europe, with the biggest drop being registered in the US. From all social media content, 6,7% of posts by US based companies in 2024 included diversity related topics, while in 2025 only 1,3% were about diversity. For European companies, the scenario is similar. In 2024, 12,6% of social media posts by European companies touch upon diversity content which dropped to 7,0% in the same period of 2025. 
In general, European companies posted more on diversity than American companies both in 2024 and in 2025. These results show us that while the drop in diversity related talk by corporations was more accentuated in the US, other geographies seem to also replicate the trend.

articles.title: Backcasting Semantic Risk Indicators in Historical Travel Advisories: Enriching a Longitudinal Web Corpus
articles.authors: Christian Oswald; Dominik Allen
articles.abstract: Travel warnings can affect the political and economic situation in the target countries. However, data to systematically investigate these links are lacking. Previous work has introduced and validated a crawler pipeline to obtain time series of government-issued travel advisories via the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine. Governments may change the type and amount of information they provide in their advisories. For example, the United States began to provide numerical travel warning levels for individual countries and tags to categorize advisories in 2018. We illustrate an approach to using these \textit{labeled} data points to extend the variable for travel advisories before 2018 and for other issuing countries. In addition, we show how to extract additional information, such as whether the advisory concerns an entire country or specific regions or cities. This paper documents a further step towards a harmonized and unified dataset and a multilingual text corpus of government-issued travel advisories for the social sciences, humanities, and beyond.

articles.title: Expanding the utility of protest event datasets with automated variable extraction from event summaries
articles.authors: Dominik Allen; Christian Oswald
articles.abstract: Previous research shows that civil resistance works. Various event datasets emerged and led to a large body of disaggregated analyses of protest dynamics. Although observations in all event datasets are based on text sources, such as news articles and reports, they provide different and often distinct variables. As a result, scholars with particular research questions and applications are restricted to using one or only a few of these datasets. Many of them are no longer maintained, further restricting applied researchers and other users. However, some datasets provide event summaries for each observation, from which additional variables can be generated. Using the Armed Conflict and Location Event Data, we generate additional variables present in four other datasets with BERT and large language models. Performance varies by target concept. Under their respective primary evaluation settings, supervised encoder models achieve 0.95 average categorical accuracy, while the strongest few-shot decoder model achieves 0.87. Human intercoder reliability similarly varies across categorical variables, with lower agreement concentrated among more interpretive concepts. We enable enhancing the usage of an existing dataset for new descriptive, explanatory, and predictive applications, including future robustness analyses of empirical findings, and ultimately answering previously out of reach research questions due to variable compartmentalization. We contribute to the study of protest and mobilization by showing how natural language processing can be used to reliably expand dataset usage.

articles.title: Population Development In The Roman Empire
articles.authors: Ulrik Vachet Rasmussen
articles.abstract:
This paper addresses the problem of reconstructing the population development of 
the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire despite the scarcity, inconsistency, and indirect 
nature of the available evidence. Its primary objective is to produce a continuous population 
curve spanning from 508 BC to AD 395, which is internally consistent in the assumptions of 
underlying growth and other factors over time. To achieve this, the study critically integrates 
multiple methodological approaches, including Beloch’s area-and-density estimates, Lo 
Cascio’s revisions, and Scheidel’s demographic critiques, alongside archaeological, 
economic, and comparative demographic evidence.  
By combining these methods and cross-validating their results, a coherent framework 
is established for estimating both population levels and growth rates. It adopts moderate 
empire-wide growth assumptions, 2-3‰ annually, while allowing for significant variation 
between core and newly incorporated territories. This enables the interpolation between key 
chronological benchmarks and the extension of estimates across periods lacking direct 
evidence.  
The resulting reconstruction yields a continuous demographic trajectory showing the 
full consequences of the growth assumptions.

articles.title: Integrating Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) in Participatory Research Practice with Young Children with Disabilities. A Scoping Review.
articles.authors: Anna Beyer; Annika Endres
articles.abstract:
Objective: Young children with disabilities often face barriers to participation in research, as many of them do not use verbal speech. This limits the representation of their views concerning designing research processes, policies, support systems or education. Assuming that the integration of Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC) into research methods could be a suitable approach to deconstruct these barriers, this review explores the implementation of AAC into participatory research with this group.
Method: A scoping review was conducted (Tricco et al., 2018). Following a systematic search in scientific databases and two screening rounds, 8 studies were included. Full texts were analysed concerning the use of AAC and the modalities of children’s communication by means of Qualitative Content Analysis (Kuckartz & Rädiker, 2024). 
Results: Only three studies reported unaided or low-tech AAC-use for data collection. Additionally, a wide range of other child-friendly modalities for children to express themselves were identified which facilitated communication, but did not classify as AAC. These strategies were mostly applied during data collection (e.g. within interviews), while decision-making concerning the research process (e.g. choosing a research question of methods) relied on verbal communication.
Conclusion: The potential of AAC for participatory research has not yet been realized to its maximum. Nevertheless, other multimodal and child-friendly forms of facilitating children’s communication also are very valuable. Both forms should be extended to support children’s decision-making concerning the research process. Future research should focus on using this potential to involve all children – including those with disabilities - into participatory research.

articles.title: The Geography of Life Chances and Intergenerational Mobility
articles.authors: Dylan Shane Connor
articles.abstract: We have entered a new era of soaring inequalities in income and wealth, patterns driven by a highly differentiated landscape of opportunity. This economic reality has propelled the geographies of intergenerational mobility and life chances to the forefront of the social science agenda. While geographers are increasingly engaging with these topics, the field of economic geography provides a critical, yet underutilized, theoretical foundation for this work. This chapter proposes the People-Experience-Places (PEP) framework, a model for analyzing the geographic differentiation of life chances across space and time. Drawing from core schools of thought within economic geography, the framework identifies the foundational mechanisms that produce spatially differentiated opportunity regimes and their impact on intergenerational mobility. The chapter concludes with a call for economic geographers to return to the core concerns of understanding and addressing inequalities in livelihood possibilities.

articles.title: Ready for What? Rethinking AI and Robotics Preparedness for Adoption and Policy
articles.authors: Peng Wang
articles.abstract: Efforts to accelerate AI and robotics adoption require evidence about where communities are prepared to act and where support is still needed. However, conclusions based mainly on average differences between people or stakeholder groups can obscure relationships that emerge when the same person evaluates different challenges. We address this problem using a repeated card-based survey in which 982 participants provided 15,200 evaluations of 17 AI and robotics challenges. Each challenge was rated on common 1-5 measures of significance, complexity and readiness, where readiness refers to perceived community preparedness and available resources rather than personal competence or realised adoption. Because each participant evaluated multiple challenges, the design separates stable differences between respondents from challenge-specific deviations within the same respondent. This distinction materially changes the interpretation of preparedness. Within the same respondent, a challenge rated one point more complex than their usual level is associated with approximately 0.21 points lower readiness ($p<0.001$). By contrast, respondents who generally rate challenges as more complex do not systematically report lower readiness ($p=0.29$). Significance is positively associated with readiness, while unusually high complexity modestly weakens this challenge-specific alignment. These relationships also vary strongly across challenge families, and professional background remains associated with adjusted preparedness assessments. On applied cards, confidence, trust and related perceptions provide substantial additional information about readiness, including for held-out participants. For policymakers and organisations, the findings show that averaging across stakeholders can hide challenge-specific barriers. Readiness assessments should therefore preserve both differences between stakeholder groups and variation within the same stakeholders across challenges. Effective adoption and literacy strategies should ask not only \emph{who} appears ready, but \emph{which challenges} they find unusually difficult and whether the likely constraint concerns implementation, capability, assurance or resources.

articles.title: Computational Discourse Analysis: A Methodological Framework
articles.authors: Audrey Alejandro
articles.abstract: Computational Discourse Analysis is an emerging methodological approach that bridges discourse analysis with quantitative text analysis and natural language processing. While computational discourse analysis is gaining traction across a growing number of case studies, this momentum has not yet been matched by the development of dedicated methodological resources. This article addresses this gap by developing a methodological framework that makes sense of the diverse and scattered works falling under the scope of computational discourse analysis to legitimise this innovative approach and make it accessible to a broad audience. I begin by tracing the methodological traditions that underpin computational discourse analysis: discourse analysis and quantitative text analysis/ natural language processing. I then identify two primary modes through which it is currently practised: “mixed-method” computational discourse analysis and “text-as-discourse” computational discourse analysis. Building on this foundation, I address terminological and practical confusions and clarify what computational discourse analysis is and is not. Finally, I outline the core rationale and key benefits of adopting a computational discourse analysis approach: enhanced rigour, greater efficiency, and increased analytical value. In doing so, the article provides conceptual grounding for a broader methodological conversation at the intersection of qualitative and computational text analysis.

articles.title: The Social in International Relations: Mapping IR Theory through Social Theory
articles.authors: Audrey Alejandro; Gustav Meibauer
articles.abstract: What conceptions of ‘the social’ underpin International Relations (IR) theories? Despite the growing engagement of IR scholarship with ‘the social’ dimensions of international politics, the concept remains surprisingly under-specified. Existing debates are theoretically rich but fragmented, offering limited guidance for understanding how different traditions conceptualise the social or how these assumptions are transmitted through the pedagogical accounts of the discipline encountered by students. This article argues that IR theories are underpinned by distinct yet often implicit conceptions of the social that function as unacknowledged ontological commitments. We develop a typology of six conceptions of the social grounded in social theory—functionalist, Marxist, rational choice, systems-theoretical, structuralist, and poststructuralist—and use it to re-read the traditions through which students most commonly encounter the discipline, from liberalism and neorealism to constructivism and critical approaches. We then trace how these conceptions have been reproduced and transformed through the discipline’s pedagogical canon taking widely assigned IR textbooks as our pedagogical point of departure. We show that the coexistence of heterogeneous conceptions renders the social both ubiquitous and under-specified, generating analytical and pedagogical ambiguities. By making these assumptions explicit, the article offers students, teachers, and scholars a clearer vocabulary for analysing, teaching, and debating IR theory.

articles.title: A good climate for solutions? The adaptation of solutions journalism within Surinamese climate journalism
articles.authors: Lucas Verhoeven; Alice Fleerackers
articles.abstract: This study explores how climate journalists’ role conceptions and media system constraints shape their perceptions and practices of solutions journalism. It does so through a reflexive thematic analysis of in-depth interviews with five of the six practicing climate journalists in Suriname. Findings suggest that journalists express concerns about environmental injustices, particularly those affecting Indigenous communities, yet remain reluctant to adopt interventionist roles. They define their primary task as informing and providing context rather than promoting specific solutions, with objectivity functioning as a professional norm and strategic resource in a fragile media environment where access to sources is precarious. Solutions journalism is further reinterpreted in the Surinamese context, with solutions only introduced after problems have been thoroughly portrayed. Overall, the findings suggest that professional role conceptualizations and solutions journalism approaches cannot be generalised along Global North/Global South lines but are instead reshaped within specific political, economic, and structural conditions.

articles.title: Kommunale Bürgerumfrage 2019
articles.authors: Amt für Statistik und Wahlen Stadt Leipzig
articles.abstract: Bei der Kommunalen Bürgerumfrage handelt es sich um eine Mehrthemenbefragung (Omnibusbefragung). Die inhaltlichen Schwerpunkte ergeben sich aus den Informations­bedürfnissen der Stadtverwaltung. Der vorliegende Ergebnisbericht wertet ausgewählte Fragestellungen der Kommunalen Bürgerumfrage 2019 grafisch und textlich aus.

articles.title: Through Rose-Tinted Smart Glasses: Tech Myths and the Normalisation of Wearable Harms
articles.authors: Milica Stilinovic; Joanne E. Gray; Sanika Vekhande; Ben Egliston; Wenqi Tan; Ryan Stanton; Marcus Carter
articles.abstract: Smart glasses are marketed as lifestyle devices that enhance productivity, creativity, and social connection. However, a growing body of evidence suggests these devices are facilitating new harms relating to privacy, bystander consent, and human agency. This paper examines how branded social media content contributes to the normalisation of smart glasses usage while obscuring their associated risks. Focusing on Instagram as a key promotional environment, this study conducts a quantitative content analysis of 768 branded posts featuring Meta’s market leading Ray-Ban glasses alongside emerging competitors Xiaomi, Rokid, Even Realities, and XReal. We analyse how smart-glasses practices are visually and narratively represented and evaluate how recording visibility is addressed and how potential harms are downplayed or obscured. Results suggest that even within highly commercial advertising environments, social and ethical harms remain embedded in the representation of the technology itself. Branded content therefore plays a critical role in legitimising these devices through the construction of powerful technological myths.

articles.title: Technological complexity and the nature of adaptive problem-solving in small-scale societies
articles.authors: Marcus John Hamilton; Briggs Buchanan; Robert S. Walker; Mark Collard; Nicholas Gala
articles.abstract: Technological complexity is a defining eature of human adaptation, yet the processes determining how much technology societies require remain poorly understood. Existing explanations emphasize environmental risk, resource productivity, or demographic factors, but provide limited insight into why technological systems respond differently across subsistence economies. Here, we propose that technological complexity reflects the computational burden imposed by environmental uncertainty. In seasonal environments, survival requires solving a sequential decision problem in which risks accumulate multiplicatively across the year, increasing demand for technological buffering. Technologies reduce this uncertainty but are costly to produce and maintain, generating an optimization problem balancing risk reduction against technological costs. We further argue that niche construction fundamentally alters this relationship by smoothing environmental variability and transforming exogenous uncertainty into managed, endogenous processes. From this framework we derive the prediction that technological complexity should increase with environmental seasonality among hunter-gatherers but become increasingly independent of climate as niche construction intensifies. We test these predictions using data on toolkit richness and component-part diversity from 127 small-scale societies. We find the richness of hunter-gatherer technologies increases exponentially with environmental seasonality, whereas farming technologies remain largely invariant across climatic regimes. These findings suggest that technological complexity responds to the informational and computational demands environmental conditions impose. More broadly, these results imply that agriculture represents not simply a new mode of energy acquisition, but a transition in the computational architecture of human adaptation, in which farming reduces the effective depth of adaptive problems by restructuring the environments that generate uncertainty.

articles.title: The Atlantic Axis of Football Dominance: An Empirical investigation of FIFA World Cup Winners.
articles.authors: Nerhum Sandambi
articles.abstract: The domain and influence of majority European Countries, was naturally evidenced on this approach in particular, where the study for example evidence many European Countries won the world cup tournament, these Countries are naturally strong riches, Countries such as France, England, Italy, Germany and Spain show naturally this particularly, mainly relatively with the existence of high economic performance in general. articles.title: 从宗教圣地到茶道名片——汉口亚历山大·涅夫斯基教堂的百年变迁   From Sacred Sanctuary to Tea Trade Landmark: The Century-Long Transformation of the Hankou Alexander Nevsky Church
articles.authors: Emmanuel A. Waung
articles.abstract:
本文以武汉现存唯一的东正教建筑——汉口阿列克桑德聂夫堂（亚历山大·涅夫斯基教堂）为研究对象，系统梳理了其自1876年草创、历经晚清“东方茶港”繁荣、民国常态化发展直至建国后高度式微的百年历史变迁。文章结合实地考察，深入探讨了该建筑在2013年依托中俄“万里茶道”地缘历史叙事重获抢救性修缮的风貌复原过程。同时，作者指出，在当下的世俗化利用与展览叙事中，当局呈现出一种既渴望吸纳历史建筑的外交红利、又刻意回避其本源宗教属性与制度化衰落历史的矛盾心态。本研究不仅丰富了近代通商口岸异质信仰群体的微观历史，也为审视当代历史遗产保护中的意识形态焦虑与话语置换提供了参考。

Taking the Alexander Nevsky Church, the only surviving Orthodox architectural heritage in Wuhan, as the research object, this paper systematically delineates its century-long historical evolution, tracing its origins in 1876, its flourishing period during the late Qing Dynasty when Hankou served as the "Oriental Tea Port," its regularized development during the Republican era, and its post-1949 institutional decline. Based on field observations, the study examines the facade restoration process initiated in 2013, which was driven by the geopolitical and historical narrative of the Sino-Russian "Great Tea Road." Furthermore, the author points out a nuanced paradox in the contemporary secular utilization and exhibition narratives of the property: the authorities eagerly embrace the diplomatic dividends and cultural prestige of the historic building, while deliberately avoiding its fundamental religious attributes and the complex history of its institutional decline. This study not only enriches the microhistory of heterogeneous religious groups in modern treaty ports, but also provides empirical insights into ideological anxieties and discourse displacement in contemporary historical heritage conservation.

articles.title: The Peacekeeping Dilemma: Understanding the  Challenges of UN Peacekeeping in Modern Conflicts
articles.authors: William George Nomikos; Ipek Ece Sener; Rob Williams
articles.abstract: An abundance of evidence demonstrates that United Nations (UN) peacekeeping operations (PKOs) enhance the prospects for peace in conflict and post-conflict settings. Yet existing work also suggests that peacekeeping succeeds at some tasks while failing at others—often within the same mission. We argue that UN peacekeepers cannot eliminate all forms of violence because actions that reduce one type of violence create conditions that contribute to an increase in another type—a phenomenon we call the peacekeeping dilemma. Two countervailing mechanisms generate this dilemma: a deterrence mechanism, through which peacekeepers raise the costs of violence for non-state actors, and a collaboration mechanism, through which the UN's reliance on host-government consent facilitates government violence against civilians. We test this framework using a geographic regression discontinuity design around the border of Mali and Burkina Faso, where the UN mission MINUSMA operated from 2013 until its forced withdrawal in 2023. We find that UN peacekeeping reduces conflict between non-state rebel groups and communal violence between civilians, but not violence between governments and rebels. More troubling, we find evidence that UN peacekeeping increases government violence against civilians.

articles.title: Linking Media Effects with Political Talk: A Theoretical Review
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: Political talk has been a central focus of political communication research. However, grounded in a micro-conversational perspective often fall short in explaining the emergence of diverse forms of political discourse, as well as recent declines in both news use and participation in political talk. By presenting a macro-structural view of political talk and revisiting two classical media effects, this article provides a theoretical review on how agenda-setting and framing effects of general media and mediated communication can shape political talk, across cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions. Theoretically linking media effects with political talk contributes to explaining macro-structural conditions for various political talk to happen, integrates both traditional and non-institutionalized forms of political talk, and generates a set of propositions and research questions to guide future empirical inquiry.

articles.title: Japanese has effectively only two accent patterns: A quantitative and information-theoretic approach to lexical predictability
articles.authors: Thomas Pellard; Akiko Takemura
articles.abstract: Japanese pitch accent is traditionally described as a free accent system allowing up to n + 1 possible patterns for an n-mora word. However, Japanese accentuation is heavily constrained by factors such as word length, prosodic structure, and lexical stratum, leading to the hypothesis that the system fundamentally reduces to only two dominant patterns: unaccented and thematic (antepenultimate). Evaluating this claim requires moving beyond raw counts of empirically attested patterns to quantify the skewness of their distribution. In this study, we introduce information-theoretic metrics, specifically Shannon's conditional entropy and ecological effective numbers of diversity, to measure the uncertainty an diversity of accent patterns in a representative sample of 8,173 Japanese common nouns. Our findings show that while overall pattern richness reaches the theoretical maximum (7 patterns), global effective diversity remains low (3.12 by type frequency, 3.43 by token frequency). Crucially, with knowledge of word length, prosodic structure, and lexical stratum the number of accent patterns is reduced to effectively two (2.1) dominant patterns, providing a precise, quantitative validation of the two-pattern hypothesis. We further demonstrate that prosodic structure is the single most informative factor, reducing accentuation uncertainty by 23%, and that native nouns exhibit greater residual uncertainty than Sino-Japanese and foreign words. Finally, the strong alignment between type and token results confirms that dictionary-based word lists closely mirror natural speech distributions in phonological diversity.

articles.title: Determinants of Patent Applications across European Regions: Evidence from Panel Estimators, K-Means Clustering and Predictive Validation
articles.authors: Angelo Maurizio Galiano; Giuseppe Dell'Erba; Alberto Costantiello; Angelo Leogrande
articles.abstract: Europe measures the innovative performance of its regions largely by counting patents, and allocates public resources accordingly. This paper asks what regional patenting actually reflects, drawing on Regional Innovation Scoreboard data for 245 European regions observed annually between 2016 and 2023. Three candidate drivers are considered: the research effort of firms, the intensity of formal collaboration between the research base and industry, and the propensity to protect intangible assets through trademarks. Business research effort emerges as the dominant correlate throughout, science–industry collaboration as a weaker but consistent one, and trademark activity as a positive one, suggesting that firms which protect brands are not forgoing patents but exercising a single appropriation capability across several instruments. Two findings carry implications beyond measurement. Regional innovative capacity proves remarkably immobile: differences between regions account for roughly 95 per cent of the variation in the data, and differences within a region over the eight years for the remainder, so the short-run movements on which policy evaluation typically relies carry very little information, and the returns to innovation investment should be sought over horizons far longer than a programming cycle. And when the 245 regions are grouped into four innovation profiles rather than treated as a single population, the relationship that holds on average holds almost nowhere in particular: it is strong among leading and lagging regions, statistically absent in the largest group, and displaced by brand-led appropriation in a fourth group of 27 regions whose innovation is real but largely non-technological. Uniform innovation policy prescriptions and uniform managerial benchmarks are correspondingly difficult to justify.

articles.title: Beyond the Rural Designation: Geographic Aggregation as a Justice Problem in Psychiatric–Mental Health Nursing
articles.authors: Josef V. Hodgkins
articles.abstract:
Objective: To argue that the geographic category "rural," as operationalized in disparities research and federal shortage-area designation, conceals the rural populations who fare worst, and what follows for psychiatric–mental health (PMH) nursing.

Methods: Critical analysis of literature on rural mental health disparities, rurality measurement, and racially and sexually minoritized rural populations, spanning 2002, when the field was urged past counting rural disorder toward how place shapes it, through 2026.

Results: Prevalence findings have stayed inconsistent for two decades, substantially because rurality is measured dichotomously. On disaggregation, the rural–urban axis often proves the wrong one: among American Indian and Alaska Native veterans, urban–rural comparison yields no significant difference while comparison with White veterans yields large ones. Because shortage-area designation is geographic, the aggregate does not merely describe disparity; it drives allocation.

Conclusions: Aggregation is not a neutral convenience. A category that renders the worst-off invisible and governs resource distribution is a justice concern for a specialty supplying much of rural America's mental health workforce. PMH nursing should assess structural position rather than residence, adopt continuous and intersectional measures of rurality, and contest designation methodology as professional advocacy.

articles.title: Public Health Emergencies and Executive Power in Nepal: Balancing Liberty and Security in a Fragile Federal System
articles.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles.abstract: Public health crises leave governments with difficult choices. One side is liberty, the freedom to move, to work, to meet others and to live without too much state control. In contrast, the goal is security: to protect people from disease, to maintain public order and prevent a collapse of health systems. In a democracy these two values must be carefully balanced. Nepal’s experience of COVID-19 is a useful case study of how this balance can be lost when emergency powers are invoked without robust legal safeguards. Nepal is especially important as it has a new federal system and a weak legal framework for public health emergencies. The government has used old and vague laws during the pandemic to put in place lockdowns and other restrictions. This paper describes how Nepal used these powers, the impact of the restrictions on civil liberties and what lessons can be learned for the future. The core argument is that the Nepal experience highlights the perils of relying on old, vague laws instead of clear constitutional emergency procedures. Without strong legal protections, the balance between liberty and security can be tipped too far in favor of executive control.

articles.title: The Economics of Conditional Grants: Local Health Service Delivery in Nepal's Federal System
articles.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles.abstract: Fiscal federalism in Nepal has conditional grants as one of its key features. These grants are a way for the federal government to send money to state and local governments for certain purposes, especially for health and education. This paper explores whether conditional health grants translate into better delivery of local health services, or are mostly an administrative burden for local governments. The analysis, which is based on publicly available data from the National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission, the Ministry of Health and Population, the Ministry of Finance and international organizations including the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and the World Health Organization, presents a mixed picture. Conditional health grants have increased local health expenditure and helped to sustain basic health services during Nepal's transition to federalism. For example, local governments now constitute a significant proportion of total public health expenditure and immunization coverage has been sustained in the face of significant institutional reforms. But the grant system also creates a lot of administrative work, limits local flexibility, slows the flow of funds and does not always result in better health outcomes. However, many municipalities have continued to experience low health grant execution rates and key health indicators such as stunting and neonatal mortality have not improved significantly. The paper argues that conditional grants are a transitional mechanism that maintains service continuity while local governments build their own capacity. It proposes reforms to simplify conditional grants, increase local discretion through block grants, strengthen performance-based elements and build local capacity for health planning and financial management. The findings contribute to the larger literature on intergovernmental transfers and local service delivery in decentralized systems.

articles.title: Love at First Swipe: Online Dating and Relationship Outcomes in Europe
articles.authors: Zerui Tian
articles.abstract: This article examines whether unions formed through online dating differ from other unions in relationship trajectories across nine European countries. Using harmonised Generations and Gender Survey data, I estimate country-specific survival and current-union models for union dissolution, marriage, shared biological childbearing, relationship satisfaction, and break-up consideration. Adjusted dissolution hazards are higher in Austria, Estonia, and Croatia, lower in Germany, and not significant elsewhere or among recent unions. Among surviving unions, online dating is more often associated with lower marriage and shared childbearing, especially in Croatia and the United Kingdom, than with poorer relationship quality. Overall, online dating appears more strongly associated with how unions are institutionalised and converted into family life and the findings do not support the idea of a uniform pan-European relationship difference associated with online dating.

articles.title: Governments as Adopters and Regulators of AI: A Challenge for Democracy?
articles.authors: Philipp Trein; Martino Maggetti
articles.abstract: This paper explores the dual role of governments as both adopters and regulators of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on the implications for democratic governance. As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in public administration – from policymaking to service delivery – they offer opportunities for improving efficiency and personalization but also raise concerns about transparency, accountability, and fairness. To deal with these questions, this paper examines how AI is framed as a policy problem, the regulatory approaches adopted in different political systems, and the politicization of AI governance. It also analyzes the democratic risks posed by algorithmic decision-making, polarization, and corporate concentration of power, while highlighting the potential of AI to enhance democratic quality through improved public services, inclusive discourse, and citizen engagement. The paper concludes by identifying key areas for future research, including legitimacy, trust, regulatory design, and equity in AI governance.

articles.title: Analysis of the effectiveness of the procurement and receipt process of goods in supporting retail store operations
articles.authors: Muhammad Rangga; Sherin Azra Damila
articles.abstract: CV Chiko Mitra Abadi is a retail company in Bandung Regency operating a one-stop shop concept that combines a supermarket, furniture, and playground facilities. Because the company depends on suppliers for all merchandise sold, the effectiveness of its procurement and receipt of goods process is central to maintaining stock availability, data accuracy, and smooth store operations. This report was compiled from Practical Work carried out in the administrative section of CV Chiko Mitra Abadi from June 29 to August 7, 2026, during which the author was directly involved in supplier data management, Purchase Order (PO) preparation, goods receiving, SKU/PLU verification, price and margin updates, and the preparation of promotional media. The report describes the company's procurement and receipt workflow, identifies the operational obstacles encountered during implementation, and evaluates the process using SWOT analysis. The findings show that CV Chiko Mitra Abadi already applies clear procedures supported by formal Purchase Order documentation and generally good coordination among the Administrative, Receiving, warehouse, and supplier-facing functions. However, several weaknesses remain, including administrative tasks that are still performed manually, price and margin updates that are not yet system-integrated, and inspection procedures that slow down when incoming volumes are high, compounded by suppliers' delivery reliability. Based on these findings, the report recommends greater use of integrated information systems, closer and more structured supplier coordination, standardized receiving checklists, and regular employee training, together with a more consumer-centric view of how these administrative improvements ultimately affect customer experience on the sales floor. These recommendations are intended to help the company run its procurement and receiving process more effectively and sustain the smooth operation of its retail store.

articles.title: Optimizing Recovery Value in Public Asset Disposal: Business Process Mapping (As-Is vs. To-Be) Analysis of State-Owned Asset Sales and Write-Offs at Indonesia's Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs
articles.authors: Anissa Rahmarani; Danang Indrajaya
articles.abstract: Efficient management of state-owned assets (Barang Milik Negara, BMN) is a critical determinant of fiscal accountability and non-tax state revenue (Penerimaan Negara Bukan Pajak, PNBP) optimization in public sector organizations. This study examines the process of proposing, verifying, and executing the sale and write-off of low-value BMN (below IDR 100 million) at the Bureau of Finance and State Assets, Secretariat General, Indonesia's Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs (KOMDIGI), where delegated approval authority under Minister of Finance Regulation (PMK) No. 4/PMK.06/2015 was, in practice, insufficiently leveraged to accelerate administrative throughput. Employing a qualitative, participant-observation-based case study design conducted over a six-week practicum period, this research applies Business Process Mapping (As-Is vs. To-Be) to document the existing workflow, identify bottlenecks and non-value-added activities, and design a redesigned process architecture. The As-Is analysis reveals three structural inefficiencies: (1) duplicated manual verification between spreadsheet-based checklists and the State Asset Management Information System (SIMAN); (2) recurrent data mismatches across unit nomenclature, asset codes, and book values; and (3) an undifferentiated verification pathway that fails to exploit the risk-based delegation of authority for low-value assets. A SWOT matrix further situates these findings within the organization's internal capabilities and external opportunities, generating SO, WO, ST, and WT strategic alternatives. The proposed To-Be process (anchored on system integration, a risk-based fast-track lane, and standardized correspondence templates) is theorized to compress processing lead time and thereby preserve the economic value of assets pending disposal, directly reinforcing recovery value and PNBP contributions. This study contributes to the limited empirical literature on business process reengineering in Indonesian public asset governance and offers a replicable diagnostic-to-design framework for other line ministries operating under similarly delegated regulatory regimes.

articles.title: Measuring and Repairing Document Conversion Errors in the Michigan Child Welfare Policy Manual
articles.authors: Nanyi Deng
articles.abstract:
Author Note (August 18, 2026): This preprint is currently undergoing systematic review and revision. An updated version will be posted upon completion. Readers are encouraged to consult the latest version of the manuscript.
Child welfare practice is governed by documents written for people to read. A state policy manual specifies how quickly a caseworker must see a child after the child returns home, and it does so in a PDF laid out for the eye. Any system that answers questions from such a manual must first convert it into text, and that conversion step is rarely measured. This study measures it. Five test documents were constructed to replicate the layout of the Michigan Children’s Protective Services Manual, with identifiers replacing its words. The identifiers run consecutively, so that a loss reads as a gap in a counted run and a person can see it without tooling, and each one ends in a check code, so that a converter driven by a language model cannot supply a convincing replacement for whatever it dropped. The same artifact is therefore verifiable by a person reading it and by a script counting it, and the tool under test cannot repair the evidence before either of them looks at it.
Four converters were evaluated on the test documents, and the two generations of the commercial service were evaluated on the manual itself, for a total of 31 documents and 328 pages. No converter was adequate for every property required by a retrieval corpus. The older generation invented 43 section headings that appear nowhere in the source, and the corpus assembled from it labels a column in a contact-standards table with the wrong requirement, so it lists three contacts with each child at intensive risk, where the manual states one. The current generation’s cheapest tier deletes the opening line of every paragraph beginning Exception:, which is how this manual marks the cases a rule does not cover. None of these failures garbles the text. Each produces fluent prose that reads as policy and states a rule the manual does not contain. The study then reports a repair procedure that derives document structure from the PDF’s geometry, and fifteen checks that halt conversion if any fail. Every check passes across all 31 documents, measured against the same documents from which the repair rules were derived. A fourth failure property emerged only after presence, level, and order had all reached their best values: 380 paragraph boundaries across 200 of the 328 pages were marked in the source by vertical spacing that the converter does not read.

articles.title: Financial Risk Management Practices in a State-Owned Energy Enterprise: A Process-Based Case Study of Market Research Operations at PT Pertamina (Persero)
articles.authors: Alya Putri; Danang Indrajaya
articles.abstract: Financial risk management (FRM) has become a strategic function within state-owned energy enterprises exposed to volatile commodity prices, exchange rate fluctuations, and interest rate movements. While a substantial body of literature examines the determinants and firm-level consequences of financial risk exposure and hedging behavior, comparatively little empirical or practice-based work documents how such risk-monitoring functions are operationally structured and executed within large state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in emerging markets. This study addresses that gap through a process-based case study of the Market Research sub-function within the Financial Risk & Insurance Center (FRIC) of PT Pertamina (Persero), Indonesia's national energy company. Using Business Process Modeling (BPM) with BPMN notation and a SWOT analysis supported by Internal Factor Analysis Summary (IFAS) and External Factor Analysis Summary (EFAS) matrices, this study maps the daily workflow of market monitoring and Morning Market Flash Report preparation, identifies operational strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, and formulates strategic recommendations. The findings indicate that the process exhibits strong internal verification controls (a multi-tier review chain and the use of integrated tools such as Bloomberg Terminal and the FRAME application) but remains constrained by manual data-entry processes and tight pre-market deadlines. Positioned in Quadrant I (Growth/SO) of the SWOT matrix, the function is well placed to pursue an aggressive strategy centered on automation and standardization. The study contributes a practice-grounded account of financial risk monitoring operations that complements the predominantly econometric literature on FRM determinants and offers actionable recommendations for both corporate practice and academic curricula in financial risk education.
